This paper presents the development of Cantonese and Irish treebanks within the Parallel Grammar (ParGram) Project, where linguistic parallelism is maintained at an abstract functional level. We also investigate the methodological potential and limitations of using multilingual LLMs to support grammar engineering, focusing on Cantonese-Irish translation and the generation of formal syntactic structures using OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b model. The results show that translation performance was generally unsatisfactory and unaffected by prompt language. For syntactic structure generation, the model produced some structurally meaningful outputs, but performed poorly on tasks requiring cross-linguistic abstraction. Nonetheless, LLM-generated outputs may still offer some reference value by suggesting alternative analyses and (partially) capturing predicate-argument relations. Overall, our findings highlight both the potential and limitations of using LLMs in collaborative grammar engineering, while underscoring the continued importance of expert-driven analysis and verification.

</details>


### [47] [Natural Language Processing Psychometrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07316)
*Edoardo Sebastiano De Duro,Emma Franchino,Massimo Stella*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces "NLP Psychometrics," a framework treating psychological prediction from text as a psychometric problem. Using LLM personas (cognitive digital shadows) completing questionnaires with explanations, the authors extracted emotional and syntactic-semantic network features. Combined with personality/sociodemographic variables in ablated random forests, these features explained up to 76% of variance in psychological outcomes. Models generalized to real human diaries and clinical transcripts without retraining, though the authors caution synthetic data cannot replace human validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NLP models predicting mental health outcomes typically fail to specify whether they measure contextual knowledge, emotional content, or syntactic structure. This ambiguity undermines interpretability and validity. The authors propose NLP Psychometrics to link predictive scores to interpretable linguistic evidence, making measurement constructs explicit and testable.

Method: Nine LLMs were conditioned on controlled personas (cognitive digital shadows) and completed psychometric questionnaires (SWLS, PHQ-9, DASS-21) with textual explanations per item. Emotional profiles and syntactic-semantic structure were extracted via textual forma mentis networks. These features, combined with personality (Big Five) and sociodemographic variables, fed ablated random forest regressors with SHAP analysis. Generalization was tested on real human diaries and clinical transcripts without retraining.

Result: Full RF models explained up to 70.8% of variance in life satisfaction (SWLS), 55.7% in depression (PHQ-9), and 68.5–76.0% across DASS-21 subscales. Sociodemographics alone explained no meaningful variance in depression/anxiety/stress but did for life satisfaction (emotion features + income were strongest predictors). Neuroticism and network topology dominated depression/anxiety, with reversed directionality between them. Without retraining, models separated diary-based personas (r up to 0.91) and classified clinical vs. controls from real transcripts at up to 68% accuracy using only network/emotion features.

Conclusion: LLM personas can expose model biases, recover patterns consistent with clinical rumination, and support psychometric prediction from human text without matched questionnaires, but cannot substitute for human validation. NLP Psychometrics renders these distinctions explicit, measurable, and testable through interpretable AI and network/emotional features.

Abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) models predicting mental health outcomes rarely specify what they measure: contextual knowledge, emotional content, or syntactic structure. NLP Psychometrics treats psychological prediction from text as a psychometric problem, linking scores to interpretable linguistic evidence and testing beyond the training text format. Nine LLMs, conditioned on controlled personas (cognitive digital shadows), completed psychometric questionnaires with textual explanations per item. We extracted emotional profiles and syntactic-semantic structure via textual forma mentis networks, combined with personality and sociodemographic variables in ablated random forest (RF) regressors, using SHAP to identify which features drove performance and in which direction. Full RF models explained up to 70.8% of variance in life satisfaction (SWLS), 55.7% in depression (PHQ-9), and, for DASS-21, 68.5% depression, 76.0% anxiety, 72.4% stress. Sociodemographics alone explained no meaningful variance in depression, anxiety, or stress, but did so for life satisfaction, where emotion features and income were the strongest predictors; neuroticism and network topology instead dominated depression and anxiety, reversing direction between them. Without retraining, RF models separated diaries from low- and high-score personas ($r$ up to 0.91) and, using only network/emotion features, classified clinical from control participants in real transcripts with up to 68% accuracy. These results show the promise and limits of synthetic data: LLM personas can expose model biases, recover patterns consistent with clinical rumination, and support psychometric prediction from human text without a matched questionnaire, but cannot substitute for human validation. NLP Psychometrics makes these distinctions explicit, measurable, and testable through interpretable AI and network/emotional features.

</details>


### [48] [Zero Gap Is Not Restoration: Stratified Per-Question Probability Evaluation and Step-wise Mitigation of Benchmark Contamination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07341)
*Ruijie Hou,Yueyang Jiao,Zhao Wang,Yingming Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies flaws in the prevailing contamination mitigation metric (G-AP), proposes a new metric (SA-PPG) that uses per-question probability gaps stratified by clean model solve rates, and introduces RailCap, a decoding-time mitigation strategy that caps greedy tokens to suppress memorization without requiring contamination estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public benchmark data leaks into pretraining corpora, inflating evaluation scores via memorization. Current contamination mitigation evaluation relies on G-AP, which is fundamentally flawed: binary correct/incorrect signals lose granularity, averaging before differencing allows over- and under-suppression to cancel out, and uniform weighting incentivizes strategies that exploit the clean model's high-frequency solve probabilities. A more rigorous metric and more effective mitigation strategy are needed.

Method: SA-PPG (Stratified Aggregate of Per-question Probability Gaps): estimates each question's solve probability via sampling, computes per-question gaps against the clean model, and aggregates within strata defined by the clean model's solve probability. RailCap: a decoding-time intervention that detects when a generated token falls back onto the greedy trajectory and caps it to the runner-up token, accumulating suppression until the response distribution becomes sufficiently dispersed — no prior contamination estimation required.

Result: SA-PPG reveals that prior mitigation strategies' restoration performance is substantially overestimated. RailCap achieves the lowest SA-PPG across multiple contaminated models and benchmarks, demonstrating superior and more genuine contamination mitigation.

Conclusion: Contamination mitigation evaluation requires per-question probabilistic metrics like SA-PPG rather than coarse aggregate correctness gaps. Decoding-time interventions like RailCap, which operate without explicit contamination estimation, can more effectively suppress memorization and reveal a model's true underlying capability.

Abstract: Test data from public benchmarks inevitably leaks into pretraining corpora, inflating evaluation scores once memorized. \textbf{Contamination mitigation evaluation} intervenes in the decoding process to suppress memorization and restore a contaminated model's genuine capability, but its prevailing metric, the \textbf{G-AP} (\textbf{G}ap of \textbf{A}ggregate \textbf{P}erformance), is flawed. Discrete correct/incorrect readouts cannot characterize per-question performance, averaging before differencing lets over- and under-suppression cancel out, and uniform per-question weighting invites strategies to push solve probabilities onto the clean model's high-frequency values. We propose \textbf{SA-PPG} (\textbf{S}tratified \textbf{A}ggregate of \textbf{P}er-question \textbf{P}robability \textbf{G}aps): estimate each question's solve probability by sampling, difference it against the clean model per question, and aggregate within groups defined by the clean model's solve probability. Existing mitigation strategies first estimate where contamination lies and then operate on the estimate, so they are only as correct as the estimate. \textbf{RailCap} instead judges contamination during generation: whenever a sample falls back onto the greedy trajectory, the next trajectory token is capped to the runner-up, accumulating suppression until the response distribution becomes sufficiently dispersed. Across multiple contaminated models and benchmarks, SA-PPG reveals that prior strategies' restoration is substantially overestimated, while RailCap attains the lowest SA-PPG.

</details>


### [49] [LitTraceQA: A Benchmark for Multi-Stage Grounding and Verification in Scientific Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07370)
*Xuye Liu,Yimu Wang,Peng Shi,Bo Xue,Xiangrui Ke,Songcheng Cai,Kath Choi,Di Wu,Freda Shi,Krzysztof Czarnecki*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LitTraceQA is a benchmark for scientific literature QA that requires systems to retrieve papers, locate specific evidence (tables, figures, text, equations, citations), and produce faithful answers in multiple formats, with separate evaluation of retrieval, grounding, and answer accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current language models and RAG systems can generate fluent text from scientific literature but often fail to produce verifiable, evidence-backed answers. Existing benchmarks lack the demand for explicit evidence grounding—connecting answers to concrete locations within papers. There is a need for a benchmark that tests whether systems can reliably identify relevant papers, pinpoint supporting evidence, and generate faithful answers rather than unsupported summaries.

Method: The authors construct LitTraceQA with a three-output requirement: (1) canonical paper identifiers, (2) supporting evidence locations (tables, figures, text spans, equations/algorithms, citation contexts), and (3) answers in free-form text, multiple-choice, or structured tables. The public split has 55 examples (26 single-paper, 29 multi-paper). A larger collection contains 4,978 unique-question records over 4,859 unique gold papers. Evaluation is disaggregated into three axes: paper retrieval, evidence grounding, and answer accuracy.

Result: The benchmark defines a structured task and provides gold-annotated papers, evidence locations, and answers. The public development split enables local validation. The larger annotation collection (≈5K question records, ≈4.9K gold papers) demonstrates scale and coverage across diverse evidence types.

Conclusion: LitTraceQA offers a testbed for building and evaluating scientific QA systems that produce verifiable, evidence-grounded answers, moving beyond unsupported summarization toward accountable, traceable responses grounded in the literature.

Abstract: Scientific literature is increasingly used as a knowledge source for language models, retrieval-augmented generation systems, and research assistants, but answering research questions from papers requires more than fluent generation. A reliable system must identify the relevant papers, locate the concrete evidence that supports the answer, and produce a response that is faithful to that evidence. We present LitTraceQA, a benchmark for literature-grounded question answering over scientific papers. Given a research question and a metadata pool of papers, a system must return three connected outputs: canonical paper identifiers, supporting evidence locations, and answers in one or more requested formats, including free-form text, multiple-choice answers, and structured tables. LitTraceQA targets evidence types common in scientific reading: tables, figures, text spans, equations or algorithms, and citation contexts. The public development split contains 55 examples, including 26 hidden-source single-paper questions and 29 multi-paper questions, and provides gold papers, evidence annotations, and answers for local validation. We also analyze a larger final annotation collection with 4,978 unique-question records over 4,859 unique gold papers. By evaluating paper retrieval, evidence grounding, and answer accuracy separately, LitTraceQA provides a testbed for scientific QA systems that produce verifiable answers rather than unsupported summaries.

</details>


### [50] [An Exploratory Evaluation of LLM-Assisted Rewriting of Moderate-Complexity Financial Sentences for DisCoCat-Based Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07439)
*Brian Llinas,Nikos Chrisochoides*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM-assisted rewriting of moderate-complexity financial sentences can drastically reduce quantum circuit costs (over 70% fewer qubits/gates) for DisCoCat-based QNLP sentiment analysis, with GPT-4.1-mini achieving 0.550 mean accuracy vs. 0.521 baseline, though larger training splits surprisingly correlate negatively with performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior DisCoCat-based QNLP for financial sentiment analysis suffers from parser sensitivity, high simulation costs, and inability to handle longer sentences. The authors seek to extend applicability beyond low-complexity sentences by leveraging LLM rewriting to make moderate-complexity inputs compatible with existing DisCoCat pipelines.

Method: An LLM-assisted preprocessing workflow using controlled rewriting to compress, simplify, or decompose moderate-complexity financial sentiment sentences into parser-compatible, circuit-efficient variants. Multiple prompting strategies, language models (including GPT-4.1-mini), and filtering configurations are compared against the low-complexity-only DisCoCat baseline from Stein et al. Evaluation uses qubit/gate counts, accuracy across repeated training runs, and Pearson correlation between training-split size and performance.

Result: The strongest compression variants reduce average qubit and gate counts by >70% vs. raw moderate-complexity inputs. GPT-4.1-mini with Prompt B achieves highest mean accuracy of 0.550±0.035 vs. baseline 0.521±0.050. Training-split size shows a moderately negative association with accuracy (Pearson r=-0.446), indicating larger splits do not improve performance.

Conclusion: LLM-assisted rewriting can make moderate-complexity financial sentiment sentences tractable for DisCoCat QNLP, but prompt design, filtering, and circuit-aware preprocessing are critical. The negative correlation between training size and accuracy warrants further investigation, and results are exploratory rather than definitive.

Abstract: Quantum natural language processing (QNLP) provides a grammar-aware framework for text modeling, and Distributional Compositional Categorical (DisCoCat) is one of its theoretically grounded formulations. Prior work on financial sentiment analysis has identified practical limitations of DisCoCat, including parser sensitivity, high simulation cost, and difficulty handling longer sentences. We study an LLM-assisted preprocessing workflow that uses controlled rewriting to compress, simplify, or decompose moderate-complexity financial sentiment sentences into parser-compatible, circuit-efficient variants while preserving sentiment-bearing meaning. We compare prompting strategies, language models, and filtering configurations with the low-complexity-only DisCoCat baseline of Stein et al. At the circuit level, the strongest compression variants reduce average qubit and gate counts by more than 70 percent relative to the raw moderate-complexity subset. Across repeated training runs, GPT-4.1-mini with Prompt B achieves the highest observed mean accuracy, $0.550 \pm 0.035$, compared with $0.521 \pm 0.050$ for the baseline. Larger training splits do not necessarily improve downstream performance; across evaluated configurations, training-split size has a moderately negative association with accuracy (Pearson $r=-0.446$). These results provide exploratory evidence that LLM-assisted rewriting can make some moderate-complexity inputs usable within the evaluated DisCoCat configuration, while highlighting prompt design, filtering, and circuit-aware preprocessing as considerations for more scalable QNLP-based financial sentiment analysis.

</details>


### [51] [CreativeInstruct: Scalably Teaching LLMs to Balance Quality, Creativity, and Diversity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07460)
*Ananya Sahu,Mohit Bansal,Elias Stengel-Eskin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CreativeInstruct is a scalable instruction-tuning method that teaches LLMs to balance creativity with quality by injecting [StartCreativity] spans, improving output diversity without sacrificing quality and boosting RL performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training improves LLM capabilities but reduces output diversity and creativity, harming both explicitly creative tasks (story generation) and implicitly creative ones (RL). Existing solutions require multiple models at inference time. A method is needed to maintain post-training quality while recovering base-model diversity.

Method: CreativeInstruct injects special [StartCreativity] tokens that bias generation toward creative, base-model-like outputs. A structural diversity metric based on graph edit distance captures narrative-level variation. GRPO is applied to CreativeInstruct checkpoints for RL tasks.

Result: On narrative generation, CreativeInstruct matches/exceeds diversity of multi-model baselines without sacrificing quality. Human evaluation shows 70.3% preference for CreativeInstruct generations as more creative. For RL, GRPO on CreativeInstruct improves ~4% on AMC and ~5% on MATH over post-trained checkpoints.

Conclusion: CreativeInstruct effectively restores creativity in post-trained LLMs via trainable creativity spans, benefiting both generative tasks and RL performance, all within a single-model, single-inference framework.

Abstract: While post-training improves the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), it generally lowers their output diversity and creativity, negatively impacting tasks that explicitly require creativity (e.g., story generation) as well as those that require it implicitly, e.g., reinforcement learning (RL). We instead propose CreativeInstruct, a scalable instruction-tuning method that teaches LLMs to balance creative, base-model-like generations with the quality of post-trained models, by learning to inject special [StartCreativity] spans that bias generation toward creativity. Furthermore, we introduce a structural diversity metric based on graph edit distance, which captures narrative level variation missed by purely lexical and semantic metrics. On narrative generation, CreativeInstruct matches or exceeds the diversity of both multi-model baselines and distilled variants of their outputs, without sacrificing quality or requiring multiple models at inference time. These results are mirrored in our human evaluation, where we find that annotators rate CreativeInstruct generations as more creative than the post-trained LLMs' generations in 70.3% of cases. We also show the benefits of creative models as a substrate for RL: GRPO applied to a CreativeInstruct checkpoint improves by ~4% on AMC and ~5% points on MATH over the same training applied to the post-trained checkpoint.

</details>


### [52] [Mitigating Scoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge via Random Number Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05726)
*Yuma Asato,Kiyoaki Shirai,Natthawut Kertkeidkachorn*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM evaluators exhibit scoring bias (tendency to favor certain scores regardless of context). This paper proposes measuring an LLM's latent numerical bias via random number generation prompts, then rectifying token probabilities during evaluation to debias scores. The method outperforms baselines across four tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators suffer from scoring bias, where models systematically favor certain scores irrespective of the text being evaluated. Existing debiasing/calibration methods are insufficient, and bias patterns vary across LLMs, tasks, and score ranges, necessitating a task-specific, context-aware debiasing approach.

Method: The proposed method works in two stages: (1) Latent bias measurement — the LLM is prompted to randomly generate number tokens; by comparing the observed distribution to a uniform distribution, the LLM's inherent numerical preference (latent number bias) is quantified. A downstream task definition is prepended to these prompts to capture task-specific bias. (2) Rectification — during actual LLM evaluation, the token generation probabilities for score outputs are adjusted (rectified) using the measured latent number bias to produce debiased scores.

Result: Experiments on four tasks — LLM alignment evaluation, summarization evaluation, Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), and Semantic Textual Relatedness (STR) — show the proposed method outperforms baselines including an unmodified LLM evaluator and prior calibration methods. Additionally, scoring bias is shown to vary across different LLMs, task types, and score ranges, validating the need for case-specific bias measurement.

Conclusion: Latent number bias is a significant source of scoring distortion in LLM evaluators and can be effectively mitigated by measuring it via random number generation and rectifying output probabilities accordingly. The variability of bias across models, tasks, and score ranges underscores the importance of task-specific debiasing, making the proposed method a practical and robust solution for improving LLM-as-a-Judge reliability.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are often used as evaluators of text quality, known as LLM-as-a-Judge, which can outperform conventional automatic evaluation metrics that rely on reference texts. However, LLM evaluators tend to generate particular scores regardless of the context of the evaluated text, which is known as scoring bias. This study proposes a novel method to mitigate this scoring bias. An LLM is instructed to randomly generate number tokens, and the latent numerical bias of the LLM is identified by measuring the deviation of the observed distribution of numbers from the uniform distribution. A definition of a downstream task, for which an LLM evaluator is used, is added to the prompts for random number generation to measure task-specific latent number bias. In the evaluation by an LLM, the token generation probabilities for a given input are rectified considering the LLM's latent number bias. Results of the experiment on four different tasks, evaluation of LLM alignment, evaluation of summarization, Semantic Textual Similarity, and Semantic Textual Relatedness, demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the baselines, including an LLM without debiasing and previous calibration methods. In addition, it is confirmed that scoring bias varies across LLMs, tasks, and score ranges, indicating the importance of measuring latent number bias as the case may be.

</details>

### [53] [Latent Fact-Checking: Detecting Misinformation through Activation Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06417)
*Pedro Barcelos,Otávio Parraga,Marcelo M. Mussi,Lucas M. Fraga,Lucas S. Kupssinskü,Rodrigo C. Barros*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a misinformation detection method that identifies a "falsehood direction" in the residual stream of transformer LMs via contrastive activation differences, enabling classification through last-token projection onto this direction without fine-tuning or external evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing misinformation detection relies on surface-level linguistic features or external knowledge retrieval. The authors hypothesize that truthfulness is a structured, geometrically separable property within a language model's latent representation space, motivating an interpretability-driven approach that bypasses fine-tuning and retrieval.

Method: Using Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), the method contrasts activations from paired truthful and false statements to isolate a "misinformation direction" in the residual stream. At inference, the last-token activation of an unseen claim is projected onto this direction, and the resulting representation is fed to an MLP classifier. The backbone model remains frozen; only the direction estimation and MLP training require the contrastive pairs.

Result: Evaluated across 11 models (Gemma, Llama, Qwen; 270M–12B params) on AVeriTeC, LIAR, and FACTors benchmarks, the falsehood direction proved recoverable across scales and architectures. Last-token projection matched or exceeded zero-shot and few-shot prompting baselines on LIAR and FACTors, with largest gains for smaller models. AVeriTeC performance was limited, attributed to its evidence-grounded labeling scheme.

Conclusion: Truthfulness appears to be a linearly separable concept in pretrained LM latent space. Activation-engineering-based detection offers a practical, interpretability-driven complement to retrieval-based misinformation pipelines, particularly effective for smaller models.

Abstract: The proliferation of misinformation online has driven demand for scalable detection systems. While most existing approaches rely on surface-level linguistic features or external knowledge retrieval, we examine truthfulness as a geometric property of a language model's representation space. We introduce a misinformation detection framework grounded in activation engineering, which leverages the latent geometry of transformer models. Our approach elicits a misinformation direction in the residual stream by contrasting activations from paired truthful and false statements, following the difference-in-means principle of Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). At inference time, the last-token activation of an unseen claim is projected onto this direction, and the projected representation is fed to an Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) for classification. The procedure requires no fine-tuning of the backbone model, no external evidence retrieval, and no task-specific supervision beyond the contrastive pairs used to estimate the direction. We evaluate the method across 11 models from the Gemma, Llama, and Qwen families, ranging from 270M to 12B parameters, on three fact-checking benchmarks: AVeriTeC, LIAR, and FACTors. The falsehood direction is recoverable across model scales and architectural families, and last-token projection matches or surpasses zero-shot and few-shot prompting baselines on LIAR and FACTors, with the largest gains observed for smaller models. Performance on AVeriTeC is more limited, which we attribute to its evidence-grounded labeling scheme. These findings provide evidence that truthfulness is a structured, linearly separable concept in the latent space of pretrained language models, and point toward interpretability-driven misinformation detection as a practical complement to retrieval-based pipelines. The code is available on https://github.com/Malta-Lab/LaFaCt.

</details>


### [54] [Risk-Aware Decision Policies for Agents Under Noisy Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06420)
*David Szczecina*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An artificial life predator-prey model demonstrates that uncertainty-aware foraging strategies dramatically outperform naive trust in noisy perceptual labels, with agents exhibiting qualitative behavioral regime shifts from exploratory to conservative as perceptual uncertainty increases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biological perception is inherently noisy, yet organisms must make high-stakes decisions (e.g., foraging vs. fleeing) under uncertainty. The authors aim to understand how different decision-making policies that account for perceptual noise affect survival outcomes, bridging risk-sensitive foraging theory with artificial life and robust learning under noisy labels.

Method: The authors construct an Artificial Life predator-prey model where agents forage under noisy perception. They compare multiple decision policies — ranging from blindly trusting perceptual labels to uncertainty-aware strategies — under controlled symmetric and asymmetric perceptual noise conditions. Agent performance is evaluated on survival and fatal error rates.

Result: Blind trust in noisy perceptual labels leads to catastrophic failure as noise increases. Uncertainty-aware policies significantly improve survival and reduce fatal errors. A qualitative regime shift is observed: agents transition from exploratory to conservative foraging behavior as uncertainty rises. Explicit information gathering emerges as a mechanism for improving robustness under unreliable perception.

Conclusion: Uncertainty-aware decision-making is critical for robust performance under perceptual noise. The model provides an interpretable artificial life analogue to robust learning with noisy labels and highlights the evolutionary importance of explicit information gathering when perception is unreliable.

Abstract: Perception in biological systems is inherently noisy, requiring organisms to make decisions under uncertainty where misclassification can be costly or fatal. We present an Artificial Life predator-prey model of foraging under noisy perception, and compare agent performance when using various policies that take into account their noisy predictions. Through controlled experiments under both symmetric and asymmetric perceptual noise, we show that blindly trusting perceptual labels leads to catastrophic failure as noise increases, while uncertainty-aware strategies significantly improve survival and reduce fatal errors. We further observe qualitative regime shifts in behaviour, with agents transitioning from exploratory to conservative strategies as uncertainty increases. Our model links risk-sensitive foraging, ecological information use, and Artificial Life by showing that explicit information gathering can improve robustness when perception is unreliable. These results highlight the importance of uncertainty-aware decision-making and provide an interpretable artificial life analogue to robust learning with noisy labels.

</details>


### [55] [Sharding Prevents LLM Oversight Failures and Adversarial Exploitation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06422)
*Victor Akinwande,J. Zico Kolter,Aran Nayebi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLM judges suffer from "overload": as the number of verdicts per call increases, agreement with experts drops. Sharding—partitioning requirements across separate calls—mitigates this, improving accuracy under fixed budgets and showing robustness against adversarial presentation attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based evaluators are increasingly used for oversight tasks requiring multiple simultaneous judgments. The authors identify that packing many verdicts into a single call degrades decision quality, even with ample compute budgets. This "overload" phenomenon threatens reliability in high-stakes domains like research replication, legal review, and clinical-trial assessment.

Method: The paper proposes "sharding": splitting a set of evaluation requirements into smaller groups, dispatching each to an independent LLM call, and aggregating results. The authors compare sharded panels against single holistic calls under matched total budgets (tokens/tools) and per-decision budgets. They also test robustness via best-of-N adversarial attacks (varying presentation only, holding underlying work fixed) and debate-style countermeasures for criterion-specific persuasion.

Result: Sharding consistently improves expert agreement over single holistic calls. A sharded weaker judge can outperform a stronger holistic judge and match it even when the latter receives the full panel budget. Sharding eliminates the adversarial advantage of best-of-N attacks that exploit overload, keeping over-acceptance of unmet criteria low. For attacks targeting individual criteria, debate-style opposition atop sharding provides robustness.

Conclusion: Overload is a systematic failure mode in model-based oversight. Sharding offers a simple, budget-neutral intervention that improves accuracy and adversarial robustness. The findings suggest that decomposition strategies should be a first-class design consideration when deploying LLM judges for multi-criterion evaluation.

Abstract: Giving an LLM judge more compute does not necessarily make it check more requirements. When one call must return many verdicts, some decisions become weakly grounded in the evidence, even when that call receives the same token or tool budget as a panel of separate calls. Across expert-graded research replications, legal work, and clinical-trial assessments, agreement with experts falls as the number of verdicts per call grows. We identify sharding as the intervention that mitigates this failure in model-based oversight. Sharding partitions the requirements into smaller groups, assigns each group to a separate call, and aggregates the verdicts. Against a single call with the panel's full budget, sharding improves agreement while holding the model, evidence, total budget, and per-decision budget fixed. Overall, we find that a sharded weaker judge can outperform a more capable holistic judge and match that judge even when the latter receives the panel's full budget. Additionally, we find that sharding exhibits robustness against adversaries. A best-of-N adversary can hold the underlying work fixed, vary only its presentation, and increase an overloaded judge's acceptance of genuinely unmet criteria severalfold. Wherever sharding reduces baseline error, it removes this adversarial advantage, keeping over-acceptance low even as the adversary's search widens. Sharding does not address attacks that persuade the judge separately on each criterion rather than exploiting overload. In that setting, we find that debate-style opposition on top of sharding withstands such adaptive re-optimization.

</details>


### [56] [Adversarial Causal Intervention Falsification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06427)
*Mojtaba Eslami*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A game-theoretic framework where a causal generator and an adversarial experimentalist compete: the generator proposes causal models with interventional distributions, while the experimentalist selects interventions to falsify the generator. The framework clarifies distinctions between observational fit, interventional equivalence, and point identification, with theoretical guarantees for equilibria, convergence, and sequential design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative models can match observational data while encoding wrong causal structures. Existing evaluation focuses on observational fidelity, which is insufficient for causal claims. The authors aim to formalize adversarial testing of causal models through interventions, bridging causal generative modeling, active causal discovery, and experimental design.

Method: The authors introduce Adversarial Causal Intervention Falsification (ACIF), a sequential two-player game. The generator proposes a structural causal model (observational + interventional distributions). The discriminator/adversary selects an intervention to maximize discrepancy between the generator's predicted post-intervention distribution and the true one. Both oracle and implementable versions are formulated. The objective reduces to a worst-intervention integral probability metric. Analysis covers equilibria, finite-sample convergence, margin-based model selection, and disagreement-driven sequential experimental design.

Result: Key theoretical results for finite model/intervention classes: (i) adversarial objective reduces to a worst-intervention integral probability metric; (ii) identification up to interventional equivalence, with point identification under a separating intervention family; (iii) mixed-strategy Nash equilibria exist; (iv) finite-sample uniform convergence and margin-based model selection guarantees; (v) logarithmic elimination guarantee for disagreement-driven sequential design under balanced separation. A linear-Gaussian example demonstrates two observationally indistinguishable causal directions separated by one well-chosen intervention.

Conclusion: ACIF clarifies what adversarial causal discriminators can and cannot certify, and provides a principled bridge between causal generative modeling, active causal discovery, and experimental design. It formalizes the insufficiency of observational fit and the necessity of interventional testing for causal claims.

Abstract: Generative models can reproduce an observational distribution while encoding an incorrect causal structure. We study a sequential game in which a structural causal generator proposes observational and interventional distributions, while an adversarial experimentalist selects interventions intended to maximally falsify the generator. The discriminator is therefore not merely a real-versus-synthetic classifier: it is indexed by an intervention and tests whether the generator reproduces the corresponding post-intervention law. We introduce Adversarial Causal Intervention Falsification (ACIF), formulate oracle and implementable versions of the game, and distinguish three objects that are often conflated: observational fit, interventional equivalence over an admissible query class, and point identification of a structural causal model. For finite model and intervention classes, we prove: (i) an exact reduction of the adversarial objective to a worst-intervention integral probability metric; (ii) identification up to interventional equivalence, with point identification under a separating intervention family; (iii) existence of mixed-strategy equilibria; (iv) finite-sample uniform convergence and margin-based model-selection guarantees; and (v) a logarithmic elimination guarantee for a disagreement-driven sequential design under a balanced-separation condition. We also give a complete linear-Gaussian example in which two observationally indistinguishable causal directions are separated by a single well-chosen intervention. The framework clarifies what an adversarial causal discriminator can and cannot certify, and provides a principled bridge between causal generative modeling, active causal discovery, and experimental design.

</details>


### [57] [Fixed and Adaptive Topological DeepONets: Functional Measurements on Hausdorff Locally Convex Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06428)
*Khemraj Shukla,George Em Karniadakis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper extends DeepONets by replacing fixed pointwise discretizations with continuous linear functionals from the dual of a locally convex space, enabling both fixed and adaptive functional measurement systems. The framework yields a discrete error decomposition with Barron-rate refinement and demonstrates strong performance on PDE problems including Navier-Stokes, where the adaptive variant achieves 1.685% error with 128 coordinates while requiring far less memory and training time than FNO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard DeepONets encode input functions via point values on a fixed discretization, which ties the model to a specific resolution, fails to exploit the continuous dual structure of function spaces, and cannot handle non-normable locally convex input spaces. There is a need for a discretization-independent, compact, and interpretable encoding scheme that leverages continuous linear functionals, supports adaptivity, and provides theoretical error control.

Method: Building on the Topological DeepONet of Ismailov, the authors replace point samples with continuous linear functionals from the continuous dual V' of a Hausdorff locally convex space (V, {p_α}), whose topology is generated by a point-separating family of seminorms. They develop both fixed and adaptive functional measurement systems. Measurements are combined with the coefficient-space Two-Step procedure of Lee and Shin, and a training-only decoder plus regularization stabilizes the adaptive coordinates. A discrete error decomposition is derived, separating measurement error, output-basis error, and neural-approximation error, with a Barron-rate refinement.

Result: On heterogeneous Darcy flow, functional models achieve nearly resolution-independent errors of 5.5–5.6% on unseen grids. For the controlled operator, adaptive measurements reduce mean error below 1.2%. On fixed-time Navier-Stokes, the Adaptive Topological DeepONet reaches 1.685% ± 0.017% mean relative L² error with 128 functional coordinates. A comparably sized FNO achieves 0.832% ± 0.172% but requires the full 64×64 input field, twice the training time, and 10.7× greater peak GPU memory. The method also handles the antiderivative operator on a non-normable locally convex input space and time-evolving Navier-Stokes vorticity.

Conclusion: The functional measurement formulation yields compact, interpretable, and discretization-portable coordinates in the continuous dual V', applicable even to non-normable input spaces. The adaptive variant offers a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off compared to grid-based methods like FNO, providing strong performance with substantially lower computational cost.

Abstract: Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets; arXiv:1910.03193) typically encode an input function through point values on a fixed discretization. Building on the Topological DeepONet framework of Ismailov (arXiv:2603.11972), we replace point samples by continuous linear functionals drawn from the continuous dual of a Hausdorff locally convex space $({V},\{p_α\}_{α\in A})$, whose topology is generated by a point-separating family of seminorms rather than a single norm, and develop fixed and adaptive functional measurement systems. Measurements are combined with the coefficient-space Two-Step procedure of Lee and Shin (arXiv:2309.01020), while a training-only decoder and regularization stabilize the adaptive coordinates. We derive a discrete error decomposition separating measurement, output-basis, and neural-approximation errors, together with a Barron-rate refinement. The framework is evaluated on the antiderivative operator, a non-normable locally convex input space, heterogeneous Darcy flow, a controlled operator, and fixed-time and time-evolving Navier-Stokes vorticity operators. In the heterogeneous Darcy problem, the functional models retain nearly resolution-independent errors of 5.5-5.6% on unseen grids, while in the controlled problem adaptive measurements reduce the mean error below 1.2%. For the fixed-time Navier-Stokes problem, the Adaptive Topological DeepONet is the most accurate DeepONet-based model, attaining a mean relative $L^2$ error of 1.685% +/- 0.017% using 128 functional coordinates. A comparably sized Fourier neural operator (FNO; arXiv:2010.08895) achieves the lower error 0.832% +/- 0.172%, but requires the full 64x64 input field, twice the training time, and 10.7x greater peak GPU memory. The formulation provides compact, interpretable, and discretization-portable coordinates in the continuous dual $V'$, including for non-normable input spaces.

</details>


### [58] [MiGHT-EHR: A Multi-task Graph Transformer for Heterogeneous Temporal Electronic Health Records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06430)
*Anirudh Rayas,Yuan Wang,Pavan Turaga*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MiGHT-EHR is a multi-task graph transformer that models heterogeneous clinical entities, longitudinal patient trajectories, and shared task dependencies in EHR data using a unified heterogeneous graph framework, achieving SOTA performance on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV across four clinical prediction tasks while preserving interpretable structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing EHR learning methods fail to jointly capture three critical properties: (1) heterogeneous clinical entities and their interactions, (2) longitudinal patient trajectories across visits, and (3) shared statistical dependencies across related clinical prediction tasks. Most methods address only a subset of these, limiting their effectiveness.

Method: MiGHT-EHR constructs a heterogeneous graph from EHRs where nodes represent clinical entities (patients, visits, diagnoses, prescriptions, procedures) and edges connect statistically associated entities identified via normalized point-wise mutual information (NPMI). A multi-task graph transformer is then applied to learn unified representations that jointly model all three properties, supporting multiple downstream clinical prediction tasks simultaneously.

Result: MiGHT-EHR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on average across four tasks — drug recommendation, length-of-stay prediction, mortality prediction, and readmission prediction — on both MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets, with particularly strong gains in mortality and readmission. Post-hoc analysis shows patient neighborhoods cluster by clinical outcomes, salient medical concepts are encoded as linear directions, and task probabilities are well calibrated.

Conclusion: MiGHT-EHR demonstrates that jointly modeling heterogeneity, temporality, and multi-task dependencies yields superior predictive performance while producing clinically interpretable representations, advancing EHR representation learning for diverse clinical prediction tasks.

Abstract: Learning from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has gained significant attention due to its potential to improve clinical prediction. However, effective learning remains challenging because EHRs encode heterogeneous, temporally ordered clinical interactions. In particular, EHRs contain: (i) heterogeneous clinical entities, including patients, visits, diagnoses, prescriptions, and procedures, together with their heterogeneous interactions, (ii) longitudinal patient trajectories across hospital visits and (iii) shared statistical dependencies across related clinical prediction tasks. Existing EHR learning methods capture only a subset of these properties. To bridge this gap, we propose Multi-task Graph transformer for Heterogeneous Temporal EHRs (MiGHT-EHR), which jointly models all three within a unified representation learning method. MiGHT-EHR constructs a heterogeneous graph from EHRs in which nodes represent clinical entities and edges connect statistically associated entities identified via normalized point-wise mutual information. Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets, MiGHT-EHR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on average across four tasks: drug recommendation, prediction of length-of-stay, mortality, and readmission, with particularly strong improvements in mortality and readmission prediction. Furthermore, a post-hoc analysis of the learned representations reveals that patient neighborhoods are organized by clinical outcomes, salient medical concepts are recoverable as linear directions in the representation space, and task probabilities are well calibrated. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that MiGHT-EHR representations support diverse prediction tasks while preserving clinically interpretable structure.

</details>


### [59] [SNI-GNN: SmartNIC-Assisted Full-Graph GNN Training with In-Network Embedding Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06441)
*Guofan Yu,Sitian Chen,Zhenheng Tang,Xiaowen Chu,Amelie Chi Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SNI-GNN is a SmartNIC-assisted full-graph GNN training system that uses in-network linear-trend prediction of remote embeddings to reduce inter-node communication by 21–45%, achieving 1.3–3.6× speedups with negligible accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full-graph GNN training suffers from heavy, irregular inter-node embedding exchanges on multi-server clusters, limiting scalability despite high accuracy. Existing solutions (partitioning, compression) have trade-offs; this work explores SmartNIC-based in-network prediction as a complementary approach to reduce communication while preserving accuracy.

Method: SNI-GNN deploys a lightweight linear-trend predictor on NVIDIA BlueField-3 SmartNICs to predict remote embeddings from cached historical values, avoiding full communication. It incorporates: (1) an importance-based boundary-node sampling policy, (2) an asynchronous DPU–GPU data pipeline with intermediate-result reuse. Theoretical error and convergence bounds are provided, showing controlled predictor bias under bounded second-order dynamics and standard non-convex convergence with inexact gradients.

Result: SNI-GNN cuts communication by 21–45%, achieves 1.3–3.6× end-to-end speedups over BNS-GCN and up to 1.29× over SANCUS, with accuracy loss ≤ 0.01, and scales to 16 GPUs on graphs with tens of millions of edges.

Conclusion: SmartNIC-based in-network prediction is a practical complement to partitioning and compression for communication-efficient full-graph GNN training at scale.

Abstract: Full-graph GNN training delivers high accuracy but scales poorly on multi-server clusters due to heavy, irregular inter-node embedding exchanges. We present SNI-GNN, a SmartNIC-assisted full-graph training system that reduces communication while preserving accuracy by predicting remote embeddings in-network. SNI-GNN deploys a lightweight linear-trend predictor on SmartNICs to refine cached historical embeddings, coupled with an importance-based boundary-node sampling policy and an asynchronous DPU--GPU data pipeline with intermediate-result reuse. We provide error and convergence bounds showing that predictor bias remains controlled under bounded second-order dynamics and yields standard non-convex convergence with inexact gradients. Implemented on NVIDIA BlueField-3, SNI-GNN integrates with state-of-the-art full-graph systems, cuts communication by 21--45\%, achieves 1.3--3.6$\times$ end-to-end speedups over BNS-GCN and up to 1.29$\times$ over baseline SANCUS, with accuracy loss $\leq 0.01$, and scales efficiently to 16 GPUs on graphs with up to tens of millions of edges. These results indicate SmartNIC-based in-network prediction is a practical complement to partitioning and compression techniques for communication-efficient full-graph GNN training at scale.

</details>


### [60] [ED-CSP: Crystal Structure Prediction from Electron Diffraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06448)
*Germain Poloudenny,Yaël Frégier,Arnaud Demortière*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ED-CSP is a machine learning framework that predicts 3D crystal structures from sparse, unindexed electron diffraction patterns combined with composition data. It uses a relational set encoder, multi-view aggregation, and periodic flow generator to jointly predict lattice parameters and atomic coordinates, achieving 57.49% MR@5 on held-out materials and scaling to 66.27% with more training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recovering 3D periodic crystal structures from sparse, unindexed electron diffraction (ED) observations is an inherently difficult generative inverse problem. Existing methods are limited to predicting crystallographic labels, reconstructing from already-indexed reflections, or retrieving from finite libraries, rather than performing true generative structure prediction from raw ED data.

Method: ED-CSP integrates three components: (1) a relational set encoder for processing ED spot sets, (2) permutation-invariant multi-view aggregation to combine information across multiple detector-plane observations, and (3) a periodic flow generator that jointly predicts lattice parameters and fractional atomic coordinates. The authors also construct ED-CS, a large-scale simulated dataset of 4.85 million multi-view ED structures drawn from seven materials repositories, deduplicated and filtered to avoid overlap with the CHILI-100K benchmark.

Result: On 2,075 held-out CHILI-100K materials, ED-CSP trained solely on CHILI achieves 57.49% MR@5, outperforming PXRDGen (52.92%). Initializing from a one-million-structure precursor raises MR@5 to 66.27%. On 1,024 compositions absent from the training library, the model still attains 53.52% MR@5, confirming genuine generative capacity. Ablation: replacing target ED with diffraction from non-isomorphic structures of the same composition reduces MR@5 by 22.09 percentage points, verifying dependence on input diffraction rather than composition alone.

Conclusion: ED-CSP and the accompanying ED-CS dataset establish a benchmark for generative crystal structure prediction from sparse ED observations and lay groundwork for future transfer to experimental electron diffraction data.

Abstract: Recovering a periodic 3D crystal structure from sparse, unindexed electron diffraction (ED) observations is a challenging generative inverse problem. Existing ED-based learning methods mainly predict crystallographic labels, reconstruct structures from indexed reflections, or retrieve candidates from finite structure libraries. Here, we introduce ED-CSP, a machine learning framework that predicts crystal structures from chemical composition, atom count, and multiple detector-plane ED spot sets. ED-CSP combines a relational set encoder, permutation-invariant multi-view aggregation, and a periodic flow generator to jointly predict lattice parameters and fractional atomic coordinates.
  To train the model, we construct ED-CS, a dataset of 4.85 million simulated multi-view ED crystal structures, deduplicated across seven materials repositories and filtered to exclude CHILI-100K overlaps. On 2,075 held-out CHILI-100K materials, ED-CSP trained only on CHILI achieves a structural match rate of 57.49% MR@5, outperforming PXRDGen (52.92%), a state-of-the-art crystal structure prediction model conditioned on powder X-ray diffraction. Scaling training data further improves performance: initializing from a one-million-structure precursor raises MR@5 to 66.27%. On 1,024 compositions absent from the training retrieval library, the model still achieves 53.52% MR@5, demonstrating true generative capability beyond exact-formula retrieval. Replacing target ED observations with diffraction from non-isomorphic structures of identical composition decreases MR@5 by 22.09 percentage points, confirming that predictions depend on the input diffraction patterns rather than composition alone. ED-CSP and ED-CS establish a benchmark for generative crystal structure prediction from sparse ED observations and provide a foundation for future transfer to experimental data.

</details>


### [61] [Beyond Attention: Signed Integrated Gradients Attribution in a BiomeGPT-Style Microbiome Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06486)
*Oren Nelson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes using Integrated Gradients with a source-derived baseline for feature-tokenized transformers (like BiomeGPT) to overcome limitations of [CLS] attention weights in microbiome classification. This signed, fusion-aware method separates pathogenic from protective signals and, combined with Integrated Hessians, reveals community interaction rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior interpretability methods for feature-tokenized transformers (e.g., BiomeGPT) rely on [CLS] token attention weights to rank input importance. These are limited because: (1) they are nonnegative and cannot distinguish disease-supporting from health-supporting evidence, and (2) they operate post-fusion, obscuring how the fixed token identity (species S) and variable measurement (abundance A) individually contribute to predictions.

Method: The authors apply Integrated Gradients — a signed, fusion-aware attribution method — to feature-tokenized transformers. They propose a source-derived baseline T' = S + A₀, which preserves species identity as a fixed biological coordinate while isolating abundance variation effects. Second-order Integrated Hessians are recommended to uncover interaction rules between microbial community members (how perturbing one species alters sensitivity to another).

Result: The gradient-based approach reveals species-abundance directional relationships and sensitivity diagnostics that are entirely invisible to unsigned [CLS] attention weights. It explicitly separates pathogenic from protective microbial signals along the disease-health decision margin. The method generalizes to any smooth, differentiable feature-tokenized transformer.

Conclusion: Integrated Gradients with a source-derived baseline provides a principled, signed, and fusion-aware explainability framework for feature-tokenized transformers like BiomeGPT. Supplementing with Integrated Hessians further enables discovery of higher-order community interaction rules. Code is publicly available.

Abstract: In a feature-tokenized transformer (arXiv:2106.11959) such as BiomeGPT (doi:10.64898/2026.01.05.697599), each input token is built by fusing a fixed identity with a sample-specific measurement: a fixed species and a variable abundance, T = S + A. To interpret downstream classification in such models, prior work inspects the attention weights of the special [CLS] token (arXiv:2106.11959, arXiv:1810.04805, BiomeGPT) to rank sample tokens by importance. These weights have two critical limitations: they are nonnegative, so they cannot separate disease-supporting from health-supporting evidence (arXiv:2201.12114), and they act after token fusion, obscuring how the input sources S and A each affect the output.
  To address this we use Integrated Gradients (arXiv:1703.01365), a signed, fusion-aware attribution method, and propose a source-derived baseline T' = S + A_0 for feature-tokenized models such as BiomeGPT, which preserves species identity as a fixed biological coordinate while isolating the effect of abundance variation. Applied to a disease-versus-health decision margin, it yields polarity that explicitly separates pathogenic from protective microbial signals. We show that this gradient-based approach uncovers species-abundance directional relationships and sensitivity diagnostics entirely obscured by unsigned [CLS] attention weights. We further recommend second-order Integrated Hessians (arXiv:2002.04138) to expose microbiome community interaction rules: how a perturbation in one member alters the model's sensitivity to another, and which other species drive ambiguous cases toward disease or health at a given abundance level. This provides a principled approach to explainability in BiomeGPT that generalizes to other smooth and differentiable feature-tokenized transformers. Code is available at https://github.com/nohren/token-source-attribution

</details>


### [62] [Toward Reliable Context Compression for Long-Horizon Agents: An Empirical Study of Execution Instability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06503)
*Guanghui Min,Liang Wu,Mayank Darbari,Chen Chen,Liangjie Hong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recurrent context compression can degrade agent behavior; the authors propose TRACE, a verifier-guided framework that optimizes compression prompts via paired continuations, improving task performance, reliability, and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recurrent context compression is used to manage context growth in long-horizon agents, but its behavioral side effects—such as weakened recency influence, blocked actions, repeated exploration, and instability—are poorly understood and underexplored.

Method: TRACE evaluates individual compaction events using paired closed-loop continuations from the same environment state (compressed vs. uncompressed) and uses summary preference optimization to tune a natural-language compression prompt, keeping all models frozen throughout.

Result: Initial experiments on AppWorld demonstrate improvements over existing compression baselines in task performance, multi-run reliability, and context-execution efficiency.

Conclusion: The findings offer early evidence that boundary-local evaluation is a promising direction for developing reliable agent context compression methods.

Abstract: Recurrent context compression controls context growth in long-horizon agents, but its behavioral effects remain poorly understood. In this preliminary empirical study, we show that compression can weaken the influence of recent interactions, increasing blocked actions, repeated exploration, and instability across runs. Motivated by these observations, we introduce TRACE, a verifier-guided framework that evaluates individual compaction events through paired closed-loop continuations from the same environment state and uses summary preferences to optimize a natural-language compression prompt while keeping all models frozen. Initial results on AppWorld show improvements over existing compression baselines in task performance, multi-run reliability, and context--execution efficiency. These findings provide early evidence for boundary-local evaluation as a promising direction for reliable agent context compression.

</details>


### [63] [Unmasking Removal-Budget Confounding: A Matched Operating-Point Evaluation Framework for Adaptive Data Cleaning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06511)
*Wei-Hsiang Chen,Pin-Hsuan Yu,Chen-Hsuan Fang,Jung-Hua Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adaptive data-cleaning methods suffer from removal-budget confounding, where apparent performance gains stem from removing fewer samples rather than better corruption detection. The authors propose an operating-point-aware evaluation framework using matched-budget and matched-recall controls plus threshold-independent metrics, revealing that most claimed improvements vanish under equalized comparison.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adaptive data-cleaning methods are evaluated naively at their own induced operating points, which confounds removal budget size with discrimination quality. Changing partition granularity shifts decision boundaries and alters how many samples are removed, creating an illusion of improvement when metrics like precision or FPR improve simply because fewer samples are flagged. A rigorous evaluation framework is needed to isolate genuine corruption-discrimination ability from budget effects.

Method: The authors introduce an operating-point-aware evaluation framework with three components: (1) matched-budget controls that equalize the number of removed samples across methods, (2) matched-recall controls that equalize the fraction of corrupted samples detected, and (3) threshold-independent metrics (AUROC, AUPRC). They also propose a multi-cue adaptive cleaner redesign incorporating a reweighted learning-difficulty cue, an auxiliary Euclidean-distance cue, and increased partition granularity to isolate clean-but-difficult samples. False-positive decomposition is used to trace error sources (clean-but-difficult vs. other clean samples) across corruption severity levels.

Result: Naive evaluation shows substantial performance gains for the redesigned cleaner, but these gains disappear under matched-budget and matched-recall controls. Clean-but-difficult samples dominate false positives at low corruption rates, become threshold-dependent at moderate corruption, and are negligible under severe corruption. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 confirm most differences shrink or vanish at low-to-moderate corruption; true ranking advantages persist only in specific low-prevalence settings and high-recall regions under severe corruption.

Conclusion: Adaptive cleaning methods must be benchmarked at matched operating points; otherwise, reported improvements may reflect reduced removal budgets rather than genuine gains in corruption discrimination. The proposed evaluation framework provides a principled solution to removal-budget confounding.

Abstract: Adaptive data-cleaning methods replace manual filtering thresholds with data-driven partitions. However, changing the partition granularity, the number of groups used to segment samples by estimated corruption risk, can implicitly shift the decision boundary and alter the overall number of removed samples. This creates a bias known as removal-budget confounding, where apparent gains in metrics like precision or false-positive rate reflect a smaller removal budget rather than superior corruption discrimination. To address this evaluation bias, we introduce an operating-point-aware evaluation framework that evaluates methods using matched-budget and matched-recall controls alongside threshold-independent metrics (AUROC and AUPRC). We test this framework on a multi-cue adaptive cleaner redesign featuring a reweighted learning-difficulty cue, an auxiliary Euclidean-distance cue, and increased partition granularity intended to isolate clean-but-difficult samples. While naive evaluations (assessing configurations at their own induced operating points) suggest substantial performance improvements for the redesign, these gains disappear once operating points are equalized. False-positive decomposition reveals that clean-but-difficult samples primarily drive error counts at low corruption rates, become threshold-dependent at moderate corruption, and contribute negligibly under severe corruption. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 demonstrate that most performance differences observed in naive evaluation shrink or vanish at low-to-moderate corruption when operating points are matched. True ranking advantages only remain in specific low-prevalence settings and in high-recall regions under severe corruption. These findings highlight that adaptive cleaning methods must be benchmarked at matched operating points to ensure performance gains reflect genuine corruption discrimination.

</details>


### [64] [Target-Weighted Neyman Allocation: Experimental Design for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects under Population Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06512)
*Hoang Dang,Luan Pham,Minh Nguyen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TWNA is a two-stage stratified experimental design that optimizes sample allocation by balancing group importance in the deployment population with statistical precision needs, using pilot variance estimates to target weighted average treatment effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard experimental designs either waste budget on rarely-appearing groups (experimental proportions) or under-sample hard-to-measure groups (deployment proportions). Neither approach optimally balances deployment relevance with statistical precision when the experimental population differs from the deployment population.

Method: TWNA uses a two-stage stratified design: a pilot stage estimates group-arm outcome variances, then a final stage allocates sample sizes and treatment probabilities according to a closed-form oracle rule that weights groups by both their deployment importance and measurement difficulty. The plug-in rule converges to the oracle as pilot estimates stabilize. Extensions handle deployment composition uncertainty and outcome distribution issues (skewness, rare events, contamination).

Result: Simulations and real-covariate benchmarks demonstrate that TWNA yields the largest precision gains precisely when groups are both important in deployment and statistically difficult to measure, outperforming both experimental-proportion and deployment-proportion allocation strategies.

Conclusion: TWNA provides a principled, robust framework for designing experiments intended to inform decisions in a different target population, with strong theoretical guarantees and practical performance improvements over conventional allocation methods.

Abstract: Randomized experiments are often run in one population to guide decisions in another. Allocating by experimental proportions wastes budget on groups that rarely appear in deployment, whereas allocating by deployment proportions under-samples groups that are hard to measure precisely. We propose \textbf{TWNA} (Target-Weighted Neyman Allocation), a two-stage stratified design that uses pilot estimates of group--arm outcome variances to allocate final-stage sample sizes and treatment probabilities for target-weighted group average treatment effect (GATE) precision. The oracle rule has a closed form and balances deployment importance with statistical difficulty; the plug-in rule recovers it as pilot variance estimates stabilize. We also extend TWNA to handle uncertainty about deployment composition, remaining robust whether the target mix is roughly known or entirely unknown. Finally, we distinguish this weight robustness from a pilot-robust variant for skewed, rare-event, or contaminated outcomes. Simulations and real-covariate benchmarks show the largest gains when groups are both deployment-important and difficult to measure.

</details>


### [65] [CertBind from Multimodal Connectivity to Certifiable Retrieval Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06516)
*Shuheng Cao,Zhenhao Zhang,Ruiqi Chen,Renjie Cao,Weijia Zhang,Siyu Zhang,Jiaxin Liu,Xiangyu Zeng,Haotian Geng,Fan Gu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CertBind is a framework that provides certifiable composition for frozen multimodal encoders connected via lightweight connectors, ensuring that cross-modal routing does not degrade native retrieval capabilities through multiscale (node, edge, path, query) theoretical guarantees with finite-sample recovery bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While lightweight connectors enable frozen multimodal encoders to be composed at the representation level, deployment reveals a critical second problem: connecting routes can expand cross-modal reach but simultaneously degrades established native retrieval performance. The paper addresses the lack of formal guarantees for when composed multimodal systems will preserve or harm native task decisions.

Method: CertBind proposes a multiscale theory of certifiable composition spanning four scales: (1) Node scale — native anchors define exact task identification boundaries under a chart model; (2) Edge scale — contract-aware conformal ranks provide graph-wide family-wise error control; (3) Path scale — an overlap-aware budget with clean calibration yields a finite-sample recovery radius; (4) Query scale — the recovery radius produces a covered top-k candidate set that becomes a point certificate when its size equals k. Based on these, CertBind classifies queries into four outcomes: Direct (supported routes), flagged routes sent to recovery, Certified (decisive recovery), and Abstain (unresolved).

Result: On the C-MCR shared route benchmark, connecting routes reduced native CLIP R@1 from 0.524 to 0.290. The CertBind production fallback recovered 0.963 ± 0.002 of clean retrieval performance, while the passing branch achieved a no-harm value of 1.000, indicating perfect preservation of native capability where applicable.

Conclusion: CertBind extends multimodal composability beyond connected representations to certifiable task decisions, providing formal guarantees through its multiscale framework and demonstrating near-complete recovery of degraded native retrieval with a perfect no-harm score on preserved routes.

Abstract: Lightweight connectors make frozen multimodal encoders composable at the representation level. Deployment exposes a second problem at the level of task decisions. A connected route can expand cross-modal reach while changing an established native retrieval capability. We introduce CertBind, a multiscale theory of certifiable composition for frozen multimodal connector graphs. At the node scale, native anchors establish the exact task identification boundary under the stated chart model. At the edge scale, contract-aware conformal ranks provide graph-wide family-wise error control. At the path scale, an overlap-aware budget and clean calibration yield a finite-sample recovery radius under declared conditions. At the query scale, this radius yields a covered top-k candidate set that becomes a point certificate when its size equals k. CertBind therefore retains supported routes as Direct, sends only flagged routes to recovery, returns Certified for decisive recovery, and returns Abstain for unresolved queries. The evaluated C-MCR shared route reduced native CLIP R@1 from 0.524 to 0.290. The production fallback recovered 0.963 +- 0.002 of clean retrieval, while the passing branch recorded a no-harm value of 1.000. CertBind extends multimodal composability from connected representations to certifiable task decisions.

</details>


### [66] [Online Security Learning in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems under Hidden Byzantine Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06520)
*Ximing Sun,Yue Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies online cooperative multi-agent control under Byzantine attacks, where compromised agents can overwrite planned actions. The authors formalize the problem as a robust MDP whose geometry depends on attacker information (s- or (s,a)-rectangular), establish fundamental lower bounds on security regret involving a cumulative response gap, and propose an algorithm achieving near-optimal regret bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide theoretical and algorithmic foundations for reliable multi-agent systems operating under Byzantine attacks, where a fixed unknown subset of agents can stealthily overwrite the team's planned joint action after observing it, making standard cooperative multi-agent learning methods vulnerable.

Method: The authors formalize the setting as a robust Markov decision process. They analyze two attacker models: one that observes the planned action (inducing (s,a)-rectangular robust MDPs with convex-hull uncertainty sets) and a blind attacker (inducing s-rectangular models). They derive information-theoretic lower bounds via two indistinguishable horizon-one instances, and develop a stage-tied robust estimation-to-decisions (STRED) learner with regret guarantees.

Result: Security regret decomposes into return regret plus a cumulative response gap D_K. A lower bound of Ω(K) expected security regret is unavoidable even when return regret is zero. The proposed STRED algorithm achieves Õ(H²S√(AK)) + E[D_K] regret, matching the lower-bound dependence on D_K.

Conclusion: The paper provides comprehensive theoretical and algorithmic foundations for reliable multi-agent systems under Byzantine attacks, characterizing the geometry induced by attacker information, establishing fundamental limits, and proposing a near-optimal learning algorithm.

Abstract: We study online cooperative control of a multi-agent system under Byzantine attacks. Namely, an unknown, fixed subset of agents are Byzantine comprised and can stealthily overwrite its own coordinates of the team's planned joint action after observing that plan. The learner observes planned actions, public rewards, and public states, but neither the overwrite nor the executed joint action. Our objective is security: to optimize the team performance against the worst overwrites and achieve the optimal security value. We first show that the attacker's information determines the geometry. An attacker that observes the planned action induces an exact $(s,a)$-rectangular robust Markov decision process (MDP) whose rows are convex hulls of overwrite-induced public-outcome laws, whereas a blind attacker induces an $s$-rectangular model. We then identify the information-theoretic limit of security learning, showing that the security regret decomposes exactly into return regret against the response generating the data and a cumulative response gap $D_K$. Two indistinguishable horizon-one instances force $Ω(K)$ expected security regret while return regret is zero, showing that dependence on $D_K$ is unavoidable. Finally, we develop a stage-tied robust estimation-to-decisions learner and prove a regret bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(H^2S\sqrt{AK}\right)+\mathbb E[D_K]$. Our studies thus provide comprehensive theoretical and algorithmic foundations of reliable multi-agent systems under Byzantine attacks.

</details>


### [67] [Robust Average-Reward Markov Decision Processes: Minimax-Optimal Learning via Plug-in Reductions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06545)
*Yuepeng Yang,Yuxin Chen,Yuejie Chi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes minimax-optimal sample complexity bounds for learning robust policies in average-reward distributionally robust MDPs with TV uncertainty sets, revealing a phase transition at perturbation scale σH₀ between high- and low-tolerance regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While distributionally robust MDPs (DR-MDPs) are well-studied in the discounted setting, the sample complexity of learning robust policies under the average-reward criterion remains unexplored. The average-reward setting introduces unique challenges because the robust Bellman operator involves bias functions, and the perturbation radius σ interacts nontrivially with the nominal span H₀.

Method: The authors consider a generative model with N samples per state-action pair from the nominal kernel, under (s,a)-rectangular total-variation uncertainty sets. They derive matching upper and lower bounds via reduction-based plug-in estimators: a span-informed procedure that uses known H₀ and H_σ to select between nominal and robust reductions with appropriate discount factors, and a span-agnostic procedure that estimates these parameters from data using confidence-bound techniques.

Result: The minimax sample complexity exhibits a phase transition: in the high-tolerance regime (ε ≳ σH₀), the complexity is Θ̃(SA·min{H₀,H_σ}/ε²), matching nominal AMDP rates; in the low-tolerance regime (ε ≲ σH₀), an additional robustness penalty term Θ̃(SA·σH_σ²/ε²) emerges. The perturbation scale σH₀ cleanly separates these regimes.

Conclusion: Robustness incurs no extra sample cost in the high-tolerance regime, while a fundamental penalty appears in the low-tolerance regime. The reduction-based approach, connecting robust AMDPs to discounted robust MDPs via span considerations, is both statistically optimal and practically implementable with data-driven parameter selection.

Abstract: Distributionally robust Markov decision processes provide a principled framework for sequential decision making under model uncertainty. We study how many samples are necessary and sufficient to learn an $\varepsilon$-optimal robust policy under the average-reward criterion. A generative model provides samples from the nominal transition kernel, whereas policy performance is evaluated over $(s,a)$-rectangular total-variation uncertainty sets of radius at most $σ$.
  Let $H_0$ and $H_σ$ denote the nominal and robust optimal bias spans, respectively. We identify $σH_0$ as the perturbation scale separating high- and low-tolerance regimes.
