Our matching upper and lower bounds show that, up to logarithmic factors, the minimax total sample complexity is $$ NSA \asymp \frac{SA}{\varepsilon^2}\begin{cases} \min\{H_0,H_σ\}, & \varepsilon\gtrsimσH_0,\\ \min\{H_0,H_σ\}+σH_σ^2, & \varepsilon\lesssimσH_0. \end{cases} $$ Here $S$ and $A$ are the numbers of states and actions, and $N$ is the number of samples per state-action pair. The sample complexity consists of a linear-span term that resembles the nominal AMDP results and a robustness-specific term that appears only in the low-tolerance regime. We attain these rates using reduction-based plug-in procedures that select the reduction---nominal or robust---and its discount factor: a span-informed procedure that makes these choices using known span parameters, and a span-agnostic procedure that calibrates both choices from data.

</details>


### [68] [Newton-Schulz Retraction-Based Inference Enables Hidden Quantum Markov Models to Outperform Classical HMMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06554)
*Ning Ning*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NS-RIS is a scalable algorithm for learning Hidden Quantum Markov Models that uses Newton-Schulz orthogonalization on the Stiefel manifold, achieving the first benchmark evidence where an HQMM significantly outperforms EM-trained HMMs on non-quantum-generated data, with gains of up to 50.6% on synthetic benchmarks and up to 17.9% error reduction on real-world splice classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing HQMM learning methods have failed to consistently outperform EM-trained HMMs on data not generated by quantum processes, limiting their practical utility. There is a need for a scalable, theoretically grounded HQMM learning algorithm that can demonstrate practical advantages over classical HMMs on real-world and synthetic benchmarks.

Method: NS-RIS employs Newton-Schulz retraction-based inference on the Stiefel manifold to learn trace-preserving HQMMs. It computes a polar-factor search direction using Newton-Schulz orthogonalization, maintaining Stiefel-manifold feasibility without expensive matrix decompositions, and comes with a finite-time stationarity guarantee under standard smoothness, stochastic gradient, and finite-accuracy assumptions.

Result: On synthetic HMM-generated data, NS-RIS outperforms EM and COSM by an average of 38.5% (up to 50.6%). On synthetic HQMM data, it improves the test metric over COSM by 18.9% with 12.0% faster runtime. On Splice classification, it reduces mean error by 17.9% (dim=6) and 14.9% (dim=8) relative to COSM, providing the first evidence of HQMM superiority over EM-HMM on non-quantum data.

Conclusion: NS-RIS moves HQMMs beyond theoretical generalizations of HMMs, establishing them as practical and expressive models for scientific sequence data. The results demonstrate that properly trained HQMMs can significantly outperform classical HMMs even on data from non-quantum sources.

Abstract: Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are widely used probabilistic models for discrete sequential data but can be limited when hidden dynamics are complex. Hidden quantum Markov models (HQMMs) generalize HMMs by replacing probability vectors with density matrices and stochastic transitions with quantum operations, enabling richer latent representations. However, existing HQMM learning methods have not consistently outperformed Expectation--Maximization (EM)-trained HMMs on data not generated by quantum processes, limiting their practical applicability. We introduce NS-RIS, Newton--Schulz Retraction-based Inference on the Stiefel manifold, a scalable algorithm for learning trace-preserving HQMMs. NS-RIS uses Newton--Schulz orthogonalization to compute a polar-factor search direction while preserving Stiefel-manifold feasibility, avoiding costly matrix decompositions. We further establish a finite-time stationarity guarantee under standard assumptions on smoothness, stochastic gradients, and finite Newton--Schulz accuracy. Empirically, NS-RIS provides the first benchmark evidence that an HQMM can significantly outperform an EM-trained HMM on data not generated by a quantum model. On synthetic HMM-generated benchmarks, NS-RIS outperforms both EM and the state-of-the-art HQMM method COSM, improving the evaluation metric by an average of 38.5% and by up to 50.6%. On a synthetic HQMM benchmark, it improves the test metric over COSM by 18.9% while reducing runtime by 12.0%. On the real-world Splice classification benchmark, NS-RIS also surpasses both EM and COSM in higher-dimensional latent regimes, reducing mean classification error by 17.9% for latent dimension 6 and 14.9% for latent dimension 8 relative to COSM. These results move HQMMs beyond a theoretical generalization of HMMs and establish them as practical and expressive models for scientific sequence data.

</details>


### [69] [Bootstrap-Conditioned Action Selection with Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06559)
*Devansh Gupta,Shiv Tavker,Dmitry Efimov,Suchitra Sathyanarayana,Gitanjali Bhutani,Boris N. Oreshkin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes BC-ICL, a method that turns pre-trained tabular foundation models with in-context learning into randomized contextual bandit policies via bootstrap resampling, achieving strong early-round regret on standard benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practical deployment of contextual bandits is hindered by sparse, biased interaction data, unreliable uncertainty estimates, and severe cold-start problems. The authors investigate whether pre-trained tabular foundation models with in-context learning can be leveraged as randomized policies to address these challenges.

Method: BC-ICL (Bootstrap-conditioned action selection using ICL) operates by: (1) drawing a bootstrap resample of the interaction history at each round, (2) conditioning a frozen pre-trained ICL model on that resample, (3) scoring all actions, and (4) selecting the action with the highest sampled score. An arm-context conditioning architecture is introduced to share statistical strength across actions and mitigate bootstrap failure modes common in isolated-arm bandits.

Result: The proposed policy demonstrates strong early-round regret and overall regret performance on standard contextual bandit suites, outperforming established baselines under a strict online protocol.

Conclusion: Pre-trained tabular foundation models with ICL, when paired with bootstrap-based randomized action selection and proper arm-context conditioning, can serve as effective online decision-making policies for contextual bandits, particularly in data-scarce and cold-start regimes.

Abstract: Contextual bandits offer a natural framework for sample-efficient personalization, but practical deployment remains difficult under sparse, biased interaction data, unreliable uncertainty estimates, and severe cold starts. We study whether pre-trained tabular foundation models with in-context learning can be turned into randomized policies for online decision making. We propose BC-ICL (Bootstrap-conditioned action selection using ICL), which at each round draws a bootstrap resample of the interaction history, conditions a frozen pre-trained ICL model on that resample, scores all actions, and selects the action with the highest sampled score. We further introduce an arm-context conditioning architecture that promotes shared statistical strength across actions and helps avoid common bootstrap failure modes of isolated-arm bandits. Empirically, this policy delivers strong early-round regret and regret performance on standard contextual bandit suites, outperforming established baselines under a strict online protocol.

</details>


### [70] [Theoretical Foundations of Communication-Efficient, Robust, and Practical Distributed and Federated Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06563)
*Grigory Malinovsky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The thesis addresses seven challenges in federated learning and distributed optimization, introducing novel algorithms—ProxSkip, Variance Reduced ProxSkip, and methods for partial participation, server-side stepsizes, gradient-difference compression, Byzantine-robust clipping, and low-rank adaptation—each supported by theoretical guarantees and experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern large-scale training relies on classical optimization, but the constraints of distributed systems (communication bottlenecks, heterogeneity, partial participation, Byzantine faults) demand revised theoretical foundations. The work aims to bridge theory and practice at key bottlenecks in federated learning.

Method: The thesis develops seven algorithmic and theoretical contributions: (1) ProxSkip for communication acceleration via local steps; (2) Variance Reduced ProxSkip to eliminate stochastic neighborhood error; (3) analysis of local steps under partial client participation; (4) server-side stepsizes with sampling without replacement; (5) gradient-difference compression for Random Reshuffling; (6) gradient-difference clipping for simultaneous Byzantine robustness and partial participation; (7) a theoretical framework for low-rank adaptation using randomized asymmetric chains.

Result: ProxSkip provides the first theoretical proof that local gradient steps accelerate communication. Variance Reduced ProxSkip balances communication and computation while eliminating neighborhood error. Local steps retain communication acceleration under partial participation. Server-side stepsizes and sampling without replacement improve convergence in heterogeneous settings. Gradient-difference compression outperforms gradient compression both theoretically and practically. Gradient-difference clipping achieves Byzantine robustness with partial participation. The randomized asymmetric chain framework yields new insights into fine-tuning large models.

Conclusion: The thesis introduces novel algorithmic frameworks with sharp guarantees under realistic assumptions, supported by numerical experiments, advancing both the theory and practice of federated learning and distributed optimization across seven fundamental challenges.

Abstract: Machine learning and optimization have advanced together, with practical demands motivating new theory and theoretical breakthroughs enabling new applications. Modern large-scale training relies on classical optimization principles, but the constraints of distributed systems require these foundations to be reconsidered. This thesis addresses seven challenges at the intersection of theory and practice, focusing on key bottlenecks in federated learning and distributed optimization. First, we introduce ProxSkip and prove that local gradient steps can accelerate communication, providing a theoretical foundation for this widely used heuristic. Second, we develop Variance Reduced ProxSkip, which eliminates the neighborhood error of stochastic local updates while balancing communication and local computation. Third, we show that local steps retain their communication acceleration under partial client participation. Fourth, we prove that server-side stepsizes and sampling without replacement improve convergence in heterogeneous settings. Fifth, for Random Reshuffling, we demonstrate that compressing gradient differences rather than gradients yields better theoretical and practical performance. Sixth, we establish that Byzantine robustness and partial participation can be achieved simultaneously using gradient-difference clipping. Finally, we develop the first theoretical framework for low-rank adaptation based on randomized asymmetric chains, providing new insights into fine-tuning large models. Across these contributions, we introduce novel algorithmic frameworks, establish sharp guarantees under realistic assumptions, and support the theory with numerical experiments.

</details>


### [71] [Quantization Damage Is Multiplicative, Not Additive](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06564)
*Zekun Wu,Swati Dhiman,Adriano Koshiyama*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Quantization below 4 bits silently damages LLM decisions through "margin shrinkage" — a multiplicative collapse of the decision margin — causing tool-use failures and safety refusal losses that benchmarks miss, with the effect predictable per-model and unrecoverable without adding bits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work models quantization as additive fixed-size noise, implying confident (high-margin) decisions remain safe. The authors challenge this assumption, noting that real-world deployment failures (e.g., agents silently ceasing tool calls, losing safety refusals) occur without benchmark degradation, and no one can predict which specific decisions will flip at a given bit-width.

Method: The authors measure the decision margin (score of chosen option minus score of best alternative) before and after quantization across 16 models from 8 families, three quantization methods, and bit-widths from 8 down to 2 bits. They analyze the relationship between original margin and post-quantization margin, fit a multiplicative shrinkage model, validate it on held-out flips, and test cost-matched repair strategies.

Result: Quantization multiplicatively shrinks the margin: median shrinkage factors are 0.86 at 4-bit, 0.33 at 3-bit, and 0.00 at 2-bit. At 3 bits, tool-calling collapses toward inaction while tool-choice is preserved. Additive-noise models never win on damaged tool/safety decisions. The fitted model predicts flip rates within 1.8 percentage points median error on held-out decisions, with ECE of 0.004 over 131,758 predictions. The multiplicative form is universal across models, but constants are model-specific. No repair method beats simply using one more bit under cost-matched comparison.

Conclusion: Quantization damage is multiplicative margin shrinkage, not additive noise. A small paired margin set per model and bit-width can cheaply estimate which decisions break, and adding one more bit remains the cheapest repair.

Abstract: Quantization is how large language models are actually deployed, and below four bits it is known to hurt. What nobody can say is which of the model's decisions will change at a given bit-width. The damage is silent: a compressed agent stops calling its tools, then loses half its safety refusals, yet benchmark scores barely move. Prior work assumes quantization adds noise of a roughly fixed size, which would make confident decisions safe. We measure the decision itself instead. The margin of a two-way decision is the model's score for the option it picks minus the score of its best alternative; we track it before and after quantization across 16 models from 8 model families, three quantization methods, and bit-widths from 8 down to 2. Quantization does not add fixed-size noise to the margin. It multiplies the margin by a factor that collapses with bit-width (median 0.86 at 4 bits, 0.33 at 3, 0.00 at 2); we call this margin shrinkage. This contraction reduces the protection a large margin affords; the model's own small biases pick the direction of failure: at 3 bits the decision to call a tool collapses toward inaction while the choice of which tool is untouched. In fitted statistical comparison, additive-noise accounts never win on the damaged tool and safety decisions. The fitted relation predicts flip rates within a median of 1.8 percentage points on held-out decisions, though no flip was used in the fit; per decision, the predicted flip probabilities are calibrated uncertainty estimates (expected calibration error 0.004 over 131,758 predictions). The same form holds in every model we measure, but the constants are each model's own and do not transfer. A small paired margin set, measured per model and bit-width, estimates which decisions break without full generative evaluation; under our cost-matched tests, nothing repairs damage more cheaply than one more bit.

</details>


### [72] [CrystalGRPO: Target-Aligned and Coverage-Preserving Reinforcement Learning for Flow-Based Crystal Structure Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06582)
*Kaixiang Su,Hongfei Xue,Qiang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CrystalGRPO is a post-training framework for flow-based CSP models that jointly optimizes coordinate and lattice parameters using both energy and structure-matching rewards, with two variants: one prioritizing single-draw recovery and another preserving Top-N coverage via trajectory regularization and coverage-aware group advantage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing flow-based CSP models are pretrained on objectives that do not directly optimize target crystal structure recovery. RL-based post-training uses energy rewards and coordinate-only policies, but predicted energy fails to identify the reference polymorph, and reward-driven concentration hurts candidate coverage needed for Top-N recovery.

Method: CrystalGRPO extends ODE-to-SDE policy constructions to the joint coordinate-lattice state. It combines MACE-predicted energy with a StructureMatcher-based recovery score. Two modes are introduced: CrystalGRPO-Q prioritizes single-draw recovery; CrystalGRPO-C uses full-trajectory reference regularization and a coverage-aware group advantage to improve finite-budget Top-N recovery.

Result: On MP-20 and MPTS-52 with PXRDGen and OMatG backbones, both CrystalGRPO variants reduce 1- and 20-sample RMSE vs. coordinate-only RL across all four backbone-dataset settings. CrystalGRPO-Q consistently improves Top-1, while CrystalGRPO-C achieves higher Top-20 in all settings.

Conclusion: Joint coordinate-lattice RL post-training with hybrid energy-plus-structure rewards effectively improves both single-draw accuracy and Top-N recovery in flow-based CSP, with the coverage-aware variant being essential for preserving diversity under finite sampling budgets.

Abstract: Flow-based generative models can efficiently produce candidate structures for crystal structure prediction (CSP), but their pretrained objectives do not directly optimize downstream target recovery. Reinforcement-learning post-training offers a flexible solution, yet existing approaches rely primarily on energy rewards and coordinate-only stochastic policies. Predicted energy does not identify the reference polymorph, while reward-driven concentration can reduce the candidate coverage required for Top-N recovery. We introduce CrystalGRPO, a CSP-aligned post-training framework that extends existing ODE-to-SDE policy constructions to the joint coordinate--lattice state. CrystalGRPO combines MACE-predicted energy with a StructureMatcher-based recovery score and provides two operating modes: CrystalGRPO-Q, which prioritizes single-draw recovery, and CrystalGRPO-C, which combines full-trajectory reference regularization with a coverage-aware group advantage to preserve finite-budget target recovery. Across MP-20 and MPTS-52 with PXRDGen and OMatG backbones, both variants reduce one- and twenty-sample RMSE relative to coordinate-only reinforcement in all four backbone--dataset settings. CrystalGRPO-Q consistently improves Top-1, whereas CrystalGRPO-C achieves a higher Top-20 across all settings.

</details>


### [73] [Flowing Through States: Neural ODE Regularization for Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06595)
*Mohamed Ghanem,Bernd Finkbeiner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a neural ODE-based regularization method that explicitly aligns latent representations with environment dynamics in sequential decision-making, yielding significant performance gains in Actor-Critic RL algorithms on Atari and gridworld benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In standard neural network agents for sequential decision-making, latent state transitions are left implicit, creating a potential misalignment between how semantic states evolve under environment dynamics and how their latent representations evolve. The authors aim to resolve this by explicitly modeling latent dynamics.

Method: The authors draw an analogy between MDP trajectories and ODE flows (both satisfy that the current state fully determines successors) and introduce a neural ODE-based regularization term that enforces latent embeddings to follow consistent ODE-governed flows. This regularizer is integrated into Actor-Critic algorithms (A2C, PPO).

Result: The method achieves major performance gains on standard Atari benchmarks using A2C and on gridworld environments using PPO.

Conclusion: Explicitly aligning latent representation learning with environment dynamics via neural ODE regularization is broadly applicable and empirically beneficial for deep reinforcement learning agents.

Abstract: Neural networks applied to sequential decision-making tasks typically rely on latent representations of environment states. While environment dynamics dictate how semantic states evolve, the corresponding latent transitions are usually left implicit, creating a potential misalignment between the two. We propose to model latent dynamics explicitly by drawing an analogy between Markov decision process (MDP) trajectories and ordinary differential equation (ODE) flows: in both cases, the current state fully determines its successors. Building on this view, we introduce a neural ODE-based regularization method that enforces latent embeddings to follow consistent ODE flows, thereby aligning representation learning with environment dynamics. Although broadly applicable to deep learning agents, we demonstrate its effectiveness in reinforcement learning by integrating it into Actor-Critic algorithms. Our approach yields major performance gains across various standard Atari benchmarks for A2C and gridworld environments for PPO.

</details>


### [74] [Retrofitting Linear Attention into Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06628)
*Jinha Kim,Younghun Roh,Jaeyeon Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLaDA-Hybrid accelerates diffusion language model inference by replacing softmax attention over prior blocks with linear attention, achieving up to 1.7× throughput gains with minimal post-training (≈60 hours) and negligible quality loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) use blockwise semi-autoregressive decoding where each denoising step must attend to all previous blocks, incurring expensive prefix-attention costs that bottleneck inference speed despite KV caching.

Method: Introduces block-hybrid attention: exact softmax attention is retained within the active denoising block, while linear attention is applied to all previous blocks. This is retrofitted into LLaDA 2.1 (16B) by converting 6 of 20 attention layers using a LoLCAT-inspired approach, requiring only ~60 hours of post-training.

Result: LLaDA-Hybrid preserves benchmark performance: HumanEval (72.0% vs 75.6%), MBPP+ (63.0% vs 57.7%), CMATH (86.7% vs 88.3%). With a Triton implementation, it achieves up to 1.7× higher decoding throughput and supports more concurrent requests before memory exhaustion.

Conclusion: Pretrained dLLMs can be efficiently linearized for faster inference via hybrid attention with minimal post-training, offering a practical path to accelerate diffusion-based text generation without sacrificing quality.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer a promising alternative to autoregressive models by accelerating inference through parallel decoding. Recent dLLMs commonly use blockwise semi-autoregressive decoding, generating blocks autoregressively while denoising tokens within each active block in parallel. However, despite KV caching, each denoising step still attends to all previous blocks, repeatedly incurring prefix-attention cost. Motivated by this bottleneck, we ask whether dLLM inference can be further accelerated by linearizing attention over previous blocks. We introduce block-hybrid attention, which retains exact softmax attention within the active denoising block while applying linear attention over previous blocks. We show that this hybrid attention can be retrofitted into a pretrained dLLM with minimal post-training: LLaDA-Hybrid replaces 6 of the 20 attention layers in LLaDA~2.1, a 16B open-source dLLM, largely following LoLCAT (Zhang et al, 2024). The conversion takes only approximately 60 hours while preserving benchmark performance: 72.0% vs. 75.6% on HumanEval, 63.0% vs. 57.7% on MBPP+, and 86.7% vs. 88.3% on CMATH. With a Triton implementation, LLaDA-Hybrid achieves up to $1.7\times$ higher decoding throughput and supports more concurrent requests before exhausting memory, showing that pretrained dLLMs can be efficiently linearized for faster inference. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Diuven/LLaDA-Hybrid.

</details>


### [75] [The Sparsity Whisperer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06630)
*Linghao Kong,Inimai Subramanian,Micah Adler,Dan Alistarh,Dan Gutfreund,Nir Shavit*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes difference-informed pruning methods (Wisp, Wisp+, Whisper) for LLMs that preserve not just activations but the differences between outputs, showing consistent improvements over baselines like Wanda and SparseGPT across various model scales and sparsity settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing pruning criteria focus on preserving large activations (e.g., Wanda) or reconstructing layer outputs (e.g., SparseGPT). The authors argue this overlooks a critical function of sparsity-sensitive neurons in MLP up/gate projections: separating similar inputs into dissimilar outputs. Effective pruning should therefore preserve output differences, not just activations.

Method: They introduce three difference-informed pruning methods: (1) Wisp — a first-order, update-free method scoring weights via input-difference norms; (2) Wisp+ — refines Wisp neuron-wise using the input pairs each neuron separates most strongly; (3) Whisper — a second-order method using a lightly regularized difference Hessian as its reconstruction objective. These criteria can also augment existing techniques like RIA and ALPS.

Result: Across Llama 2 and 3.1 models (7B–405B), Whisper consistently outperforms reconstruction baselines; Wisp/Wisp+ outperform activation-aware baselines, especially in constrained settings. Improvements extend to structured sparsity, downstream tasks, and other model families. Augmenting stronger methods (RIA, ALPS) with difference-informed criteria yields further gains at negligible cost.

Conclusion: Preserving output differences is a broadly useful and composable signal for post-training LLM sparsification, shifting the accuracy–runtime frontier outward with minimal additional overhead.

Abstract: Pruning reduces the inference cost of large language models, but existing criteria primarily preserve large activations or reconstruct layer outputs. We argue that this overlooks a key computation performed by particularly sparsity-sensitive neurons in the MLP up and gate projections: separating similar inputs into dissimilar outputs. This suggests that effective pruning should preserve not only activations, but also the differences between outputs more broadly. We introduce a family of difference-informed pruning methods built upon this principle. Wisp is a first-order, update-free method that scores weights using input-difference norms, and Wisp+ refines this score neuronwise using the input pairs each neuron separates most strongly. Finally, Whisper is a second-order method that uses a lightly regularized difference Hessian as its reconstruction objective. Across Llama 2 and 3.1 models from 7B to 405B parameters, our second-order variant consistently improves over strong reconstruction-based baselines, while our update-free variants improve over activation-aware baselines, especially in constrained settings. The improvements over Wanda and SparseGPT extend to structured sparsity, downstream evaluations, and other model families. Augmenting stronger techniques such as RIA and ALPS with our difference-informed criteria yields further improvements, shifting the overall accuracy-runtime frontier outward at negligible additional cost. These results suggest that preserving output differences is a broadly useful and composable signal for post-training LLM sparsification.

</details>


### [76] [Cryptanalytic Extraction of Isolated Bias-Free GLU Feed-Forward Blocks by Antipodal Separation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06631)
*Chunhui Shi,Xinwen Fu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a cryptanalytic method to recover weights from bias-free Gated Linear Unit (GLU) feed-forward blocks in language models using forward queries only. By exploiting finite-difference curvature and paired observations at x and -x, the attack achieves sub-percent median validation error on high-precision targets. However, the method requires isolated block access and does not constitute an end-to-end model extraction attack.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cryptanalytic extraction methods handle ReLU networks, componentwise activations (GELU/SiLU), and final projection matrices, but fail to cover the bias-free GLU feed-forward blocks prevalent in modern LLMs. GLU blocks have a two-branch structure (gated linear projection multiplied by a value projection) absent from previously addressed architectures, motivating a dedicated extraction primitive.

Method: A multi-stage, forward-query-only recovery primitive: (1) finite-difference curvature is used to propose candidates for gate-direction vectors; (2) paired observations at inputs x and -x are leveraged to disentangle gate magnitude, orientation, and the coupling between the gate and value branches. This recovers the two weight matrices of an isolated bias-free GLU block.

Result: Across high-precision targets: six Qwen layers, an 8,192-unit Llama subproblem, and a full-dimensional Gemma block all achieve sub-percent median validation error. Four finite-precision configurations stay below 5% median error, though none perfectly reproduces every stored weight. End-to-end extraction from final model outputs remains unsolved.

Conclusion: Bias-free GLU blocks are cryptanalytically extractable via forward queries alone when isolated block responses are available. The attack achieves high fidelity in the isolated setting, but deriving the required internal responses from black-box model outputs is an open problem, so this does not yet represent a practical end-to-end model-API attack.

Abstract: Cryptanalytic extraction has been demonstrated for ReLU networks, for networks using componentwise activations such as GELU or SiLU, and for a Transformer's final projection matrix. These methods do not recover the bias-free Gated Linear Unit (GLU) feed-forward blocks used in many modern language models. Such a block multiplies an activated linear projection by a second learned linear projection within each hidden unit, a two-branch structure absent from the network classes and final-layer setting addressed by those methods. We give a constructive, multi-stage forward-query recovery primitive for isolated bias-free GLU blocks. Finite-difference curvature supplies gate-direction candidates, and paired observations at x and -x separate gate magnitude, orientation, and value-branch coupling. Across high-precision targets, six Qwen layers, an 8,192-unit Llama subproblem, and a full-dimensional Gemma block all reach sub-percent median validation error. Four finite-precision configurations remain below 5 percent median error, but none reproduces every stored weight. These isolated-block experiments are not an end-to-end model-API attack: deriving the required internal block responses from final model outputs remains unsolved.

</details>


### [77] [Bypassing Krum: Selection-Aware Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06637)
*Srinivasan Subramanian,Md. Abdullah Al Hafiz Khan,Kazi Aminul Islam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Krum-Proxy, a two-stage optimization attack that actively crafts malicious updates to infiltrate the dense core of benign distributions, bypassing distance-based Byzantine-robust aggregation rules like Krum and Multi-Krum in federated learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing distance-based robust aggregation methods (e.g., Krum, Multi-Krum) assume benign updates form a compact cluster and select updates closest to the majority. However, adaptive adversaries can exploit these geometric assumptions. The authors aim to expose this vulnerability by designing a selection-aware attack that can consistently bypass such defenses.

Method: The Krum-Proxy attack uses a two-stage optimization: (1) separating task-specific attack objectives from geometry-aware refinement, and (2) employing a nearest-neighbor proxy, stochastic reference modeling, and anchor-guided alignment to craft adversarial updates. A projection mechanism constrains updates within realistic norm and variance bounds to maintain stealth.

Result: Experiments on standard federated learning benchmarks demonstrate that Krum-Proxy achieves higher attack success rates while preserving clean accuracy, revealing the vulnerability of distance-based aggregation to selection-aware adversaries.

Conclusion: Distance-based Byzantine-robust aggregation methods are fundamentally vulnerable to selection-aware attacks like Krum-Proxy, which actively optimize malicious updates to be favored during the aggregation process rather than relying on naive perturbation strategies.

Abstract: Robust aggregation methods are widely used in federated learning to mitigate the impact of adversarial client behavior. Distance-based aggregation rules, such as Krum and Multi-Krum, select updates that are closest to the majority under the assumption that benign updates form a compact cluster. However, these methods rely on geometric properties that can be exploited by adaptive adversaries. We introduce the Krum-Proxy attack, a selection-aware backdoor injection strategy that consistently bypasses Byzantine-robust aggregation. Rather than relying on naive scaling or constraining, our method actively optimizes malicious updates to infiltrate the dense core of the benign distribution. The proposed method constructs adversarial updates that are not only similar to benign updates but are also optimized to lie in regions of the update space that are favored during aggregation. This is achieved through a two-stage optimization procedure that separates task-specific attack objectives from geometry-aware refinement, using a nearest-neighbor proxy, stochastic reference modeling, and anchor-guided alignment. To maintain stealth, we introduce a projection mechanism that constrains adversarial updates within realistic norm and variance bounds. Experiments on standard federated learning benchmarks show that Krum-Proxy achieves higher attack success while preserving clean accuracy, highlighting the vulnerability of distance-based aggregation to selection-aware adversaries.

</details>


### [78] [Dirichlet Follow-the-Leader Closes the Gap in Simultaneous Multiclass U-Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06656)
*Pahan Dewasurendra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A one-line forecaster—drawing the next prediction from Dir(c_{t-1}) after observing class counts—closes dimension gaps in both worst-case and smooth proper loss regimes. It achieves optimal regret rates: 4√(S_T T) ≤ 4√(KT) for bounded proper losses and (5/2)β(1+log T) for β-smooth proper losses, using a telescoping Jensen gap identity and a one-count likelihood ratio stability bound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work using self-concordant perturbation achieved roughly K^{5/4}√T worst-case regret and an additional β√K log K for β-smooth losses, leaving dimension-dependent gaps relative to known lower bounds. The goal is a single algorithm attaining the optimal regret rate for every bounded proper loss while simultaneously adapting to every smooth proper loss, without dimension gaps.

Method: The forecaster is a Dirichlet perturbation (Bayesian bootstrap): at round t, after observing cumulative class counts c_{t-1}, draw the next prediction from Dir(c_{t-1}) restricted to the face of classes seen so far. The core analytical tool is an exact identity: the expectation of any bounded proper loss under Dir(α) equals a discrete derivative of its Dirichlet-averaged Bayes risk. This makes the Be-The-Perturbed-Leader (BTPL) term telescope into a nonpositive Jensen gap. Stability is bounded via a one-count likelihood ratio, yielding an inverse square root dependence on the class count.

Result: The single, horizon-free algorithm satisfies sup_ℓ E[Reg_ℓ] ≤ 4√(S_T T) ≤ 4√(K T) for bounded proper losses, and E[Reg_ℓ] ≤ (5/2)β(1+log T) for every β-smooth proper loss. Here S_T is the number of observed classes. Both rates match known lower bounds in their nontrivial regimes. The proof handles nondifferentiable losses and changes of the active simplex face.

Conclusion: The Dirichlet-perturbed forecaster simultaneously achieves optimal worst-case and smooth-loss regret rates, closing both gaps left by prior self-concordant perturbation methods. The simplicity of the algorithm (a one-line Bayesian bootstrap) combined with the exact identity linking Dirichlet-averaged loss to discrete Bayes risk derivatives provides an elegant, tight analysis that extends to nondifferentiable losses and evolving simplex faces.

Abstract: Can one forecaster attain the optimal regret rate for every bounded proper loss and also adapt to every smooth proper loss? Recent work answered this up to a dimension gap. Its self-concordant perturbation gives roughly $K^{5/4}\sqrt{T}$ worst-case regret and incurs an additional $β\sqrt{K}\log K$ for $β$-smooth losses. We close both gaps with a one-line forecaster. After observing class counts $c_{t-1}$, draw the next prediction from $\operatorname{Dir}(c_{t-1})$, on the face of classes seen so far. This is a fresh Bayesian bootstrap of the outcomes. The analysis rests on an exact identity: averaging any bounded proper loss under $\operatorname{Dir}(α)$ equals a discrete derivative of its Dirichlet-averaged Bayes risk. The identity makes the be-the-perturbed-leader term telescope to a nonpositive Jensen gap. A one-count likelihood ratio then bounds stability by the inverse square root of that class's count. The resulting single, horizon-free algorithm satisfies $\sup_{\ell}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Reg}_{\ell}\leq 4\sqrt{S_T T}\leq 4\sqrt{K T}$ and $\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Reg}_{\ell}\leq \frac{5}{2}β(1+\log T)$ for every $β$-smooth proper loss. Here $S_T$ is the number of observed classes. Known lower bounds show that both rates are optimal in their nontrivial regimes. The proof covers nondifferentiable losses and changes of the active simplex face.

</details>


### [79] [EpiFlow: A framework for improving the utility of wastewater signals for disease forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06671)
*Aniruddha Adiga,Jingyuan Chou,Gursharn Kaur,Andrew Warren,Srinivasan Venkatramanan,Baltazar Espinoza,Bryan Lewis,Justin Crow,Alexandra Lorentz,Rekha Singh,Madhav Marathe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Wastewater viral load data improves real-time COVID-19 hospital admission forecasting, yielding a 20 percentage point gain in forecast coverage, even under low prevalence and reporting delays.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional disease surveillance indicators degrade during low-prevalence periods due to reporting fatigue, yet hospital burden can fluctuate substantially. The authors investigate whether wastewater viral loads can serve as a robust leading indicator to improve real-time infectious disease forecasts when conventional signals become unreliable.

Method: The authors apply entropy measures to assess WVL predictability, use causality tests to capture temporal dynamics and leading-indicator behavior between WVL and burden indicators, and develop a time-varying forecasting model that adapts to the evolving WVL-burden relationship. They also simulate the impact of WVL reporting delays. The approach is validated by forecasting COVID-19 hospital admissions across Virginia and its health regions.

Result: Incorporating WVL improves forecast accuracy over baseline models, especially during critical epidemic phases, and yields a 20 percentage point improvement in forecast coverage. WVL signals remain beneficial even under low disease prevalence or delayed reporting.

Conclusion: Wastewater-based surveillance provides actionable leading-indicator signals that enhance infectious disease forecasting. The proposed principled framework for processing and integrating WVL data can strengthen real-time outbreak response, particularly when conventional surveillance data deteriorate.

Abstract: Wastewater-based surveillance is an effective tool for disease monitoring and can provide early warning of outbreaks. Although wastewater viral loads (WVL) correlate with disease burden, their utility for improving real-time forecasting remains under investigation. During the early phases of an epidemic, many indicators can effectively monitor disease spread, but their reliability may decline because of reporting fatigue and low prevalence. Hospital burden can vary substantially even during low-prevalence periods, making accurate forecasting of burden indicators essential for minimizing disease impacts.
  In this paper, we present principled approaches for processing wastewater data, characterizing its relationship with burden indicators, and generating real-time forecasts. We assess the predictability of WVL using entropy measures. We analyze the relationship between WVL and burden indicators using causality tests that capture temporal dynamics and the leading-indicator behavior of WVL. We incorporate these insights into a time-varying forecasting model that accounts for the evolving relationship between the signals. We also evaluate the effects of delays in WVL reporting through simulations.
  We test the utility of our methods by forecasting COVID-19 hospital admissions across Virginia and its health regions during periods of varying disease prevalence. Incorporating WVL improves forecast accuracy relative to baseline models, particularly during critical epidemic phases, and results in a 20 percentage point improvement in forecast coverage. Our results demonstrate that WVL signals can improve infectious disease forecasting even under conditions of low prevalence or delayed reporting.

</details>


### [80] [A Transferable Autologistic Model for Predicting Rare Failures in Heterogeneous Equipment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06695)
*Islam Benamirouche,Djemel Ziou,Feriel Fass*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A probabilistic model for predictive maintenance that transfers failure-pattern knowledge across heterogeneous equipment within a family, producing calibrated failure-probability estimates despite varying sensor configurations and rare failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predictive maintenance faces three core challenges: rare failure events, heterogeneous sensor configurations across equipment of the same family, and the need for anticipatory (not diagnostic) failure prediction. Existing approaches struggle when these conditions co-occur.

Method: A common-to-target probabilistic model that learns shared failure-related patterns across a family of heterogeneous equipment and then adapts parsimoniously to a specific target unit. The model explicitly incorporates sensor heterogeneity, operating context, and degradation dynamics to generate calibrated failure-probability estimates.

Result: Performance was evaluated on a synthetic refrigerator dataset with 27 simulated units featuring varying sensor configurations, operating conditions, and failure types, providing a controlled benchmark for assessing the model's anticipatory capability.

Conclusion: [The abstract is truncated — a definitive conclusion cannot be extracted from the incomplete provided text.]

Abstract: Predicting failures before they occur remains a major challenge in predictive maintenance, particularly when failures are rare, when equipment of the same family differ in sensor configurations, and when the goal is anticipation rather than diagnosis of an already observed fault. This paper proposes a common-to-target probabilistic model that learns shared failure-related patterns across a family of heterogeneous equipment and adapts parsimoniously to target equipment. The model explicitly accounts for sensor heterogeneity, operating context, and degradation dynamics to produce calibrated failureprobability estimates suitable for maintenance planning. Its performance is evaluated on a synthetic refrigerator dataset comprising 27 simulated refrigerators with varying sensor configurations, operating conditions, and failure types, providing a controlle

</details>


### [81] [Dueling World Models: Advantage-Style Action Channels for Common-Mode Distractor Rejection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06706)
*Jiazhuo Li,Yiming Fei,Zhiruo Zhou,Heikichi Hayashi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: World models suffer from "action-blindness" when distractors dominate predictions. The authors propose subtracting the mean prediction across actions at readout time—a dueling-inspired cancellation—to isolate the agent's controllable effect, requiring no extra loss, reward, or reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent world models trained to predict future states become "action-blind" in scenes with uncontrolled motion: different actions yield indistinguishable predictions because action-independent variation (distractors) dominates the loss. Existing solutions add reconstruction, reward, or auxiliary objectives, introducing complexity and assumptions. A minimal, assumption-free solution is needed.

Method: The method borrows the dueling decomposition from reinforcement learning: for any action-conditioned prediction, subtract the empirical mean prediction over all actions. This cancels the action-independent component (where distractors reside), isolating a residual that reflects only the action's unique effect. The subtraction occurs solely at readout time, requires no retraining or auxiliary losses, and applies to any frozen pretrained model. For discrete action sets the cancellation is exact; for continuous actions, sampling is used. Theoretical finite-sample guarantees are provided.

Result: The isolated channel successfully recovers the agent's controllable effect across gridworld, synthetic generators, distracting continuous control, and Atari benchmarks—cases where entangled predictors fail. Nuisance leakage is indistinguishable from zero. Applied post hoc, it surfaces an action channel in off-the-shelf models missed by raw readouts and enables goal-reaching control in gridworld.

Conclusion: A simple mean-subtraction at readout time suffices to cure action-blindness in world models, without reward, reconstruction, or auxiliary losses. The cancellation is exact in finite samples. Limitations include distractors whose motion tracks the action, discussed in the appendix.

Abstract: Latent world models plan by predicting future states from an action, but when a scene contains motion the agent does not control, they quietly go action-blind: predictions for different actions become indistinguishable even as the training loss keeps improving. Existing remedies suppress this distraction with reconstruction, task reward, or auxiliary objectives, each adding machinery or assumptions. We show that a minimal alternative suffices, borrowed from the dueling decomposition of value into a state baseline and an action advantage: in latent dynamics, subtracting a prediction's mean effect over actions cancels whatever the actions share--the action-independent variation where distractors live--leaving a clean, controllable channel, with no reward, no reconstruction, and no distractor-specific auxiliary loss. Because this is only a subtraction at readout time, it applies unchanged to any action-conditioned world model, including frozen pretrained ones. Across a gridworld, synthetic generators with known factors, distracting continuous control, and natural-pixel Atari, the isolated channel recovers the agent's own effect where entangled predictors fail, with nuisance leak indistinguishable from zero; applied post hoc it surfaces an action channel in off-the-shelf models that their raw readouts miss, and it converts into goal-reaching control in the gridworld. We prove the cancellation is exact in finite samples for both discrete and sampled action sets, and we state its measured boundary--distractors whose motion tracks the action--together with the remaining limitations in the appendix.

</details>


### [82] [Multi-Level Modeling of Large Language Model Inference Latency and Energy via Hybrid Analytical--Machine-Learning Predictors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06723)
*Saeid Shokoufa,Mohammad Erfan Sadeghi,Mehdi Kamal,Massoud Pedram*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HYMELL is a hybrid three-level framework that combines analytical modeling with machine learning to accurately estimate LLM inference latency and energy, achieving <5% error for LLaMA 3 8B on an NVIDIA H100 GPU while supporting dense/MoE architectures and MHA/GQA attention mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid scaling of LLMs has dramatically increased computational costs, energy consumption, and inference latency. Accurate estimation of these metrics is critical for sustainable AI deployment and hardware-aware design, yet existing approaches struggle to balance accuracy with generality across diverse architectures and execution phases.

Method: HYMELL employs a three-level hierarchical approach: (1) analytical modeling of primitive operations, (2) ML-based prediction of higher-level components, and (3) an end-to-end model capturing system-level overheads. The framework covers both prefill and decode phases and supports diverse architectures including dense/MoE FFNs and MHA/GQA attention.

Result: Evaluated on an NVIDIA H100 GPU, HYMELL achieves high predictive accuracy, with less than 5% error for LLaMA 3 8B across both prefill and decode phases. It enables fast, hardware-free design space exploration using only architectural parameters.

Conclusion: HYMELL demonstrates that a hybrid analytical-ML approach can deliver accurate, generalizable LLM inference cost estimation, facilitating sustainable, energy-efficient model design and deployment without requiring physical hardware benchmarking.

Abstract: The rapid scaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly increased computational cost, energy consumption, and inference latency, making accurate estimation essential for sustainable artificial intelligence deployment and hardware-aware design. In this work, we introduce Hybrid Modeling for Energy and Latency of LLMs (HYMELL), a hybrid three-level framework for estimating LLM inference latency and energy by combining analytical modeling with machine learning (ML). HYMELL models LLM execution through a three-level hierarchy: analytical estimation of primitive operations, ML prediction of higher-level components, and an end-to-end model that captures system-level overheads across both prefill and decode phases. The framework supports diverse architectures, including dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) feed-forward networks (FFNs), as well as multi-head attention (MHA) and grouped-query attention (GQA) mechanisms. Evaluated on an NVIDIA H100 graphics processing unit (GPU), HYMELL achieves high predictive accuracy; notably, for LLaMA 3 8B, it attains less than 5% error for both prefill and decode phases. By predicting execution costs directly from architectural parameters, it enables fast, hardware-free design space exploration and energy-efficient optimization.

</details>


### [83] [Solver-Guided Reasoning for Mixed-Equilibrium Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06741)
*Han Wang,Philippe Beardsell,Boning Li,Aaron Sasmita,Shuai Li,Hongyuan Zha,Baoxiang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLMs struggle with equilibrium reasoning in complex games because human data biases toward pure strategies. The authors propose Mixed-Strategy Decision Tree (MDT), which distills solver-generated equilibrium outputs into interpretable strategic rules. Using 250M+ solver decisions from No-Limit Texas Hold'em, MDT reduces ℓ₁ distance to equilibrium by 52.6% across 8 LLM configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human gameplay data is suboptimal for training LLMs in game-theoretic reasoning because humans rely on intuition and heuristics, deviating from equilibrium—especially in mixed-strategy settings where human behavior is heavily biased toward pure strategies. Conditioning on such data yields weak strategies. The authors seek to instead elicit equilibrium play from LLMs using solver-generated outputs.

Method: The authors propose Mixed-Strategy Decision Tree (MDT), which translates the implicit optimality of game-theoretic equilibrium solutions into sparse, interpretable strategic rules understandable by both humans and LLMs. They query a solver oracle for over 250 million mixed-strategy decisions in No-Limit Texas Hold'em, using solver output rather than human annotation to enable generalization to arbitrary new states and continuations. Ablation studies include a Route-only test (measuring contribution of shadow-based contrast), River-endgame experiments, and Liar's Dice for evaluating strategic fidelity and portability beyond NLH.

Result: MDT, combined with other techniques, reduces the ℓ₁ distance to equilibrium by 52.6% across 8 different LLM configurations. The Route-only ablation isolates the incremental contribution of shadow-based contrast. River-endgame and Liar's Dice experiments confirm strategic fidelity and demonstrate portability beyond the original No-Limit Hold'em communication setting.

Conclusion: Solver-generated equilibrium data, structured through MDT into interpretable strategic rules, significantly improves LLM equilibrium reasoning in complex imperfect-information games compared to human-data conditioning. The approach generalizes across models and game settings.

Abstract: Reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often grounded in human text, human demonstrations, and human-generated rationales. For equilibrium reasoning in complex games, however, relying on human data can be suboptimal. In fact, human play is often guided by intuition and heuristics and can deviate substantially from game equilibrium. This discrepancy is amplified in games with mixed-strategy equilibria, where human data is heavily biased toward pure strategies. Consequently, conditioning LLMs on this data yields weak game strategies. To grant LLMs the reasoning capacity in games, in this work, we study how to elicit equilibrium play using solver output. We propose Mixed-Strategy Decision Tree (MDT), which articulates the silent optimality of the equilibrium into sparse strategic rules that both humans and LLMs could understand. Using solver output rather than human annotation allows us to extend the input to arbitrarily new states and continuations. We instantiate this study on No-Limit Texas Hold'em by querying a solver oracle for over \textbf{250 million mixed-strategy decisions}; MDT together with other techniques \textbf{reduces the $\ell_1$ distance to the equilibrium by $52.6\%$} across $8$ different LLM configurations. A Route-only ablation tests the incremental contribution of the shadow-based contrast, while complete River-endgame and Liar's Dice experiments evaluate strategic fidelity and portability beyond the original NLH communication setting.

</details>


### [84] [KReF: Training-Free Retrieval for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting and Predictive Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06748)
*Yang Zhang,Rui Su*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KReF is a training-free retrieval framework for probabilistic long-term time-series forecasting that uses historical lookback-future pairs as an empirical predictive distribution, achieving state-of-the-art CRPS and interval scores without gradient-based fitting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing probabilistic LTSF methods require trained models. Training-free conformal methods only provide intervals (not full distributions) around a point forecaster, and sequential variants suffer from delayed feedback at long horizons. The authors identify a gap for training-free methods that natively represent complete predictive distributions.

Method: KReF preprocesses data (robust scaling), embeds lookback windows using either handcrafted statistics or frozen random Fourier features, retrieves similar historical lookback-future pairs via similarity weighting, and uses these weights to define predictive masses, quantiles, CRPS, and a weighted-mean point forecast. It also applies a probability-integral-transform (PIT) map on the query lookback and uses validation-selected expansion/shrinkage rates to adapt interval boundaries.

Result: Across 6 LTSF benchmarks and 4 horizons, KReF achieves the lowest CRPS in all 12 dataset-embedding settings and the lowest IS90 in 9 settings. Its point forecasts match or surpass trained baselines on 2 of 6 datasets. An archive-oracle analysis reveals substantial headroom under finer horizon- and channel-wise routing.

Conclusion: Retrieval-based methods represent a useful and underexplored inductive bias for long-term time-series forecasting, offering competitive performance without gradient-based training while natively providing full predictive distributions.

Abstract: Probabilistic long-term time-series forecasting commonly relies on trained models. Training-free conformal methods typically construct intervals around a pre-existing point forecaster and do not natively represent a complete predictive distribution; sequential variants additionally suffer from increasingly delayed feedback at long horizons. We propose KReF, a training-free retrieval framework that treats retrieved historical futures as a querylocal empirical predictive distribution. After robust preprocessing, KReF embeds each lookback using handcrafted statistics or frozen random Fourier features and retrieves similar historical lookback-future pairs. Their similarity weights directly define predictive masses, quantiles, CRPS, and a weighted-mean point forecast. KReF further uses the observed query lookback to construct a probability-integral-transform map and applies validation-selected expansion and shrinkage rates to adapt interval boundaries. Across six LTSF benchmarks and four horizons, KReF obtains the lowest CRPS in all 12 dataset-embedding settings and the lowest IS90 in 9 settings. Without gradient-based fitting, its point forecasts also match or surpass trained baselines on two of six datasets. An archive-oracle analysis further reveals substantial headroom under finer horizon- and channel-wise routing. These results establish retrieval as a useful and underexplored inductive bias for LTSF.

</details>


### [85] [Sub-Quadratic Bisimulation Metrics via Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Coverage-Augmented Guarantees and Computable Two-Sided Certificates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06762)
*Ibne Farabi Shihab,Joyanta Jyoti Mondal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a sub-quadratic algorithm for computing bisimulation metrics in MDPs by using approximate nearest-neighbor indexing to selectively update only a subset of state pairs, with certificate-carrying lower/upper bounds that enclose the exact metric and provide guarantees on recovery of exact clustering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Exact bisimulation metric computation via the Wasserstein fixed-point operator requires updates on all O(|S|²) state pairs, making it prohibitively expensive. The authors aim to reduce this quadratic cost for MDPs with bounded transition support by leveraging low-dimensional state embeddings to guide selective, sparse updates while retaining formal correctness guarantees.

Method: The method uses an approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) index over state embeddings to select which pairs receive exact restricted-operator updates each sweep. Monotone lower and upper bound sequences (runs) are maintained for all pairs, sandwiching the true metric. The algorithm returns the observable sandwich width as a certificate; agreement between induced lower and upper clusterings certifies exact recovery of the covered aggregation. Theoretical analysis yields a coverage-augmented anytime bound: limiting error ≤ max(ρ, ε_op/(1−γ)), where ρ depends on the unknown exact metric. Lower bounds are also proved: a reward-oblivious lower bound showing sub-quadratic ANN coverage cannot eliminate the coverage term, and an adaptive lower bound requiring Ω(|S|) pair evaluations.

Result: Exact-operator experiments confirm identity and enclosure in every seeded run. Timing experiments demonstrate quadratic vs. sub-quadratic scaling under both cheap and full Wasserstein backups. On a grouped |S|=64 benchmark, exact restricted refinement reaches the exact-metric skyline once retrieval covers ~50% of pairs, while MICo and DBC baselines remain 22–33× above the skyline. On a 2500-state gridworld, the method improves over a reward-only metric by 28.6% using only 12.8% of one quadratic sweep. The Taxi domain shows the certificate correctly abstaining under an uninformative embedding.

Conclusion: The proposed certificate-carrying, index-guided partial-update scheme successfully achieves sub-quadratic bisimulation metric approximation with formal error bounds and practical utility. The sandwich-width certificate enables reliable abstention when the embedding is insufficiently informative, and the method significantly outperforms learned bisimulation baselines (MICo, DBC) in metric accuracy at comparable or lower computational budgets.

Abstract: Bisimulation metrics quantify behavioral similarity in Markov decision processes, but their Wasserstein fixed-point operator updates every state pair and incurs quadratic pairwise work. We give a certificate-carrying sub-quadratic method for MDPs with bounded transition support and a useful low-dimensional indexing representation: an approximate-nearest-neighbor index selects the pairs updated by the exact restricted operator, while monotone lower and upper runs enclose the exact metric at every sweep. The main analytical result is a coverage-augmented anytime bound: local index quality alone cannot control global error, because uncovered pairs retain their initialization gap. The limiting error is at most $\max(ρ,\eop/(1-γ))$, and with exact covered backups the lower arm satisfies $\|\dann-d\|_\infty=ρ$. Because $ρ$ depends on the unknown exact metric, the algorithm returns the observable sandwich width instead; agreement of the induced lower and upper clusterings certifies exact recovery of the covered aggregation. A reward-oblivious lower bound shows sub-quadratic index-first coverage cannot remove the coverage term, while a separate adaptive lower bound requires $Ω(|\Scal|)$ pair evaluations. Exact-operator experiments verify the identity and enclosure in every seeded run, and timing experiments recover quadratic versus sub-quadratic scaling under both cheap and full Wasserstein backups. On the grouped $|\Scal|=64$ benchmark, exact restricted refinement reaches the exact-metric skyline once retrieval covers roughly half of all pairs, while independently trained MICo and DBC baselines stay $22$-$33\times$ above that skyline at every retrieval budget. Taxi shows the certificate abstaining under an uninformative embedding, while a $2500$-state gridworld improves over a reward-only metric by $28.6\%$ using $12.8\%$ of one quadratic sweep.

</details>


### [86] [CubicQuant: Parametric Non-Uniform Codebooks for High-Throughput LLM Inference with 1-8-Bit Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06763)
*Xuetian Gao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CubicQuant introduces a parametric non-uniform scalar quantization format using monotonic cubic curves to adapt reconstruction levels within weight groups, achieving lower reconstruction error than uniform integer and finite floating-point formats while maintaining GPU-executable dense integer code streams.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing weight quantization methods face a trade-off: uniform integer quantization is hardware-efficient but rigid; low-bit floating-point has fixed structure; learned codebooks are flexible but incur irregular decoding overhead and extra metadata. A format is needed that combines adaptive non-uniform reconstruction with regular, dense integer encoding for efficient GPU inference.

Method: CubicQuant uses a monotonic cubic curve parameterized by two shape parameters and one scale to map uniformly-spaced integer magnitude codes to non-uniform reconstruction levels. The format supports 1–8 bit payloads, subsumes symmetric uniform quantization as a special case, and has effective bit width B + 64/G. The authors derive population distortion analytically under Uniform, Gaussian, and Laplace distributions, formulate continuous and Dynamic-A8-carrier-aware fitting objectives, and describe direct packed-weight GPU kernel execution.

Result: For G=128 with 15,360 samples per distribution, W4 CubicQuant reduced reconstruction RMSE vs. optimally clipped 4-bit uniform integer quantization by 3.90% (Uniform), 13.49% (Gaussian), and 28.14% (Laplace). Vs. best enumerated 4-bit finite floating-point, reductions were 3.90%, 9.44%, and 6.27%. Preliminary H200 kernel benchmarks show model-dtype execution is faster for narrow GEMV, while Dynamic A8 becomes favorable as row count increases.

Conclusion: CubicQuant demonstrates representational advantages and direct GPU executability. However, downstream model quality and cross-device end-to-end performance remain open evaluation questions.

Abstract: Weight quantization for large-language-model inference must balance adaptive reconstruction levels with representations regular enough for efficient GPU execution. Uniform integers constrain each group to a linear grid. Low-bit floating-point formats use a fixed exponent-mantissa structure, while learned codebooks gain flexibility at the cost of irregular decoding and additional metadata.
  We introduce CubicQuant, a parametric non-uniform scalar format that preserves a dense integer code stream while adapting reconstruction levels within each weight group. A monotonic cubic curve, specified by two shape parameters and one scale, maps uniformly spaced magnitude codes to non-uniform levels. The family spans 1-8-bit weight payloads, contains symmetric uniform integer quantization as an exact special case, and has effective width B + 64/G bits per weight for payload width B and group size G. We derive population distortion under Uniform, Gaussian, and Laplace distributions, formulate continuous and Dynamic-A8-carrier-aware fitting objectives, and describe direct packed-weight GPU execution.
  For finite groups of G=128 with 15,360 samples per distribution, W4 CubicQuant reduced reconstruction RMSE relative to optimally clipped four-bit uniform integer quantization by 3.90% on Uniform, 13.49% on Gaussian, and 28.14% on Laplace samples. Relative to the best enumerated four-bit finite floating-point format, the reductions were 3.90%, 9.44%, and 6.27%. Preliminary H200 kernel measurements show a workload-dependent crossover: model-dtype execution is faster for narrow GEMV, while Dynamic A8 becomes favorable as row count grows. The results establish the format's representational promise and direct executability; downstream model quality and cross-device end-to-end performance remain open evaluation questions.

</details>


### [87] [Hidden Gauge Controls Feature Specialization in ReLU Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06766)
*Tongxi Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In overparameterized ReLU networks, the paper identifies "feature ownership" — which neuron among initially identical ones learns a teacher feature — and shows it can be controlled by a positive-homogeneous scaling gauge, a parameter choice invisible to the initial predictor. Opposite gauges yield a sharp Θ(D²) separation in specialization time, enabling deterministic selection and functional pruning of redundant neurons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether the identity of the neuron that learns a particular feature (feature ownership) can be controlled independently of the network's initial function, challenging the assumption that the initial predictor determines both when and which neuron learns a feature.

Method: Uses a tractable Gaussian teacher-student model with overparameterized ReLU networks. Fixes the complete initial function and varies only a positive-homogeneous scaling gauge. Employs an exact reaction-transport decomposition to analyze mobility differences for changing feature coefficients versus directions, and proves global selection and functional pruning under gradient descent.

Result: Opposite gauges produce distinct feature trajectories with a Θ(D²) separation in specialization time. Among initially duplicate students, assigning the favorable gauge deterministically selects one as the feature owner and drives others' contributions to zero. Results are extended to finite-time selection with visible perturbations and small-step full-batch gradient descent, verified in both population and finite-sample training.

Conclusion: The initial predictor determines neither when a feature is learned nor which neuron learns it; feature ownership is instead governed by the scaling gauge, a symmetry of the parameterization invisible in function space.

Abstract: Training changes a network's predictions while allocating task-relevant structure across its internal units. In an overparameterized ReLU network, several neurons can begin with exactly the same functional role, yet one may acquire a teacher feature while the others become redundant. We call the identity of that neuron feature ownership and ask whether it can be controlled by a parameter choice invisible to the initial predictor. In a tractable Gaussian teacher--student model, we fix the complete initial function and vary only a positive-homogeneous scaling gauge. Opposite gauges produce distinct feature trajectories and a sharp $Θ(D^2)$ separation in specialization time that no global change of clock can explain. Among any fixed number of initially duplicate students, assigning the favorable gauge to one neuron deterministically selects it as the owner and drives the remaining functional contribution to zero. An exact reaction--transport decomposition attributes the effect to different mobilities for changing a feature's coefficient and direction. We prove global selection and functional pruning, extend finite-time selection to visible perturbations and small-step full-batch gradient descent, and verify the predicted loss, alignment, pruning, and dissipation trajectories in population and finite-sample training. The initial predictor therefore determines neither when the feature is learned nor which neuron learns it.

</details>


### [88] [ArchEGraph: A Large-Scale Graph Dataset for Geometry-Topology-Physics Aligned Building Energy Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06772)
*Yihui Li,Yihui Chen,Kaidi Zha,Xiaoyue Yan,Zhexuan Yu,Shiqi Dai,Jun Xiao,Jun Yin,Ramon Elias Weber,Borong Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ArchEGraph is a large-scale benchmark dataset representing buildings as heterogeneous graphs with geometry, topology, weather, and thermal load data. It contains 5,481 buildings and 49,326 simulation cases, supporting two benchmark tasks: graph reconstruction from meshes and topology-informed load prediction, with standardized evaluation protocols for developing scalable surrogate models in building energy modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale datasets mapping building geometry to energy performance are needed to understand design impacts and calibrate ML models for rapid early-stage design feedback. Existing resources lack explicit geometry-topology-performance coupling, motivating a unified benchmark.

Method: The authors construct ArchEGraph by representing buildings as heterogeneous graphs with aligned geometry, topology, weather data, and zone-level thermal loads. They define two benchmark tasks with standardized evaluation protocols: (1) graph reconstruction from polygonal meshes, and (2) topology-informed load prediction using graph structure and temporal weather conditions. Cross-building and cross-climate generalization experiments assess model robustness.

Result: ArchEGraph comprises 5,481 buildings, 49,326 validated building-weather simulation cases, over 133,000 space nodes, and 1.44 million face nodes, capturing substantial geometric and topological complexity. Standardized protocols and generalization experiments are established, though specific quantitative performance baselines are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: ArchEGraph provides a unified testbed for studying geometry-topology-physics coupling in building energy modeling, enabling development and evaluation of scalable, generalizable surrogate models for carbon-neutral building design.

Abstract: Accurate estimation of building energy use is essential for achieving carbon neutral and sustainable buildings. To better understand the influence of design decisions on building energy use and calibrate machine learning models that can give architects and engineers rapid design feedback, large-scale datasets are needed that explicitly map building geometry to performance. We present ArchEGraph, a large-scale benchmark dataset that represents buildings as heterogeneous graphs with aligned geometry, topology, weather, and zone-level thermal loads. The dataset contains 5,481 buildings and 49,326 validated building-weather simulation cases. In total, it includes over 133,000 space nodes and 1.44 million face nodes, reflecting substantial geometric and topological complexity. Based on ArchEGraph, we define two benchmark tasks: (i) graph reconstruction from polygonal meshes, aiming to recover topological structure from geometric representations; and (ii) topology-informed load prediction, which leverages graph structure and temporal weather conditions to forecast zone-level response time series. We further introduce standardized evaluation protocols for both tasks and conduct cross-building and cross-climate generalization experiments to assess model robustness. ArchEGraph provides a unified testbed for studying geometry-topology-physics coupling in building energy modeling, enabling the development and evaluation of scalable and generalizable surrogate models.

</details>


### [89] [Faster Query-Key Learning Sharpens Attention in Self-Attention Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06776)
*Rahul Vashisht,Harish G. Ramaswamy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Collapsed vs. factorized parameterizations of self-attention circuits induce implicit differences in relative learning rates; faster query-key learning relative to output-value learning yields sharper, more interpretable attention without sacrificing predictive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how different parameterizations (collapsed vs. factorized) of the query-key and output-value circuits in self-attention affect attention patterns, parameter dynamics, and interpretability, even when training loss is similar.

Method: Gradient-flow analysis of single-layer self-attention models trained for next-token prediction, deriving closed-form dynamics for parameter trajectories and characterizing how factorization induces implicit rescaling of learning rates in the two circuits.

Result: Factorization causes query-key and output-value parameters to move along a line with different relative speeds. Faster query-key learning relative to output-value learning produces sharper attention by concentrating attention mass on relevant tokens. This improves attention interpretability proxies while maintaining comparable predictive performance.

Conclusion: The relative learning rates of the query-key and output-value circuits govern attention concentration. Factorization-induced implicit learning rate rescaling is the mechanism by which certain parameterizations yield sharper, more interpretable attention patterns.

Abstract: A standard self-attention layer consists of two interacting circuits: the query-key circuit that governs attention allocation, and the output-value circuit that maps attended representations to predictions. Collapsed and factorized parameterizations of the query-key and output-value circuits lead to qualitatively different attention patterns. In particular, some parameterizations give sharper attention to task-relevant tokens, at a similar training loss. We analyze how the parameterizations of these circuits shape the parameter trajectories in single-layer self-attention models trained for next-token prediction. Through gradient-flow analysis, we show that factorization induces implicit rescaling of the two circuits' learning rates. We derive closed-form dynamics showing that output-value and query-key parameters move along a line, with relative speeds determined by their learning rates. Faster query-key learning relative to output-value learning thus produces sharper attention, as the model compensates for slower output-value learning by increasing attention mass on relevant tokens. Experiments show that differences in the relative learning rates of the two circuits govern attention concentration. This improves attention interpretability proxies while maintaining comparable predictive performance.

</details>


### [90] [Understanding Differentiable Embeddings Through Differential and Integral Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06809)
*Xinyu Zhang,Klaus Mueller*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper unifies existing diagnostics for nonlinear dimensionality reduction embeddings—projection glyphs, map-continuity scores, and transport-based analyses—under a single differential-geometric framework. The differential view recovers local diagnostics and quantifies curvature-based trust; the integral view detects path-dependence. The authors prove the integral view is irreducible to local measurements and validate their framework on synthetic and single-cell data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diagnostics for assessing trustworthiness of nonlinear dimensionality reduction embeddings (projection glyphs, map-continuity scores, transport-based analyses) appear fragmented and unrelated, with no common framework to explain when they agree or disagree. Analysts lack a principled way to decide whether an embedding can be trusted.

Method: The authors identify a single geometric object induced by every differentiable embedding. They decompose this into two complementary views: (1) a differential (local) view where first-order terms recover projection glyphs and second-order curvature bounds linear approximation reliability; (2) an integral view that follows the geometry along high-dimensional paths to reveal whether the embedding is state-dependent or path-dependent. They prove that map-continuity is a prerequisite for other diagnostics and that the integral view cannot be reduced to any finite collection of local measurements at any derivative order.
