Result: The framework theoretically unifies three previously disparate diagnostic families. The integral view is proven irreducible to local measurements, establishing a fundamental distinction from pointwise diagnostics. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets validate theoretical predictions, demonstrate curvature-based trust estimates on single-cell embeddings, and show the integral analysis can distinguish single-valued embeddings from path-dependent optimization-based embeddings where existing pointwise diagnostics fail.

Conclusion: The proposed differential-geometric framework provides a complete and unified theory for embedding diagnostics derived from geometry, clarifying the relationships and limitations of existing methods. The irreducibility of the integral view implies that trustworthy local behavior does not guarantee global consistency, and that path-dependence must be assessed via integral, not purely local, analysis.

Abstract: How can an analyst decide whether a nonlinear dimensionality reduction embedding can be trusted? Existing diagnostics provide only partial answers: projection glyphs characterize local sensitivity, map-continuity scores measure local conditioning, and transport-based analyses reveal path-dependent inconsistencies. However, these methods appear unrelated and provide no common framework for understanding when they agree or not. We show that they are all derived from a single geometric object induced by every differentiable embedding, whether defined implicitly through optimization or explicitly by a learned mapping. This framework provides two complementary geometric views of an embedding. The differential view explains local behavior: its first-order term recovers projection glyphs, while its second-order curvature quantifies how far their linear approximation remains reliable. The integral view follows the same geometry along high dimensional paths and determines whether an embedding depends only on the current state or also on the path taken to reach it. We further show that map-continuity is a prerequisite for the other analyses. The framework is theoretically complete for diagnostics derived from the embedding geometry, and we prove the integral view irreducible: no amount of local measurement at any number of points, to any order of derivative, reproduces what it detects. Classical rank-based metrics form a complementary class based on finite-scale neighborhood relationships. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets validate theoretical predictions, demonstrate accurate curvature-based trust estimates on single-cell embeddings, and show that the integral analysis distinguishes single-valued embeddings from path-dependent optimization-based embeddings in ways that existing pointwise diagnostics cannot.

</details>


### [91] [Multiscale Reward Hedging from Correct Demonstrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06825)
*Pahan Dewasurendra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses learning from demonstrations where multiple answers may be correct, with the learner receiving only a demonstrated action (not its own correctness or any reward). It provides the first horizon-free guarantee for continuous reward classes via a novel "shared vote" hedging mechanism over tolerant optimality tests at multiple accuracy scales, yielding cumulative hidden gap bounds expressed as metric-entropy integrals. For polynomial entropy classes, this gives $O(d\log A)$ total gap and $O(d/m)$ statistical rates, with a concrete $O(d)$ regret bound for bounded linear contextual recommendation with arbitrary compact menus — the first such polynomial finite bound without structural menu restrictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reward-hedging guarantees for learning from correct demonstrations (where the learner sees a valid answer but no reward or feedback on its own prediction) are restricted to finite reward classes. The authors aim to extend these guarantees to continuous classes without dependence on the time horizon, enabling application to rich, practical settings like contextual recommendation.

Method: The core technique is hedging via a single shared vote over tolerant optimality tests at every accuracy scale. For each target reward, one proxy survives per scale; a prediction whose optimality gap exceeds that scale doubles the proxy's weight. This yields a simultaneous tail bound $|\{t:\ell_t>2^{-j}\}|\leq \log_2\mathcal N(\mathcal G,2^{-j-1})+j$, where $\mathcal G$ is the class of optimality-gap functions. Integrating these tails produces a cumulative hidden gap bound expressed as a metric-entropy integral, independent of the number of rounds. The method supports polynomial-time implementation for one-dimensional Lipschitz parameter curves and includes robust extensions and empirical validation.

Result: Key theoretical results include: (1) horizon-free cumulative gap bounds via metric-entropy integrals for continuous classes; (2) $O(d\log A)$ total gap and $O(d/m)$ statistical rate for polynomial entropy $(A/\varepsilon)^d$; (3) $O(d)$ regret for bounded linear contextual recommendation with arbitrary compact menus (first polynomial finite bound without structural restrictions, though improper); (4) an $\Omega(d)$ lower bound; (5) corollaries for low-rank and bounded ReLU networks; (6) a robust theorem accounting for demonstrator suboptimality. Empirically, a MovieLens audit runs in 1.7 CPU seconds across ten users, improving mean latent gap over both a demonstrated-rating policy and a proper online baseline.

Conclusion: The paper establishes that learning from demonstrations over continuous reward classes is possible with horizon-free guarantees, overcoming the prior limitation to finite classes. The scale-adaptive hedging mechanism via shared voting provides a general framework with tight bounds, polynomial-time implementations for structured settings, and practical empirical performance, all while the learner never observes rewards or losses — only action demonstrations.

Abstract: Learning from correct demonstrations is harder than supervised learning when many answers are correct: after predicting, the learner sees one valid answer but not whether its own answer was valid, nor any reward. Existing reward-hedging guarantees consequently assume a finite reward class. We give the first horizon-free guarantee for continuous classes. The key is to hedge in one shared vote over tolerant optimality tests at every accuracy scale. A target reward has one surviving proxy per scale, and a prediction with gap above that scale doubles the proxy. This yields the simultaneous tail bound $|\{t:\ell_t>2^{-j}\}|\leq \log_2\mathcal N(\mathcal G,2^{-j-1})+j$, where $\mathcal G$ is the class of optimality-gap functions. Integrating the tails gives cumulative hidden gap bounded by a metric-entropy integral, independently of the number of rounds. Polynomial entropy $(A/ε)^d$ gives $O(d\log A)$ total gap and a fast $O(d/m)$ statistical rate. For bounded linear contextual recommendation, the result is $O(d)$ regret for arbitrary compact menus. This is the first polynomial finite bound without structural restrictions on the menus, at the price of improper prediction. Although the general vote can be expensive, it is exactly polynomial-time for one-dimensional Lipschitz parameter curves. Fixed-radius rank-two recommendation takes $O(KT^2)$ time for menus of size $K$. We also prove an $Ω(d)$ lower bound, low-rank and bounded ReLU-network corollaries, and a robust theorem that adds only the demonstrator's cumulative suboptimality. A reproducible adaptive stress test illustrates the predicted scale adaptation. After factorization, an exact MovieLens audit runs in 1.7 CPU seconds across ten users and improves mean latent gap over both a demonstrated-rating policy and a proper online baseline. The learner uses only action demonstrations and never observes a reward or a loss.

</details>


### [92] [Graph Machine: Exploring Edge Mechanisms as an Inductive Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06834)
*Lintai Hou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Graph Machine introduces two explicit edge mechanisms—edge-augmented attention and edge-centric referral—that allow Transformers to dynamically construct and revise relational graphs across layers. Tested on Sudoku, it outperforms Transformer baselines by discovering compact edge-based geometric representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Transformers excel at global content-based matching but lack a strong inductive bias for iterative traversal of latent relations. The authors hypothesize that reasoning tasks, particularly those requiring relational structure inference, benefit from explicit, differentiable edge manipulation mechanisms.

Method: The authors propose Graph Machine, augmenting the Transformer with two key mechanisms: (1) edge-augmented attention, where learned edge representations modulate attention weights between node pairs; and (2) edge-centric referral, where nodes exchange address-like information to update edge states. These mechanisms operate across layers, enabling dynamic construction and revision of a latent relational graph. The architecture is evaluated on Sudoku under controlled settings with ablation studies and mechanistic analysis.

Result: Graph Machine outperforms Transformer baselines on Sudoku. Ablation studies attribute performance gains directly to the edge mechanisms. Mechanistic analysis reveals that the model spontaneously discovers a compact, edge-based construction for representing Sudoku grid geometry, suggesting the inductive bias effectively guides relational structure learning.

Conclusion: Explicit edge mechanisms constitute a promising architectural direction for reasoning tasks, warranting broader evaluation beyond Sudoku. The model's ability to discover interpretable relational structures supports the value of this inductive bias.

Abstract: Transformers provide a powerful architecture for global content-based matching, but reasoning problems may benefit from a stronger inductive bias toward iterative traversal of latent relations. We introduce Graph Machine, an architecture with two explicit edge-based mechanisms: Edge-augmented attention, in which edges modulate attention between nodes, and edge-centric referral, in which nodes exchange addresses to update their edges. Conceptually, this enables the model to dynamically and differentiably construct and revise relational graphs across layers. We study this inductive bias using Sudoku under controlled settings and find that Graph Machine outperforms Transformer baselines, with ablation studies and mechanistic analysis attributing the gains to the edge mechanisms. Surprisingly, we found that the model discovers a compact edge-based construction for Sudoku geometry. Our results support explicit edge mechanisms as a promising architectural design, motivating broader evaluation.

</details>


### [93] [Mathematical Principles and Experimental Discoveries of the Emergence of Symbolic Patterns in Artificial Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06839)
*Quanshi Zhang,Qihan Ren,Siyu Lou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ANNs trained on diverse tasks naturally develop sparse symbolic interactions that explain their inference logic. The authors prove that two common mathematical criteria drive this emergence, empirically validate it across many models, and demonstrate the interactions' faithfulness via transferability and generalization power.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the black-box nature of ANNs by investigating whether their complex inference logic can be exhaustively and concisely explained as sparse symbolic patterns, and whether such emergence reflects a natural law.

Method: The authors theoretically prove that two implicit mathematical criteria across tasks lead to the emergence of sparse symbolic interactions in ANNs. They then empirically verify these criteria hold for most input samples across diverse models and demonstrate interaction faithfulness through sample-to-sample and model-to-model transferability experiments, as well as generalization power analysis.

Result: Symbolic interactions emerge broadly across ANNs trained on diverse tasks. The two mathematical criteria hold for the majority of input samples. The interactions exhibit strong transferability and can explain the overall generalization power of ANNs.

Conclusion: The findings provide a solid foundation for symbolic explanations of ANNs, offer novel insights into generalization power, highlight the potential of a communicative learning paradigm where inference logic can be inspected and tuned at the symbolic level, and suggest similar symbolic representations may emerge in other black-box systems under certain conditions.

Abstract: Artificial Neural networks (ANNs) are often treated as black-box models, making explainability a central challenge in deep learning. Many engineering methods have been proposed to approximately explain the ANN from various perspectives, such as feature attribution and visualization. However, it remains a long-standing open question whether the complex inference logic of an ANN can be explained exhaustively and concisely as sparse symbolic patterns. This raises a deeper inquiry: does the emergence of symbolic patterns reflect a natural law rather than chance? Here, we show that across a broad class of ANNs trained on diverse tasks, their inference logic can indeed be reformulated as sparse symbolic interactions. We further prove that two common mathematical criteria, which are implicitly required across tasks, lead to the emergence of such sparse symbolic interactions. Empirical evidence confirms that the two criteria hold for the majority of input samples in diverse models. Furthermore, the faithfulness of these interactions is also demonstrated by their strong sample-to-sample and model-to-model transferability, as well as their ability to explain the overall generalization power of ANNs. Our theoretical analysis and extensive experiments provide a solid foundation for symbolic explanations of ANNs, and offer novel insights into the ANN's generalization power. Our findings also highlight the potential of communicative learning, a paradigm in which the inference logic of an ANN can be directly inspected and tuned at the level of symbolic patterns, thus complementing traditional end-to-end learning paradigm. Finally, the observed emergence of symbolic patterns in ANNs suggests that similar symbolic representations may also emerge in other types of black-box systems under certain conditions, because our proof does not depend on any specific ANN architecture.

</details>


### [94] [Bridging the Gap Between Hyperdimensional Computing and Kernel Methods via the Nyström Method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06860)
*Quanling Zhao,Anthony Hitchcock Thomas,Ari Brin,Xiaofan Yu,Tajana Rosing*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NysHD introduces a Nyström method-based encoding for hyperdimensional computing, enabling any user-defined positive-semidefinite similarity kernel to be mapped into HDC space, achieving 11% and 17% average accuracy gains on graph and string classification tasks, respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The effectiveness of HDC in machine learning is critically dependent on how raw data is encoded into high-dimensional random vectors. Existing encoding methods are limited in scope, and there is a vast literature on kernel-based similarity functions that remains inaccessible to HDC. The authors aim to bridge this gap.

Method: NysHD leverages the Nyström method for kernel approximation to construct an HDC encoding map. Given any user-specified positive-semidefinite similarity (kernel) function, the method uses Nyström sampling (random Fourier features for shift-invariant kernels, or standard Nyström with landmark points) to produce a deterministic mapping into high-dimensional vector representations compatible with HDC operations.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows NysHD outperforms existing HDC encoding methods, achieving on average 11% higher classification accuracy on graph datasets and 17% higher accuracy on string datasets.

Conclusion: NysHD provides a simple, principled mechanism to import arbitrary positive-semidefinite similarity functions into the HDC framework, significantly expanding the class of problems addressable by HDC and yielding substantial accuracy improvements over existing encoding schemes.

Abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is an approach from the cognitive science literature for solving information processing tasks using data represented as high-dimensional random vectors. The technique has a rigorous mathematical backing, and is easy to implement in energy-efficient and highly parallel hardware like FPGAs and "processing-in-memory" architectures. The effectiveness of HDC in machine learning largely depends on how raw data is mapped to high-dimensional space. In this work, we propose NysHD, a new method for constructing this mapping that is based on the Nyström method from the literature on kernel approximation. Our approach provides a simple recipe to turn any user-defined positive-semidefinite similarity function into an equivalent mapping in HDC. There is a vast literature on the design of such functions for learning problems. Our approach provides a mechanism to import them into the HDC setting, expanding the types of problems that can be tackled using HDC. Empirical evaluation against existing HDC encoding methods shows that NysHD can achieve, on average, 11% and 17% better classification accuracy on graph and string datasets respectively.

</details>


### [95] [SkillAligner: Treating Retrieved Skills as Adaptable Drafts at Execution Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06880)
*Qinfeng Li,Dalin He,Yuntai Bao,Ying Yang,Ruoxi Chen,Xinyan Yu,Lizhou Liang,Ge Su,Wenqi Zhang,Xuhong Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SkillAligner is a training-free framework that adapts retrieved skills at execution time by resolving mismatches between skill assumptions and task/interface realities, then consolidates them into a compact execution guide, improving agent performance while reducing inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieved skills, while semantically relevant, often contain procedural assumptions that conflict with the current task, execution environment, or other retrieved skills — a problem termed the "skill–execution misfit." Semantic relevance alone does not guarantee execution utility.

Method: SkillAligner performs a one-time joint adaptation of retrieved skills before execution: (1) it specializes useful skill fragments to the task requirements, (2) aligns procedural assumptions with the available execution interface, (3) resolves inter-skill dependencies, conflicts, and redundancy, and (4) consolidates the adapted content into a compact execution guide reused throughout the trajectory. The framework is training-free.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse agent benchmarks and model backbones demonstrate that SkillAligner substantially improves task performance over existing skill-use baselines, reduces skill-induced regressions at the instance level, and lowers total inference cost.

Conclusion: Treating retrieved skills as adaptable drafts rather than fixed instructions, and performing joint adaptation at execution time, effectively mitigates the skill–execution misfit problem and yields both performance gains and efficiency improvements for language agents.

Abstract: General-purpose skills promise reusable procedural knowledge for language agents, yet semantic relevance does not guarantee execution utility: a retrieved skill may encode assumptions that conflict with the current task, execution environment, or other retrieved skills. We formalize this problem as the skill--execution misfit. To address it, we propose SkillAligner, a training-free execution-time skill adaptation framework that treats retrieved skills as adaptable drafts rather than fixed instructions. Before execution, SkillAligner performs a one-time joint adaptation that specializes useful skill fragments to task requirements, aligns their procedural assumptions with the available execution interface, and composes the resulting guidance by resolving dependencies, conflicts, and redundancy across skills. The adapted content is consolidated into a compact execution guide and reused throughout the subsequent trajectory. Extensive experiments across diverse agent benchmarks and model backbones show that SkillAligner substantially improves task performance over existing skill-use baselines, reduces skill-induced regressions at the instance level, and lowers total inference cost.

</details>


### [96] [PRISM: Principled Reference Identification for Schrodinger Bridge Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06893)
*Forouzan Fallah,Yezhou Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PRISM formalizes the design of reference processes in Schrödinger bridge models, proving that under infinite compute all admissible references recover the true posterior, but under finite steps the optimal noise spectrum matches the destroyed-information spectrum, with real-image deviations traced to non-Gaussian per-mode statistics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Schrödinger bridge models typically use heuristically chosen white noise references with hand-tuned schedules. The paper seeks to develop a principled theory for reference process design, addressing when and why reference choice matters.

Method: The authors characterize exactly tractable time-varying Gaussian references (those with commuting instantaneous covariances and per-mode schedules), prove an invisibility principle showing all admissible references recover the true posterior with exact drift and infinite steps, derive the finite-step objective in closed form, and prove the optimal noise spectrum is proportional to P_k (the spectrum of destroyed information) with constant x*(T). Empirical validation includes Gaussian experiments, FFHQ image experiments, and a pre-registered mechanism study isolating non-Gaussian per-mode statistics as the source of real-image deviations.

Result: In the Gaussian regime, the optimal finite-step noise spectrum is proportional to P_k with constant x*(T) = (2 ln T)^(-1/2)(1+o(1)). Noise color and temporal scheduling are interchangeable, and regularization shifts optimal references toward white noise. On FFHQ, white noise outperforms the matched reference despite theoretical predictions; a pre-registered study rules out ridge whitening, and a 2x2 mechanism study traces the inversion to non-Gaussian per-mode statistics.

Conclusion: PRISM transforms reference design from hyperparameter tuning into a principled calculation in the Gaussian regime and precisely identifies where real-image statistics break the theory, namely in the non-Gaussian per-mode structure.

Abstract: Schrödinger bridge models restore a clean signal from a degraded observation by following the conditional bridges of a reference process, yet this reference is chosen heuristically, typically white noise with a hand-tuned schedule. We develop PRISM, a theory of bridge reference design. We characterize the time-varying Gaussian references that remain exactly tractable with per-mode schedules: precisely those whose instantaneous covariances commute. We then prove an invisibility principle: with the exact drift and unlimited solver steps, every admissible reference recovers the true posterior. The choice of reference therefore matters only under finite computational resources. For a fixed step budget, we derive the finite-step objective in closed form and prove that every optimal noise spectrum is proportional to Pk, the spectrum of information destroyed by the sensor, with a mode-independent constant x*(T) = (2 ln T)^-1/2 (1 + o(1)). The analysis shows that noise color and temporal scheduling are interchangeable, and regularization provably shifts the optimal reference toward white noise. Experiments in Gaussian settings confirm the predicted orderings and the closed-form loss floors. On FFHQ, the distortion-- perception trade-off and spectral localization transfer, but white noise outperforms the matched reference; a pre-registered study that changes the training regime refutes ridge whitening as the explanation. A 2x2 mechanism study then traces the inversion to the non-Gaussian per-mode statistics of real images. PRISM turns reference design from a hyperparameter sweep into a calculation in the Gaussian regime, and locates exactly where real images break it.

</details>


### [97] [Recent advances in weakly supervised learning: New supervision paradigms, assumption relaxations, and practical solutions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06896)
*Wei Wang,Gang Niu,Masashi Sugiyama*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This chapter surveys recent advances in weakly supervised learning, introducing confidence-difference binary classification, complementary-label learning with relaxed assumptions, and a fair evaluation framework for partial-label learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning requires high-quality, well-annotated training data, which is often unavailable in real-world applications. Weakly supervised learning addresses this gap by enabling model training under incomplete, inexact, or inaccurate supervision.

Method: The authors present three contributions: (1) a new binary classification problem called confidence-difference classification with consistent solving approaches; (2) complementary-label learning methods for multi-class classification under relaxed data-generation assumptions compared to existing consistent approaches; and (3) an evaluation framework for partial-label learning designed to enable fair and realistic algorithm comparison.

Result: The chapter reports new consistent approaches for confidence-difference classification, relaxed-assumption methods for complementary-label learning, and a standardized evaluation framework for partial-label learning. Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: The chapter demonstrates progress in weakly supervised learning through novel problem formulations (confidence-difference classification), relaxed theoretical assumptions (complementary-label learning), and improved evaluation practices (partial-label learning framework), collectively advancing the field toward more practical real-world applicability.

Abstract: Deep learning has achieved great success in recent years thanks to the availability of high-quality, well-annotated training data. However, this requirement is often not met in real-world applications. Weakly supervised learning aims to train an accurate model with incomplete, inexact, or inaccurate supervision. In this chapter, we will discuss recent advances in this field, including new supervision paradigms, relaxed assumptions, and practical solutions. First, we introduce a new weakly supervised binary classification problem called confidence-difference classification and propose consistent approaches to solve it. Next, we investigate complementary-label learning, a weakly supervised multi-class classification problem. Our proposed approaches are based on more relaxed assumptions about the data generation process than existing consistent approaches. Lastly, we present an evaluation framework for partial-label learning, another popular multi-class weakly supervised learning problem, in order to promote fair and realistic evaluation of algorithms in this field.

</details>


### [98] [MiCoPro: End-to-End Mixed Precision HW/SW Co-design with HW-aware Proxy Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06916)
*Zijun Jiang,Yangdi Lyu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MiCo is a holistic mixed-precision quantization framework that searches for accuracy-optimal quantization configurations under strict latency constraints, with MiCoPro extending it via a Hardware-Aware Proxy for improved prediction accuracy and direct deployment from PyTorch to bare-metal C code, achieving up to 40% latency reduction with <3% accuracy drop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mixed-precision quantization exploration algorithms suffer from limited flexibility and efficiency. Conventional methods struggle to comprehend the complex impacts of different MPQ schemes on post-training quantization and quantization-aware training. Moreover, no end-to-end framework exists for both optimization and deployment of MPQ models on edge devices.

Method: The MiCo framework employs a novel optimization algorithm that searches for accuracy-optimal quantization configurations under strict latency constraints. MiCoPro extends this with a Hardware-Aware Proxy (HAP) model that incorporates target-specific latency modeling, enabling rapid exploration and direct compilation from PyTorch models to bare-metal C code for deployment.

Result: The framework was demonstrated on both the BitFusion accelerator and SIMD-extended RISC-V processors, achieving up to 40% latency reduction while maintaining less than 3% accuracy degradation.

Conclusion: MiCo/MiCoPro provides a versatile, end-to-end solution for mixed-precision quantization exploration and deployment on edge AI hardware, bridging the gap between optimization and practical deployment through hardware-aware proxy modeling.

Abstract: Quantized Neural Networks~(QNN) with low-bitwidth data have proven promising in efficient storage and computation on edge devices. To mitigate accuracy degradation while maximizing speedup, layer-wise mixed-precision quantization~(MPQ) becomes a popular solution. However, existing algorithms for exploring MPQ schemes are limited in flexibility and efficiency. Comprehending the complex impacts of different MPQ schemes on post-training quantization and quantization-aware training results is a challenge for conventional methods. Furthermore, an end-to-end framework for the optimization and deployment of MPQ models is missing in existing work.
  To address these challenges, we propose the MiCo framework, a holistic MPQ exploration and deployment framework for edge AI applications. The framework adopts a novel optimization algorithm to search for accuracy-optimal quantization configurations under strict latency constraints. We further extended the framework to MiCoPro, which introduces a robust Hardware-Aware Proxy (HAP) model to enhance prediction accuracy and hardware versatility. By leveraging target-specific latency modeling, MiCoPro enables rapid exploration and direct deployment from PyTorch models to bare-metal C code. We demonstrate the versatility of our framework on both the BitFusion accelerator and SIMD-extended RISC-V processors, achieving up to 40\% of latency reduction with less than 3\% of accuracy drop.

</details>


### [99] [Walkable to Whom? Capturing Subjective Variability in Walkability Perception Using Multimodal Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06934)
*Moloud Damandeh,Meead Saberi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A dataset of ~30K walkability ratings from ~1.2K respondents links sidewalk-view imagery with rater attributes. The proposed user-conditioned multimodal deep learning model improves rank agreement by 65% over image-only baselines, demonstrating that observer identity is predictive beyond image content alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing walkability perception studies (1) reduce diverse individual judgments to aggregated scores assuming uniform perception, and (2) rely on vehicle-mounted street-view imagery that misrepresents the pedestrian visual experience. There is a need for models that account for inter-individual variability and use pedestrian-perspective imagery.

Method: The authors collected 29,870 walkability ratings from 1,196 respondents using sidewalk-view imagery across urban, suburban, and regional Australian environments. They conducted a viewpoint-comparison study (sidewalk-view vs. matched street-view) and developed the first user-conditioned multimodal deep learning framework that fuses visual features from sidewalk images with respondent-level representations for personalized walkability prediction.

Result: Sidewalk-view images received significantly higher walkability ratings than matched street-view images, confirming imagery source matters. The user-conditioned model achieved a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.47 versus 0.29 for the image-only baseline — a 65% improvement in rank agreement with observed ratings.

Conclusion: The field should move from aggregated, observer-independent walkability scores toward user-conditioned models that represent diverse users, enabling more inclusive assessment of pedestrian environments.

Abstract: Visual perception of walkability varies substantially across individuals, reflecting differences in personal characteristics, experiences, and preferences. Existing studies, however, often reduce these diverse judgements to aggregated scores, implicitly assuming uniform perception, and commonly rely on vehicle-mounted street-view imagery that does not reflect the pedestrian's visual experience. This paper introduces a dataset of 29,870 walkability ratings from 1,196 respondents, linking sidewalk-view imagery across urban, suburban, and regional Australian environments with individual rater attributes, and proposes the first user-conditioned multimodal deep learning framework for walkability perception, fusing visual features with respondent-level representations. A viewpoint-comparison study shows that sidewalk-view images receive significantly higher walkability ratings than matched street-view images, indicating that imagery source is a substantive design decision in perception surveys. The user-conditioned model improves rank agreement with observed ratings by 65% over an image-only baseline (quadratic weighted kappa 0.47 vs. 0.29), demonstrating that who is evaluating an environment carries predictive indication beyond image content alone. These findings support moving from aggregated, observer-independent walkability scores toward models that represent diverse users, enabling more inclusive assessment of pedestrian environments.

</details>


### [100] [ELMZip: Onboard Satellite Image Compression via Extreme Learning Machines for Efficient Downlink](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06942)
*Woojin Cho,Junghwan Park,Sangcheol Sim,Steve Andreas Immanuel,Junhyuk Heo,Darongsae Kwon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ELMZip is a framework that uses Extreme Learning Machines with domain decomposition for efficient, resolution-free onboard neural representation of multispectral imagery, enabling high compression rates without backpropagation by transmitting only compact output weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small satellites like CubeSats face severe downlink bottlenecks due to high-volume multispectral data and limited communication windows. Traditional onboard image compression methods struggle with nonlinear, multi-band, multi-resolution statistics, and prior neural representation approaches require iterative optimization with full parameter transmission — both of which are ill-suited for resource-constrained platforms.

Method: ELMZip employs Extreme Learning Machines (random-feature single-layer networks) that reformulate image fitting as a convex least-squares problem, eliminating backpropagation. It uses a domain decomposition strategy for resolution-free neural representation and an asymmetric transmission protocol where only the compact output weights — not full network parameters — are downlinked, achieving high compression.

Result: ELMZip achieves significant compression efficiency while maintaining high reconstruction fidelity, enabling immediate image reconstruction for analysis on resource-constrained platforms.

Conclusion: ELMZip offers a practical and efficient onboard compression solution for small satellites, advancing real-time AI-powered Earth observation by maximizing data return under severe bandwidth constraints.

Abstract: The acquisition of multispectral imagery via small satellites (e.g., CubeSats) presents significant data downlink challenges due to high data volumes and restricted communication windows. While onboard image compression is critical to address this bottleneck, traditional methods often struggle to adapt to the nonlinear statistics of multi-band, multi-resolution data. To overcome these limitations, we propose ELMZip, a novel framework based on Extreme Learning Machines (ELM) and domain decomposition strategies for efficient, resolution-free onboard neural representation. ELMZip formulates the fitting process as a convex least-squares problem using random-feature single-layer networks, thereby eliminating the need for computationally expensive backpropagation. By adopting an asymmetric transmission protocol that sends only the compact output weights, the proposed method significantly reduces the downlink payload. Unlike previous neural representation approaches that rely on iterative optimization and require transmitting full network parameters, ELMZip achieves significant compression efficiency while maintaining high reconstruction fidelity. This capability enables immediate image reconstruction for analysis, allowing resource-constrained platforms to maximize data return and advancing real-time AI-powered Earth observation.

</details>


### [101] [A Rate Separation for Agnostic Direct Sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06951)
*Mihir More,Aritra Das,Debayan Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper shows that the single-instance agnostic PAC learning rate does not determine the learning rate for direct sums, providing counterexamples with two function classes that share the same single-instance rate (n^{-1/2}) but differ in direct-sum behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2024) posed the open question of how the agnostic PAC learning curve of a direct sum C^r depends on the single-instance learning curve ε_agn(n | C) and on r. This paper investigates whether the single-instance learning rate alone determines the direct-sum learning rate.

Method: The authors construct two simple function classes as counterexamples: F (the class of two constant binary functions) and G (consisting of the zero function and the identity function). Both classes are shown to have agnostic learning curves of order n^{-1/2}. The direct-sum learning behavior of these classes is then analyzed to demonstrate divergence.

Result: Despite both F and G having identical single-instance agnostic learning rates of order n^{-1/2}, their direct-sum learning behaviors differ. This proves that the single-instance learning rate does not determine the direct-sum rate, answering the question raised by Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2024) in the negative.

Conclusion: The single-instance agnostic learning rate is insufficient to characterize the direct-sum learning rate. The structure of the function class beyond its individual learning curve matters for understanding how learning scales when combining instances.

Abstract: Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine \cite{HannekeMoranWaknine2024} asked how the agnostic PAC learning curve of the direct sum $C^r$ depends on the single-instance learning curve $\epsagn(n\mid C)$ and on $r$. We show that the single-instance learning rate does not determine the direct-sum rate. Let $\F$ be the class of the two constant binary functions and let $\G$ consist of the zero function and the identity function. Both classes have agnostic learning curve of order $n^{-1/2}$.

</details>


### [102] [How Molecular Generative Models Organize Molecular Identity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06956)
*Raul Ortega-Ochoa,Tejs Vegge,Jens S. Bakander,Luis Mantilla Calderon,Alan Aspuru-Guzik,Tonio Buonassisi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates how molecular generative models internally organize chemical identities in latent space, revealing a piecewise-constant partitioned repertoire shaped by representation, identity conventions, and training dynamics. It argues that latent spaces cannot be assumed chemically navigable without first characterizing this internal organization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While generative models for molecules are widely used for sampling and latent-space navigation, little is known about how these models internally structure discrete chemical identities. The authors aim to expose the model's internal repertoire — the fixed set of molecular identities it can produce — and understand how this organization emerges during training.

Method: The authors formalize molecular identity explicitly and perform a "pullback" through the generative process: they probe latent regions that decode to the same molecule, mapping the model's internal partition. They analyze three molecular generative architectures, varying the representation (e.g., SMILES, graphs), identity convention, decoder stochasticity, and distance metrics to characterize how piecewise-constant regions and coarse-to-fine boundaries form and evolve during training.

Result: Across architectures, the model's repertoire consists of piecewise-constant regions separated by coarse-to-fine boundaries. Local chemical organization stabilizes during training, but the number of distinct identities per neighborhood continues to fluctuate. The partition's structure depends on representation type, identity convention, stochasticity, and the comparison metric.

Conclusion: Internal chemical organization in generative latent spaces must be empirically characterized rather than assumed. The fixed, partitioned nature of the model's output repertoire has implications for using latent spaces as proxies for chemical space navigation and novelty generation.

Abstract: Generative models for matter are often evaluated as samplers over output representations, and their latent spaces are commonly used as proxies for navigating chemical space. Much less is known about how these models internally arrange discrete chemical identities within those representations. We study this arrangement by making molecular identity explicit and pulling it back through the generative process. Through these pullbacks we probe the regions that generate the same object, exposing the trained model's internal repertoire: a fixed partition that determines which objects (novel or not) the model can produce.
  Across three molecular generative architectures, we find that this repertoire is arranged into piecewise-constant regions separated by recurring coarse-to-fine boundaries. Its organization depends on the representation probed, the identity convention, decoder stochasticity, and the metric used to compare coordinates. During training, local chemical organization stabilizes while the number of distinct molecular identities represented within each neighborhood continues to change. Internal organization must therefore be characterized, rather than assumed, before a generative space can be treated as chemically navigable.

</details>


### [103] [Density-aware Hierarchical Clustering Based on Element-Categorized Connection Subgraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06990)
*Yuning Yu,José Rodríguez-Piñeiro,Xuefeng Yin,Bin Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DHC-ECS is a novel density-aware hierarchical clustering method that integrates hierarchical, density-based, and graph clustering by introducing a new inter-cluster similarity metric based on KNN connection subgraphs, kernel density estimation, and local connectivity. It outperforms baselines on heterogeneous benchmarks in accuracy and parameter robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional hierarchical clustering methods compute inter-cluster similarity solely from pairwise distances, ignoring density variations and structural graph connectivity. This limitation motivates a unified approach that leverages density and graph structure for more accurate and robust clustering.

Method: DHC-ECS integrates three clustering paradigms. The core novelty is an inter-cluster similarity metric that combines (1) element categorization within KNN connection subgraphs, (2) kernel density estimation (KDE), and (3) local connectivity within sub-clusters. This metric guides the agglomerative/divisive merging or splitting decisions, and the method also explores an intrinsic threshold to reduce manual parameter dependence.

Result: Extensive evaluations on heterogeneous benchmark datasets show DHC-ECS achieves superior clustering accuracy and parameter robustness compared to AChameleon, RNN-DBSCAN, McDPC, and G-RMS, particularly for low-dimensional data.

Conclusion: The method demonstrates strong potential for low-dimensional clustering by exploiting the duality of vertices and edges (density + graph connectivity) and shows promise in determining intrinsic thresholds to minimize manual parameter tuning.

Abstract: Clustering is a fundamental data mining technique for pattern recognition through unsupervised learning. Among various clustering methods, hierarchical clustering, density-based clustering, and graph clustering stand out as representative approaches. For hierarchical clustering, it can be categorized into agglomerative and divisive modes to construct clusters in a recursive manner. The key aspect of both modes is the calculation of inter-cluster similarity, which determines whether to merge the sub-clusters into one cluster or divide a current cluster into sub-clusters. Traditionally, the similarity is derived from pairwise distances, often overlooking density variations and structural connectivity in graphs. To address this, we propose a density-aware hierarchical clustering method based on element-categorized connection subgraphs (DHC-ECS), which effectively integrates the hierarchical clustering, density-based clustering, and graph clustering. Particularly, a novel inter-cluster similarity metric is introduced that considers not only distances but also the element categorization in the KNN connection subgraphs, kernel density estimation, and local connectivity within sub-clusters. Extensive evaluations on heterogeneous benchmark datasets demonstrate that DHC-ECS exhibits superior overall performance in terms of clustering accuracy and parameter robustness compared with the baseline methods (including AChameleon, RNN-DBSCAN, McDPC, and G-RMS). The work indicates the great potential of the proposed clustering algorithm for low-dimensional datasets by leveraging local density and graph-structured connectivity (i.e., the duality of vertices and edges), as well as the possibility to determine an intrinsic threshold, reducing the reliance on manual parameter tuning.

</details>


### [104] [Beyond Foundation Models: Dimension-Aware Neural Architecture Search with Small-Data Representation Models for Cryocooler Lifetime Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06993)
*Gregor Molan,Grafika Jati,Francesco Barchi,Andrea Acquaviva,Aljaž Osterman,Martin Molan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes FSD-RM, a paradigm using capacity-controlled unsupervised representation learning with established encoders (CNN1D, LSTM, GRU, Transformer) and dimension-aware NAS for small-data telemetry, demonstrating competitive performance on cryocooler lifetime prediction without large-scale pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale pretrained time-series models require abundant, diverse data that industrial and scientific domains often lack. There is a need for practical representation learning approaches tailored to limited, domain-specific telemetry data where large-scale pretraining is infeasible.

Method: The FSD-RM paradigm employs capacity-controlled unsupervised representation learning using established encoder architectures (CNN1D, LSTM, GRU, Transformer) selected for small-data suitability and interpretability. These encoders are trained on multivariate telemetry and integrated into a two-stage pipeline for downstream lifetime prediction. Dimension-aware neural architecture search (NAS) jointly optimizes model capacity and input dimensionality to systematically examine architectural trade-offs under data constraints.

Result: Experiments on cryocooler telemetry data show the proposed approach achieves competitive predictive performance for lifetime prediction while reducing training cost and model complexity compared to large-scale pretrained alternatives.

Conclusion: Effective representation learning can be achieved without large-scale pretraining when appropriate inductive bias and capacity control are applied. The NAS-driven FSD-RM framework provides a coherent, practical solution for small-data industrial time-series domains.

Abstract: Large-scale pretrained time-series models achieve strong results through large-scale pretraining and task-agnostic representation learning, but they rely on abundant, diverse data that industrial and scientific domains often lack. We therefore propose the FSD-RM (Family of Small-Data Representation Models) paradigm as a practical alternative for limited, domain-specific telemetry. Rather than relying on large-scale pretraining, we focus on capacity-controlled representation learning using established encoder architectures (CNN1D, LSTM, GRU, Transformer), selected for their suitability in small-data settings and interpretability.
  These encoders are trained unsupervised on multivariate telemetry data and integrated into a two-stage pipeline for downstream lifetime prediction. To systematically examine architectural trade-offs under data constraints, we employ \textbf{dimension-aware neural architecture search (NAS)} to jointly optimize model capacity and input dimensionality.
  Experiments on cryocooler telemetry show that the proposed approach achieves competitive predictive performance while reducing training cost and model complexity. The contribution lies in combining established representation learning techniques within a coherent, NAS-driven framework tailored to small-data regimes, with explicitly defined parameter settings and design choices. The results indicate that effective representation learning can be achieved without large-scale pretraining when appropriate inductive bias and capacity control are applied.

</details>


### [105] [Every Cache Entry Earns Its Place: Global Allocation of Resolution and Coverage for KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07001)
*Haolin Tian,Yuzhe Liu,Tonghan Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GraceKV reformulates KV cache compression as a global resource allocation problem under a fixed budget, using a prototype tree structure to dynamically balance information coverage and local resolution across layers, heads, and context slots. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse long-context tasks without additional training, ranking first in 24 of 32 settings and remaining robust up to 128× compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KV cache compression methods rely on fixed, predefined rules (either token eviction or merging) that prevent free flow of cache resources across layers, heads, and context slots, and cannot jointly balance local resolution and information coverage. This motivates a global, adaptive allocation approach.

Method: GraceKV treats each (layer, head, slot) combination as an atomic unit and constructs a prototype tree where leaves are token-level KV entries and internal nodes use a single prototype to compress their children's KV space. A set of non-overlapping nodes forms each atomic unit's representation. Two actions—adding a new tree root (expanding coverage) or splitting a selected node (improving resolution)—compete globally for a shared cache budget. The final retained nodes across all trees form the compressed KV cache, adaptively determining allocation globally. No training is required; compression and inference run entirely on GPU.

Result: GraceKV ranks first in 24 out of 32 experimental settings across diverse long-context tasks and compression ratios, and remains robust even at 128× compression.

Conclusion: Global budget allocation that jointly coordinates information coverage and local resolution is highly effective for KV cache compression, as demonstrated by GraceKV's leading performance and robustness under extreme compression ratios.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long contexts, KV cache storage and repeated access have become a major bottleneck. Existing KV cache compression methods rely on predefined, fixed compression rules and are typically developed around either token eviction or merging. As a result, cache resources can neither flow freely across layers, heads, and context slots, nor be jointly allocated to balance local resolution and information coverage. Therefore, we propose GraceKV, a global approach for the allocation of resolution and coverage in KV cache compression, and formulate the compression process as a global resource allocation problem under a fixed cache budget. GraceKV treats each layer-KV head-slot combination as an atomic unit and builds a prototype tree. Leaf nodes correspond to token-level KV entries, while each internal node uses a single prototype to compress the KV space covered by its children. A set of non-overlapping nodes in the tree forms the representation of an atomic unit. Adding the root of a new tree expands information coverage, whereas splitting a selected node improves local resolution. All candidate actions compete globally for a shared cache budget. Finally, the nodes retained across all trees form the compressed KV cache. This process adaptively determines the allocation of cache resources among atomic units globally and the balance between resolution and coverage. GraceKV requires no additional training, and the entire compression and inference process is performed on the GPU. Systematic experiments across diverse long-context tasks and compression ratios show that GraceKV ranks first in 24 of 32 settings and remains robust up to 128-fold compression. These results validate the effectiveness of global budget allocation in coordinating information coverage and local resolution.

</details>


### [106] [Hyperbolic Graph Embedders for Link Prediction and Topology Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07029)
*Robert Jankowski,Maksim Kitsak,Dorota Celińska-Kopczyńska*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A benchmark of 13 unsupervised hyperbolic graph embedding methods reveals that maximum-likelihood and representation-learning approaches (including hybrids) perform best overall, though no single method dominates all tasks. Performance aligns more with embedding paradigm than disciplinary origin, with clear guidance on which methods suit different network regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hyperbolic embeddings are widely used for complex network representation, yet systematic, cross-disciplinary comparisons of embedding methods remain lacking. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a unified benchmark that evaluates both link prediction and structural preservation across diverse network types.

Method: The authors benchmark 13 unsupervised hyperbolic graph embedding methods from machine learning, network science, and algorithmics under a unified evaluation protocol. Evaluation covers link prediction (missing-link recovery) and topology reconstruction (preservation of local and global network structure), tested on both synthetic and empirical networks spanning different structural regimes.

Result: Maximum-likelihood and representation-learning-based approaches, including hybrid variants, achieve the strongest overall performance. However, no single method excels across all tasks and network regimes. Performance correlates more strongly with the embedding paradigm (e.g., distance-based vs. optimization-based) than with the disciplinary origin of the method.

Conclusion: The study identifies which embedding paradigms succeed or fail under specific network regimes and provides practical guidance for practitioners selecting hyperbolic embedding methods for downstream applications. It underscores the need for task- and structure-aware method selection rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

Abstract: Hyperbolic embeddings provide compact geometric representations of complex networks in hyperbolic spaces, but systematic comparisons of methods developed in machine learning, network science, and algorithmics remain rare. We benchmark 13 unsupervised hyperbolic graph embedders under a unified protocol for link prediction and topology reconstruction on synthetic and empirical networks. The protocol captures both missing-link recovery and the preservation of local and global network structure. Maximum-likelihood and representation-learning-based approaches, including hybrid variants, achieve the strongest overall performance, although no method dominates across all tasks and structural regimes. Performance is more strongly associated with embedding paradigm than with disciplinary origin. We identify the network regimes in which different paradigms succeed or fail and provide practical guidance for method selection in downstream applications.

</details>


### [107] [Accounting Graph Transformer for Short-History Multi-KPI Forecasting in Small Businesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07037)
*Shrutendra Harsola,Vignesh Subrahmaniam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AGT, a 5.3M-parameter graph transformer, jointly forecasts 13 financial KPIs across four statement types from 71 monthly ledger series, outperforming LightGBM, TimeMixer, and SOFTS on 11,993 forecast origins from 1,060 unseen small businesses, with relational attention and recency path ablations confirming each component's contribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small businesses typically have limited accounting history (12–24 months), yet financial planning and risk assessment workflows demand coordinated, multi-statement forecasts. Existing approaches fail to jointly model the structural relationships across income statements, balance sheets, cash flows, and working-capital KPIs in a unified manner.

Method: The Accounting Graph Transformer (AGT) encodes 71 monthly ledger series as masked tokens, applies typed attention over a fixed accounting-relation graph to exchange information, pools target-specific context, and fuses this with a gated three-month recency path. A single 5.3M-parameter model produces all 156 aligned forecasts (13 KPIs × 12 months) without company-specific fitting.

Result: AGT achieves sample-weighted KPI-macro MAE of 0.6990 ± 0.0013 versus LightGBM's 0.7378 ± 0.0014. Paired bootstrap gives a LightGBM-minus-AGT difference of 0.0395 (95% CI [0.0350, 0.0439]). AGT wins on all 13 KPIs against LightGBM, TimeMixer, and SOFTS. Ablations confirm relational attention, accounting topology, and recency path each improve accuracy. On 7,094 additional unseen 2025 companies, AGT achieves 0.7548 MAE versus SOFTS's 0.7694.

Conclusion: AGT provides a single, unified forecasting layer for integrated planning, liquidity, and working-capital analysis, demonstrating that explicitly encoding accounting-structure priors into a transformer architecture yields robust multi-KPI forecasts from limited historical data.

Abstract: Small businesses often have only 12-24 months of accounting history, yet planning and risk workflows require coordinated forecasts across financial statements. We study joint 12-month forecasting of 13 income-statement, balance-sheet, cash-flow, and working-capital key performance indicators (KPIs) from 71 monthly ledger series. We introduce the Accounting Graph Transformer (AGT), which represents each ledger series as a masked token, exchanges information through typed attention on a fixed accounting-relation graph, pools target-specific context, and fuses it with a gated three-month recency path. Across 11,993 forecast origins from 1,060 unseen companies, AGT achieves sample-weighted KPI-macro mean absolute error (MAE) $0.6990 \pm 0.0013$ over three independent seeds, compared with $0.7378 \pm 0.0014$ for the strongest baseline, LightGBM. At the pre-specified seed 42, a paired company-clustered bootstrap gives a LightGBM-minus-AGT difference of 0.0395 with 95% confidence interval (CI) $[0.0350,0.0439]$. AGT is best on all 13 KPIs against LightGBM, TimeMixer, and SOFTS in the matched seed-42 comparison, while final-architecture ablations show that relational attention, accounting topology, and the recency path each improve validation and test accuracy. On 7,094 additional unseen companies with origins sampled from January-May 2025, AGT obtains 0.7548 MAE versus 0.7694 for SOFTS. A single 5.3M-parameter model produces 156 aligned forecasts without company-specific fitting, providing one forecasting layer for integrated planning, liquidity, and working-capital analysis.

</details>


### [108] [Beyond Isolation: Unlocking Reinforcement Learning Component Synergy for Sample-Efficient Continuous Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07086)
*Qi Zhao,Guozheng Ma,Yilun Kong,Lu Li,Haoyu Wang,Zilin Wang,Tiantian Zhang,Yuxing Wang,Jian Sha,Yongzhe Chang,Xueqian Wang,Dacheng Tao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates interdependencies among RL components (model-based representation, optimization stability, experience replay), finds that naive stacking causes emergent issues like compounded non-stationarity, and proposes ROSER — a principled framework coordinating these three dimensions that achieves 17.60% gains over naive stacking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL system design requires jointly accounting for many tightly coupled factors, yet the functional interdependencies between algorithmic components (whether they exhibit synergy or interference) remain underexplored. The authors aim to systematically understand these interactions and develop principled coordination strategies.

Method: Systematic investigation of component interactions across tasks, followed by distillation of actionable design insights. Based on these, ROSER is proposed as a coordinated framework spanning three dimensions: Model-based Representation, Optimization Stability, and Experience Replay. Evaluated on diverse continuous-control benchmarks.

Result: Component efficacy is strongly task-dependent; naive stacking of SOTA techniques often fails to yield gains and triggers emergent challenges like compounded non-stationarity. ROSER consistently outperforms vanilla baselines with 17.60% improvement over naive stacking.

Conclusion: Holistic, coordinated design is necessary in RL system development. Principled coordination of components enables sample-efficient agents and avoids the pitfalls of naive composition.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning systems are significantly more complex than other machine learning paradigms due to inherent properties, causing RL system design to jointly account for many tightly coupled factors. Despite advances in individual algorithmic components, their functional interdependencies remain underexplored: do they exhibit mutual synergy or counterproductive interference? To bridge this gap, we conduct a systematic investigation and find that the efficacy of different components exhibits significant task-dependency, and naively stacking state-of-the-art techniques does not necessarily yield performance gains; instead, it often triggers emergent challenges, such as compounded non-stationarity. Building upon these findings, we distill a suite of actionable insights into the principled coordination of these components. Guided by these insights, we propose ROSER, an RL framework that coordinates three critical dimensions: Model-based Representation, Optimization Stability, and Experience Replay. Across diverse continuous-control benchmarks, ROSER consistently outperforms vanilla baselines and achieves 17.60% gains over naive stack. Our findings underscore the necessity of a holistic perspective in RL system design and paves the way for developing sample-efficient agents.

</details>


### [109] [Synthetic LiDAR Data Generation and Deterministic Downsampling for Point Cloud Classification on the Edge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07106)
*Niclas Meyer,Stefan Reitmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a hardware-constrained 3D deep learning pipeline for the Raspberry Pi 5, using a Critical Points Layer to compress point clouds and achieve ~50 FPS inference at 88.36% accuracy, while demonstrating the importance of sensor-aware synthetic LiDAR training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying 3D deep learning on low-power embedded processors is bottlenecked by unstructured spatial data and expensive distance-sorting algorithms. Additionally, there exists a reality gap between clean CAD datasets and real-world sensor data that degrades model performance.

Method: The authors construct a synthetic LiDAR dataset via physics-based simulation to bridge the CAD-to-real gap. They then integrate a feature-driven Critical Points Layer (CPL) as a frontend filter to replace traditional geometric preprocessing, deterministically compressing 1024-point clouds to 40–60 unique coordinates. The full pipeline is profiled on the ARM Cortex-A76 of a Raspberry Pi 5.

Result: Cross-dataset evaluation reveals a substantial accuracy drop when CAD-trained networks are tested on synthetic LiDAR data, validating the need for sensor-aware training. The CPL-based pipeline achieves ~50 FPS inference throughput with 88.36% instance classification accuracy on the embedded processor.

Conclusion: Deterministic real-time 3D perception at the edge is viable through sensor-aware synthetic training and learned point cloud compression via the Critical Points Layer, enabling efficient native execution on resource-constrained embedded hardware like the Raspberry Pi 5.

Abstract: Deploying three-dimensional deep learning frameworks to low-power embedded processors is bottlenecked by the unstructured nature of spatial data and the resource-intensive distance sorting algorithms often used before neural network inference. To address this gap, this paper presents a hardware-constrained workflow optimized for native execution on the Raspberry Pi 5. To account for the reality gap between noiseless, clean computer-aided design (CAD) datasets and real-world sensor data, we use physics-based simulation to construct a synthetic LiDAR dataset. Cross-dataset evaluations demonstrate a substantial drop in classification accuracy when networks trained on clean CAD data are evaluated on synthetic LiDAR sensor data, highlighting the critical need for sensor-aware training. To address the latency bottleneck of traditional geometric preprocessing on edge CPUs, we integrate an isolated, feature-driven Critical Points Layer (CPL) as a frontend filter. Our results show that the pretrained CPL deterministically compresses raw 1024-point clouds to a subset of 40 to 60 unique coordinates. When profiled on the ARM Cortex-A76 processor, the complete pipeline achieves an inference throughput of approximately 50 FPS while maintaining an instance classification accuracy of 88.36%, demonstrating the viability of deterministic real-time 3D perception at the edge.

</details>


### [110] [Modular TTT: Rethinking Test-Time Training as Composable Modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07110)
*Bohao Tang,Zhen Qin,Yuqi Pan,Zheng Li,Pengfei Liu,Ya Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Modular TTT is a framework that decomposes test-time training into explicit design dimensions (fast-weight network, loss, learning rate, weight decay, normalization), enabling systematic ablation. Key findings: small LR initialization, weight decay, and single-layer nonlinearity help; deeper networks and normalization hurt; the resulting 410M–1.45B models match Gated DeltaNet on 100B tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TTT variants are hard-coded independently, obscuring which components matter and impeding the design of new methods. A unified, modular framework is needed to systematically isolate and evaluate each design choice.

Method: The authors propose Modular TTT, which represents the inner learner as a directed acyclic graph. It decomposes TTT into five design dimensions (fast-weight network, loss function, learning rate, weight decay, normalization) and auto-composes primitive-level train-view forward/backward and causal query-view rules into the full graph-level computation, including fast-weight state transitions.

Result: Small learning-rate initialization, weight decay, and a single-layer nonlinearity improve performance. MSE and inner-product losses perform similarly. Deeper fast-weight networks and normalization hurt due to excessively large activations. Residual connections and gating offer marginal benefit. Models at 410M and 1.45B parameters trained on 100B tokens achieve training loss and benchmark performance comparable to Gated DeltaNet.

Conclusion: Modular TTT enables principled ablation of TTT components, revealing that simplicity (shallow networks, no normalization, small LR init, weight decay) suffices for strong performance. The framework facilitates future TTT research by making design choices explicit and composable.

Abstract: Test-time training (TTT) views sequence modeling as an online learning problem in which fast weights are updated by an internal learning rule. Despite the growing number of TTT variants, existing approaches typically hard-code each variant separately, which makes it difficult to design new TTT methods and to isolate the role of each component. To address this, we propose Modular TTT, a framework that represents the inner learner as a directed acyclic graph and exposes the fast-weight network, loss function, learning rate, weight decay, and normalization as explicit design dimensions. Modular TTT automatically composes primitive-level train-view forward, train-view backward, and causal query-view rules into the full graph-level TTT computation, including the fast-weight state transition. Using Modular TTT, we systematically ablate the components of TTT and find that small learning-rate initialization, weight decay, and a single-layer nonlinearity improve performance, while MSE and inner-product losses perform similarly. Deeper fast-weight networks and normalization tend to hurt performance because they induce excessively large activations, while residual connections and gating provide little measurable benefit. Guided by these findings, we train the best resulting variant as 410M- and 1.45B-parameter models on 100B tokens, and observe training loss and benchmark performance comparable to Gated DeltaNet.

</details>


### [111] [Online Conformal Prediction Beyond Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07139)
*Joar Skalse,Edoardo Pona,Osvaldo Simeone,Nicola Paoletti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces OCP with queries (OCPQ), a method for online conformal prediction where the learner cannot receive feedback on deployed predictions and must instead explicitly query labels. By framing this as a partial monitoring game and adapting a label-efficient forecaster, OCPQ achieves strong coverage guarantees with minimal label queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many safety-critical applications, deployed prediction sets cannot be directly evaluated (no feedback), making standard online conformal prediction infeasible. The authors aim to provide principled uncertainty quantification in this "beyond feedback" setting where the learner must choose between outputting a prediction set or querying the true label—but cannot do both simultaneously.

Method: The problem is reduced to a partial monitoring game with two action types: prediction actions (which yield no observation) and query actions (which reveal the label). The reward function is designed to balance small prediction sets with high coverage probability. The authors adapt the label-efficient forecaster of Cesa-Bianchi, Lugosi, and Stoltz (2004) to develop OCPQ, which strategically decides when to query labels versus when to output prediction sets.

Result: For any black-box classifier and non-i.i.d. oblivious data stream of length T, OCPQ achieves O(T^{2/3}) expected regret and expected coverage of at least β - O(T^{-1/3}), while querying only an expected T^{-1/3} fraction of rounds. Experiments on real-world datasets validate the approach's effectiveness.

Conclusion: OCPQ provides coverage guarantees comparable to bandit-based OCP methods but crucially requires no feedback from deployed prediction sets. This expands the applicability of online conformal prediction to settings where direct evaluation of predictions is impossible or impractical.

Abstract: Uncertainty quantification is essential when deploying machine learning models in safety-critical applications. Online conformal prediction (OCP) provides theoretically principled uncertainty quantification for arbitrary black-box classifiers and non-i.i.d. data streams by constructing prediction sets that are guaranteed to contain the true label at a user-specified frequency. OCP usually updates prediction sets using feedback from previously deployed predictions. We instead study an OCP setting beyond feedback: on each round, the learner can either output a prediction set or query the correct label, but not both. Thus, no deployed prediction is ever evaluated directly. We reduce this problem to a partial monitoring game in which prediction actions return no observation and a separate query action reveals the label. The reward function is constructed in a way that encourages the learner to output small prediction sets while ensuring that the correct label is covered with a sufficiently high probability. To solve this game, we develop OCP with queries (OCPQ) by adapting the label efficient forecaster of Cesa-Bianchi, Lugosi, and Stoltz (2004) to our setting. For any black box classifier and any (non-i.i.d.) oblivious data stream of length $T$, OCPQ has $O(T^{2/3})$ expected regret and expected coverage at least $β-O(T^{-1/3})$ for a user-defined $β$, while querying only an expected $T^{-1/3}$ fraction of rounds. This provides coverage comparable to bandit-based OCP methods while requiring no feedback from deployed prediction sets. Experiments on real-world datasets further demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

</details>


### [112] [Interpretable reinforcement learning with decision-tree pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07151)
*Mark Leon Ringer,Michel Tokic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A pruning process is proposed to simplify decision-tree rules extracted from reinforcement learning policies, balancing interpretability and task performance. It uses structural operators and re-execution-based evaluation to transform complex policies into compact, auditable forms, validated on classic control and MuJoCo benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning policies are opaque and difficult to interpret, yet trustworthiness requires transparency. Converting policies to decision-tree rules helps, but the resulting trees often remain too complex for human comprehension. A method is needed to simplify these rule-based policies without sacrificing performance.

Method: The authors define a small set of structural and usage-aware pruning operators. Candidate edits are evaluated by re-executing the policy to measure both return (task performance) and interpretability proxies. This iterative process exposes a transformation pathway from complex to compact policy structures.

Result: On classic control and MuJoCo benchmarks, the pruning traces consistently show improved interpretability metrics while maintaining high task performance. The approach produces more compact, auditable decision-tree policies.

Conclusion: The pruning process effectively simplifies rule-based RL policies into more interpretable forms without degrading performance, making edits auditable and increasing trustworthiness of the resulting policies.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning policies are difficult to inspect, but interpreting them is a prerequisite for trustworthiness. Converting a trained policy into explicit decision-tree rules improves transparency and the resulting artifacts often remain too complex for human understanding. We present a pruning process that simplifies such rule-based policies while preserving task performance and making edits to the policy auditable. The process defines a small set of structural and usage-aware operators and evaluates candidate edits by re-executing the policy to measure return and interpretability proxies. This exposes an transformation process from complex to compact policy structures. We investigate this approach on classic control and MuJoCo benchmarks, where pruning traces reveal consistent interpretability improvements while maintaining high performance.

</details>


### [113] [Machine Learning-Based Inter-Crystal Scatter Recovery for Ultra-High Resolution PET Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07155)
*Alexandre Bernier,Roger Lecomte,Jean-Baptiste Michaud*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A feed-forward neural network recovers inter-crystal scatter events in ultrahigh-resolution PET, increasing sensitivity by 70–106% while preserving sub-millimeter spatial resolution (down to 1.6 mm), enabling shorter scans and lower radiation doses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events in UHR-PET, exacerbated by smaller pixelated detectors, force a trade-off: rejecting ICS events reduces sensitivity, while accepting them with suboptimal positioning degrades spatial resolution. There is a need for a method that recovers ICS events without compromising image quality.

Method: A feed-forward neural network that infers the line-of-response corresponding to the first Compton interaction from ICS events. Validated on Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data from fully pixelated LabPET-II preclinical and brain UHR-PET scanners.

Result: Sensitivity increased by 70% to 106% while maintaining sub-millimeter spatial resolvability (down to 1.6 mm) compared to conventional methods.

Conclusion: The neural network-based ICS recovery approach effectively compensates for the lower detection efficiency of small pixelated detectors in UHR-PET, enabling reduced scan times and lower radiation doses while largely preserving image quality.

Abstract: Inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events pose a significant challenge in ultrahigh- resolution positron emission tomography (UHR-PET), especially as detector crystals become smaller and their readouts increasingly segmented. Current approaches either reject these events, reducing sensitivity, or accept them with suboptimal positioning algorithms, degrading image resolution. We present a feed forward neural network to optimize ICS event recovery by inferring the line-of-response belonging to the first Compton interaction. Our approach was validated using both Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data from the fully pixelated LabPET-IIbased preclinical and brain UHR-PET scanners.Results demonstrate a 70% to 106% increase in sensitivity while preserving sub-millimeter spatial resolvability (down to 1.6 mm) compared to conventional methods.
