This ICS recovery approach is an effective solution that compensates for the lower detection efficiency of small, pixelated detectors in UHR-PET, enabling reduced scan times and lower radiation doses while largely preserving image quality.

</details>


### [114] [Capacity Confounds and Coverage Guarantees in Adaptive Sub-model Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07157)
*Alireza Moayedikia,Alicia Troncoso Lora*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In sub-model federated learning, using server-observed updates to estimate client data heterogeneity for capacity allocation is fundamentally confounded by device capacity. HAS-FL experiments reveal that update-based heterogeneity estimates correlate negatively with capacity, not data, and adaptive allocation fails unless full parameter coverage is guaranteed. Random allocation matches adaptive methods given equal budgets, suggesting coverage—not allocation intelligence—drives accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work in sub-model FL allocates sub-model widths based solely on device resources. A repeatedly suggested natural extension is to also allocate capacity according to each client's data heterogeneity, estimated from the updates the server already receives. This paper investigates whether that step is actually feasible and beneficial.

Method: The authors use HAS-FL, an adaptive capacity-allocation framework, as a test case. They (1) validate update-divergence estimates against ground-truth label-distribution divergence across reproducible partitions, (2) test adaptive allocation under varying coverage conditions, and (3) run matched-budget control experiments comparing adaptive, random, and uniform allocation strategies on both image benchmarks and a naturally partitioned text benchmark.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Update-divergence estimates of client heterogeneity are dominated by capacity, correlating strongly and negatively with device capacity; no data signal remains after controlling for capacity. (2) Adaptive allocation has a hidden failure mode where uncovered parameters (when all clients are capped below full width) stay at random initialization and progressively corrupt the global model; a simple coverage guarantee removes this failure. (3) Random allocation with matched average budget performs identically to adaptive on image benchmarks; on the text benchmark, adaptive is the weakest strategy while consuming the most capacity.

Conclusion: Sub-model training is valuable for admitting constrained clients at quadratically reduced cost, but what protects accuracy is parameter coverage rather than allocation intelligence. Apparent benefits of adaptive methods stem from capacity budgeting and coverage. Future designs need heterogeneity signals that are separable from capacity effects.

Abstract: Sub-model federated learning lets resource-constrained clients train width-reduced versions of a global model, but existing methods allocate capacity by device resources alone. A natural next step, allocating capacity by each client's data heterogeneity as estimated from the updates the server already observes, has been repeatedly suggested. We ask whether that step is possible, using HAS-FL, an adaptive capacity-allocation framework, as a test case. Our findings are threefold. First, validated against ground-truth label-distribution divergence on reproducible partitions, update-divergence estimates of client heterogeneity are dominated by capacity rather than data: across two corrected estimators, multiple datasets, and all seeds, the estimates correlate strongly and negatively with device capacity, and no data signal remains once capacity is controlled for. This previously undocumented confound affects any method estimating client statistics from sub-model updates. Second, adaptive allocation has a hidden failure mode: when every client is capped below full width, the uncovered parameters stay at random initialization and progressively corrupt the global model. A simple coverage guarantee removes the failure and explains why uniform allocation collapses. Third, a matched-budget control settles what adaptivity contributes: random allocation to the same average budget performs no differently on both image benchmarks, and on the naturally partitioned text benchmark the adaptive policy is the weakest of the three strategies while consuming the most capacity. Sub-model training remains valuable because it admits constrained clients at quadratically reduced cost, but what protects accuracy is parameter coverage rather than allocation intelligence. Its apparent benefits come from capacity budgeting and coverage, and future designs need heterogeneity signals separable from capacity effects.

</details>


### [115] [Edge Sparsification via Temporal Forman-Ricci Curvature for Dynamic Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07158)
*Poupak Azad,Cuneyt Gurcan Akcora,Kiarash Shamsi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRicci proposes a Forman-Ricci curvature-based edge sparsification framework for temporal graphs, achieving ~80% sparsification and ~56% reduction in training/inference time without significant performance loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning from large-scale temporal graphs is computationally challenging, especially when networks are dense and rapidly changing. Existing methods lack principled sparsification techniques that preserve temporal-structural information critical for downstream tasks.

Method: TRicci extends classical Forman-Ricci curvature to directed weighted temporal graphs by incorporating three components: structural support, temporal recency, and local interaction competition. Edges with low temporal curvature scores are pruned, yielding a sparse subgraph that retains predictive temporal-structural information.

Result: On 9 transaction networks and 3 temporal graph benchmark datasets, TRicci achieved approximately 80% edge sparsification while reducing end-to-end training and inference time by an average of 55.94%, without substantial degradation in predictive performance across multiple graph-level prediction tasks.

Conclusion: Temporal curvature provides a principled and effective basis for scalable temporal graph learning, enabling substantial sparsification while preserving critical predictive information.

Abstract: Temporal graph learning has become essential for analyzing real-world systems whose interactions continuously evolve over time, including financial transaction networks, communication systems, and online social platforms. However, learning from large-scale temporal graphs remains computationally challenging when networks are dense and rapidly changing. To address this limitation, we propose a network-curvature-inspired edge sparsification framework for dynamic graph learning. Our proposed method, TRicci, extends classical Forman-Ricci curvature to directed weighted temporal graphs by capturing structural support, temporal recency, and local interaction competition.
  Experiments on 9 transaction networks and 3 temporal graph benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework preserves predictive performance across multiple graph-level prediction tasks. The results show that TRicci sparsifies temporal graphs by approximately 80% while reducing end-to-end downstream training and inference time by an average of 55.94%, without substantial degradation in predictive performance. Our findings suggest that temporal curvature can serve as a principled basis for scalable temporal graph learning by preserving predictive temporal-structural information under substantial sparsification.

</details>


### [116] [Fluid-DiT: Graph-Free Diffusion Transformers for Fluid Flow Simulations Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07161)
*Shentong Mo,Guolin Ke*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fluid-DiT introduces a graph-free diffusion transformer for simulating complex fluid flows, replacing hand-crafted graph message passing with attention-based denoising in latent space. It achieves superior distributional accuracy and scalability over graph-based methods across laminar and turbulent benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph-based diffusion models (e.g., DGNs) for fluid simulation are limited by hand-crafted architectural constraints, restricted receptive fields in message passing, and expensive multi-scale designs, hindering scalability to larger, more complex domains.

Method: Fluid-DiT employs a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) operating in latent space. The latent formulation disentangles geometric fidelity from distributional learning, reducing high-frequency artifacts. The transformer's global self-attention replaces graph message passing, naturally capturing both local structures and long-range correlations without hierarchical graph coarsening.

Result: Fluid-DiT consistently outperforms graph-based diffusion baselines on laminar cylinder wakes, ellipse-flow systems, and turbulent 3D wing experiments, achieving higher R² correlations and lower Wasserstein distances. It generalizes robustly from short, incomplete trajectories to unseen Reynolds numbers and geometries.

Conclusion: Eliminating explicit graph design via transformer-based diffusion in latent space yields a scalable, accurate framework for distribution-aware fluid simulation that surpasses graph-based approaches in both quality and generalization.

Abstract: Simulating complex fluid flows requires capturing full equilibrium distributions rather than just mean trajectories, yet high-fidelity solvers remain computationally prohibitive. Recent advances, such as Diffusion Graph Networks (DGNs), have combined diffusion models with graph neural networks to sample equilibrium states directly from unstructured meshes, enabling distributional accuracy even from short simulations. However, graph-based diffusion approaches suffer from hand-crafted architectural constraints, limited receptive fields in message passing, and costly multi-scale designs, which restrict scalability to larger and more complex domains. We propose Fluid-DiT, a Graph-Free Diffusion Transformer that replaces graph message passing with attention-based denoising, eliminating explicit graph design while preserving the ability to model distributions of chaotic flows. Our framework introduces a latent-space formulation that disentangles geometric fidelity from distributional learning, reducing high-frequency artifacts and accelerating sampling. By leveraging the transformer's global receptive field, Fluid-DiT naturally captures both local flow structures and long-range correlations without requiring hierarchical graph coarsening. On canonical benchmarks including laminar cylinder wakes, ellipse-flow systems, and turbulent 3D wing experiments, Fluid-DiT consistently outperforms graph-based diffusion baselines in both sample quality and distributional accuracy, achieving higher $R^2$ correlations and lower Wasserstein distances. Moreover, it generalizes robustly from short, incomplete trajectories to unseen Reynolds numbers and geometries, demonstrating strong scalability.

</details>


### [117] [Momba: Network Modernization Improves Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07180)
*Adam Štafa,Santeri Heiskanen,Petr Novotný,Joni Pajarinen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Integrating modern neural network design techniques—input/feature normalization, weight normalization, and distributional return modeling—into a multi-objective RL algorithm significantly improves solution set quality across standard continuous control benchmarks, without modifying the core algorithm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-objective RL (MORL) research has focused heavily on algorithmic innovations while neglecting neural network architecture design. Since optimal policies and value functions vary substantially with different trade-off preferences, the commonly used simple feedforward networks conditioned on trade-offs may limit performance. The authors hypothesize that more expressive function approximators could yield better results.

Method: The paper integrates three recent neural network advances into an entropy-regularized MORL algorithm: (i) observation and feature normalization, (ii) weight normalization, and (iii) distributional modeling of returns. These architectural improvements are evaluated without altering the underlying MORL algorithm.

Result: The empirical evaluation across standard continuous control benchmarks shows that these architectural changes substantially improve the quality of the produced solution sets (i.e., the set of policies balancing trade-offs among conflicting objectives).

Conclusion: Neural network architecture design is an underexplored yet impactful dimension in MORL. Simple architectural enhancements borrowed from single-objective deep RL can significantly boost MORL performance without requiring algorithmic changes, suggesting a promising direction for future MORL research.

Abstract: Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (RL) have shown that improving neural network architectures can yield substantial gains in sample efficiency and asymptotic performance without altering the underlying algorithms. In contrast, work on multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), which aims to discover a set of policies that balance trade-offs among conflicting objectives, has predominantly focused on algorithmic innovations, leaving the area of architectures underexplored. While the optimal policies and value functions can differ significantly depending on the trade-offs, MORL algorithms commonly represent them with simple feedforward networks conditioned on the trade-off. This raises the question of whether the performance of the algorithms could be improved with more expressive function approximators. In this paper, we integrate recent advances in neural network design: (i) observation and feature normalization, (ii) weight normalization, and (iii) modeling of distributional returns with an entropy-regularized MORL algorithm. The empirical results across standard continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that these changes substantially improve the quality of the produced solution sets without requiring major changes to the underlying algorithm.

</details>


### [118] [Conformal Fusion Under Missing Modalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07183)
*Alireza Moayedikia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MCCF combines modality-dropout-trained fusion, evidential Dirichlet heads, Dempster-Shafer combination, and Mondrian conformal calibration to provide formal, modality-conditioned coverage guarantees under arbitrary missing modalities without sacrificing accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal fusion research treats missing modalities as a prediction-accuracy problem, neglecting whether model confidence estimates remain calibrated when entire input streams are missing. The authors argue that missing-modality robustness and calibrated uncertainty are fundamentally coupled and should be addressed jointly.

Method: MCCF integrates four components: (1) a multimodal bottleneck fusion backbone trained with modality dropout; (2) per-modality evidential heads that produce modality-decomposed Dirichlet distributions; (3) a Dempster-Shafer combination rule that fuses per-modality evidence, where absent modalities contribute vacuous evidence that is structurally ignored; and (4) a Mondrian conformal calibration module keyed on the modality-presence mask, providing finite-sample group-conditional coverage guarantees for every non-empty modality subset.

Result: Across a synthetic problem and three real multimodal benchmarks, MCCF maintains target coverage on every modality-presence subset, substantially narrows the coverage gap between full and partial modalities versus a marginal split-conformal baseline, and imposes no measurable accuracy cost relative to temperature-scaled and evidential baselines.

Conclusion: MCCF is the first method to provide formal coverage guarantees under arbitrary modality availability through architectural integration rather than post-hoc recalibration. The evidential decomposition also yields per-modality vacuity scores that localize uncertainty to the absent modality responsible.

Abstract: Multimodal fusion architectures typically assume all modalities are available at inference, yet sensor failures, acquisition variability, and cost constraints routinely produce incomplete observations. Existing work treats modality absence as a prediction-accuracy problem, leaving a more basic question unanswered: whether a model's confidence estimates remain calibrated when an entire input stream is removed. We argue that missing-modality robustness and calibrated uncertainty are a single coupled property, and introduce Modality-Conditioned Conformal Fusion (MCCF), an architecture that addresses both at once. MCCF combines a multimodal bottleneck fusion backbone trained with modality dropout, per-modality evidential heads producing modality-decomposed Dirichlet distributions, and a Dempster-Shafer combination rule that fuses the per-modality evidence into a joint predictive distribution; an absent modality contributes vacuous evidence that is structurally ignored, so the fused uncertainty automatically reflects the reduced information without test-time imputation. A Mondrian conformal calibration module keyed on the modality-presence mask then provides finite-sample group-conditional coverage for every non-empty modality subset. MCCF is, to our knowledge, the first method with formal coverage guarantees under arbitrary modality availability through architectural integration rather than post-hoc recalibration, and the evidential decomposition yields per-modality vacuity scores that localise uncertainty to the absent modality responsible. Across a synthetic problem and three real multimodal benchmarks, MCCF holds its target coverage on every modality-presence subset, substantially narrows the coverage gap between full and partial modalities relative to a marginal split-conformal baseline, and imposes no measurable accuracy cost relative to temperature-scaled and evidential baselines.

</details>


### [119] [MAUPITI: On-Device Prototype-Based Learning on a Smart Infrared Sensor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07192)
*Beatrice Alessandra Motetti,Tanguy Dugas du Villard,Matteo Risso,Alessio Burrello,Francesco Daghero,Enrico Macii,Massimo Poncino,Marco Castellano,Alfio Basile,Daniele Jahier Pagliari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A smart IR sensor combining a 16×16 thermal MOSFET array with a RISC-V microcontroller uses a prototype-based Nearest Class Mean classifier for on-device, privacy-preserving pose and gesture recognition under severe resource constraints (~1.5 mW, <32 kB memory), enabling online adaptation without backpropagation or replay buffers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable privacy-preserving, low-power human sensing on embedded devices by circumventing the memory and computational overhead of traditional on-device learning (backpropagation, replay buffers) for continual adaptation.

Method: A CNN encoder is trained and quantized offline to extract features. On-device, a Nearest Class Mean (NCM) classifier stores and incrementally updates class prototypes in streaming mode, while low-precision SIMD extensions on the RISC-V core accelerate inference. No backpropagation or replay buffer is required.

Result: The approach achieves accuracy comparable to conventional classifiers with negligible latency overhead (<0.29% for both classification and prototype update phases) on two pose/gesture datasets.

Conclusion: Prototype-based NCM with offline-quantized CNN encoders is a viable strategy for ultra-low-power, on-device continual learning in smart IR sensors, matching conventional accuracy while avoiding memory-heavy training components.

Abstract: Low-resolution infrared (IR) array sensors represent an interesting solution for privacy-preserving human sensing in embedded systems. In this letter, we describe a smart multi-pixel IR sensor integrating a 16$\times$16 thermal MOSFET (TMOS) array and a RISC-V microcontroller extended with low-precision SIMD instructions, capable of on-device learning and continual adaptation for pose and gesture recognition tasks under tight memory and power constraints ($<$32kB on-chip memory, $\approx$1.5mW). To avoid the memory overheads of backpropagation and replay buffers, we adopt a prototype-based Nearest Class Mean (NCM) classifier in which a simple Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) encoder is trained and quantized offline, while class prototypes are stored and updated on the device in streaming mode. With experiments on two datasets, we show that this approach yields accuracy on par with a conventional classifier, with negligible latency overheads in both the classification and the prototype update ($<$0.29% considering both phases), effectively enabling online adaptation of the perception framework.

</details>


### [120] [An AI4AI Framework for Visual Token Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07193)
*Zhen Liu,Wenli Huang,Wei Song,Yuhan Liu,Zhiqin Yang,Jingwen Fu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoPrune uses LLMs to automatically design visual-token pruning policies for MLLMs, introducing a domain-specific language (TPDSL) with 131 reusable atoms and a residual search formulation, achieving near-lossless performance even when removing 94.4% of visual tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual-token pruning methods for MLLMs depend on fixed, handcrafted heuristics requiring costly expert trial and error. As pruning objectives, budgets, and model architectures diversify, manual design becomes infeasible. The authors ask whether LLMs can automate this design process, but note that translating LLMs' general algorithmic knowledge into domain-specific pruning solutions is nontrivial without an appropriate search-state representation.

Method: AutoPrune is a training-free framework where an LLM searches over a Token Pruning Domain-Specific Language (TPDSL) containing 131 reusable atoms spanning budget control, token scoring, selection constraints, and token reassembly. Each search state is represented as a residual modification of a strong base policy, which narrows the search space and focuses the LLM on the most consequential policy components. The LLM iteratively proposes, evaluates, and refines pruning policies using this structured representation.

Result: Evaluated on 14 multimodal benchmarks with three MLLM backbones, AutoPrune achieves over 99% of full-token performance while removing 94.4% of visual tokens, reducing FLOPs by 9.9× and prefill latency by 6.4×. The discovered policies demonstrate effectiveness, efficiency, and transferability across architectures.

Conclusion: An appropriately designed search-state representation — concretely, TPDSL with its residual formulation — successfully bridges LLMs' general reasoning capabilities with the structural constraints of visual-token pruning, enabling automated, training-free design of highly effective pruning policies that significantly outperform handcrafted baselines.

Abstract: Visual-token pruning can substantially reduce the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing methods largely rely on fixed, handcrafted heuristics and costly expert trial and error. As pruning objectives, budgets, and model architectures diversify, manually navigating the expanding design space becomes increasingly difficult. This paper aims to build an AI4AI framework for visual-token pruning by addressing a natural question: Can large language models automatically design effective visual-token reduction algorithms? Although LLMs possess broad algorithmic knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, translating such general knowledge into effective solutions for a specialized task remains nontrivial. We argue that the key lies in designing an appropriate search-state representation that connects the internal knowledge of LLMs with the structural requirements and constraints of visual-token pruning. Based on this insight, we propose AutoPrune, a training-free framework for LLM-driven visual-token pruning policy design. At its core, AutoPrune introduces a Token Pruning Domain-Specific Language (TPDSL) comprising 131 reusable atoms for budget control, token scoring, selection constraints, and token reassembly. A key property of TPDSL is that it represents each search state as a residual modification of a strong base policy. This residual formulation narrows the search space and directs the LLM's attention toward the policy components that are most consequential for performance. Experiments on 14 multimodal benchmarks and three MLLM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness, efficiency, and transferability of AutoPrune. Even when removing 94.4% of visual tokens, AutoPrune preserves more than 99% of full-token performance while reducing FLOPs by 9.9x and prefill latency by 6.4x.

</details>


### [121] [Stochastic Autoregressive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07224)
*Ilan Doron-Arad,Idan Mehalel,Elchanan Mossel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces a PAC-learning model for binary stochastic autoregressive generation, contrasting three supervision forms (one-step, chain-of-thought, end-to-end). Shows fundamental differences from deterministic theory: no universal comparison between tasks at fixed scale, but tight upper bounds exist after scale adjustment (CoT ≤ base at ε/M²; e2e ≤ (M/ε)·CoT). Validates with logistic function analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs generate outputs by iteratively sampling next-token distributions. Existing deterministic autoregressive learning theory (Joshi et al., COLT 2025) does not capture the stochastic nature of this process. The authors aim to develop a PAC-learning framework for stochastic autoregressive models and understand the sample complexity relationships among three natural supervision paradigms.

Method: Formalizes a binary stochastic autoregressive model where a fixed generator assigns Bernoulli distributions to prompts. Three supervision types are defined: (1) base one-step samples, (2) chain-of-thought (CoT) samples revealing full length-M trajectories, (3) end-to-end (e2e) samples revealing only final tokens. Sample complexities m_base, m_CoT, m_e2e are analyzed under squared loss ε, using PAC-learning techniques to establish upper and lower bounds, including scale-altered comparisons and dimension-d logistic function case studies.

Result: At fixed scale ε, no universal comparison exists: both m_CoT/m_base and m_e2e/m_CoT can be made arbitrarily larger than M/ε. After scale adjustment: CoT at ε ≤ base at ε/M²; e2e at ε ≤ (M/ε)·m_CoT(Θ(ε)) up to logarithmic factors. These dependencies are essentially tight. Logistic function analysis confirms results.

Conclusion: Stochastic autoregressive learning fundamentally differs from the deterministic counterpart. While no universal sample complexity ordering holds at fixed scales, meaningful and tight upper bounds emerge after appropriate scale adjustments, revealing intrinsic relationships among base, CoT, and e2e supervision paradigms.

Abstract: Motivated by LLMs, which generate outputs by iteratively sampling from next-token distributions, we introduce a PAC-learning model for binary stochastic autoregressive learning. This generalizes the deterministic autoregressive learning framework of Joshi et al., COLT 2025. In our model, one fixed generator assigns a Bernoulli next-token distribution to every prompt string. Starting from an input prompt, a token is sampled and appended to the prompt; the same generator is then applied again to this expanded prompt; this procedure is repeated for $M$ steps. Three forms of supervision are considered: base one-step samples, chain-of-thought (CoT) samples that reveal full random trajectories of length $M$, and end-to-end (e2e) samples that reveal only the final token of length $M$ trajectories. For a generator class, we study the minimum number of samples $m_{base}(\varepsilon),m_{CoT}(\varepsilon), m_{e2e}(\varepsilon)$, resp., required to learn the one-step probabilities in the base model, and the final-token probability in the CoT and e2e models, under squared loss error~$\varepsilon$.
  We show that stochastic autoregressive learning fundamentally differs from the deterministic theory. At scale $\varepsilon$, there is no universal comparison between the three learning tasks: both $m_{CoT}/m_{base}$ and $m_{e2e}/m_{CoT}$ can be made simultaneously arbitrarily larger than $M/\varepsilon$, the natural analogue for the existing deterministic results. Nevertheless, after altering scales, for every class, CoT learning at scale $\varepsilon$ is upper-bounded by base learning at scale $\varepsilon/M^2$, whereas e2e learning at scale $\varepsilon$ is upper-bounded, up to logarithmic factors, by $(M/\varepsilon) m_{CoT}(Θ(\varepsilon))$. These dependencies and scales are essentially tight. We complement these bounds by studying dimension $d$ logistic functions in our model.

</details>


### [122] [Trajectory-Relative Hindsight Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07371)
*Haoyu Zheng,Yun Zhu,Qing Wang,Wenqiao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRIAL is a hindsight distillation framework for RL that allocates dense, turn-aligned supervision across a trajectory by comparing ordinary and hindsight-conditioned response probabilities, normalizing turn-level magnitudes jointly to fix the average multiplier. It outperforms GRPO and other methods on WebShop and ALFWorld.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic RL methods exploit hindsight to generate dense reward signals from sparse outcome rewards, but they lack a principled mechanism for allocating many hindsight signals across decision turns within a rollout. This allocation problem is critical because improper distribution can lead to noisy or suboptimal credit assignment.

Method: TRIAL (Trajectory-Relative Hindsight Distillation) uses a unified turn-aligned scoring protocol: for each decision turn, it computes an outcome view by evaluating the response under both an ordinary context and a hindsight-conditioned context (informed by the eventual outcome). The signed log-probability gap between these two evaluations determines the direction and local strength of token-level supervision. Turn-level magnitudes are then normalized jointly over the realized trajectory such that the eligible-token-weighted mean of the allocation multipliers equals one, redistributing dense supervision while preserving the average multiplier.

Result: On WebShop and ALFWorld across different backbones, TRIAL outperforms GRPO on all eight (backbone × environment × metric) combinations and achieves best or tied-best among six methods on six of them. With Qwen3-1.7B on WebShop, success rate rises from 56.4% to 75.2% and task score from 78.7% to 85.7%. Ablations confirm that trajectory-relative turn allocation yields significant gains beyond dense hindsight distillation alone.

Conclusion: TRIAL provides an effective, principled approach to hindsight credit assignment in agentic RL by jointly normalizing turn-level supervision along a trajectory. The strong empirical results and ablation evidence support the importance of trajectory-relative allocation as a distinct contributor to performance.

Abstract: Recent agentic reinforcement learning methods use hindsight to complement sparse outcome rewards. However, a completed rollout can yield many such signals, leaving their appropriate allocation across turns unclear. We introduce TRIAL, a trajectory-relative hindsight distillation framework with a unified turn-aligned scoring protocol. For each decision turn, TRIAL extracts an outcome view of that decision's realized consequence and evaluates the same response under ordinary and hindsight-conditioned contexts. The signed log-probability gap determines the direction and local strength of token-level supervision, while turn-level magnitudes are normalized jointly over the realized trajectory. The resulting allocation multipliers have an eligible-token-weighted mean of one, redistributing dense supervision across turns while fixing its average multiplier. Experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld with different backbones show that TRIAL outperforms GRPO across all eight combinations of backbone, environment, and evaluation metric, while achieving the best or tied-best performance among six methods on six of them. On WebShop with Qwen3-1.7B, TRIAL improves the success rate from 56.4% to 75.2% and the task score from 78.7% to 85.7%. Controlled ablations further show that trajectory-relative turn allocation provides substantial gains beyond those of dense hindsight distillation alone.

</details>


### [123] [Learning Suffers More Than the Policy Class Under Partial Observability: A Closed-Form Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07228)
*Idil Gözel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In partially observed RL, even when a good policy is representable, standard actor-critic fails due to a critic bias that misattributes unexplained observation variation as value curvature, pulling the actor away from the optimum. The fix is adjusting the look-ahead horizon (TD-λ), not adding memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard intuition holds that poor performance in partially observed RL stems from the policy class being insufficiently expressive. The authors challenge this, demonstrating that even when a near-optimal policy is representable and the value function approximator can capture it exactly, learning still converges to a substantially worse policy — implying the problem lies in the learning dynamics, not in representational capacity.

Method: The authors analyze a partially observed linear-quadratic (LQ) control problem where actor-critic dynamics admit closed-form solutions. They derive exact expressions for: (1) the policy the algorithm converges to, (2) its cost relative to the optimal representable policy, and (3) the mechanism by which the critic's bias arises — specifically, the critic misinterprets variation caused by unobserved state components as high curvature in its own value estimates. They also derive the role of the look-ahead parameter (TD-λ/bootstrap horizon) in mitigating this bias. Predictions are validated with deep RL experiments.

Result: At the default setting, the best representable policy costs 10.4% more than the fully observable optimal controller, but actor-critic converges to a policy 35% worse than that best representable one. The critic's bias is the root cause: it attributes observation noise to sharp value curvature, steering the actor away from the optimum. Memory (e.g., recurrence) does not resolve this; shortening the bootstrap horizon does. Deep RL experiments closely match the theoretical predictions.

Conclusion: The failure mode in partially observed actor-critic is not primarily a representation problem but a learning bias problem: the critic develops systematic errors due to partial observability that misguide the actor. The effective intervention is not adding memory but adjusting how far the agent looks ahead (TD-λ/bootstrap horizon), which reduces the critic's reliance on its own biased estimates.

Abstract: When a reinforcement learning agent cannot observe the full state, we usually blame its policies: it cannot see enough to represent a good one. We show that in a solvable case the bigger problem lies elsewhere. Even when a good policy is available and the agent's value function is expressive enough to describe it exactly, learning still ends up somewhere far worse.
  We study a partially observed linear-quadratic problem in which a standard actor-critic learner can be solved in closed form. At our default setting the best policy the agent can represent is already close to optimal, costing 10.4% more than the ideal controller that observes everything. Learning does not find it. The algorithm instead comes to rest at a policy that is 35% worse than the best one available to it, and we can say exactly where and why.
  The cause is a bias in what the critic learns rather than a limit on what the actor can express. Because the agent cannot attribute what it sees to the part of the state it cannot observe, the critic misreads that unexplained variation as sharp curvature in its own value estimates, and the actor follows that error away from the optimum. We derive closed-form expressions for the resulting policy, for its cost, and for the one design choice that removes the problem, which is how far the learner looks ahead before trusting its own value estimates. Deep reinforcement learning experiments follow these predictions closely. Notably, giving the agent memory of past observations does not help, while changing how far it looks ahead does.

</details>


### [124] [TOFD: Target-Oriented Feature Decoupling against Poisoning Attacks in Split Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07274)
*Yuhan Xie,Jingrong Huang,Chen Lyu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TOFD is a three-stage unified defense framework for Split Federated Learning that proactively detects and mitigates diverse poisoning attacks via target inference, sample purification, and decoupling optimization, achieving state-of-the-art robustness with low overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Split Federated Learning's split architecture creates unique vulnerabilities to poisoning attacks, yet existing defenses fail to leverage this paradigm for early-stage malicious behavior detection and containment.

Method: TOFD operates in three stages: (1) Target Inference using class-specific Margin Perturbation (MP) to refine safe zones and identify attack targets; (2) Sample Purification via adaptive filtering of poisoned smashed data using cross-class min-max normalized MP thresholds; and (3) Decoupling Optimization employing an adversarial guidance model to capture attack patterns and decouple their influence. Theoretical convergence guarantees are provided.

Result: Extensive experiments on five datasets show TOFD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art defenses across diverse attack scenarios, achieving superior robustness with low computational overhead suitable for practical deployment.

Conclusion: TOFD is a unified, theoretically grounded framework that effectively addresses diverse poisoning attacks in SFL by exploiting the split paradigm for early detection and robust optimization, demonstrating both superior performance and practical deployability.

Abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) facilitates privacy-preserving collaborative training with reduced client-side overhead. However, its split architecture introduces unique attack surfaces, rendering it vulnerable to diverse poisoning attacks. Most existing defenses fail to exploit the split paradigm, limiting their ability to detect and contain malicious behaviors at an early stage. To bridge this gap, we propose Target-Oriented Feature Decoupling (TOFD), a unified framework that jointly enables proactive detection and robust optimization against a wide range of poisoning attacks. TOFD operates in three stages: (1) Target Inference, which identifies potential attack targets by refining class-wise safe zones via class-specific Margin Perturbation (MP); (2) Sample Purification, which adaptively filters poisoned smashed data using thresholds calibrated through cross-class min-max normalization of MP; and (3) Decoupling Optimization, which leverages an adversarial guidance model to capture attack-induced patterns and decouple their influence during optimization, thereby suppressing residual adversarial effects. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of TOFD. Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate that TOFD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art defenses under diverse attack scenarios, achieving superior robustness with low computational overhead suitable for practical deployment.

</details>


### [125] [A foundation-model approach to pediatric headache classification from rs-fMRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07287)
*Guilherme S. Imai Aldeia,Clara Moon,Julie Shulman,Navil Sethna,Allison Smith,Alyssa Lebel,William G. La Cava,Scott Holmes*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Using NeuroSTORM, a foundation model for rs-fMRI, fine-tuned on 189 scans from 110 children, headache vs. non-headache classification achieved AUROC 0.82/AUPRC 0.93, outperforming standard functional connectivity approaches. Multiclass classification of headache subtypes (chronic migraine vs. others) yielded macro-AUROC 0.69, with better discrimination of chronic migraine than other subtypes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Headache is the most common pediatric neurological disorder and significantly impairs quality of life, yet objective neuroimaging-based diagnostic tools are lacking. The authors sought to determine whether rs-fMRI combined with machine learning could support pediatric headache classification, particularly under data-limited conditions.

Method: Resting-state fMRI data (189 scans, 110 individuals, two visits, 74% headache prevalence) were encoded using NeuroSTORM, a recently developed foundation model, and fine-tuned for two tasks: (1) binary classification of headache vs. healthy controls, and (2) multiclass classification among healthy controls, chronic migraine, and non-chronic headache subtypes (post-viral, new daily persistent, post-traumatic). Performance was compared against standard functional connectivity (FC) matrix-based models.

Result: NeuroSTORM achieved AUROC 0.82 (95% CI: 0.82–0.82) and AUPRC 0.93 (0.93–0.94) for headache vs. non-headache discrimination, substantially outperforming FC-based models (AUROC 0.67, AUPRC 0.85). Multiclass macro-AUROC was 0.69 (0.68–0.69). NeuroSTORM distinguished chronic migraine effectively but struggled to differentiate other headache subtypes from chronic migraine.

Conclusion: NeuroSTORM captures latent rs-fMRI representations that transfer to headache-related classification without relying on handcrafted FC features, providing proof of concept for fMRI-based pediatric headache prediction. The approach shows promise for subtype identification and individualized treatment strategies, though discriminating non-chronic headache subtypes remains challenging.

Abstract: Headache is the most common neurological disorder in children and substantially affects quality of life. We investigated whether resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) can support pediatric headache classification using machine learning. We encoded rs-fMRI data using NeuroSTORM, a recent foundation model, and fine-tuned it to distinguish healthy controls from children with headache and subsequently classify headache subtypes. We compared NeuroSTORM with a standard neuroscience approach using functional-connectivity (FC) matrices derived from brain activity as predictors. Using 189 rs-fMRI scans from 110 individuals collected across two visits (prevalence of any headache: 74%), NeuroSTORM achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.82 (95% CI, 0.82-0.82) and an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.93 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) for discriminating headache from non-headache. In contrast, models trained on FC matrices showed lower performance (AUROC, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.67-0.67]; AUPRC, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.85-0.85]). In multiclass classification of healthy controls, chronic migraine, and non-chronic headaches (e.g., post-viral headache, new daily persistent headache, post-traumatic headache), NeuroSTORM achieved a macro-AUROC of 0.69 (95% CI, 0.68-0.69). Results suggest that the approach can distinguish chronic migraine but has difficulty differentiating other headache subtypes from chronic migraine. Overall, under limited-data conditions, NeuroSTORM appears to capture latent rs-fMRI representations that transfer to headache-related tasks without relying on FC features. These findings provide proof of concept for fMRI-based prediction of pediatric headache and highlight potential future utility for subtype identification and individualized treatment strategies.

</details>


### [126] [FUSE: Feature-Wise Unified Specialization with Cross-Column Exchange for Mixed-Type Tabular Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07294)
*Suman Cha,Seongchan Lee,Dohyun Ko,Hyunjoong Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FUSE introduces a variational flow matching framework for mixed-type tabular data that explicitly decouples feature-specific processing from cross-column interactions via separate adaptive mixture modules for numerical and categorical features, with joint attention for information exchange. The paper also provides theoretical bounds on generation error and demonstrates strong empirical performance across eight datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing variational flow matching methods for tabular data rely on factorized distributions and a shared backbone that implicitly handles both feature-specific processing and cross-column dependencies. This implicit treatment limits the model's ability to tailor transformations to distinct feature types (numerical vs. categorical) while maintaining rich cross-column interactions.

Method: FUSE adopts a dual-pathway architecture: (1) separate adaptive mixture modules for numerical and categorical features, where each feature learns to combine shared specialized subnetworks for feature-wise processing; (2) joint attention mechanisms that preserve information exchange across all columns. The authors also derive a theoretical characterization of excess population risk due to restricted conditioning contexts and bound the continuous 2-Wasserstein generation error by the endpoint-prediction risk.

Result: Comprehensive experiments on eight tabular datasets show that FUSE achieves strong and consistent performance on both distributional fidelity metrics and downstream utility metrics, outperforming or matching prior methods.

Conclusion: Explicitly separating feature-wise specialization from cross-column information exchange via FUSE yields a more effective generative model for mixed-type tabular data, with theoretical guarantees linking generation quality to prediction error.

Abstract: Generating mixed-type tabular data requires jointly modeling diverse feature distributions and their complex cross-column dependencies. Variational flow matching handles distinct endpoints via factorized distributions, yet leaves feature-specific processing and cross-column interactions implicit within a shared backbone. We introduce Feature-wise Unified Specialization with cross-column Exchange (FUSE) to explicitly separate these roles. FUSE applies separate adaptive mixture modules to numerical and categorical features, allowing each feature to combine shared specialized subnetworks, while joint attention preserves information exchange across all columns. We also characterize the excess population risk from restricted conditioning contexts and bound the continuous Wasserstein generation error by endpoint-prediction risk. Comprehensive experiments on eight tabular datasets demonstrate that FUSE achieves strong and consistent performance across distributional fidelity and downstream utility metrics.

</details>


### [127] [From Optimal Actions to World Models: Identifiability of Transition Kernels in Discounted MDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07301)
*Neal Batra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies identifiability of Markov decision process (MDP) transition probabilities when only optimal actions — not Q-values — are observed. For state-action rewards, two transition kernels are observationally equivalent iff they are related by a specific linear transformation involving an invertible matrix L. Near strictly positive kernels, this yields an n(n−1)-dimensional family of indistinguishable kernels. The paper also compares identifiability under state-only and next-state-dependent reward structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work by Letcher et al. addressed recovering MDP dynamics from Q-values, but in many practical settings (e.g., imitation learning, observational data), only optimal actions are observable — not the numerical values. The authors ask: what can be inferred about transition probabilities from optimal actions alone, for every reward in a given class?

Method: The authors characterize observational equivalence of transition kernels: two kernels P and Q yield identical optimal actions for all state-action rewards r(s,a) iff they satisfy a linear algebraic relation Q_{s,a} = (P_{s,a} + (1/γ)e_s^T(L−I))L^{−1} for some invertible L with L1=1. They analyze the dimension of this equivalence class near strictly positive kernels, yielding n(n−1) degrees of freedom. They then compare identifiability under alternative reward structures: r(s) (state-only) and r(s,a,s') (next-state-dependent).

Result: For state-action rewards, transition kernels are not uniquely identifiable; an n(n−1)-parameter family of kernels yields identical optimal actions. This holds even when restricting to rewards with unique optimal actions. Next-state rewards r(s,a,s') are far more informative: rows at states with ≥2 actions are fully determined; only rows at single-action states may remain ambiguous. State-only rewards r(s) are least informative: two kernels are equivalent iff every deterministic policy is optimal for the same set of rewards.

Conclusion: The form of the reward function critically determines what can be learned about MDP dynamics from optimal actions alone. State-action rewards leave significant ambiguity (n(n−1) parameters), next-state rewards nearly recover the full kernel, and state-only rewards reveal the least. These results delineate the fundamental limits of inverse reinforcement learning and imitation learning from action observations.

Abstract: We study what can be recovered about the transition probabilities of a Markov decision process from optimal actions alone. This is closely related to the inverse problem considered by Letcher et al., who ask when the dynamics can be recovered from numerical \(Q\)-values. Here the numerical values themselves are not observed; only the optimal actions are known, for every reward in a given class.
  For state-action rewards \(r(s,a)\), knowing the optimal actions for every reward also tells us how much better one action is than another when each is followed by the same fixed policy. This is still not enough to determine the transition probabilities uniquely. We prove that two kernels give the same optimal actions for every reward exactly when \[ Q_{s,a} =
\Bigl(P_{s,a}+\tfrac1γe_s^{\mathsf T}(L-I)\Bigr)L^{-1} \] for one invertible matrix \(L\) satisfying \(L\mathbf 1=\mathbf 1\). Near a kernel with strictly positive entries, there is an \(n(n-1)\)-dimensional family of different kernels with this property. The result is unchanged if we consider only rewards having a unique optimal action at every state.
  We then compare this with rewards of the forms \(r(s)\) and \(r(s,a,s')\). Rewards that depend on the next state can usually recover the transition kernel itself: every row at a state with at least two actions is determined, and we describe exactly when a row at a state with one action can remain hidden. State rewards reveal less: two kernels give the same optimal actions exactly when every deterministic policy is optimal for the same set of rewards. The results show how the form of the reward affects what can be learned about the dynamics from optimal actions alone.

</details>


### [128] [Is SwiGLU's Open Positive Tail Necessary? Evidence from Closed-Tail Gating with MemGLU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07323)
*Yuting Ge,Pengju Yang,Mingkai Nie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper tests whether SwiGLU's open positive tail is necessary for decoder-only language model FFNs. Introducing MemGLU (a closed-tail alternative inspired by memristive branch geometry), paired pretraining runs at 9M and 30M scales show MemGLU matches SwiGLU within ~0.1% validation NLL, suggesting the open positive tail is not required at these scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SwiGLU is widely used in transformer FFNs, but whether its defining characteristic — an unbounded positive tail in the gating function — is actually necessary for performance remains an open question. The authors aim to determine whether this architectural feature is essential or merely incidental.

Method: The authors introduce MemGLU, a closed-tail gating comparator derived from a memristive branch geometry. They conduct paired pretraining runs at 9M and 30M parameter scales across three seeds, comparing MemGLU and SwiGLU on validation NLL. They also perform post-hoc tail-suppression experiments on trained SwiGLU checkpoints and use mechanism diagnostics to analyze how the two models utilize their gating mechanisms differently.

Result: MemGLU achieves validation NLL within ~0.1% of SwiGLU across all runs. However, trained SwiGLU checkpoints are sensitive to positive-tail suppression (post-hoc clamping degrades performance). Mechanism diagnostics reveal that despite nearly identical losses, SwiGLU and MemGLU learn divergent gating strategies, indicating models adapt to the available gate geometry during pretraining.

Conclusion: At the tested scales (9M–30M), SwiGLU's open positive tail is not necessary for decoder-only language model FFN performance. Models adapt their gating behavior to whatever geometry is present during training, suggesting the SwiGLU tail is an architectural choice rather than a functional requirement at these scales.

Abstract: We test whether decoder-only language-model FFNs require SwiGLU's open positive tail. We introduce MemGLU as a closed-tail comparator derived from a memristive branch geometry. Across paired 9M and 30M pretraining runs with three seeds, MemGLU remains within about 0.1% of SwiGLU in validation NLL. Trained SwiGLU checkpoints are sensitive to positive-tail suppression, while mechanism diagnostics show that the two models use their gates differently despite similar losses. These results suggest that models adapt to the gate geometry available during pretraining. At the tested scales, SwiGLU's open positive tail is not necessary for decoder-only language-model FFNs.

</details>


### [129] [When GNNs Fail: Quantifying and Overcoming Temporal Correlation Volatility in Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07333)
*Chen Shao,Yue Wang,Zhenyi Zhu,Zhanbo Huang,Tobias Käfer,Zonghan Wu,Danai Koutra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies that GNNs for multivariate time series forecasting degrade under dynamic graph topologies, proposes a metric (TCV) to quantify this drift, and introduces GLIDE — a novel GNN layer with path-based message passing and static/dynamic propagation separation — achieving up to 85.7% improvement in high-volatility settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current GNN-based multivariate time series forecasters assume static graph topology, but real-world pairwise correlations evolve over time. The authors observed that popular models (including Transformers) underperform simple baselines in high-volatility dynamic settings, motivating a formal characterization of this failure mode and a principled solution.

Method: (1) Introduce Temporal Correlation Volatility (TCV), a model-agnostic metric measuring distributional evolution of latent correlation structures. (2) Propose GLIDE, a GNN layer with two mechanisms: (D1) Path-based Message Passing — aggregates information over multi-hop path neighborhoods to capture richer structural context; (D2) Static and Dynamic Propagation Separation — uses local static approximation to identify optimal propagation dynamics, decoupling static and dynamic components for robust learning under topology drift.

Result: On synthetic and real-world benchmarks, GLIDE improves average forecasting performance by up to 45.6% across static and dynamic settings, with maximum gains reaching 85.7%. TCV is shown to correlate strongly with performance degradation across multiple model classes.

Conclusion: Graph topology volatility is a critical yet underexplored factor in multivariate time series forecasting. TCV effectively diagnoses this issue, and GLIDE's dual mechanisms provide a robust solution that excels in both static and dynamic regimes, significantly outperforming existing GNN and Transformer baselines.

Abstract: Modeling multivariate time series by representing them as graphs, where individual series act as nodes and pairwise temporal corre- lations serve as edges, has gained significant traction. Recent advances in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated strong perfor- mance by assuming a static graph topology and aggregating information from neighboring series. In this work, we investigate the representa- tional power of GNNs for forecasting under both static and dynamic settings (i.e., when pairwise correlations evolve drastically over time) and identify critical limitations in current architectures. To formalize this, we first propose Temporal Correlation Volatility (TCV), a model- agnostic metric designed to quantify the distributional evolution of these latent structures. We establish a clear connection between TCV and performance degradation, demonstrating that many popular models, including Transformers, generalize poorly in high-TCV settings and are often outperformed by simple structure-agnostic baselines. To address these limitations, we propose Graph Layer for Inference in Dynamic En- vironments (GLIDE), a novel GNN layer enhanced by two theoretically grounded design mechanisms: (D1) Path-based Message Passing, which captures path-based neighborhoods and (D2) Static and Dynamic Propagation Separation, which identifies optimal dynamics via local static approximation. These components significantly improve learning under dynamic topology while preserving robustness in static scenarios. Ex- tensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that GLIDE improves average performance by up to 45.6% across static and dynamic settings, with the largest gain reaching 85.7%. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenS676/GLIDE.

</details>


### [130] [Aftab: A Comprehensive Benchmark of CNN Encoders and Advanced Value Functions in Parallelized Q-Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07335)
*Taha Shieenavaz,Shabnam Zareshahraki,Loris Nanni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates CNN architectural design for the Parallelized Q-Network (PQN) algorithm, proposing a composite architecture called Aftab that integrates Hadamax encoding with advanced Q-learning extensions (distributional, ensemble, dueling heads). Aftab achieves superior sample efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization on Atari-57 and Procgen Hard benchmarks under strict parameter constraints, without using replay buffers or target networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While PQN offers stable off-policy learning without replay buffers or target networks—making it computationally efficient—the representational capacity and parameter efficiency of visual encoders in such buffer-free settings remain underexplored. There is a need to systematically identify optimal CNN architectures that maximize sample efficiency under strict parameter constraints in parallelized, unbuffered RL paradigms.

Method: The authors design and evaluate eight distinct CNN topologies for PQN under strict parameter constraints. They integrate the Hadamax encoding paradigm and advanced Q-learning extensions—distributional RL, ensemble methods, and dueling network heads—into these architectures. The resulting composite architecture, Aftab, is benchmarked on Atari-57 (using IQM Human-Normalized Score and Probability of Improvement) and evaluated for structural resilience on the non-stationary Procgen Hard benchmark.

Result: Aftab achieves an IQM Human-Normalized Score of 6.479 on Atari-57 with a 0.86 Probability of Improvement over the PQN baseline. On Procgen Hard, it yields an IQM Normalized Score of 0.418 versus the baseline's 0.382, confirming out-of-distribution generalization. The framework is open-sourced with all model definitions, training configs, and logs.

Conclusion: The paper establishes Aftab as an efficient, probabilistically superior structural reference for model-free RL, demonstrating that careful architectural design combined with advanced encoding and value-estimation enhancements can significantly boost performance while preserving the simplicity and memory efficiency of unbuffered, parallelized optimization.

Abstract: Recent advancements in deep reinforcement learning have increasingly favored simplified, highly parallelized paradigms. Notably, the Parallelized Q-Network (PQN) algorithm achieves stable off-policy learning without relying on computationally expensive replay buffers or target networks. However, the representational capacity and parameter efficiency of visual encoders operating in these buffer-free settings remain underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the architectural design space of Convolutional Neural Networks for PQN. We design and rigorously evaluate eight distinct CNN topologies, optimizing for sample efficiency under strict parameter constraints. Furthermore, we study the impact of representation and value estimation enhancements by integrating the Hadamax encoding paradigm and advanced Q-learning extensions, including distributional, ensemble, and dueling heads. Extensive experiments on the Atari-57 benchmark demonstrate that our proposed composite architecture, Aftab, achieves an Interquartile Mean (IQM) Human-Normalized Score of 6.479, establishing a 0.86 Probability of Improvement over the standard PQN baseline. Additionally, structural resilience evaluations on the highly non-stationary Procgen Hard benchmark confirm out-of-distribution generalization, with Aftab yielding an IQM Procgen Normalized Score of 0.418 compared to the baseline's 0.382. Ultimately, this work establishes an efficient, probabilistically superior structural reference for model-free reinforcement learning, all while preserving the simplicity and memory efficiency of unbuffered, parallelized optimization.
  The complete Aftab framework, including all model definitions, training configurations, and raw experimental logs, is open-sourced and available on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/tahashieenavaz/aftab

</details>


### [131] [Residual Algebra for Representation-Preserving Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07349)
*Yao Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a formal algebraic framework where representations are typed objects owning both coordinate systems and residuals. Learning becomes an ordered composition of operators that respect type. Implemented via Fold (conditional-mean fields on rank grids) and FPRC-PQ (relax-aggregate-close algebra), the method achieves significant gains on Chinese A-share data, raising net returns from 13.52% to 19.10% and Sharpe from 1.42 to 2.09, outperforming controls through explicit residual ownership rather than more features or capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard heterogeneous representation learning relies on feature concatenation, which discards information about which representation produced which error. This erases the provenance of residual structure, preventing learners from exploiting representation-specific correction opportunities. The authors argue that preserving representation identity (typing) throughout the learning pipeline enables more principled residual decomposition and correction.

Method: Representations are formalized as typed objects with coordinate systems and residuals. Learning is structured as an ordered composition of type-preserving operators. The Fold construction instantiates representations as point-in-time conditional-mean fields on 10×10 rank grids. The FPRC-PQ algebra follows relax-aggregate-close: (1) each field is relaxed via a correction fitted to its own residual in its own coordinates; (2) corrected fields meet at a fixed mean serving as the identity-erasure boundary; (3) a shared learner closes only the aggregate's fresh residual. This telescopes into representation, local residual estimate, and residual-of-residual estimate. A reflective rumination operator further reads and reflects the displacement from the aggregate anchor, with gain fixed by orthogonal projection.

Result: On 3.67 million Chinese A-share stock-day observations (2023–2026) under a frozen point-in-time protocol, the base algebra raises net-of-cost return from 13.52% to 19.10% and Sharpe ratio from 1.42 to 2.09. Matched-capacity, unified-residual, identity-free two-stage, and pairwise-only controls all trail the proposed method. Refitting the closer along backbone perturbations yields first-order coupled-path mean orthogonality.

Conclusion: The performance gain is attributable not to increased features or model capacity, but to making residual ownership and composition explicit while representation identity remains available. The algebraic typing of representations and their residuals enables a disciplined decomposition that standard concatenation-based pipelines cannot replicate.

Abstract: Learning from heterogeneous representations is usually reduced to feature concatenation, which erases which representation produced an error. We instead algebraize the residual: a representation is a typed object that owns both a coordinate system and the residual it leaves unresolved, and learning is an ordered composition of operators that preserve or deliberately erase that type. Fold realizes the objects as point-in-time conditional-mean fields on 10x10 rank grids. FPRC-PQ realizes the algebra as relax-aggregate-close: each field is relaxed by a correction fitted to its own residual in its own coordinates; corrected fields meet at a fixed mean that is the sole identity-erasure boundary; and a shared learner closes only the aggregate's fresh residual. The composition telescopes exactly into representation, local residual estimate, and residual-of-residual estimate. Its aggregate is a learned control-variate interface with population variance reduction, while refitting the closer along perturbations of the backbone yields first-order coupled-path mean orthogonality. As an analytical extension, a reflective rumination operator reads the displacement of a global reconstruction from the aggregate anchor, reflects it, and fixes its gain by a unique orthogonal projection rather than return-tuned grid search. On 3.67M Chinese A-share stock-day observations (2023-2026) under a frozen point-in-time protocol, the evaluated base algebra raises net-of-cost return from 13.52% to 19.10% and Sharpe from 1.42 to 2.09. Matched-capacity, unified-residual, identity-free two-stage, and pairwise-only controls all trail it. The gain is therefore not explained by more features or more trees, but by making residual ownership and composition explicit while representation identity is still available.

</details>


### [132] [Omni-modal decomposition autoencoders learn full-stack wearable disentangled representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07385)
*Ioannis Ziogas,Ensieh Khazaei,Bilal Taha,Aamna Al Shehhi,Ahsan H. Khandoker,Leontios J. Hadjileontiadis,Dimitrios Hatzinakos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OmniDecVAE is a unified framework that learns disentangled, interpretable representations from arbitrary multi-modal wearable time-series data, jointly addressing classification, fusion, generative modeling, and interpretability in a single lightweight model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-modal wearable computing methods fail to simultaneously deliver task-specific classification, disentangled representation learning, multi-modal fusion, and generative modeling in a unified full-stack processor. There is a need for a scalable, single-model solution that handles heterogeneous time-series from arbitrarily many modalities.

Method: OmniDecVAEs extend DecVAEs with a shared asymmetric autoencoder architecture and a multi-view self-supervised decomposition loss to learn modality-conditioned time-frequency latent subspaces. The framework jointly performs disentangled representation learning, fusion, classification, and generative reconstruction across up to 30 modalities.

Result: On omni-modal HAR with up to 30 modalities, OmniDecVAE achieves +1.01% accuracy for activity recognition and +6.75% for identity recognition over transformer/VAE baselines. It improves MAE by 76.84% and MMD by 13.85% for synthetic data generation, all with only 4.1M parameters.

Conclusion: OmniDecVAE demonstrates strong potential as a lightweight, real-time full-stack wearable processor suitable for edge intelligence and clinical healthcare, unifying multiple processing requirements in a single model with modality-invariant spatial complexity.

Abstract: Learning disentangled representations is a key requirement for developing versatile, general-purpose, and sustainable models in multi-modal wearable computing. However, existing approaches do not operate as full-stack wearable processors, i.e., they do not simultaneously address task-specific classification performance, disentangled and interpretable representation learning, fusion, and generative modeling of highly heterogeneous multi-modal time series. To address this gap, we introduce Omni-modal Variational Decomposition Autoencoders (OmniDecVAEs), a framework that efficiently learns multi-purpose representations in a unified and scalable manner from arbitrarily many modalities. OmniDecVAEs extend DecVAEs by learning modality-conditioned time-frequency latent subspaces through a multi-view self-supervised decomposition loss and a shared asymmetric autoencoder (AE) architecture. Results on a challenging omni-modal human activity recognition (HAR) setting with up to thirty modalities, demonstrate the ability of OmniDecVAEs to learn full-stack wearable representations. When compared to transformer-based and VAE-based methods, OmniDecVAEs full-stack disentangled representation properties lead to accuracy improvements of 1.01% and 6.75% in activity and identity recognition, respectively. Furthermore, OmniDecVAEs synthesize realistic omni-modal time-frequency data that manifest with enhanced reconstructions (mean absolute error improves by 76.84%) and distributional similarity between real and synthetic data (maximum mean discrepancy improves by 13.85%). Our results highlight OmniDecVAEs potential as a lightweight model suitable for intelligent edge wearables and clinical healthcare, unifying processing requirements and abilities in a single model, through its enhanced representational capacity, modality-invariant spatial complexity (4.1M parameters), and real-time latency.

</details>


### [133] [FedDOSE: Federated Learning Framework Decomposing Site Effects for Modeling Brain Dynamic Functional Connectivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07393)
*Deepank Girish,Yi Hao Chan,Yubin Zheng,Sukrit Gupta,Jagath C. Rajapakse*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedDOSE is a federated learning framework that addresses site heterogeneity in multi-site fMRI analysis by decomposing site-specific differences, encoding dynamic functional connectivity via modularity-guided Tucker decomposition, and aligning class prototypes across sites using optimal transport and Procrustes analysis, achieving state-of-the-art results on ASD and ADHD diagnosis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-site fMRI consortia are essential for training generalizable deep learning models, but statistical heterogeneity across sites undermines standard federated learning. Existing FL methods also rely on static functional connectivity, ignoring dynamic brain network information. Both limitations motivate a framework that handles site differences while leveraging dynamic FC.

Method: FedDOSE consists of three core components: (1) a Modularity-Guided Tucker Decomposition block that encodes high-dimensional dynamic FC tensors to capture modular-level spatio-temporal patterns efficiently; (2) class-specific prototype generation across sites; and (3) global prototype alignment using Optimal Transport barycenter formulation combined with Procrustes analysis to harmonize site differences in the federated setting.

Result: Extensive experiments on three multi-site resting-state fMRI datasets — ABIDE-I, ABIDE-II, and ADHD-200 — demonstrate that FedDOSE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in detecting both Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).

Conclusion: FedDOSE effectively learns robust representations from multi-site fMRI datasets by explicitly modeling and decomposing site differences while preserving dynamic functional connectivity information. The framework's superior diagnostic performance underscores its promise for reliable, privacy-preserving collaborative analysis of neuroimaging data in clinical applications.

Abstract: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging ( fMRI ) data are often pooled into collaborative multi-site consortia, as deep learning models for analyses require large datasets to generalize well. While Federated Learning (FL) offers a privacy-preserving paradigm for collaborative training, standard approaches continue to struggle with statistical heterogeneity. In particular, site differences pose a key challenge in multi-site data settings. Additionally, existing FL approaches for fMRI rely on static Functional Connectivity ( FC), omitting dynamic information in brain networks. To address this, we propose FedDOSE, a novel framework that explicitly decomposes site differences for analysis of dynamic FC (dFC). FedDOSE introduces a Modularity-Guided Tucker Decomposition block to encode high-dimensional dFC tensors and capture modular-level spatio-temporal patterns efficiently. Class-specific prototypes are generated across all sites and subsequently aligned at the global level by using a combination of Optimal Transport (OT) barycenter formulation and Procrustes analysis. Extensive experiments for diagnosing Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) on three multi-site resting-state fMRI datasets: ABIDE-I, ABIDE-II, and ADHD-200, demonstrate that FedDOSE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in ASD and ADHD detection. Our results highlight its effectiveness in learning robust representations from multi-site datasets for reliable analysis.

</details>


### [134] [Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling: Bilevel Optimization for LLM Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07419)
*Ruochen Jin,Zhanliang Wang,Zongyu Dai,Jiancong Xiao,Bojian Hou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a bilevel optimization method that maximizes predictive entropy during training to calibrate LLMs, avoiding domain-dependent post-hoc temperature scaling. A first-order approximation makes it practical at scale, yielding well-calibrated models with strong out-of-domain generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preference alignment (e.g., RLHF) makes LLMs overconfident and poorly calibrated. Traditional temperature scaling is post-hoc and domain-dependent—a temperature fitted on one domain fails to generalize to others. This motivates a training-time intervention that modifies model parameters to improve intrinsic calibration across domains.

Method: A bilevel optimization framework: the lower level trains the model under a parametric loss, while the upper level selects loss hyperparameters to maximize the entropy of predictive distributions (directly penalizing overconfidence). To scale to LLMs, a first-order approximation is used to avoid expensive second-order gradient computation.

Result: The method produces well-calibrated LLMs on both multiple-choice and open-ended generative QA tasks, with particular advantages in out-of-domain generalization compared to post-hoc temperature scaling.

Conclusion: Training-time entropy maximization via bilevel optimization is an effective and scalable approach to calibrating LLMs, overcoming the domain-dependence limitations of post-hoc temperature scaling while maintaining strong generalization.

Abstract: Preference alignment often makes large language models (LLMs) overconfident and poorly calibrated. Traditional post-hoc temperature scaling is inherently domain-dependent: a temperature fitted on one domain does not generalize across domains. This motivates us to modify model parameters during training to improve calibration. We propose maximizing the entropy of predictive distributions as the calibration objective, which directly targets overconfidence by discouraging overly concentrated predictions. Inspired by temperature scaling, we realize this through a bilevel optimization formulation, where the lower level trains the model under a parametric loss and the upper level selects loss hyperparameters to maximize entropy. To make the framework practical at LLM scale, we adopt an efficient first-order approximation that avoids explicit second-order computation. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended generative question answering, experiments demonstrate that our method yields well-calibrated LLMs with particular advantages in out-of-domain generalization.

</details>


### [135] [Beyond Myopic World Models: Long-Horizon End-to-End Training for Direct Future Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07420)
*Xinyi Li,Zaishuo Xia,Chenjie Hao,Yubei Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Current world models suffer from a mismatch: they're trained with local few-step prediction but deployed recursively for long horizons, amplifying errors. The authors propose Direct Prediction World Model (DPWM), which compresses arbitrary-length action sequences into a single embedding and predicts the endpoint in one forward pass, enabling stable end-to-end long-horizon training. DPWM substantially outperforms recursive baselines, with gains growing as horizon increases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models are typically trained with few-step (local) prediction objectives but are expected to perform long-horizon imagination via recursive rollout. This creates a fundamental mismatch: local losses treat all transitions uniformly regardless of their downstream influence on the endpoint, and small local errors compound through recursive inference. The authors argue that optimizing directly for endpoint prediction accuracy — rather than local transition fidelity — is the key to better long-horizon performance.

Method: The authors introduce the Direct Prediction World Model (DPWM), a non-recursive architecture that compresses an action sequence of arbitrary length into a single embedding vector and predicts the final endpoint observation in a single forward pass. This eliminates recurrent rollout entirely — both during inference and during gradient backpropagation — making end-to-end long-horizon training practical at scales where unrolled autoregressive training becomes unstable. The core design choice is shifting the training objective from local transition prediction to direct endpoint prediction.
