Result: DPWM achieves substantial improvements in long-horizon endpoint prediction over recursive world-model baselines on both continuous-control and pixel-based benchmarks. The performance gap widens as the prediction horizon increases. Additionally, when recurrent baseline architectures are retrained with the same long-horizon endpoint objective, they show similar gains, supporting the claim that the training objective — not the specific backbone — is the primary driver of long-horizon accuracy.

Conclusion: World models benefit significantly from being trained and evaluated at the temporal scales where they are ultimately deployed. The field should shift focus from local transition modeling toward long-horizon predictive accuracy, and end-to-end endpoint objectives offer a practical path to achieving this. The non-recursive DPWM design enables stable gradient propagation over long horizons that recursive methods cannot handle.

Abstract: World models are expected to support imagination over extended temporal horizons, yet most are still trained through local few-step prediction objectives and deployed by recursively rolling out their own predictions. This creates a fundamental mismatch: few-step losses optimize local transition fidelity, while long-horizon prediction depends on how errors and gradients propagate through the entire trajectory. As a result, transitions with different downstream influence on the endpoint are treated uniformly during training, and small local errors are amplified through recursive inference. We argue that long-horizon accuracy is better achieved by optimizing directly, through an end-to-end endpoint prediction objective. To instantiate this paradigm, we introduce the Direct Prediction World Model (DPWM), a non-recursive architecture that compresses an action sequence of arbitrary length into a single embedding and predicts the endpoint observation in a single forward pass. This design avoids recurrent rollout in both prediction and gradient propagation, making long-horizon end-to-end training practical at horizons where unrolled autoregressive training becomes unstable. Empirically, DPWM substantially improves long-horizon endpoint prediction over recursive world-model baselines on continuous-control and pixel-based benchmarks, with larger gains as the prediction horizon increases. We further show that recurrent baselines benefit similarly when retrained with the same long-horizon endpoint objective, supporting our central claim that the training objective, rather than the particular backbone choice, is the main driver of long-horizon prediction accuracy. Our results suggest that world models can benefit from being trained and evaluated at the temporal scales where they are ultimately used, shifting the focus from local transition modeling toward long-horizon predictive accuracy.

</details>


### [136] [Diffusion LLMs as Targets and Adversaries: Mechanistic Safety Exploits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07430)
*Elena Dumitrescu,Gert Lek,Lydia Y. Chen,Jérémie Decouchant*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates safety vulnerabilities in Diffusion Large Language Models (DLLMs), demonstrating that safety alignment is sparse, transferable across architectures, and easily bypassed via neuron-level attacks. The authors further propose SN-Guided Diffusion, a black-box jailbreak method achieving near-perfect prompt separability and high transfer attack success rates against both open and proprietary models at low computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DLLMs are an emerging paradigm replacing autoregressive decoding with iterative denoising, but their safety mechanisms are poorly understood. The authors aim to characterize how safety alignment manifests in DLLMs mechanistically (sparsity, transferability) and to develop efficient jailbreaking methods exploiting these properties.

Method: Two-pronged approach: (1) Mechanistic analysis — safety neuron mapping, pruning, and transfer pruning across DLLM architectures (LLaDA, Dream, Fast-dLLM) and their autoregressive predecessors (Qwen2.5). (2) SN-Guided Diffusion — a black-box jailbreak framework that computes a weighted safety neuron loss to steer the diffusion sampling trajectory away from safety-triggering regions, evaluated on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite.

Result: Self-pruning raises ASR from 2.6%→73.8% (LLaDA) and 1.9%→86.6% (Dream). Transfer pruning from Qwen2.5 achieves 1.9%→73.2% (Dream) and 7.0%→86.3% (Fast-dLLM). SN-Guided Diffusion attains AUROC=1.0 for benign-vs-jailbreak discrimination and transfer ASR up to 77.1% (Llama-3), 86.9% (Qwen2.5), and 74.3% (Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite) using only 20 generation episodes per prompt.

Conclusion: Safety alignment in DLLMs is mechanistically sparse and inheritable from autoregressive predecessors, making them vulnerable to neuron-level attacks. SN-Guided Diffusion provides a highly efficient, fully offline black-box jailbreak framework that significantly outperforms prior methods in cost-effectiveness while achieving competitive transferability across both open-source and proprietary models.

Abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (DLLMs) replace autoregressive next-token prediction with iterative parallel denoising, yet their internal safety mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate DLLMs both as targets and as adversaries, exposing mechanistic vulnerabilities in diffusion-based alignment.
  We first show that safety alignment in DLLMs remains sparse and transferable across architectures. DLLMs initialized from autoregressive predecessors inherit the same mechanistic safety footprint as their source models, enabling transfer attacks via direct safety neuron mapping and pruning. Self-pruning increases attack success rates (ASR) from 2.6% to 73.8% on LLaDA and from 1.9% to 86.6% on Dream, while transfer pruning from Qwen2.5 increases ASR from 1.9% to 73.2% on Dream and from 7.0% to 86.3% on Fast-dLLM.
  Building on these findings, we introduce SN-Guided Diffusion, a fully offline black-box jailbreak framework that steers the diffusion process away from safety-triggering regions using a weighted safety neuron loss, which achieves near-perfect prompt separability (AUROC = 1.0 for benign-vs-jailbreak discrimination). Across multiple open and proprietary targets, our method achieves a transfer ASR of up to 77.1% on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, 86.9% on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and 74.3% against Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, while requiring only 20 generation episodes per prompt. Compared to prior jailbreaking frameworks, our method achieves competitive transferability with orders-of-magnitude lower generation cost.
  Our codebase is available at https://github.com/ellyoana/sn-guided-diffusion.

</details>

# cs.IR [[Back]](#toc)

### [137] [Progressive Alignment of Recommender Foundation Model through Multi-Phase Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06792)
*Oseong Choi,Hoeinn Kim,Jihoon Lee,Byungsoo Kang,Taeyeong Jang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A three-phase progressive post-training framework (LP→FFT→RFT) for adapting foundation models to recommendation, separating task adaptation from business-metric alignment. Linear Probing stabilizes new heads, Full Fine-Tuning specializes the model, and Reinforcement Fine-Tuning aligns policy with business objectives via a learned reward model trained on sparse business signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models for recommendation excel at long-horizon sequential modeling, but adapting a pretrained FM to downstream surfaces via SFT on task-specific objectives (clicks, likes) does not align with true business metrics that define recommendation quality. Direct optimization on sparse business targets is also ineffective.

Method: A three-phase progressive post-training pipeline: (1) Linear Probing (LP) — freeze pretrained backbone, train only randomly initialized downstream heads to stabilize representations; (2) Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) — jointly fine-tune the entire model for the target task on top of the stabilized policy; (3) Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) — align the policy with business metrics using a learned reward model, where the policy trains on dense implicit feedback and business-metric supervision is used only for reward modeling, avoiding direct optimization on sparse targets.

Result: Offline experiments show LP-FFT-RFT outperforms single-phase alternatives; reward-based alignment yields a stronger serving policy than directly using the reward model for ranking. Large-scale online A/B tests confirm improved production recommendation quality over a conventional non-foundation baseline.

Conclusion: Progressive post-training with explicit separation of downstream adaptation and business-metric alignment is effective. The LP→FFT→RFT pipeline provides a robust recipe for adapting foundation models to real-world recommendation systems with improved business outcomes.

Abstract: Foundation model(FM) for recommendation has shown strong ability to model long-horizon sequential user behavior. In practice, a single pretrained foundation model is often adapted to diverse downstream serving surfaces through Supervised Fine-Tuning(SFT). However, optimizing task-specific objectives such as clicks or likes does not necessarily align the serving policy with the business metrics that determine recommendation quality.
  We propose a three-phase progressive post-training framework that explicitly separates downstream adaptation from business-metric alignment. The adaptation stage is decomposed into Linear Probing(LP) and Full Fine-Tuning(FFT): LP first stabilizes randomly initialized downstream heads within a frozen pretrained representation space, and FFT then jointly specializes the full model for the target task. On top of this stabilized policy, Reinforcement Fine-Tuning(RFT) aligns the model with practical business objectives using a learned reward model. Rather than directly optimizing the serving policy on sparse business targets, we train the policy on dense implicit feedback and use business-metric supervision only for reward modeling.
  Offline experiments show that the progressive LP-FFT-RFT framework outperforms single-phase alternatives, and that reward-based alignment yields a stronger serving policy than directly using the reward model itself for ranking. Large-scale online A/B tests further show that the proposed framework improves production recommendation quality over a conventional non-foundation baseline. A reference implementation is available at https://github.com/webtoon/rec-fm-progressive-alignment

</details>


### [138] [Rhetorical-Role-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Legal Question Answering over Indian Supreme Court Judgments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06828)
*Sayed Ayaan Ahmed Sha,Sangeetha Sivanesan,Anand Kumar Madasamy,Navya Binu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A domain-specific RAG framework for Indian Supreme Court judgments that combines rhetorical chunking, fusion retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and chat history-aware query reformulation, achieving strong contextual recall and answer relevancy on legal QA tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose RAG systems lack the domain-specific enhancements needed to handle the unique structural and rhetorical characteristics of legal documents, particularly Indian Supreme Court judgments, which impairs retrieval quality and reasoning accuracy in legal question-answering.

Method: An enhanced RAG framework with four key components: (1) rhetorically-based chunking that respects the argumentative structure of legal texts; (2) fusion-based retrieval combining multiple retrieval strategies; (3) cross-encoder reranking to refine retrieved document relevance; and (4) chat history integration with query classification and rewriting to handle multi-turn conversational context and user intent. The framework also accounts for structural features like judge names.

Result: Evaluation using the DeepEval framework demonstrated strong performance on contextual recall and answer relevancy metrics, validating the framework's effectiveness for context-heavy legal question-answering tasks.

Conclusion: Domain-specific enhancements — particularly rhetorical chunking, fusion retrieval, and query reformulation — are essential for building reliable and explainable legal AI systems. The results underscore that off-the-shelf RAG is insufficient for the legal domain without targeted adaptation.

Abstract: This research paper proposes a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that is specific to the legal field in order to assist interactive retrieval and reason about judgments from the Supreme Court of India. The solution uses an enhanced version of RAG framework which consists of rhetorically based chunking, fusion-based retrieval, and cross encoder reranking methods to increase the relevancy of the information retrieved. In order to improve conversations, the proposed framework uses chat history along with query classification and rewriting in order to understand user intention from successive queries. Additionally, there are features that take into account structural aspects of legal documents, such as isolated names of judges that could have an impact on retrieval quality. The evaluation was done using the DeepEval framework and demonstrated strong performance on metrics including contextual recall and answer relevancy, which proves that the framework is very effective in dealing with legal question-answering tasks that require a lot of context. The results emphasize the importance of domain specific enhancements in developing legal AI systems that are both reliable and explainable.

</details>


### [139] [BZKO: An Ontology for the Card Index of German Post-War Compensation Records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06918)
*Dilek Yargan,Jörg Waitelonis,Mahsa Vafaie,Harald Sack*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Presents the BZK Ontology (BZKO), a two-layer semantic framework for integrating German Holocaust compensation archival records, combining BFO-based realism with archival standards to enable provenance-preserving knowledge graph generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable semantically enriched representation, integration, and reuse of the German Central Federal Card Index (Bundeszentralkartei), which documents compensation claims by victims of National Socialist persecution. Current archival practices lack semantic interoperability for digital humanities applications.

Method: A two-layer ontology architecture: a foundational domain layer grounded in BFO (Basic Formal Ontology) realism, and an interoperability extension layer incorporating archival standards (RiC-O, PROV-O, PiCo). This separation maintains logical rigor and modularity while enabling provenance-preserving semantic integration.

Result: A publicly available OWL ontology (hosted on GitHub) that establishes a reusable semantic foundation for integrating Wiedergutmachung archival materials into digital humanities infrastructures, with support for provenance tracking.

Conclusion: The BZKO provides a rigorous, modular, and standards-aligned semantic foundation that lays the groundwork for future knowledge graph generation, ontology validation, and incorporation of additional historical entities with uncertain temporal and spatial information.

Abstract: The Central Federal Card Index (Bundeszentralkartei) of Germany is a key archival resource documenting compensation claims submitted by victims of National Socialist persecution and their relatives, within the German Wiedergutmachung process. To enable semantically enriched representation, integration, and reuse of this historically significant collection, we present the BZK Ontology (BZKO). We propose a two-layer ontology for historical archival data that separates ontologically grounded domain semantics from interoperability-oriented extension constructs. The approach combines BFO-based realism with archival standards (RiC-O, PROV-O, PiCo), enabling provenance-preserving semantic integration, while maintaining logical rigor, modularity, and reuse across digital humanities infrastructures. The proposed approach establishes a reusable semantic foundation for the integration of Wiedergutmachung archival materials into digital humanities infrastructures and lays the groundwork for future knowledge graph generation, ontology validation, and the incorporation of additional historical entities and uncertain temporal and spatial information. The ontology is available on https://github.com/ISE-FIZKarlsruhe/bzko.

</details>


### [140] [From Classification to Recommendation: Empirical Analysis of Audio Embedding Models Application for Content-Based Music Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06928)
*Qingrui Li,Haowei Lou,Chengkai Huang,Quan Z. Sheng,Lina Yao*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates six pretrained audio encoders across three types of music recommender systems (content-based, sequential, generative Semantic-ID-based), finding that audio-text-aligned representations excel when used directly, while sequential training diminishes encoder differences; it also reveals that increasing Semantic-ID capacity can introduce instability in generative recommender systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most pretrained audio models are optimized for objectives like masked prediction or contrastive learning, which do not produce representation spaces suitable for recommender systems that must capture subjective, behavior-dependent listener preferences. Furthermore, the effectiveness of audio embeddings in the emerging paradigm of generative recommender systems remains underexplored.

Method: The authors systematically evaluate six representative audio encoders (varying in pretraining objectives) across three recommender system paradigms: content-based, sequential, and Semantic-ID-based generative recommenders. They also investigate the impact of residual-quantization design choices—codebook width, quantization depth, and retained Semantic-ID prefixes—on preserving recommendation-relevant information. Experiments are conducted on two music recommendation datasets.

Result: Audio-text-aligned and music-domain-specific representations outperform others when pretrained embedding geometry is used directly. However, interaction-based sequential training substantially reduces performance gaps among different encoders. Increasing Semantic-ID capacity does not consistently improve generative recommender performance and may introduce significant instability.

Conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for selecting audio encoders and designing audio-derived Semantic IDs for music recommender systems, highlighting the importance of alignment between pretraining objectives and downstream recommendation tasks, and cautioning against indiscriminate expansion of Semantic-ID capacity.

Abstract: Pretrained audio representation models learned from large-scale corpora have achieved strong performance in audio classification and understanding. However, most existing models are optimized for objectives such as masked prediction, contrastive learning, or audio-text alignment, which do not necessarily produce representation spaces well-suited to recommender systems. Unlike classification, music recommender systems must capture item relationships shaped by subjective and behavior-dependent listener preferences. Although pretrained audio embeddings have been explored in conventional recommender systems, their effectiveness in the rapidly emerging paradigm of generative recommender systems remains underexplored. To address this gap, we systematically evaluate six representative audio encoders across three types of music recommender systems: content-based, sequential, and Semantic-ID-based generative recommender systems. We further investigate how residual-quantization design, including codebook width, quantization depth, and retained Semantic-ID prefixes, affects the preservation of recommendation-relevant information. Experiments on two music recommendation datasets show that audio-text-aligned and music-domain representations are generally more effective when pretrained embedding geometry is used directly, whereas interaction-based sequential training substantially reduces performance differences among encoders. We also find that increasing Semantic-ID capacity does not consistently improve generative recommender systems and may introduce substantial instability. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting audio encoders and designing audio-derived Semantic IDs for modern music recommender systems.

</details>


### [141] [Hierarchical Quantization with Domain-Adaptive Sparse Routing for Generative Cross-Domain Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06997)
*Haiying He,Xiaopeng Li,Yuchen Gu,Kuo Cai,Bo Chen,Jingtong Gao,Yejing Wang,Derong Xu,Ruiming Tang,Guorui Zhou,Han Li,Xiangyu Zhao*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: HD-Rec is a unified generative cross-domain recommendation framework that uses hierarchical domain-aware quantization and a domain-adaptive sparse mixture-of-experts architecture, with cross-granularity routing consistency, to model heterogeneous item semantics and user behaviors across domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing generative cross-domain recommendation methods rely on globally shared representations or lightweight domain adaptation, which lack sufficient capacity to model heterogeneous item semantics and behavioral patterns at different semantic granularities across domains.

Method: HD-Rec introduces: (1) a hierarchical domain-aware quantizer with globally shared coarse-level codebooks and adaptively routed fine-level codebooks for SID construction; (2) a domain-adaptive sparse mixture-of-experts module combining a continuously activated shared expert with a dynamically selected specialized expert; and (3) a cross-granularity routing consistency objective that regularizes token-level routing toward item-level consensus.

Result: Experiments on three public cross-domain recommendation benchmarks show that HD-Rec consistently outperforms competitive sequential, generative, and cross-domain recommendation baselines.

Conclusion: HD-Rec effectively addresses the challenge of cross-domain generative recommendation by hierarchically modeling shared and domain-specific semantics at multiple granularities, with the mixture-of-experts and routing consistency serving as key enablers for heterogeneous pattern modeling.

Abstract: Generative Recommendation (GenRec) represents a promising paradigm that achieves remarkable empirical success by encoding items as compact Semantic IDs (SIDs) and modeling user behavior via next-token prediction across diverse recommendation scenarios. Extending this paradigm to cross-domain recommendation is challenging because a unified model must accommodate heterogeneous item semantics and behavioral patterns across domains. Existing methods commonly rely on globally shared representations or lightweight domain adaptation, which may provide insufficient capacity for modeling heterogeneous patterns at different semantic granularities. To address these challenges, we propose HD-Rec, a unified generative framework for cross-domain recommendation. HD-Rec employs a hierarchical domain-aware quantizer that constructs semantic identifiers using globally shared coarse-level codebooks and adaptively routed fine-level codebooks. It further introduces a domain-adaptive sparse mixture-of-experts module that combines a continuously activated shared expert with a dynamically selected specialized expert. To improve the coherence of multi-token item representations, we develop a cross-granularity routing consistency objective that regularizes token-level routing decisions toward their item-level consensus. Experiments on three public cross-domain recommendation benchmarks show that HD-Rec consistently improves over competitive sequential, generative, and cross-domain recommendation baselines.

</details>


### [142] [MISO: Model-Internal-State-Guided Optimization for Ranking Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07035)
*Yongzhe Zhang,Xiaoyu Deng,Yifan He,Mengying Sun,Sheng Luo,Yijia Liu,Hao Yan,Zhuo Li,Yi Meng,Huiping Yao,Swathi Hrishikesh,Jing Chen,Dennis Choi,Steven Liu,Lexi Luo,Keyi Chen,Anish Khazane,Marcio Porto,Xiaoya Wang,Emmy Wang,Kangfu Zheng,Xingyuan Wang,Bilal Fadlallah,Gursharan Singh,Prabhakar Goyal,Alireza Vahdatpour,Santanu Kolay*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: MISO is a systems workflow that leverages model internal states (parameters, activations, gradients, normalization statistics) to guide local optimization decisions in ranking models, offering an adaptive, interpretable alternative to trial-and-error that outperforms both expert-driven and black-box scaling baselines in an ads ranking case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current practice for refining ranking models within established model families relies on expensive trial-and-error to decide which components to scale, replace, or retire. There is a need for a principled, data-driven method to prioritize these local optimization decisions without resorting to opaque automated search.

Method: MISO extracts model internal states (MIS) — including parameters, activations, gradients, and normalization statistics — from a trained ranking model. These MIS are aggregated into ranking, alignment, and comparison signals, which are then converted into a small set of interpretable candidate edits. MIS are re-extracted after each retraining cycle, enabling an adaptive optimization workflow that tracks evolving model behavior under shifting data distributions and system requirements.

Result: In an ads ranking case study, MISO improves normalized entropy while requiring substantially fewer validation runs than both expert-driven workflows and black-box scaling approaches.

Conclusion: MISO provides a practical middle ground between manual tuning and opaque automated search, demonstrating that leveraging internal model states can effectively and efficiently guide local optimization decisions in production ranking systems.

Abstract: Ranking models are repeatedly refined within established model families, yet the choice of which component to scale, replace, or retire is often guided by expensive trial-and-error. We present Model Internal State Optimization (MISO), a systems workflow that uses model internal states (MIS), including parameters, activations, gradients, and normalization statistics, to prioritize such local optimization decisions. MISO extracts MIS from a trained ranking model, aggregates them into ranking, alignment, and comparison signals, and converts those signals into a small set of interpretable candidate edits. Because MIS are re-extracted after each retraining cycle, MISO naturally supports an adaptive optimization workflow that tracks evolving model behavior as data distributions and system requirements shift over time. In an ads ranking case study, MISO improves normalized entropy while requiring substantially fewer validation runs than expert-driven and black-box scaling workflows, offering a practical middle ground between manual tuning and opaque automated search.

</details>


### [143] [Teacher Retains Full Tokens, Student Merges Efficiently: TM20K for E-Commerce Sequence Modeling in Ad Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07055)
*Xinchun Li,Duoru Zheng,Wenlin Zhao,Ziyi Zhou,Jingxuan Tan,Huizhi Yang,Linlan Chen,Dongjian Wang,Dongyue Wang,Xiaosong Li,Hongyue Mao,Yaocheng Tan*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: TM20K proposes a two-stage knowledge distillation framework with token merging for ultra-long (20K) behavior sequence modeling in recommender systems, balancing effectiveness and efficiency. A full-attention teacher model trained on complete sequences distills knowledge into a student model that uses token merge compression, achieving significant business metric gains (+1.036% ADSS) with minimal latency increase (+5.6%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ultra-long behavior sequences improve user interest modeling in recommenders but impose heavy burdens on training efficiency and serving throughput. Existing solutions either lose fine-grained information through search/cluster-based compression or use lightweight target-attention structures that insufficiently extract sequential features. A method is needed that balances effectiveness and efficiency without these trade-offs.

Method: TM20K employs a two-stage knowledge distillation framework with full transformer modeling. Both teacher and student use full attention (not just target-sequence attention). The teacher is heavily trained on complete sequences. The student uses purpose-designed token merge approaches to aggressively compress sequence length. Knowledge distillation transfers the teacher's superior representations to the efficient student model.

Result: Deployed in ByteDance's e-commerce advertising recommender system, TM20K scales sequence length to 20K tokens. It achieves +1.036% improvement in ADSS (a key business metric) while maintaining training/serving costs nearly equivalent to the online SOTA, with only a +5.6% increase in serving latency.

Conclusion: Full transformer modeling combined with token merging and knowledge distillation enables ultra-long sequence modeling at scale, delivering substantial business improvements without proportional cost increases. The approach is production-validated in a large-scale advertising recommender system.

Abstract: Benefiting from ultra-long behavior sequence modeling, existing recommender systems bring users a better experience via simultaneously considering their long-term and short-term interests. Nevertheless, extended sequence lengths introduce substantial burdens on training efficiency and serving throughput. Prior approaches typically utilize search-based or cluster-based compression on ultra-long sequences at the cost of fine-grained information, or rely on various lightweight target attention structures incapable of sufficient sequential feature extraction. In this paper, we balance the effectiveness and efficiency for ultra-long sequence modeling via full transformer modeling accompanied with a two-stage knowledge distillation framework. First, both teacher and student models take the full attention mechanism rather than pure target-sequence attention for effective sequence scaling. For student models, we propose several simple yet well-motivated token merge approaches, significantly compressing the sequence length while maintaining an acceptable performance. Then, a one-time teacher is heavily trained with full sequence tokens, further boosting the performance of student models via knowledge distillation. The proposed paradigm named TM20K has been successfully deployed in ByteDance's e-commerce advertising recommender system that extends the e-commerce sequence length to 20K, delivering substantial improvements in key business metrics (e.g., ADSS +1.036\%) while keeping the training and serving cost nearly the same as the online state-of-the-art model (e.g., serving latency only +5.6\%).

</details>


### [144] [Invisible to the Machine: Auditing AI Restaurant, Cafe, and Bar Recommendation Against a Complete Market Census](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07069)
*Vladimir Pitenin*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: First census-based audit of AI venue recommendations across 4,776 venues in Bali reveals 85.6% are never surfaced; visibility is driven by documentation (review volume, website, price info) rather than quality ratings, which only matter for ranking among those already recommended.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI assistants increasingly mediate local discovery with direct revenue implications for food/drink venues, yet no rigorous, population-level audit exists on which venues they surface, why, and with what reliability — prior audits rely on sampling and cannot measure true coverage or exclusion rates.

Method: Complete enumeration of 4,776 venues in two Bali markets (Canggu, Ubud) was conducted. Four systems (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity) were queried with 96 persona-conditioned prompts yielding 2,208 responses over 7 days under a pre-registered protocol. Logistic and rank-ordered logistic regression modeled two visibility margins: entry into answers and rank within answers. Foursquare POI data, venues' digital attributes, and temporal stability (test-retest) were also analyzed.

Result: 85.6% of all venues and 72.6% of established venues (50+ ratings) were never recommended. At the entry margin, documentation — review volume (OR 1.64), owning a website (OR 1.92), listed prices (OR 1.54), third-party web mentions (OR 1.44) — predicted inclusion; star rating was null (OR 0.89). At the rank margin, rating significantly predicted top position (OR 1.17). Foursquare presence showed no positive effect. Fabrication was rare (0.08%), but 93 permanently closed venues were recommended. Cross-system agreement was low (top-20 Jaccard 0.33–0.54). Temporal churn reflected sampling stochasticity, not drift.

Conclusion: AI venue recommendation exhibits systematic visibility bias driven by documentation rather than quality, creating a "two-margin" structure where different signals govern entry vs. ranking. The primary practical failure is staleness, not hallucination. Low cross-system agreement implies platform choice substantially shapes which venues are discovered, raising concerns for fair market access.

Abstract: AI assistants are becoming a primary interface for local discovery, yet almost nothing is known about which venues they surface -- especially in food and drink, where recommendations carry direct revenue consequences. We present the first census-denominated audit of AI venue recommendation: a complete enumeration of 4,776 cafes, restaurants, and bars across two bounded markets (Canggu and Ubud, Bali), against which we evaluate 2,208 search-grounded responses from four production AI systems (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity) to 96 persona-conditioned queries, collected over seven days under a pre-registered protocol. Because we observe the full market, we can measure what sampled audits cannot: 85.6% of venues were never recommended by any system -- 72.6% even among established venues with fifty or more ratings. Visibility follows a two-margin structure. Entry into answers is associated with documentation: review volume (OR 1.64), an own website (OR 1.92), listed price information (OR 1.54), and third-party web mentions (OR 1.44) -- while star rating is null at this margin (OR 0.89). Rank within answers reverses the pattern: among recommended venues, rating significantly predicts first position (OR 1.17). Presence in an open POI dataset (Foursquare), a folk-theorized visibility factor, shows no positive effect at either margin. Outright fabrication is rare (0.08% of mentions), but systems recommended permanently closed venues 93 times -- staleness, not hallucination, is the practical failure mode. Cross-system agreement is low (top-20 Jaccard 0.33-0.54). A two-week test-retest shows cross-period answer similarity comparable to same-day rerun similarity: the churn is sampling stochasticity, not temporal drift. We release our protocol, registry construction method, and derived data.

</details>


### [145] [Exact Adaptive Hybrid Retrieval Without Fixed Top-L Cutoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07152)
*Chunran Zhang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: EAHR replaces fixed-depth truncated fusion in RAG with an adaptive method that guarantees exact complete-list Top-K results by dynamically requesting ranks only when they can change the outcome, achieving 23–30× geometric-mean latency reduction over exhaustive batch execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed Top-L truncation in hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse) is problematic because: (1) unread cross-list ranks can alter Top-K membership/order even when observed candidates contain the complete-list Top-K, and (2) optimal depth varies per query and corpus snapshot, so depth selected from historical queries does not transfer reliably. The goal is to match complete-list weighted RRF fusion without a preset truncation depth.

Method: EAHR (Exact Adaptive Hybrid Retrieval) treats channel depth as request-specific execution state. It uses Per-Vector Scalar Quantization (PVS) and Posting Block-Max (PBM) to produce resumable exact dense and sparse rankings. Fusion bounds unread contributions and requests further ranks only while they can still change the Top-K. This guarantees every successful request matches complete-list fusion; otherwise execution continues safely to list exhaustion.

Result: Across 5 test collections and 5 temporal corpus snapshots: (1) complete-list weighted RRF remained competitive; (2) fixed depths from historical queries did not transfer reliably; (3) EAHR reproduced the complete-list ordered Top-20 in all 150 query-snapshot combinations; (4) geometric-mean latency ratios of exhaustive batch to EAHR were 23.35 (TREC-DL 2019) and 30.28 (TREC-DL 2020) under warm-cache, interleaved, order-balanced protocol. Anti-correlated rankings exhausted both lists; some difficult queries were slower.

Conclusion: EAHR provides exact adaptive hybrid retrieval that guarantees complete-list fusion results while adapting execution depth dynamically. It does not guarantee speedup for every request but fixes the exact result. The approach demonstrates that avoiding fixed-depth truncation is both feasible and beneficial for reliability and efficiency in RAG systems.

Abstract: Modern retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems often fuse fixed Top-$L$ results from dense and sparse retrievers, treating later contributions as zero. The cutoff therefore determines both the ranking and its execution cost. Yet truncated fusion is not generally equivalent to complete-list fusion: unread cross-list ranks can change Top-$K$ membership or order even when the observed candidates contain every item in the complete-list Top-$K$. Because channel rankings vary across queries and corpus updates, a depth selected from historical queries may not transfer reliably. We propose Exact Adaptive Hybrid Retrieval (EAHR), which fixes the ordered Top-$K$ defined by complete-list weighted RRF as the retrieval target and treats channel depth as request-specific execution state. Per-Vector Scalar Quantization (PVS) and Posting Block-Max (PBM) produce resumable exact dense and sparse rankings. Fusion bounds unread contributions and requests further ranks only while they can change the Top-$K$. Every successful request therefore matches complete-list fusion without a preset Top-$L$; otherwise, execution continues safely to list exhaustion. Across five test collections and five temporal corpus snapshots, complete-list weighted RRF remained competitive, whereas fixed depths selected from historical queries did not transfer reliably. EAHR reproduced the complete-list ordered Top-20 in all 150 query-snapshot combinations. Under a warm-cache, interleaved, order-balanced protocol, the paired geometric-mean latency ratios of exhaustive batch execution to EAHR were 23.35 on TREC-DL 2019 and 30.28 on TREC-DL 2020. Anti-correlated rankings exhausted both lists, and some difficult queries were slower with EAHR. EAHR does not guarantee a speedup for every request; it fixes the exact result while adapting execution depth to the current rankings.

</details>
