### [146] [Multimodal Drivers' Emotion Recognition and Safety-Oriented Intervention for Intelligent Transportation Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06378)
*Chang Liu,Dalai Mengke,Hanbo Zhou,Jia Hu,Peter Mihajlik,Tamas Sziranyi*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A multimodal driver assistance framework that combines speech-based emotion recognition with visual road perception to generate safety-prioritized interventions—first issuing road safety reminders, then providing emotion-aligned verbal support. A new dataset and a joint evaluation metric (CARE score) are introduced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research focuses heavily on driver emotion recognition in isolation, neglecting context-aware intervention that jointly considers both the driver's emotional state and real-time road perception. This gap limits the effectiveness of intelligent driver assistance systems under complex road conditions.

Method: The authors propose a safety-prioritized multimodal framework that (1) analyzes speech-derived emotional cues and visual road condition data, (2) generates two-tier structured interventions: road safety reminders first, followed by emotion-aligned verbal support, (3) constructs a multimodal dataset aligning emotional speech with road environment descriptors, and (4) introduces the CARE (Context-Aware Road-Emotion Evaluation) score for joint evaluation of emotion recognition, risk identification, and intervention quality.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively balances environmental risk reporting with emotion-aware verbal regulation, validating its feasibility as a safety-driven approach for intelligent transportation systems.

Conclusion: Jointly modeling driver emotion and road context enables more effective, safety-prioritized interventions than emotion recognition alone. The CARE framework offers a practical direction for integrating affective computing into intelligent transportation systems.

Abstract: Driver emotions can affect risk perception, decision-making, and vehicle control under complex road conditions. Existing studies mainly focus on driver emotion recognition, while limited attention has been given to context-aware intervention that jointly considers driver emotion and road perception. This paper proposes a safety-prioritized multimodal driver assistance framework that analyzes speech-derived emotional cues and visual road conditions to generate structured driving interventions. The framework first provides road safety reminders and then generates emotion-aligned verbal support. We construct a multimodal dataset by aligning emotional speech signals with structured road environment descriptors and introduce the CARE (Context-Aware Road-Emotion Evaluation) score to jointly evaluate emotion recognition, risk identification, and intervention generation. Experimental results show that the proposed framework balances environmental risk reporting and emotion-aware verbal regulation, providing a feasible safety-driven direction for intelligent transportation systems.

</details>


### [147] [Preventive Care Recommendations by Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06379)
*Eden Avnat,Elia Yanko,Ori Yoran,Raja-Elie E. Abdulnour*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: LLMs closely mirror physician prioritization of preventive care services, including their bias toward underprioritizing lifestyle interventions, with time constraints similarly affecting both. Some models improved performance, but consistent augmentation requires value-aligned training and real-world validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physicians often underprioritize highly effective preventive care services like lifestyle modifications despite their life-extending potential. This study investigates whether LLMs can replicate and potentially augment physician prioritization of PCS under time constraints, addressing a critical gap in clinical decision support.

Method: Using Zhang et al.'s validated survey with two patient scenarios (long and short visits), seven LLMs were compared against historical physician data. 137 simulated physician personas matching cohort demographics were generated, with three prompts tested per model. Primary outcomes included Spearman correlation for ranking concordance and Consensus-Stratified Agreement (CSA). Secondary outcomes: life-years gained per prioritized choice (LYGPC), consistency, and selectiveness. Augmentation was assessed via model revision of physician rankings under three informative prompts, quantified by delta LYGPC.

Result: LLMs showed high concordance with physicians (mean Spearman = 0.83, SD = 0.11). CSA was high at extreme agreement ranges (94%, 197/210) but low at moderate ranges (21%, 30/140), where lifestyle services were significantly underprioritized (8.8% vs. 38%, P < .001). Several models exceeded physicians in LYGPC and consistency while being more selective. Time constraints affected both LLMs and physicians similarly, increasing LYGPC and selectiveness but reducing consistency. Augmentation effects varied by model.

Conclusion: Current LLMs reproduce physicians' time-sensitivity and base-rate prioritization patterns while exacerbating the underprioritization of lifestyle interventions. Some models show improved prioritization performance, but consistent clinical augmentation requires value-aligned training, explicit time-constraint representation, and prospective real-world validation.

Abstract: Preventive care services (PCS) extend life, yet physicians often underprioritize highly effective interventions such as lifestyle modifications (Zhang et al., JAMA Network Open 2020). We evaluated whether large language models (LLMs) replicate and augment physician prioritization of PCS under time constraints. Using Zhang et al.'s validated survey with two patients assessed during long and short visits, we compared seven LLMs with historical physicians. We generated 137 simulated physician personas matching cohort demographics and tested three prompts per model. Primary outcomes were concordance with physician rankings, measured by Spearman correlation, and Consensus-Stratified Agreement (CSA), the proportion of LLM selections rated 4 or higher that matched physician consensus across agreement strata. Secondary outcomes included life-years gained per prioritized choice (LYGPC), consistency, and selectiveness. Augmentation was assessed by having models revise physician rankings under three informative prompts, with delta LYGPC quantifying impact. LLMs closely mirrored physicians (mean Spearman = 0.83, SD = 0.11), with high CSA at extreme agreement ranges (94%, 197/210) but low CSA in moderate ranges (21%, 30/140), where they underprioritized lifestyle services (8.8% vs. 38% rated 4 or higher; P < .001). Several models exceeded physicians in LYGPC and consistency while being more selective. Time constraints affected physicians and LLMs similarly, increasing LYGPC and selectiveness but reducing consistency. Augmentation effects varied by model. Current LLMs reproduced physicians' time-sensitivity and base-rate prioritization while exacerbating underprioritized lifestyle interventions. Some models improved prioritization performance, but consistent augmentation will require value-aligned training, explicit time-constraint representation, and prospective real-world validation.

</details>


### [148] [Mobile Interaction for Assessing Fatigue, Sleep, and Activity in Neurodegenerative and Chronic Diseases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06380)
*Julian Fierrez,Alejandro Peña,Aythami Morales,Ruben Tolosana,Ruben Vera-Rodriguez,Meenakshi Chatterjee,Ahmaniemi Teemu,Wan-Fai Ng,Walter Maetzler,Nikolay V. Manyakov,Jennifer Kudelka,Ralf Reilmann,C. Janneke van der Woude,Kristen Davies,Victoria Macrae,IDEA-FAST Consortium*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study investigates using passively collected smartphone interaction data (screen-time, app-usage) as objective proxies for assessing fatigue, sleep disturbances, and daily activity impairments in patients with neurodegenerative and immune-mediated inflammatory diseases, comparing these digital biomarkers against traditional patient-reported outcomes (PROs) in a cohort of 137 participants across 6 disease groups plus healthy controls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional PRO-based assessment of fatigue, sleep, and activity disturbances suffers from subjective biases and low sensitivity to temporal variability, as questionnaires are typically administered only every few months. There is a need for objective, continuous, and ecologically valid measurement methods.

Method: Data collected from 137 participants (6 disease groups + healthy controls). Smartphone screen-time and app-usage features were passively recorded. Statistical analysis employed repeated measures correlation to assess the relationship between these digital features and PRO scores collected concurrently via a smartphone app.

Result: Not specified in this abstract excerpt.

Conclusion: Not explicitly stated in this abstract excerpt; the work explores the feasibility of smartphone-derived digital markers as objective assessment tools for fatigue, sleep, and daily activity disturbances.

Abstract: Fatigue, sleep, or disturbances in daily activities are common symptoms among patients with neurodegenerative disorders (NDD) and immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMID). The current assessment of such symptoms is usually conducted using patient reported outcomes (PROs) based on standardized questionnaires that patients usually complete every few months. This assessment protocol has raised some concerns, due to its propensity to exhibit biases derived from its subjectivity nature, or the low sensibility to changes, which may lead to a failure when trying to capture variability over time. In this work, we explore the use of smartphone data, which can serve as a proxy for how patients interact with their devices, to provide an effective, reliable, and objective assessment of the symptoms mentioned above. Our study comprises data from 137 participants belonging to 6 different disease groups, plus a healthy control group. We conducted statistical analysis based on repeated measures correlation, in which we analyze the correlation between screen-time and app-usage features with scores obtained from the PROs collected from the participants using a smartphone application.

</details>


### [149] [Evaluating XAI Support From A Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning Policy in Human-Agent Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06381)
*Mateus Levi Simões Fernandes,Alberto Sardinha*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: First systematic evaluation of intrinsically explainable reinforcement learning in a benchmark environment (Overcooked-AI). Text vs. audio explanations from a hierarchical agent showed no significant performance gains, but audio explanations unexpectedly reduced working-alliance bond—suggesting spoken explanations create partnership expectations the reactive policy cannot fulfill. Modality-policy matching emerges as a key design principle.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior XAI research in human-agent collaboration relies on hand-crafted policies in custom, non-standard environments, limiting reproducibility and generalizability. There is no systematic evaluation of intrinsically explainable learned policies in established benchmarks, and no comparison of explanation modalities (text vs. audio) in real-time collaborative settings.

Method: The authors deployed the Hierarchical Ad Hoc Agents (HA²) architecture—an intrinsically explainable hierarchical RL policy—in the Overcooked-AI benchmark. Explanations are generated from the agent's subtask selections and delivered via a novel trigger-based system in either text or audio. A between-subjects experiment (n=38) compared three conditions: no explanation, text explanation, and audio explanation, measuring objective performance and subjective working-alliance bond.

Result: No statistically significant performance differences across conditions, though explanation conditions trended toward faster improvement. Crucially, audio explanations significantly reduced participants' working-alliance bond with the agent compared to the no-explanation baseline; this negative effect was absent under the text modality.

Conclusion: Explanation modality matters: spoken explanations may inadvertently invoke human-like partnership expectations that a reactive policy cannot satisfy, harming perceived alliance. Matching explanation modality to the policy's relational capacity is a critical design principle. The work establishes a replicable methodology for evaluating intrinsically explainable RL in standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) has shown promise for human-agent collaboration, yet results rely on hand-crafted policies in custom environments, limiting generalizability to state-of-the-art teaming research. We provide the first systematic evaluation of XAI support generated from an intrinsically explainable learned policy in an established benchmark. Using the Hierarchical Ad Hoc Agents (HA$^2$) architecture in Overcooked-AI, we generate real-time explanations from hierarchical subtask selections, delivered through text or audio via a novel trigger-based system. Our between-subjects experiment (n=38) found no significant performance effects, though participants with explanations showed trends toward faster performance improvement. More notably, audio explanations produced a significant reduction in participants' working-alliance bond with the agent -- an effect absent under the text modality -- suggesting that spoken explanations activate partnership expectations the underlying reactive policy cannot meet. We provide the first modality comparison in real-time human-agent collaboration and establish a baseline methodology for evaluating intrinsically explainable reinforcement learning architectures in benchmark environments. Results point to matching explanation modality to the underlying policy's capacity of sustaining the partnership its delivery implies as a potential path for more effective collaborative XAI.

</details>


### [150] [DREAMS: Diverse Reactions of Engagement and Attention Mind States Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06382)
*Monisha Singh,Gulshan Sharma,Ximi Hoque,Abhinav Dhall*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The DREAMS dataset captures facial videos of 32 users in naturalistic settings to study the bidirectional relationship between engagement and attention. Multi-task and transfer learning approaches outperform single-task methods for predicting these states, and higher engagement/attention correlates with lower cognitive load and better task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Engagement and attention are distinct but interrelated constructs crucial for learning experiences, yet their bidirectional relationship is not well understood. The authors aim to explore this relationship through a dataset and machine learning framework.

Method: The DREAMS dataset comprises facial video recordings of 32 participants watching diverse stimuli in naturalistic settings. Engagement and attention prediction is framed as a classification problem, evaluated under three paradigms: single-task learning (separate networks), transfer learning, and multi-task learning (shared network jointly predicting both states). Participants also completed video-based questionnaires and cognitive workload assessments.

Result: (a) Transfer learning and multi-task learning yield better classification performance for engagement prediction compared to single-task learning. (b) Higher engagement and attention states are associated with lower perceived cognitive load and improved task performance.

Conclusion: The DREAMS dataset and associated benchmarks demonstrate that jointly modeling engagement and attention improves predictive performance, and both states positively correlate with reduced cognitive load and enhanced task outcomes. The dataset and code are publicly available.

Abstract: Active attention and engagement are important in improving users' learning experiences. Engagement refers to the level of involvement and interest individuals show towards a particular task. Attention, on the other hand, refers to a state where someone is entirely focused on a particular task with conscious awareness. Engagement and attention are different but closely linked concepts and can influence each other bidirectionally. To explore the relationship between user engagement and attention, we introduce the Diverse Reactions of Engagement and Attention Mind States (DREAMS) dataset. The dataset includes facial video recordings of 32 users in naturalistic settings watching various stimuli to evoke diverse emotions. We then analyze user engagement and attention states in these videos by framing it as a classification problem, exploring single-task, transfer learning task, and multi-task settings. In single and transfer learning task settings, separate networks are applied to predict engagement and attention states. Whereas in multi-task settings a shared network is applied, which jointly learns to predict both engagement and attention states. Moreover, we examine participants' performance on video-based questionnaires and evaluate their perceived cognitive workload. In our findings, we observe (a) better classification performance in predicting engagement states in both transfer and multi-task learning compared to single-task learning and (b) higher engagement and attention states correlate with lower cognitive load and improved task performance. The dataset and the code are publicly available and can be accessed through https://sites.google.com/view/dreams-dataset/dataset.

</details>


### [151] [Octo's Adventure: At-home Deployment of a Pediatric Education Tool](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06684)
*Crimson Olaleye,Neda Barbazi,Ji Youn Shin,Gurumurthy Hiremath,Carlye Anne Lauff*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A one-week at-home deployment of Octo, a hybrid physical-digital tool for children with congenital heart disease (CHD), showed that children gained health understanding, expressed emotional attachment, and engaged in collaborative family communication, using child-friendly reflection and drawing-based methods embedded in daily routines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Children with CHD face educational, emotional, and communication challenges outside clinical settings, yet most pediatric health intervention studies rely on caregiver-mediated feedback, obscuring children's direct lived experiences during everyday tool use.

Method: A one-week at-home deployment study with 13 families of children diagnosed with CHD. The study embedded child-friendly reflection activities, drawing-based feedback, and emotional tracking into family routines, extending participatory design approaches into the deployment phase.

Result: Preliminary findings indicate that children gained understanding across Octo's physical and digital components, expressed emotional attachment and confidence through play, and engaged in collaborative family communication about their condition.

Conclusion: These findings will guide future refinement of Octo and inform subsequent clinical deployment across diverse care settings.

Abstract: Children with congenital heart disease (CHD) and their families often navigate educational, emotional, and communication challenges regarding care management outside clinical settings. However, many pediatric health intervention studies rely on caregiver-mediated feedback or structured evaluations, limiting visibility into children's direct experiences during everyday use. We present a one-week at-home deployment study of Octo, a hybrid physical-digital educational tool designed to support children's health literacy and reduce parental educational burden. Extending participatory design approaches into deployment, the study embedded child-friendly reflection activities, drawing-based feedback, and emotional tracking into family routines. We conducted the deployment with 13 families of children diagnosed with CHD. Preliminary findings suggest that children gained understanding across Octo's physical and digital components, expressed emotional attachment and confidence through play, and engaged in collaborative family communication about their condition. These findings will guide future refinement of Octo and inform future clinical deployment across care settings.

</details>


### [152] [CustomDance: Customized 3D Dance Generation with Coarse-to-Fine Human-Centered Interactive Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06722)
*Xulong Tang,Kaixing Yang,Xiaohu Guo,Prabhakaran Balakrishnan,Rawan Alghofaili*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: CustomDance is a coarse-to-fine interactive system for AI-assisted 3D dance choreography that combines a multimodal LLM for music/text analysis, a retrieval module for selecting dance phrases from a library, and a diffusion-based inpainter for seamless motion stitching, enabling user-guided iterative refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D dance generation methods produce technically correct but expressively shallow motions that lack alignment with users' creative vision, and fail to offer comprehensive, distinct control over multimodal inputs such as music and textual movement descriptions.

Method: CustomDance operates in three interconnected stages: (1) a multimodal LLM analyzes music and high-level text prompts to identify key temporal anchors and creative cues; (2) a multimodal retriever suggests high-quality motion clips from a dance library based on local music and text for each anchor, giving users concrete, predictable options; (3) a custom music-conditioned diffusion inpainter seamlessly connects selected phrases, supported by motion dynamics visualizations for iterative user-guided refinement.

Result: Evaluations show CustomDance outperforms competitive baselines across both quantitative metrics and qualitative comparisons, while demonstrating significant creative utility and empowering potential in AI-assisted choreography.

Conclusion: The coarse-to-fine, human-in-the-loop paradigm inspired by expert choreographer workflows effectively bridges the gap between automated generation and artistic intent, offering a more expressive, controllable, and user-empowering approach to 3D dance generation.

Abstract: With the rise of AI-generated content (AIGC) and advanced techniques for 3D human representation, the task of generating 3D dance movements has become an exciting area of research. Despite significant advancements, current methods often fail to provide comprehensive and distinct control over various multimodal inputs from users, such as music or specific descriptions of desired movements. As a result, the generated motions may be statistically plausible and technically correct, but they often lack depth, expressiveness, and alignment with the user's creative vision. To address this issue, we present CustomDance, a coarse-to-fine interactive system designed for customized 3D dance generation. Inspired by the workflows of expert choreographers, CustomDance introduces a novel paradigm to AI-assisted choreography through three interconnected stages. First, a multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) analyzes the music and a high-level text prompt to identify key temporal anchors and creative cues for the piece. Next, for each anchor, a multimodal retriever suggests high-quality motion clips from a dance library based on local music and text, empowering the user with concrete and predictable options. Finally, a custom music-conditioned diffusion in-painter seamlessly connects the selected phrases, allowing for iterative, user-guided refinement of the final composition, supported by visualizations of motion dynamics. Our evaluations demonstrate that CustomDance not only highlights the significant creative utility and empowering potential of our AI-assisted choreography paradigm, but also outperforms competitive baselines across quantitative and qualitative comparisons.

</details>


### [153] [Fact-Check Your Information (FYI): A Design Probe to Understand How People Actually Fact-Check Data-Driven Articles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06804)
*Nguyen-Truong Thinh,Yuxuan Du,Phongsakon Mark Konrad,Arpit Narechania*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: FYI is a browser extension that integrates AI-assisted fact-checking with manual data exploration. A user study (N=22) revealed three workflow archetypes—AI-first, manual-first, and parallel co-review—with visualization as the key mechanism for auditing AI. Trust in AI fluctuated based on consistency across tools. The authors recommend treating AI as a starting point, elevating visualization, and supporting flexible workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fact-checking systems isolate automated verification from manual data exploration, leaving unclear how readers coordinate AI assistance with hands-on evidence inspection in practice. The authors aim to bridge this gap by studying how people actually detect, verify, and validate data claims when both AI and manual tools are available within the reading environment.

Method: The authors developed FYI, a browser extension embedding four complementary fact-checking tools spanning from full automation to manual data exploration. They conducted an exploratory user study with 22 participants who used FYI to fact-check claims in a data-driven article. The study was structured as a design probe to observe naturalistic workflows, trust dynamics, and human-AI coordination strategies.

Result: Three distinct workflow archetypes emerged: (1) AI-first with manual confirmation, (2) manual-first with AI supplement, and (3) parallel co-review. Visualization served as the primary mechanism for auditing AI conclusions. Trust in AI shifted dynamically—growing when multiple tools converged and eroding when AI outputs were inconsistent.

Conclusion: Fact-checking systems should position AI as a starting point that human verification complements, not as a definitive authority. Visualization should be elevated as a core verification capability, and systems must support flexible, user-driven workflows rather than prescribing a single verification path.

Abstract: Data-driven journalism and policy reports frequently rely on statements grounded in statistical evidence, referred to as data claims. Verifying such a claim requires connecting it to the underlying structured dataset. However, existing systems typically isolate automated fact-checking from manual data exploration, leaving it unclear how readers coordinate AI assistance with manual inspection of the evidence in practice. We present FYI, a browser extension that embeds fact-checking in the reading environment, and use it as a design probe to study how people detect, verify, and determine the validity of data claims against the underlying dataset. FYI provides four complementary tools spanning the spectrum from full automation to manual data exploration. In an exploratory study (N=22), participants used FYI to fact-check claims in a data-driven article. We find that participants adopted three distinct workflow archetypes---AI-first with manual confirmation, manual-first with AI supplement, and parallel co-review---with visualization serving as the primary mechanism for auditing AI conclusions. Trust in AI shifted dynamically, growing when multiple tools converged and eroding when AI outputs were inconsistent. These findings suggest that fact-checking systems should treat AI as a starting point that human verification complements rather than a definitive authority, elevate visualization as a core verification capability, and support flexible, user-driven workflows. We release FYI as open-source software for further research at https://github.com/DataVisards/FYI.

</details>


### [154] [Not Always Top-Left: Untangling the Signals that Guide Dashboard Reading Order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06845)
*Nicole Sultanum,Vidya Setlur*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A mixed-methods study investigating how dashboard authors and end-users navigate dashboards, identifying factors influencing reading order (layout, visual saliency, semantics, functional roles, interaction, user context), emergent reading patterns, and implications for computational modeling of dashboard consumption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While dashboard authors design layouts to suggest a logical consumption flow, users may interpret and navigate dashboards differently due to the interplay of design features, analytical goals, and personal preferences. There is a gap in understanding how people actually make sense of dashboards through their reading sequences.

Method: A mixed-methods study with 18 dashboard authors and 16 end-users, capturing how participants design for and reason through component transitions. Both qualitative and quantitative analyses of participant-generated flows were conducted, examining aggregate measures and variability in reading patterns.

Result: Identified six key factors influencing dashboard reading order: layout, visual saliency, semantics, functional roles, interaction, and user context. Discovered emergent reading patterns and revealed areas of convergence and divergence in how users interpret dashboards.

Conclusion: The findings provide foundational knowledge for developing computational approaches that can automatically model, guide, or serialize dashboard consumption, bridging the gap between author intent and user behavior.

Abstract: Dashboards are widely used interfaces for data analysis, combining multiple visualizations, text, and interactive controls within a single view. While dashboard authors often structure layouts to suggest a logical consumption flow, users may interpret and navigate dashboards differently depending on the interplay between design features, analytical goals, and personal preferences. In this work, we investigate how people make sense of dashboards by examining their reading orders, i.e., the sequences in which users engage with dashboard components. We conduct a mixed-methods study with 18 dashboard authors and 16 end-users, capturing how participants design for and reason through these component transitions. Through qualitative and quantitative analyses of participant-generated flows, we outline a set of factors that influence dashboard reading order, including layout, visual saliency, semantics, functional roles, interaction, and user context. We also identify emergent reading patterns and analyze them through aggregate and variability measures, revealing where users converge and diverge in their interpretations. Finally, we discuss implications and opportunities for computational approaches that aim to automatically model, guide, or serialize dashboard consumption.

</details>


### [155] [The Nocturnity Scale: Measuring the Sense of Being at Night in Virtual Urban Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06904)
*Anthony Le Gourri{é}rec,Etienne Peillard,Nicolas Houel,Myriam Servi{è}res*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper introduces the construct of "nocturnity"—the subjective feeling of being at night—and proposes a theory-driven, tripartite framework (perceptual, activity, inner-state) along with a 42-item Likert-type questionnaire for assessing nocturnity in virtual urban environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Virtual urban studies increasingly employ nighttime settings, but darkness alone fails to capture the full subjective experience of night. No validated instrument exists to measure this scene-dependent feeling, which encompasses lighting structure, low-light perception, human activity, soundscape, and self-related states.

Method: A theory-driven framework was developed, structuring nocturnity into three subscales: perceptual, activity, and inner-state nocturnity. A candidate questionnaire (42 Likert-type items plus complementary global and time-related items) was constructed through a literature-informed process and reviewed by two urban lighting experts.

Result: The resulting scale comprises three diagnostic subscales (perceptual, activity, inner-state nocturnity) with supplementary global and time-related items, providing a first operational tool for comparing virtual urban scenes by perceived nocturnity.

Conclusion: The proposed questionnaire offers a foundational instrument for quantifying nocturnity in virtual urban environments and lays the groundwork for future empirical validation studies.

Abstract: Nighttime environments are increasingly used in virtual urban studies, yet darkness alone does not fully recreate the subjective sense of being at night. Prior work suggests that this experience depends not only on the absence of daylight, but also on lighting structure, low-light perception, human activity, soundscape, and self-related states. However, no existing tool directly assesses this scene-dependent subjective experience. This work introduces nocturnity as the feeling of being at night elicited by a scene and proposes a theory-driven framework structured into three subscales: perceptual, activity, and inner-state nocturnity. Based on this framework, we develop a first candidate questionnaire for virtual urban environments. Developed through a literature-informed process and reviewed by two urban lighting experts, the scale comprises 42 Likert-type items, including three diagnostic subscales and complementary global and time-related items. This work provides a first operational basis for comparing virtual urban scenes according to their perceived nocturnity and supports future empirical validation.

</details>


### [156] [Social Facilitation of Creative Reflection: AI-agents and Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06980)
*Olga Sutskova,Corey Ford*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper examines how social facilitation — the influence of others' mere presence or observation on behavior — may shape creative reflection in human-AI collaborations, exploring whether AI companions elicit similar non-verbal social dynamics as human partners and proposing methods to empirically test these effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As human-AI creative collaborations proliferate, there is a critical gap in understanding how different forms of social interaction — particularly non-verbal dynamics — influence creative reflection. It remains unclear whether AI companions can replicate the social facilitation effects that humans exert on one another during creative work, and at which stage of the creative process social intervention is most impactful.

Method: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper that reviews and synthesizes literature on social facilitation, non-verbal communication, creative reflection, and human-AI interaction. It proposes theoretical mechanisms linking social facilitation to creative practice and outlines directions for future empirical testing.

Result: The paper contributes a theoretical framework connecting social facilitation mechanisms to creative reflection in technology-mediated environments, and identifies testable propositions regarding whether AI social companionship can elicit effects comparable to human presence on creative outcomes.

Conclusion: Further empirical investigation is needed to determine how technology-mediated social environments and AI companions influence creative reflection. The paper calls for detailed examination of non-verbal social dynamics in the age of AI companionship, particularly regarding the timing and nature of social interventions in the creative process.

Abstract: Social collaboration can support people's reflection and is a crucial component of creativity. Creative technologies have been designed to support more collaborative ways of working, including using AI to simulate social partners. As human-AI creative collaborations increase, further investigation is needed into how different social interactions influence creative reflection and at which stage a social intervention is crucial to improve creative outcomes. Considering that non-verbal communication is the bedrock of human cognition and influence, non-verbal social dynamics should be examined in detail in the age of AI-companionship. For example, during social interaction, the social facilitation effect describes how the mere presence or observation of others influences how a person behaves and feels in the context. Whether changes in technology-mediated social environments influence how people reflect on their creative work needs further exploration, as does whether social AI-companionship elicits similar effects as humans. This paper discusses how theoretical mechanisms relating to social facilitation could influence creative practice and reflection, proposing ways of further testing these effects.

</details>


### [157] [Switched Reading: Toward Seamless Visual-Auditory Switching When Reading Text in Augmented/Mixed Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06985)
*Kazuyuki Fujita,Yuto Matsui,Ikuru Sato,Guanghan Zhao,Yoshifumi Kitamura*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Switched Reading is an AR/MR framework enabling seamless switching between visual and auditory text reading. It combines gaze-based voice playback and correspondence-aware transition effects, with studies showing the combined approach is most preferred, improves reading speed, and reduces gaze offsets during modality transitions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AR/MR wearable glasses enable ubiquitous information interaction, but visual displays can be inappropriate or unsafe when real-world awareness is critical (e.g., walking). Auditory output offers an alternative, but switching between visual and auditory reading modalities introduces continuity and attentional challenges that existing systems do not adequately address.

Method: The authors propose two techniques: (1) gaze-based voice playback that uses eye-tracking to synchronize auditory playback with the user's last-fixated text position, and (2) a correspondence-aware transition effect that visually highlights text as it is spoken to maintain cross-modal correspondence. These were implemented on an MR headset and tuned via a parameter-tuning user test. A VR user study (N=16) evaluated four conditions (baseline, gaze-only, transition-only, both combined) on reading performance and experience. A real-world walking application was also built and evaluated for qualitative feedback.

Result: The combined condition (gaze-based voice playback + transition effect) was the most preferred among all four conditions. Gaze-based voice playback significantly reduced gaze offsets during modality switching and improved reading speed compared to the scroll-position baseline. The walking application yielded further design implications for real-world deployment.

Conclusion: Switched Reading effectively supports modality switching for text consumption in AR/MR, with the combination of gaze-based voice playback and correspondence-aware transitions delivering the best user experience and performance. The framework opens new design directions for eyes-free, situational-awareness-preserving reading in mobile AR/MR contexts.

Abstract: Augmented/mixed reality (AR/MR) wearable glasses now permit information interaction anywhere, but visual displays can be inappropriate when real-world awareness is essential. We propose Switched Reading, a novel interaction framework for reading text in AR/MR that supports switching between visual and auditory modalities as needed. Specifically, we explore two key interaction techniques within this framework: (1) gaze-based voice playback and (2) a correspondence-aware transition effect. We implemented them on an MR headset through a parameter-tuning user test. Next, we conducted a user study (N=16) to investigate the impact of the two techniques on reading performance and overall user experience with simulated modality switching in virtual reality. The results show that the condition combining both techniques was the most preferred among four conditions. Moreover, we found that the gaze-based voice playback reduced gaze offsets when switching modalities and improved reading speed over the baseline condition using scroll position. Finally, we implemented a Switched Reading application for reading while walking and collected user feedback, yielding further design implications for practical use.

</details>


### [158] [XGait: A Multi-Modality Wireless Sensing Dataset for Indoor Human Tracking and Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07064)
*Wei Xu,Zhu Wang,Yifan Guo,Changlong Cheng,Yin Zhang,Zhihui Ren,Bin Guo,Zhiwen yu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: XGait is a multi-modal wireless sensing dataset capturing synchronized Wi-Fi and acoustic walking data from 27 participants across 3 indoor scenarios (22K+ samples), paired with a unified Doppler spectrogram representation and benchmarking pipeline to enable robust, reproducible cross-modal gait analysis for tracking and identification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-modality wireless sensing features are fragile to environmental layout and trajectory variations. Existing datasets lack trajectory diversity and multi-modal coverage, hindering robust evaluation of system generalization. There is a clear need for a standardized, multi-modal benchmark to systematically compare and combine Wi-Fi and acoustic sensing modalities.

Method: The authors introduce XGait, a dataset with synchronous Wi-Fi and acoustic transceiver recordings across three indoor scenarios, using vision-based ground truth. They propose a unified Doppler spectrogram representation that maps both Wi-Fi and acoustic signals into a shared time-frequency space, along with a standardized pipeline for pre-processing, temporal alignment, and feature construction.

Result: Extensive evaluations show that Wi-Fi and acoustic sensing exhibit complementary strengths, especially under complex trajectories and challenging propagation conditions, validating the utility of the multi-modal approach and the benchmarking framework.

Conclusion: XGait provides a foundational resource and standardized methodology that enables reproducible, cross-modal wireless sensing research, paving the way for future work in multi-modal gait tracking and identification.

Abstract: Wireless sensing has emerged as a promising approach for tracking and identification using commodity Internet of Things devices. However, the features derived from a single wireless modality are often fragile to variations in environmental layouts and walking trajectories. Furthermore, most existing studies are based on datasets collected in specific scenarios with limited trajectory diversity and sensing modalities, preventing a robust evaluation of system generalization. \textcolor{blue}{To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{XGait}, a multi-modality wireless sensing dataset that synchronously captures human walking using Wi-Fi and acoustic transceivers across three indoor scenarios, with vision-based measurements serving as ground truth. Specifically, XGait contains more than 22K walking samples from 27 participants, covering diverse directions and trajectories to support both indoor tracking and identity recognition. To bridge the heterogeneity of wireless sensing modalities, we propose a unified Doppler spectrogram representation that maps Wi-Fi and acoustic signals into a shared time--frequency space, along with a standardized benchmark pipeline for pre-processing, temporal alignment, and feature construction, enabling reproducible evaluation and systematic cross-modal analysis. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that Wi-Fi and acoustic sensing exhibit complementary strengths, particularly under complex trajectories and challenging propagation conditions, thereby paving the way for novel research in the field of multi-modality wireless sensing.} The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/warrior-087/XGait.

</details>


### [159] [Human-Centered Explainable AI for TinyML Edge Devices: A Pareto-Based Selection Framework with LLM-Guided Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07091)
*Zeinab Dehghani,Dhavalkumar Thakker,Koorosh Aslansefat,Kuniko Paxton,Bhupesh Kumar Mishra,Baseer Ahmad,Rameez Raja Kureshi*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper proposes a human-centered framework for selecting XAI methods in resource-constrained TinyML clinical deployments, using LLM-guided design interfaces to map qualitative stakeholder preferences to candidate methods, followed by feasibility filtering and Pareto optimization to balance explanation quality and deployment cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge AI in clinical settings requires both local inference under strict resource constraints and explainability to support healthcare decision-making. Selecting appropriate XAI methods for TinyML deployments is a multi-objective design problem that must jointly consider stakeholder preferences, explanation quality, and deployment feasibility — a challenge not adequately addressed by existing approaches.

Method: A three-stage framework: (1) an LLM-guided design interface that translates qualitative stakeholder preferences into candidate XAI methods; (2) deterministic feasibility filtering based on proxy deployment cost constraints; and (3) Pareto-based multi-objective optimization that exposes trade-offs among explanation fidelity, stability, and deployment cost. Proof-of-concept evaluation uses a skin lesion classification task.

Result: The framework systematically compares candidate XAI methods and identifies Pareto-efficient trade-offs between explanation fidelity, stability, and proxy-based deployment cost. The proof-of-concept demonstrates the computational selection stages, though physical MCU deployment and empirical human-expert validation remain future work.

Conclusion: The proposed framework offers a structured, human-centered approach to XAI method selection for TinyML in clinical contexts, enabling transparent trade-off analysis. Full validation requires future physical deployment and expert user studies.

Abstract: Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) enables the deployment of AI models directly on local edge devices, while such deployments are subject to strict resource constraints, particularly in clinical applications requiring local and timely inference. In such contexts, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can serve as a human-AI interface intended to support healthcare professionals' and patients' understanding of model predictions and informed decision-making. To fulfill this role, XAI method selection for TinyML deployments can be formulated as a human-centered multi-objective design problem that jointly considers qualitative stakeholder preferences, explanation quality, and proxy-based deployment cost. We propose a framework that integrates a large language model (LLM)-guided design interface that maps qualitative stakeholder preferences to candidate XAI methods, followed by deterministic feasibility filtering and Pareto-based optimization. The framework exposes trade-offs among explanation fidelity, stability, and proxy-based deployment cost while characterizing their implications for explanation quality and estimated deployment feasibility. A proof-of-concept evaluation on a skin lesion classification task illustrates how the framework systematically compares candidate XAI methods and identifies Pareto-efficient trade-offs. The present evaluation covers the computational selection stages, while physical MCU deployment and empirical human-expert validation remain outside the scope of this study.

</details>


### [160] [UncertaintyVis: Preserving Linguistic Uncertainty in Automated Text-to-Chart Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07093)
*Songheng Zhang,Emily Aurelia,Anthony Tang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: UncertaintyVis preserves linguistic uncertainty markers (e.g., "nearly," "at least") in automated chart generation, using a four-category taxonomy mapped to visual encodings. In a 12-participant study, uncertainty-aware charts achieved 85% chart-to-text matching accuracy, reduced cognitive demand, and were preferred by 75% of users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated text-to-chart systems discard linguistic uncertainty markers, producing deceptively definitive visualizations. Readers consequently over-interpret precision and misjudge author intent, undermining faithful communication of quantitative claims that were originally hedged or incomplete.

Method: First, a formative corpus analysis of 211 uncertainty expressions across 12 documents in 8 domains produced a four-category taxonomy: Surface Form Normalization, Precision Boundaries, Inferential Derivation, and Non-Inferable Gaps. Each category was then mapped to chart-specific visual encodings designed to signal uncertainty without disrupting spatial integrity. Finally, an end-to-end pipeline combining LLM-based text analysis with uncertainty-aware rendering was implemented and evaluated.

Result: In a two-part study (N=12), readers matched charts to source text with 85% accuracy and text to charts with 76% accuracy. Uncertainty-aware visualizations trended toward lower cognitive demand (mental demand effect size 0.460; effort effect size 0.769). 75% of participants preferred them over plain text, citing explicit uncertainty encodings as useful for verifying data claims. Performance varied by chart type: bar and pie encodings were consistent, while line chart encodings need redesign.

Conclusion: Explicitly encoding linguistic uncertainty in automated chart generation improves reader accuracy in recovering author intent, reduces cognitive load, and is strongly preferred by users. The taxonomy and visual encoding mapping provide a generalizable framework, though line chart encodings require further refinement.

Abstract: Data-rich documents pair narrative text with quantitative claims, and authors routinely qualify those claims with linguistic uncertainty markers such as "nearly," "approximately," or "at least." Automated text-to-chart systems discard these markers, producing visualizations that appear definitive even when the source text expresses hedged or incomplete knowledge. Readers may then over-interpret precision and misjudge author intent. We present UncertaintyVis, a system that preserves linguistic uncertainty during automated chart generation. A formative corpus analysis of 211 uncertainty expressions across 12 documents and 8 domains yielded a four-category taxonomy: Surface Form Normalization, Precision Boundaries, Inferential Derivation, and Non-Inferable Gaps. We mapped each category to chart-specific visual encodings that signal uncertainty without disturbing the spatial integrity readers rely on, and implemented an end-to-end pipeline pairing large language model text analysis with uncertainty-aware rendering. In a two-part study with 12 participants, readers matched charts to source text with 85% accuracy and text to charts with 76%. Uncertainty-aware visualizations trended toward lower cognitive demand (effect sizes 0.460 and 0.769 for mental demand and effort), and 75% of participants preferred them to plain text, describing explicit uncertainty encodings as a basis for verifying data claims. Encoding effectiveness varied by chart type: bar and pie encodings performed consistently, while line chart encodings require redesign.

</details>


### [161] [Thermodynamic Human-Computer Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07123)
*Uzafir Ahmad Rafaq,Muaz Hassan,Ali Muzaffar*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A thermodynamics-inspired framework unifies cursor and mobile target prediction, deriving Fitts' law from equilibrium thermodynamics and extending to non-equilibrium cases. It requires zero training, runs in O(1) time, and achieves 98.1% accuracy on web prefetching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing human-computer interaction models are domain-specific — cursor prediction models fail on mobile interfaces and vice versa. A unified, modality-agnostic framework is needed that generalizes across interaction types without retraining or domain adaptation.

Method: The framework models human interaction through thermodynamic phases (equilibrium and non-equilibrium). Kinetic and potential energies are assigned to a moving agent and target, allowing derivation of Fitts' law from equilibrium thermodynamics. The model scales across modalities, uses zero training data, and evaluates in constant O(1) time. Button color is treated as an independent parameter modulating attractive force on the agent.

Result: On live web prefetching tasks, the framework achieved a Fetch:Click ratio of 1.37 and predicted user targets with 98.1% accuracy. Equilibrium thermodynamics fails for large targets, a limitation the proposed non-equilibrium extension addresses.

Conclusion: Thermodynamics provides a principled, unifying lens for modeling human-computer interaction across modalities. The framework's zero-training, O(1) evaluation, and high accuracy make it practical for real-time applications like prefetching, though equilibrium models alone are insufficient for edge cases like large-target prediction.

Abstract: Traditional human-computer interaction models rely on domain-specific techniques to model target prediction; models designed for cursor interaction prediction fail to generalize to mobile interfaces and vice versa. We introduce a unifying framework grounded in thermodynamics, proposing that human interaction is composed of phases in thermodynamic equilibrium and non-equilibrium. To demonstrate this, we derive Fitts' law and the proposed target prediction model from equilibrium thermodynamics by assigning kinetic and potential energies to a moving agent and target. Subsequently, we analyze the shortcomings of the prediction model and Fitts' law in edge cases, such as predicting intent for large targets. This analysis demonstrates that large targets cannot be accurately modeled using equilibrium thermodynamics. The proposed model scales across interaction modalities without modification, requires zero training data, and evaluates in constant O(1) time. Furthermore, we show that design properties such as the color of a button act as independent parameters that influence the attractive force exerted on an agent. Applied to live web prefetching tasks, the framework achieved an efficient Fetch:Click ratio of 1.37 and predicted the user's target with an accuracy of 98.1%.

</details>


### [162] [PHOENIX: Fine-Tuned SLM-Powered Autonomous Satellite Lifetime Extension via Predictive Self-Healing and Multi-Agent AI Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07126)
*Sumaiya Islam,Harsha Kumara Moraliyage*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: PHOENIX deploys a fine-tuned Small Language Model onboard CubeSats for continuous fault monitoring and autonomous reasoning, paired with ground-based AI agents and a diffusion model for synthetic fault data generation, addressing the critical 85-minute communication gap in LEO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CubeSats in LEO suffer from an 85-minute communication blackout per 96-minute orbit, during which faults can escalate irrecoverably. With only 48-65% remaining operational after two years despite 2-5 year design lifetimes, there is a critical need for onboard autonomous fault detection and recovery capability.

Method: PHOENIX combines: (1) a fine-tuned Small Language Model (SLM) running on Aethero NxN-ECM flight-proven hardware for continuous onboard sensor monitoring and fault reasoning; (2) a memory system caching past repair solutions to avoid redundant inference; (3) once-per-orbit structured health reports replacing raw data dumps; (4) six specialized ground-based AI agents that generate validated commands within the 5-10 minute contact window; and (5) a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) to synthesize training data compensating for the extreme class imbalance (only 0.57-1.80% fault examples).

Result: Preliminary results are reported on the ESA Anomaly Detection Benchmark, which contains 14 years of data across 76 channels with 118 labeled faults.

Conclusion: Onboard edge AI using compact SLMs, combined with agentic ground-side reasoning and synthetic data augmentation, offers a promising architecture for improving CubeSat operational longevity by closing the fault-detection gap during communication blackout periods.

Abstract: Most CubeSats, small and low-cost satellites roughly the size of a shoebox, do not survive as long as they were designed to: a study of 178 missions found that only 48-65% remain operational after two years, against a designed lifetime of 2-5 years. The deeper issue is that a CubeSat in low Earth orbit (LEO) is physically unreachable from the ground for roughly 85 minutes out of every 96-minute orbit, so faults that start during that window go unnoticed until the next contact pass, by which point recovery may no longer be possible. We propose PHOENIX (Predictive Health On-orbit Edge Neural Intelligence eXtension) to give the satellite its own fault reasoning capability. A fine-tuned Small Language Model (SLM) compact enough to run on embedded hardware is deployed onboard the CubeSat, running on the flight-proven Aethero NxN-ECM computer, monitoring all sensor readings continuously, and resolving recurring faults using a memory system that stores past repairs so the same inference does not need to run twice. Once per orbit it sends a short structured health report to the ground instead of a raw data dump; six specialized AI agents on the ground read that report and generate validated satellite commands within the 5-10 minute contact window. A generative diffusion model (DDPM) creates synthetic training data because real fault examples make up only 0.57-1.80% of the dataset. We report preliminary results on the ESA Anomaly Detection Benchmark (14 years, 76 channels, 118 labeled faults).

</details>


### [163] [Incidental Visualizations: Augmented Reality as a Medium for Contextual Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07271)
*Matilde Heitor,João Moreira,Daniel Gonçalves*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Investigates "incidental visualizations" (IVs) — contextually relevant, brief, spontaneous information displays in AR — comparing them against ambient and periodic patterns. User studies with Sudoku and Connect 4 show IVs match ambient displays in comprehension accuracy while causing less disruption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ambient and glanceable visualizations, while useful for real-time data delivery, impose cognitive load and disrupt primary tasks. There is a need for information delivery mechanisms that are effective yet minimally intrusive, particularly in AR environments where displays are embedded in the user's surroundings.

Method: Controlled user studies employing logic-based game tasks (Sudoku and Connect 4) to compare three visualization patterns — ambient, periodic, and incidental — across metrics of comprehension accuracy, task performance, and disruption.

Result: Incidental visualizations deliver information as effectively as ambient displays in terms of comprehension accuracy while significantly minimizing disruption to the primary task.

Conclusion: Incidental visualizations show strong potential for adaptive, context-aware information delivery in AR environments, offering a compelling trade-off between informativeness and unobtrusiveness.

Abstract: In today's fast-paced world, delivering information efficiently and unobtrusively is essential. While ambient and glanceable visualizations provide real-time data, they can increase cognitive load and disrupt primary tasks. We investigate incidental visualizations, a novel concept in information visualization designed to present contextually relevant information briefly and spontaneously, with minimal user interaction. Augmented Reality offers an ideal medium for this integration, embedding visualizations directly within the user's environment. Through controlled user studies on logic-based game tasks (Sudoku and Connect 4), this work compares ambient, periodic, and incidental visualization patterns in terms of comprehension accuracy, performance, and disruption. Results indicate that IVs deliver information as effectively as ambient displays while minimizing disruption, highlighting their potential for adaptive, context-aware information delivery in AR environments.

</details>


### [164] [Beyond Call and Response: Modelling Reciprocal Coordination in Human-AI Vocal Ensembles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07376)
*Polina Proutskova*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper frames unconducted vocal ensembles as coupled dynamic systems and proposes a research architecture for AI vocal agents that participate in collective musical emergence rather than simply responding to individual inputs, addressing the hard case of non-isochronous repertoires.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing musical AI systems operate on a response-loop paradigm (human performs → system interprets → system responds), which fails for unconducted vocal ensembles where singers simultaneously and continuously affect one another through many-to-many reciprocal adjustment, with no fixed timing, pitch, or conductor. The authors seek to shift from AI that tracks a signal to AI that enters collective states.

Method: The paper proposes a comprehensive research architecture spanning five interconnected components: (1) multichannel field capture of ensemble singing, (2) dialect- and singing-aware acoustic representation learning, (3) collective-state inference that models group-level emergent dynamics, (4) vocal generation capable of participating in reciprocal adjustment, and (5) in-situ evaluation methods. Non-isochronous temporal contours serve as a "hard case" to test the generality of the framework.

Result: This is a position/agenda paper rather than an empirical study, so it presents a new research framing and architectural blueprint rather than experimental results. The key contribution is reframing the problem from "can an AI synchronise?" to "how does an AI's presence reorganise human coordination, leadership dynamics, stylistic evolution, and musical transmission within the ensemble?"

Conclusion: The paper argues that truly participatory AI vocal agents require moving beyond beat-tracking and turn-taking to modeling coupled dynamic systems. The proposed architecture opens a new research agenda where the core questions become sociological and musicological: how artificial agents reshape collective human musical behavior, not merely how well they mimic it.

Abstract: Musical interaction with AI is often organised as a response loop: a human performs, the system interprets that action, and the system answers, accompanies, or schedules a musical event. Unconducted vocal ensembles pose a different problem. Singers act simultaneously and continuously affect one another; neither timing nor pitch is fixed by a conductor, metronome, accompaniment, score, or tuning source. Collective organisation emerges from many-to-many reciprocal adjustment. This paper frames such ensembles as coupled dynamic systems and proposes a research architecture for vocal agents that enter, rather than merely track, their collective states. Some target repertoires are metrical, while others exhibit non-isochronous temporal contours that cannot be reduced to a beat grid; we treat the latter as a hard case for a general framework. The architecture connects multichannel capture in the field to dialect- and singing-aware representation, collective-state inference, vocal generation, and in-situ evaluation. The resulting agenda asks not only whether an artificial singer can synchronise, but how its presence reorganises human coordination, leadership, style, and musical transmission.

</details>


### [165] [Hands-Off or Hands-On? Variation in Area Chair Practices and Implications for AI Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07425)
*Ines Arous,Neha Nayak Kennard,Andrei Mircea,Emily Kuang,Jackie Chi Kit Cheung,Andrew McCallum*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Interviews with 27 AI area chairs reveal significant variation in how they manage peer review — from hands-off to hands-on — and a cautious stance toward AI tools. The study identifies key tensions (submission volume, uneven reviewer expertise, reviewer-author dynamics) and derives three design implications: tailoring AI to diverse AC practices, assisting discussion moderation, and embedding human-centered AI principles that preserve agency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Area chairs are critical to peer review, yet their challenges and perceptions of AI support tools remain poorly understood. Given growing submission volumes and the complexity of managing reviewer-author relationships, understanding AC practices is essential before designing AI interventions.

Method: Semi-structured interviews incorporating a design probe with 27 area chairs in AI venues. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify challenges, strategies, and attitudes toward potential AI tools.

Result: Three key tensions emerged: (1) growing submission volumes, (2) uneven reviewer expertise, and (3) the complexity of managing reviewer-author relationships. Crucially, the study found substantial variation in AC engagement styles — ranging from largely hands-off to deeply hands-on in guiding discussions and decisions — challenging the notion of a universal AC practice. ACs expressed cautious attitudes toward AI tools, informed by their domain expertise and awareness of AI limitations.

Conclusion: The diversity of AC practices precludes one-size-fits-all AI solutions. Three design implications are proposed: tailoring AI assistance to varied AC workflows, designing tools for discussion moderation, and embedding human-centered AI principles that preserve human agency in decision-making.

Abstract: Area chairs (ACs) play a critical role in the peer-review process, managing conflicts and ensuring fair outcomes. Although AI tools have been proposed to support ACs, little is known about the challenges they face and their perceptions of these technologies. In this paper, we conduct interviews including a design probe with 27 ACs in AI to explore their challenges, strategies, and perspectives on potential AI tools. Through thematic analysis, we identify key tensions arising from the growing volume of submissions, uneven reviewer expertise, and the complex task of managing the relationship between reviewers and authors. Most importantly, we find substantial variation in how ACs engage with submissions and influence outcomes: some adopt a largely hands-off approach, while others take a more hands-on role in guiding discussions and decisions. This variation challenges the notion of a single, universal AC practice and highlights the need to account for diverse approaches. When reflecting on the potential use of AI tools, ACs expressed a cautious stance, drawing on their domain knowledge and heightened awareness of AI limitations. From these findings, we derive three design implications: tailoring AI assistance to diverse AC practices, design assistance for discussion moderation, and embedding human-centered AI principles that preserve human agency in decision-making.

</details>
