### [166] [Flaky Test Recognition when Testing CPSs Using Hybrid Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06535)
*Zahra Sadri-Moshkenani,Justin Bradley,Gregg Rothermel*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces HyTestTF, an extension of the HyTest CPS testing framework that integrates TReVa (for validating test results) and FlaRe (for identifying flaky test cases and their underlying flaky conditions) using hybrid models, enabling detection of unreliable tests in early-stage CPS development with just one extra round of testing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CPSs operate in uncertain environments where timing, synchronization, and unexpected events cause non-deterministic behaviors, leading to "flaky" test cases that pass sometimes and fail other times. Such flaky tests undermine testing reliability, yet existing approaches lack systematic methods to identify both flaky tests and their root-cause flaky conditions early in development.

Method: The authors build on their prior test generation/execution technique HyTest and augment it with two new techniques: TReVa, which validates testing results, and FlaRe, which leverages hybrid models to recognize flaky test cases and the conditions causing flaky behavior. The combined approach, HyTestTF, operates in the early CPS development stages and requires only one additional round of testing to distinguish flaky from non-flaky tests.

Result: An empirical study demonstrates that HyTestTF effectively differentiates flaky test cases from non-flaky ones, improving the reliability of CPS testing outcomes.

Conclusion: HyTestTF provides a practical, lightweight approach (only one extra testing round) for early detection of flaky tests and their underlying conditions, yielding more trustworthy CPS validation results and enabling engineers to take corrective action before deployment.

Abstract: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) have many applications, ranging from simple thermostat systems to autonomous driving systems and medical devices. Like all systems, they need to function correctly. To this end, validation techniques such as testing that can effectively reveal faults are required. Also, CPSs usually operate in uncertain environments where various expected/unexpected events can affect their behaviors. These events together with timing and synchronization incidents may result in various/different CPS behaviors and may cause a CPS to pass a test under some conditions and fail it under others. Such test cases are called ``flaky'' test cases and we call the conditions that are responsible for them ``flaky conditions'' and call these behaviors ``flaky behaviors''. When test cases are flaky, testing results are unreliable. To achieve more reliable test results, engineers may attempt to recognize flaky test cases and remove them. In this work, beginning with a test case generation and execution technique called HyTest that we created previously, we integrate TReVa, a new technique that validates testing results provided by HyTest and FlaRe, a new technique that recognizes flaky test cases and flaky conditions using hybrid models during the early stages of CPS development in just one additional round of testing. We present the results of an empirical study evaluating the effectiveness of our new approach (which we call HyTestTF). Our results show that correctly differentiate flaky test cases from non-flaky test cases

</details>


### [167] [Understanding the Energy Impact of Software Refactoring: A Workload-Aware Study of Controlled Examples and Real-World Commits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06620)
*Haibo Wang,Heng Li,Shin Hwei Tan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A large-scale empirical study on the energy impact of code refactoring reveals that 51.8% of refactoring-workload pairs show significant energy differences in controlled settings, but only 7.5% of real-world refactoring commits do; workload variation strongly affects energy outcomes, refactoring type alone is a poor predictor, and neither metric-based nor LLM-based approaches reliably identify energy regressions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research on refactoring's energy impact is limited to isolated refactorings under fixed or simple workloads. Critical gaps remain: the effects of workload variation, real-world refactoring practices, explanatory factors, and reliable energy regression identification are insufficiently understood.

Method: The authors conducted the first large-scale empirical study using two complementary Java benchmarks: (1) a Micro-benchmark with 68 refactoring types evaluated under diverse workloads, and (2) a Practical-benchmark with 481 real-world refactoring commits from 430 GitHub projects. They employed repeated paired energy measurements to analyze workload sensitivity, refactoring patterns, explanatory factors, and the effectiveness of metric-based and LLM-based regression identification.

Result: In the Micro-benchmark, 199 of 384 refactoring-workload pairs (51.8%) showed statistically significant energy differences, with 45.3% of refactoring instances changing energy-impact classification across workloads. In the Practical-benchmark, only 36 commits (7.5%) showed significant energy changes, though two-thirds differed by at least 10%. Refactoring type alone was insufficient to predict energy outcomes, but certain recurring refactoring combinations were associated with energy reductions. Execution time changes consistently explained energy variation in the controlled benchmark but correlated weakly with energy changes in real-world commits.

Conclusion: The findings underscore the necessity of workload-diverse evaluation for assessing refactoring's energy impact. Neither existing metric-based approaches nor LLM-based predictors can reliably identify refactoring-induced energy regressions, motivating the development of more accurate prediction techniques.

Abstract: Refactoring improves software maintainability while preserving functional behavior, yet behavior preservation does not imply energy neutrality. Existing studies primarily examine isolated refactorings under fixed or simple workloads, leaving the effects of workload variation, real-world refactoring practices, explanatory factors, and energy regression identification insufficiently understood. We present the first large-scale empirical study of the energy impact of refactoring across two complementary Java benchmarks: a Micro-benchmark, comprising 68 refactoring types evaluated under diverse workloads, and a Practical-benchmark, containing 481 real-world refactoring commits from 430 GitHub projects. Using repeated paired energy measurements, we analyze workload sensitivity, refactoring patterns, explanatory factors, and the effectiveness of metric- and LLM-based regression identification. In the Micro-benchmark, 199 of 384 refactoring-workload pairs (51.8%) exhibit statistically significant energy differences, and 45.3% of refactoring instances change energy-impact classification across workloads. In the Practical-benchmark, only 36 commits (7.5%) show significant energy changes, although two-thirds differ by at least 10%. Refactoring type alone is insufficient to predict energy outcomes, while certain recurring refactoring combinations are associated with energy reductions. Changes in execution time consistently explain energy variation in the controlled benchmark but correlate weakly with energy changes in real-world commits. Our findings highlight the need for workload-diverse evaluation of the energy impact of refactoring; neither existing metric-based approaches nor LLM-based predictors can reliably identify refactoring-induced energy regressions, motivating the development of more accurate techniques for predicting the energy impact of refactoring.

</details>


### [168] [Characterizing the Quality Profile of AI-Generated C++ in Production](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06640)
*Michael Tran,Fred Lewis,Kun Yang,Saksham Thakur,Aditya Kini,Aditya Patil,Milad Hashemi,Parthasarathy Ranganathan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A large-scale empirical study (3.52M code changes over one year) at a major enterprise finds AI-generated C++ code exhibits higher coupling burdens, allocation overhead, and reliance on explicit loops over standard APIs, leading to 5-8% higher compute resource consumption. Targeted, taxonomy-informed feedback reduces static analysis warnings by 11.1% and improves efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding assistants boost engineering velocity but raise concerns about code quality and maintainability. Measuring these effects in industrial production environments is difficult due to observability barriers. This study leverages a large enterprise's thorough production observability to empirically assess the real-world quality impact of AI-generated code at scale.

Method: Large-scale empirical analysis of 3.52 million C++ code changes from April 2025 to April 2026 in a brownfield enterprise codebase serving billions of users. The study compares AI-generated code against human-written code along dimensions of quality, performance, and maintenance characteristics, leveraging the organization's per-line production observability. A follow-up intervention applies targeted, taxonomy-informed feedback to models to measure mitigation effects.

Result: AI-generated C++ code shows a distinct quality profile: higher interface/coupling burdens, increased copy and allocation overheads, and reliance on explicit loops rather than optimized standard APIs. These translate into increased review effort and a 5-8% rise in compute resource consumption. However, taxonomy-informed feedback reduces targeted static analysis warnings by 11.1% and improves computational efficiency.

Conclusion: AI-generated code introduces measurable quality degradations in production environments, but these effects are not inherent or unavoidable. Providing models with targeted, taxonomy-informed feedback can substantially mitigate quality issues, suggesting a path toward harnessing AI coding assistants without sacrificing production code quality.

Abstract: The widespread integration of AI coding assistants offers undeniable boosts to engineering velocity. Yet, recent studies point to a growing trade-off, revealing persistent challenges with code quality and maintainability. Industry leaders, including frontier AI labs, echo these concerns. As large language models are increasingly relied upon to author production code, understanding their impact on shipped software quality has become a critical priority. However, assessing these effects in industrial workflows remains difficult due to observability barriers. We study the impact of AI-generated code on production quality within a large enterprise operating global products relied upon by billions of users daily. Driven by this scale and user trust, the organization values code quality and has built thorough observability for every line of code deployed into production, enabling us to overcome measurement barriers to assess these effects.
  This study presents a large-scale empirical analysis of AI-generated C++ code from April 2025 to April 2026, tracking 3.52 million code changes across this enterprise's brownfield codebase. The core purpose is to understand the quality, performance, and maintenance characteristics of AI-generated code compared to human-written code in a production environment at scale. We find that AI-generated C++ code has a distinct quality profile, showing higher rates of interface and coupling burdens, copy and allocation overheads, and a reliance on explicit loops over optimized standard APIs. These issues translate into tangible downstream costs, including increased review effort and a 5-8% increase in compute resource consumption. However, we demonstrate that providing models with targeted, taxonomy-informed feedback can mitigate these effects, leading to an 11.1% reduction in targeted static analysis warnings and improved computational efficiency.

</details>


### [169] [Online Monitoring and Corrective Steering of Programming Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06701)
*Shuyang Liu,Saman Dehghan,Ji Young Kim,Jatin Ganhotra,Martin Hirzel,Reyhaneh Jabbarvand*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LivePlan is a real-time monitoring and correction framework for LLM-based agents fixing GitHub issues. It decouples a deterministic rule-based monitor from an LLM advisor: the monitor detects behavioral inefficiencies (plan drift, repeated failures, premature termination) without LLM overhead, and only invokes the advisor when an issue is detected. On SWE-bench Verified and Pro, LivePlan improves resolution rates by up to 15.2% (avg. 9.9%) at just $0.08 extra per instance, with gains concentrated on medium/hard problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixing GitHub issues in large-scale projects is a long-horizon task where LLM agents often exhibit behavioral inefficiencies—drifting from their plan, repeating failed actions, or terminating without a valid patch. Prior approaches that use LLMs for continuous re-planning are costly and can mislead the agent. There is a need for a lightweight, real-time mechanism to detect and correct these inefficiencies without introducing the overhead and errors of constant LLM intervention.

Method: LivePlan decouples judging from advising using a two-stage pipeline: (1) A deterministic, rule-based monitor continuously examines general signals along the agent's trajectory to detect behavioral issues (plan drift, repeated failures, premature termination) without any LLM invocation. (2) Only when an issue is detected does the system consult a separate advisor LLM, which provides a high-level, next-step correction to steer the agent back on track. This avoids the misleading re-planning and costly interventions of prior LLM-based monitoring approaches.

Result: Evaluated across SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro using five LLMs (three executors, two advisors), LivePlan achieves up to 15.2% improvement in resolution rate over vanilla SWE-agent (average 9.9%), with additional cost of only $0.08 per instance. Improvements are concentrated on medium and hard instances. LivePlan consistently outperforms alternative approaches with minimal regression on already-successful runs and achieves new successes on problems no baseline solves.

Conclusion: Decoupling issue detection from correction—using a lightweight deterministic monitor and invoking an LLM advisor only when necessary—effectively improves the long-horizon reasoning of code-fixing agents. LivePlan delivers substantial resolution gains at negligible additional cost and is particularly beneficial for harder problem instances.

Abstract: Fixing GitHub issues in large-scale projects is a long-horizon task, especially when a fix requires changes across multiple locations or the issue description lacks the information needed to localize and repair it. As a result, agents traverse long trajectories that are prone to inefficiency and error: they drift away from their intended plan, repeat failed actions, or terminate without a working patch. This paper proposes LivePlan to monitor, detect, and correct such behavioral inefficiencies and drifts in real time. LivePlan decouples judging from advising: a deterministic, rule-based monitor examines general signals over the trajectory to detect issues without invoking an LLM, and only when an issue is detected does it consult an advisor LLM for a high-level, next-step correction. This design avoids the misleading re-planning and costly interventions of prior approaches. We implement LivePlan on top of SWE-agent and evaluate it using five LLMs (three as executor agents and two as advisors) across SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro. Compared to vanilla SWE-agent, LivePlan notably improves issue resolution rates, achieving consistent gains of up to 15.2% (average: 9.9%), while incurring only an additional cost of $0.08 per instance. The additional solutions concentrate on medium and hard instances. LivePlan consistently outperforms alternative approaches in resolution rate, with minimal regression on already successful runs and new successes on problems that no baseline solves.

</details>


### [170] [Translation Tag Team: Formal Rules and LLMs Translate More Macros Together than Apart](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06705)
*Brent Pappas,Joseph Zalusky,Zachary Burkett,Paul Gazzillo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MerC is a formally-specified translator that preserves C macros when translating to Rust, avoiding the dissimilarity caused by preprocessing. Evaluated on MacroBench (a new macro translation benchmark), MerC handles 50% of cases correctly. LLMs translate more but introduce errors; a "tag team" approach combining MerC then LLMs yields the best trade-off: 32% lower failure rate than LLMs alone and 51% more coverage than MerC alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing C-to-Rust translation techniques preprocess macros away via inlining, producing translated code that is structurally dissimilar to the original. Since real-world C code heavily uses macros, there is a need for a translation approach that preserves macro usage, maintaining code familiarity and readability in the translated Rust output.

Method: The authors study shared language features between C macros and Rust, then distill these into MerC—the first formally-specified C-to-Rust translator that preserves macro constructs. They also create MacroBench, the first benchmark for macro translation, using test cases randomly sampled from real-world programs. They evaluate MerC and LLMs independently, then propose a hybrid "tag team" pipeline: run MerC first for guaranteed-correct translations, then apply LLMs to the remaining cases.

Result: MerC supports 50% of MacroBench test cases with zero incorrect translations. LLMs translate 22–77% more test cases than MerC, but 8–28% of these are incorrect. The tag team approach (MerC + LLMs) reduces the average failure rate by 32% compared to LLMs alone and translates 51% more cases than MerC alone.

Conclusion: A formally-specified approach (MerC) guarantees correctness but has limited coverage; LLMs offer broader coverage at the cost of reliability. Combining both in a pipeline yields the best overall performance, suggesting that hybrid translation strategies are the most promising direction for C-macro-to-Rust translation.

Abstract: Modern critical software infrastructure is largely written in C. Since C lacks memory safety, researchers are investigating automatic translation of C to safer languages like Rust. But real-world C software consists of more than just C code, often using named code fragments called macros which are not part of the C language proper. State-of-the-art techniques avoid translating macros by preprocessing C code first before translating it. But this approach produces translations that are dissimilar to the original C code, because preprocessing inlines all macro definitions. To preserve macro usage in translated code, we study the language features that macros and C share and distill them into the first formally-specified translator, MerC. To evaluate MerC, we introduce the first macro translation benchmark, MacroBench, with test cases based on macros randomly sampled from real-world C programs. We find that MerC supports 50% of MacroBench's macro test cases. We also use MacroBench to evaluate how effective large language models (LLMs) are at performing the previously-unstudied task of macro translation. LLMs translate 22% to 77% more of MacroBench than MerC, but with 8% and 28% of these translations being incorrect translations requiring additional validation by developers. In contrast, MerC only produces correct translations. Our key insight is that running MerC first then using LLMs on the remainder reaps greater benefits than using either technique alone. This tag team approach has an average failure rate 32% lower than that of LLMs, while also translating an average of 51% more test cases than MerC.

</details>


### [171] [AgentChaos: Chaos Engineering for Agent Systems via Programmatic Fault Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06790)
*Gou Tan,Zhensu Sun,Jieke Shi,Ting Zhang,Zilong He,Qingfu Wu,Shuai Liang,Weifeng Sun,Junda He,Pengfei Chen,Chuanfu Zhang,Lwin Khin Shar,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentChaos is a chaos engineering framework that injects faults into LLM API responses at the HTTP layer at runtime without source code modification. Using a taxonomy of crash, omission, and value faults on content and tool call fields, it evaluates agent system robustness across 65 fault configurations, finding up to 50 percentage point drops in pass@1 and that robustness depends on system implementation rather than model capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent systems depend on LLM APIs that can return server errors, truncated responses, or corrupted content, which propagate through downstream agents causing task failures. Existing fault injection methods are offline, require source code modification, or lack fine-grained field-level control. A systematic fault taxonomy is needed because different fault types affect downstream agents differently.

Method: AgentChaos injects faults at the shared HTTP interface layer common to all LLM-based agent systems, requiring no source code modification. It defines a fault taxonomy with crash, omission, and value faults targeting content and tool call fields. Faults are injected at runtime, and a verification mechanism filters untriggered tasks to avoid underestimating fault impact. The framework is evaluated across multiple agent systems, benchmarks, and backbone LLMs under 65 fault configurations.

Result: All agent systems degrade under fault injection, with pass@1 dropping by up to 50 percentage points. Robustness ranking remains consistent across backbone models, indicating system implementation determines robustness rather than model capability. Existing fault diagnosis methods achieve below 53% accuracy on fault type and below 56% on fault step, indicating significant room for improvement.

Conclusion: AgentChaos provides a systematic, non-intrusive approach to evaluating LLM agent robustness under API faults. The findings emphasize that agent system developers should focus on implementation-level resilience rather than relying on more capable models, and highlight the inadequacy of current fault diagnosis methods.

Abstract: Agent systems rely on LLM APIs for every response, but these APIs can return server errors, truncated responses, or corrupted content that propagates through downstream agents and causes task failure. Evaluating robustness under these faults is crucial for reliable deployment. Existing fault injection methods are offline, require source code modification, or cannot modify specific response fields. A comprehensive evaluation also requires a systematic fault taxonomy because different fault types affect downstream agents differently. We propose AgentChaos, a chaos engineering framework for controlled, runtime, non-intrusive LLM API fault injection. Since all agent systems access LLMs through the same HTTP interface, we inject faults at this shared layer without modifying source code. We define crash, omission, and value faults on content and tool call fields, intercept and modify LLM API responses at runtime, and verify whether each fault is triggered to filter untriggered tasks and avoid underestimating fault impact. Evaluations across agent systems, benchmarks, and backbone LLMs under 65 fault configurations show that all systems degrade under fault injection, with pass@1 dropping by up to 50 percentage points. The ranking is consistent across models, suggesting that robustness depends on system implementation rather than model capability. Existing fault diagnosis methods achieve below 53% accuracy on fault type and below 56% on fault step, leaving room for improvement. We further reveal practical findings for agent system developers.

</details>


### [172] [Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06811)
*Jiahao Zhang,Yifan Zhang,Yu Huang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PMCoder is an LLM-based repository-level issue-resolution agent that bidirectionally couples a hierarchical phase planner with episodic memory. The planner conditions memory retrieval, while memory statistics inform stuck detection and replanning. It also uses execution-based reproduction verdicts for grounded verification. On SWE-bench Verified, it resolves 25 more cases (+5.0pp) than baseline, with gains across multiple models and transfers to TerminalWorld.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing repository-level LLM agents for software issue resolution strengthen planning or memory in isolation. Long repair episodes (tens to hundreds of steps) are thus vulnerable to stale evidence, repeated failed edits, and self-reported (rather than execution-grounded) verification. A coupled approach addressing both planning and memory jointly is needed.

Method: PMCoder introduces a hierarchical phase planner coupled bidirectionally with episodic memory: the current plan phase conditions memory retrieval, while trajectory statistics from memory inform stuck detection and replanning. It also grounds verification in execution evidence via issue-reproduction verdicts when available, rather than relying on self-reported completion.

Result: On SWE-bench Verified, PMCoder resolves +25 cases (+5.0pp) over a harness-matched baseline, with gains even when the reproduction gate does not fire. On Verified-500, gains hold across Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and an OpenHands port (≥+14 cases, +2.8pp). On TerminalWorld's official sample, the plan-memory substrate transfers beyond issue reports. Ablations show coupling planning and memory outperforms either alone and reduces repeated failures, empty-patch exits, and context-window exhaustion.

Conclusion: Bidirectionally coupling hierarchical phase planning with episodic memory significantly improves LLM-based issue-resolution agents. The approach reduces common long-trajectory failure modes and generalizes across models, harnesses, and even beyond issue-report tasks, suggesting a robust substrate for agentic software repair.

Abstract: Resolving a real software issue with a large language model (LLM) agent is a long repair episode, often tens to hundreds of steps spanning exploration, hypothesis, implementation, and verification. Success depends on both the base model's local reasoning and the agent's ability to maintain an evolving plan and remember observations across phases. Existing repository-level agents typically strengthen planning or memory in isolation, leaving long trajectories vulnerable to stale evidence, repeated failed edits, and verification inferred from the agent's own claims instead of execution evidence. We present PMCoder, an issue-resolution agent that couples a hierarchical phase planner with episodic memory. The coupling is bidirectional: the current plan phase conditions memory retrieval, while memory-derived trajectory statistics inform stuck detection and replanning. When available, issue-reproduction verdicts ground verification progress in execution evidence rather than self-reported completion. On SWE-bench Verified, PMCoder resolves an average of $25$ more cases ($+5.0$pp) than a harness-matched baseline, with gains persisting even where the reproduction gate never fires. Further Verified-500 evaluations show the same positive direction across Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and an OpenHands port, with at least $14$ additional resolved cases ($+2.8$pp). Separately, evaluation on TerminalWorld's official sample suggests that the plan-memory substrate transfers beyond issue reports. Ablation and trajectory analyses show where the gains come from: coupling planning and memory outperforms either component alone and reduces repeated failed actions, empty-patch exits, and context-window exhaustion.

</details>


### [173] [How Reasoning Shapes Social Bias in LLM-Generated Code?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06829)
*Weifeng Sun,Jieke Shi,Zhou Yang,Yuchen Chen,Hongyan Li,Meng Yan,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: First systematic study of social bias in reasoning-based code generation. Finds that while reasoning reduces bias, it also degrades code quality; biased reasoning strongly predicts biased code. Proposes ProbeDebias, a framework that detects and rewrites biased reasoning traces, reducing code bias by 83.73% while largely preserving quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for code generation, but generated code can exhibit social bias via unfair treatment of sensitive demographic attributes. While direct code generation bias has been studied, bias in reasoning-based generation (chain-of-thought, etc.) remains underexplored despite the growing prominence of reasoning models.

Method: Evaluated 9 LLMs and large reasoning models (LRMs) on realistic bias-sensitive tasks across three human-centered decision scenarios. Analyzed relationship between reasoning bias and code bias, plus effects of generation configuration. Proposed ProbeDebias: a reasoning-aware framework that detects biased reasoning traces (87.76% F1) and rewrites them before code generation to mitigate bias.

Result: Reasoning reduces average bias rate from 0.64 to 0.40 but varies across models; code quality drops from 0.72 to 0.59. Biased reasoning strongly predicts biased code. ProbeDebias reduces code bias by 83.73% on average while preserving quality, outperforming SOTA baselines by 52.70%-54.42% in bias reduction and 9.79%-36.79% in quality improvement.

Conclusion: Reasoning-stage analysis and intervention is critical for trustworthy code generation. Adjusting generation configurations alone is insufficient; targeted detection and rewriting of biased reasoning traces offers a more robust mitigation strategy.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, yet generated programs may exhibit social bias through unfair or differential treatment of sensitive demographic attributes. While prior work mainly studies direct code generation, bias in reasoning-based generation remains underexplored. We conduct the first systematic study of social bias in reasoning-based code generation, evaluating 9 standard LLMs and large reasoning models (LRMs) on realistic bias-sensitive tasks across three human-centered decision scenarios. We find that reasoning generally reduces bias, lowering the average bias rate from 0.64 to 0.40, but the effect varies substantially across models. Meanwhile, code quality is not consistently preserved, with the average quality dropping from 0.72 to 0.59. Biased reasoning strongly predicts biased code, and adjusting generation configurations alone is insufficient for robust mitigation. Based on these findings, we propose ProbeDebias, a reasoning-aware framework that detects and rewrites biased reasoning traces before code generation. ProbeDebias achieves 87.76% F1 for reasoning-bias detection and reduces code bias by 83.73% on average while largely preserving quality. Compared with SOTA baselines, it further reduces average bias by 52.70%-54.42% and improves quality by 9.79%-36.79%. These results highlight the value of reasoning-stage analysis for trustworthy code generation.

</details>


### [174] [Statistical Analysis of Executability and Program Equivalence in Decompilation for IoT Vulnerability Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06960)
*Minami Yoda,Jialong Li,Yasuyuki Tahara,Yuichi Sei,Yutaka Matsuno*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A nine-dimensional metric spanning structural, behavioral, and semantic similarity is proposed to evaluate decompiled IoT firmware code quality, moving beyond binary recompilation success to capture semantically faithful decompilation. Statistical analysis of 19,625 decompilation outputs from OpenWrt shows the metric strongly predicts decompilation quality (Cohen's d=0.92 overall).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based decompilation produces highly readable code but can introduce subtle semantic deviations (e.g., altered error-handling and boundary checks) that existing metrics—focused on test-case pass rates—fail to detect. IoT firmware handling sensitive data demands a metric that quantifies internal structural fidelity.

Method: The authors propose a three-category, nine-dimensional evaluation metric: structural similarity, behavioral similarity, and semantic similarity. They tested five decompilation methods (one rule-based, four LLM-based) on 318 OpenWrt programs, generating 19,625 decompilation results, then statistically analyzed differences between recompilation-success and failure groups using Cohen's d effect sizes.

Result: The recompilation-success group significantly outperformed the failure group across the proposed metrics: overall score d=0.92, behavioral similarity d=0.96, and structural similarity d=0.69, confirming these dimensions as important predictors of decompilation quality.

Conclusion: The proposed multi-dimensional metric provides a statistical foundation for evaluating decompilation quality in IoT firmware analysis and offers a generalizable framework for assessing black-box generative model outputs beyond surface-level correctness.

Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) devices handle sensitive privacy-related information such as user audio, video, and authentication data, making it essential to detect vulnerabilities in their firmware. Decompilation, a key detection technique, has recently attracted attention because Large Language Models (LLMs) enable high readability and high recompilation success rates. However, because LLM outputs depend on probabilistic token prediction, they tend to prioritize syntactic correctness and may generate plausible-looking code that is semantically different from the original binary. Vulnerabilities often arise in details that are easily lost in this process, such as error-handling flows and boundary checks. Existing evaluation metrics focus mainly on passing test cases and cannot sufficiently identify code whose internal structure has been altered despite appearing behaviorally valid, so a metric that quantifies the internal structure of decompiled code from multiple perspectives is needed. We propose a nine-dimensional quality evaluation metric consisting of three categories: structural, behavioral, and semantic similarity. Targeting 318 programs from OpenWrt, an open-source router platform underlying many commercial routers, we generated 19,625 decompilation results using five methods (one rule-based and four LLM-based) and analyzed them statistically. The recompilation-success group achieved significantly higher overall scores than the failure group (Cohen's d=0.92); behavioral similarity showed d=0.96 and structural similarity d=0.69, demonstrating that these metrics are important predictors of decompilation quality. This study provides a statistical evaluation foundation for quantifying implementation defects in IoT devices and a framework that generalizes to quality evaluation of black-box generative models.

</details>


### [175] [What Are Developers Actually Discussing When Visual Regression Tests Fail?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07020)
*Miku Watanabe,Kosei Horikawa,Brittany Reid,Yutaro Kashiwa,Hajimu Iida*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An empirical study of 307 VRT-enabled PRs vs. 299 image-only PRs reveals VRTs slow down review (3.8× longer, 10× more comments) but predominantly catch stylistic defects (82%). Notably, ~18.5% of flagged issues are non-stylistic—such as undefined states, content disappearance, and imperceptible regressions—demonstrating VRTs' secondary role as detectors of unintended, non-local code-change consequences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The prevailing assumption is that Visual Regression Tests (VRTs) only detect stylistic regressions (layout, color, font). The authors challenge this by empirically investigating whether VRTs also surface non-stylistic defects, and how VRT integration affects the PR review process in terms of acceptance rate, resolution time, discussion volume, and code churn.

Method: The authors conduct a mixed-methods empirical study: (1) quantitative comparison of 307 VRT-PRs (using Chromatic) vs. 299 Visual PRs (image attachments, no VRT) from 103 GitHub repositories, measuring acceptance rate, resolution time, comment count, and code-change size; (2) a card-sorting analysis of 189 VRT-flagged issues to categorize defect types into seven categories (Layout, Appearance, Color, Text, State, Test, Image).

Result: VRT-PRs show no significant acceptance-rate difference but have 3.8× longer median resolution time, 10× more comments, and 1.75–4.5× larger code changes. VRT results appear mid-review and sustain discussion. Defect categories: Layout (39.7%), Appearance (27.5%), Color (14.8%), Text (9.5%), State (6.9%), Test (6.3%), Image (4.2%). ~18.5% are non-stylistic (undefined state: 13 cases; content disappearance: 17 cases; visually imperceptible regressions: 5 cases). VRTs also caught regressions from changes in seemingly unrelated files.

Conclusion: Beyond their established role as stylistic checkers, VRTs function as secondary detectors of unintended consequences from code changes, including non-local effects no targeted test would catch. This has implications for how VRTs should be integrated into maintenance toolchains—not merely as a final gate, but as an ongoing discussion-sustaining mechanism throughout review.

Abstract: Visual Regression Tests (VRTs) are widely adopted as a mechanism for detecting unintended visual changes in user interfaces. By design, VRTs operate on rendered pixel output, and the prevailing assumption is that they catch stylistic regressions such as layout shifts, color mismatches, and font alterations. We conduct an empirical analysis of 307 pull requests (PRs) from 103 GitHub repositories that incorporate VRT results via Chromatic, comparing them against 299 PRs that contain image attachments but no VRT (Visual PRs). Quantitatively, VRT-PRs show no significant acceptance-rate difference, but exhibit a 3.8 times longer median resolution time, 10 times more discussion comments, and 1.75 to 4.5 times larger code changes than Visual PRs. VRT results are typically shared around the midpoint of the review process, sustaining ongoing discussion rather than serving only as a final check. Through a card-sorting analysis of 189 VRT-flagged issues, we identify seven defect categories assigned to the analyzed issues: Layout (39.7\%), Appearance (27.5\%), Color (14.8\%), Text (9.5\%), State (6.9\%), Test (6.3\%), and Image (4.2\%). The three most frequent categories are stylistic, while approximately 18.5\% of analyzed issues (35/189) involve non-stylistic origins, including undefined component state (13 cases), content disappearance (17 cases across multiple categories), and visually imperceptible regressions (5 cases). We further document cases in which VRT detected visual regressions originating from code changes in seemingly unrelated files, exposing non-local effects that no targeted test would have been written to catch. These observations indicate that, in addition to its primary role as a stylistic checker, VRT functions as a secondary detector of unintended consequences of code changes, with implications for how VRT should be integrated into the maintenance toolchain.

</details>


### [176] [CAS2UML: A Handwritten Sketch-to-PlantUML Dataset for Class and Activity Diagrams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07036)
*Simon Scholz,Mersedeh Sadeghi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CAS2UML is a public dataset of 557 hand-drawn UML diagrams paired with manually validated PlantUML code, accompanied by validation tools and scripts to enable reproducible benchmarking of sketch-to-UML approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reproducible evaluation of automated UML generation from sketches is hindered by the lack of public datasets with executable ground-truth models. Existing work lacks standardized benchmarks due to absent validated reference implementations.

Method: The authors constructed CAS2UML, consisting of 271 class diagrams and 286 activity diagrams, each manually validated against executable PlantUML code. They also developed a PlantUML-based validation tool and reusable scripts for checking syntactic correctness and renderability of generated UML artifacts.

Result: The resulting dataset, tooling, and scripts are publicly released on Hugging Face and GitHub, along with documentation and a demonstration video, providing a foundation for standardized, reproducible evaluation of sketch-to-UML systems.

Conclusion: CAS2UML fills a critical gap in sketch-to-UML research by providing the first public, validated dataset with executable ground-truth PlantUML, enabling fair and reproducible benchmarking of multimodal AI approaches for UML generation.

Abstract: Automated UML generation from sketches and images is gaining renewed attention with the rise of large language models and multimodal AI. However, reproducible evaluation remains difficult due to the lack of public datasets with executable groundtruth models. We present CAS2UML, a public dataset of 557 handdrawn UML diagrams, including 271 class diagrams and 286 activity diagrams, each paired with manually validated PlantUML code. We also provide a PlantUML-based validation tool and reusable scripts for checking the syntactic correctness and renderability of generated UML artifacts, enabling reproducible benchmarking of sketch-to-UML approaches. The dataset, validation tool, processing scripts, documentation, and demonstration video are publicly available at: Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Seym0n /cas2uml_hand-drawn_to_plantuml_dataset; Tool and Scripts: https://github.com/Seym0n/handwritten-uml-dataset; Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KQrYeGgT3hs.

</details>


### [177] [Beyond Text Matching: Towards Reference-Free Evaluation for Human-Oriented Binary Reverse Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07038)
*Xiuwei Shang,Li Hu,Xiao Jiang,Jieke Shi,Junda He,Zhou Yang,Shaoyin Cheng,Guoqiang Chen,Weiming Zhang,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates using LLMs as judges for evaluating Human-Oriented Binary Reverse Engineering (HOBRE) tasks. The authors introduce BinJudgeBench, an expert-annotated benchmark, and propose BinJudge, a routing mechanism that adaptively selects optimal judge configurations per task/sample, achieving 4.5-24.7% better correlation with human judgment while reducing API costs to 0.06-0.84× of static configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating HOBRE outputs is challenging: human evaluation is costly and unscalable, while existing automated metrics require unavailable executables/runtime environments or inaccessible high-quality source code. The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm is promising but underexplored for HOBRE evaluation.

Method: The authors (1) systematically investigate LLM-as-a-Judge across three HOBRE tasks (function name recovery, binary code summarization, decompilation optimization); (2) construct BinJudgeBench, the first expert-annotated, reference-free, multi-dimensional benchmark; (3) analyze judge configurations (backbone LLMs, prompting strategies, decoding temperatures); and (4) propose BinJudge, a lightweight routing mechanism that adaptively selects optimal judge configurations per task and sample.

Result: LLM-as-a-Judge achieves 63.20% average correlation with human judgment on BinJudgeBench, outperforming traditional metrics at 35.04%. No single optimal configuration fits all tasks/samples. BinJudge improves correlation with human experts by 4.5-24.7% and reduces API cost to 0.06×-0.84× of static best configurations.

Conclusion: The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm is viable for HOBRE evaluation, but requires adaptive configuration. BinJudge provides a scalable, cost-effective, high-fidelity automated evaluation scheme, advancing reliable and practical assessment of HOBRE systems.

Abstract: Human-Oriented Binary Reverse Engineering (HOBRE) aims to transform decompiled pseudocode into a more human-friendly representation, thereby reducing the cognitive burden of reverse analysis and improving efficiency. However, reliably evaluating HOBRE outputs remains a fundamental challenge: human evaluation is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale, while existing automated metrics either require executable test cases and runtime environments that are often unavailable for real-world binaries, or rely on high-quality source code references that are typically inaccessible and fail to capture semantically equivalent but lexically diverse outputs. Although LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm is naturally well-suited to HOBRE evaluation, its effectiveness remains underexplored.
  This paper presents the first systematic investigation of the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm for HOBRE across three representative tasks: function name recovery, binary code summarization, and decompilation optimization. We introduce BinJudgeBench, the first expert-annotated, reference-free evaluation benchmark based on multi-dimensional human judgment, where LLM-as-a-Judge achieves an average correlation of 63.20\% with human judgment, outperforming traditional automated metrics at 35.04\%. By analyzing judge configurations across backbone LLMs, prompting strategies, and decoding temperatures, we find that no ``one-size-fits-all'' configuration exists, as the optimal setup varies across tasks and individual samples. To address this, we propose BinJudge, which employs a lightweight routing mechanism to adaptively select the optimal judge configuration for each task and sample. BinJudge improves correlation with human experts by 4.5\%-24.7\% and reduces API cost to 0.06$\times$-0.84$\times$ of that of static best configurations, providing a scalable, cost-effective, and high-fidelity automated evaluation scheme for HOBRE.

</details>


### [178] [Explanation-Guided Metamorphic Testing of Specialized Language Models: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07076)
*Xingcheng Chen,Mehmet Besenk,Andrea Stocco*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents an empirical study showing that explainability-guided metamorphic testing significantly outperforms heuristic mutation strategies for robustness testing of task-specialized language models, generating 2.30× more verified failure-inducing test cases while maintaining high semantic validity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Task-specialized language models are widely deployed in software engineering workflows, yet there is limited empirical evidence on how to effectively test their robustness and detect brittle behaviors under semantics-preserving input transformations.

Method: A large-scale empirical study across 3 datasets, 4 model architectures, and 20 testing configurations combining attribution-based token prioritization, LLM-driven mutation, and automated semantic verification. Configurations are evaluated against heuristic baselines on failure discovery capability, semantic validity, and testing efficiency.

Result: Explanation-guided metamorphic testing produces 2.30× more verified failure-inducing test cases than heuristic mutations. Semantic verification substantially improves mutation validity with high label-preservation precision. The study also reveals systematic shortcut behaviors, including over-reliance on named entities and formatting cues.

Conclusion: Explanation-guided metamorphic testing is an effective and practical approach for empirically evaluating robustness of task-specialized language models in vertical AI applications.

Abstract: \head{Background} Task-specialized language models are increasingly integrated into software engineering workflows to support vertical-domain activities such as issue triaging, document classification, and automated analysis. Despite their adoption, there is limited empirical evidence on how to test their robustness and detect brittle behaviors under semantics-preserving input transformations.
  \head{Aims} This paper investigates whether explainability-guided metamorphic testing can improve the effectiveness and validity of robustness testing for specialized language models compared to heuristic mutation strategies.
  \head{Method} We conduct a large-scale empirical study of explanation-guided metamorphic testing across three datasets, four model architectures, and 20 testing configurations derived from combinations of attribution methods and mutation strategies. The evaluated configurations combine attribution-based token prioritization, LLM-driven mutation, and automated semantic verification to generate linguistically valid test variants. We assess failure discovery capability, semantic validity, and testing efficiency against heuristic baselines.
  \head{Results} Explanation-guided metamorphic testing generates 2.30$\times$ more verified failure-inducing test cases than heuristic mutation strategies. Semantic verification substantially improves mutation validity and achieves high label-preservation precision among gate-accepted variants according to human annotation. The study further reveals systematic shortcut behaviors across models, including over-reliance on named entities and formatting cues.
  \head{Conclusions} The results provide evidence that explanation-guided metamorphic testing is an effective and practical approach for empirically evaluating the robustness of task-specialized language models used in vertical AI applications.

</details>


### [179] [Rust Coreutils: Rebuilding Unix Foundations in a Modern Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07135)
*Sylvestre Ledru,Samuel Tardieu,Stefano Zacchiroli*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents Rust coreutils, a drop-in compatible reimplementation of GNU coreutils in Rust, and reflects on how modern language features can revitalize legacy critical software infrastructure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNU coreutils is a foundational UNIX package with a decades-old C codebase that is largely feature-complete. The authors explore how one would effectively reimplement such legacy yet critical software using modern tools, and why doing so is worthwhile—specifically to enhance reliability, security, and developer engagement.

Method: The paper recounts the development process of Rust coreutils, an open-source project that reimplements ~100 core UNIX utilities (ls, cp, cat, etc.) in Rust, aiming for full compatibility as a drop-in replacement. It compares the Rust implementation with the original GNU C codebase across dimensions such as correctness, safety, performance, and community participation.

Result: Rust coreutils has achieved drop-in replacement status, achieving compatibility with most Linux distributions. The comparison highlights that modern language features (e.g., memory safety, strong type system, ergonomic error handling) can reduce bugs, attract contributors, and yield a reliable substitute for critical infrastructure.

Conclusion: Reimplementing legacy critical software in a modern language like Rust is feasible and beneficial. It improves safety and maintainability while rejuvenating developer interest in otherwise stagnant, feature-complete packages.

Abstract: GNU core utilities (coreutils) is a crucial package in modern UNIX systems. It comprises around 100 fundamental commands---like ls, cp, and cat---which run every day on millions of computers. However, GNU coreutils is also legacy software, with its C codebase dating back to the early 1990s and arguably feature-complete. If one were to consider reimplementing this essential package, how would they do so effectively, and why? This paper recounts the development of Rust coreutils, a contemporary open source reimplementation of GNU coreutils in the Rust programming language, which has reached the status of a drop-in replacement for GNU coreutils, compatible with most Linux distributions. By comparing Rust coreutils with its ancestor, we offer insights into creating a reliable substitute for critical software and highlight how modern programming features can attract development interest in legacy packages.

</details>


### [180] [Towards Assurance Closure in AI-Native Large-Scale Agile Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07317)
*Ricardo Britto*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The manifesto argues that AI-native software engineering requires "assurance closure" — a machine-operable framework for continuously establishing and validating system properties through evidence. It identifies six gaps in current practices, proposes a six-capability architecture built on a shared semantic assurance layer, and poses four research questions to realize human-on-the-loop, AI-native development.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI-assisted software engineering focuses heavily on code generation but neglects the critical need for automated, continuous assurance. As AI agents take on more engineering tasks, humans must govern intent, risk, and exceptions, which demands machine-operable assurance reasoning — the ability to establish truth, gather and judge evidence, preserve validity through change, and bound agent authority based on uncertainty.

Method: The authors survey existing mechanisms across formal methods, testing, simulation, assurance cases, digital twins, and runtime assurance. They identify six residual gaps that prevent these mechanisms from forming a coherent, machine-operable assurance pipeline. They then propose a high-level architecture with six capabilities, all built atop a shared semantic assurance layer, and formulate four research questions to guide future work toward dependable AI-native R&D.

Result: The paper identifies six gaps: (1) machine-interpretable assurance reasoning, (2) automated evidence generation and curation, (3) evidence credibility assessment, (4) change-preserving validity, (5) uncertainty quantification for authority bounding, and (6) compositional assurance across heterogeneous components. The proposed six-capability architecture addresses each gap through a unified semantic layer enabling human-on-the-loop oversight.

Conclusion: Realizing the AI-native vision requires shifting focus from code generation alone to comprehensive, automated assurance closure. The proposed architecture and research questions provide a roadmap for building systems where assurance reasoning is machine-operable, enabling safe delegation of engineering tasks to AI agents under bounded human oversight.

Abstract: The AI-Native Manifesto envisions large-scale agile software development in which humans increasingly govern intent, risk, and exceptions while agents execute more of the engineering process. Realizing that end-state requires more than better code generation: it requires assurance closure, meaning that the system can establish what must be true, determine and obtain appropriate evidence, judge the credibility of that evidence, preserve its validity through change, and use the resulting uncertainty to bound agent authority. Existing work already provides many of the necessary mechanisms across formal methods, testing, simulation, assurance cases, digital twins, and runtime assurance. We identify six residual gaps in making the surrounding assurance reasoning sufficiently machine-operable, propose a high-level architecture with six corresponding capabilities built on a shared semantic assurance layer, and formulate four research questions to turn that architecture into dependable, human-on-the-loop, AI-native R&D.

</details>


### [181] [PACE: Primitive-Aware Code Evolution for Automated Algorithm Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07395)
*Zhuoliang Xie,Ruihao Zheng,Xiang Xu,Genghui Li,Zhengkun Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PACE decouples valuable local logic from whole programs into persistent Executable Algorithmic Primitives (EAPs), enabling cross-program transfer during LLM-based automated algorithm design, with Thompson sampling guiding primitive selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based algorithm design treats programs as indivisible wholes, causing useful local algorithmic components to be lost when a program is discarded. This coupling makes it difficult to assess and preserve individual component contributions.

Method: PACE represents reusable local logic as Executable Algorithmic Primitives (EAPs) maintained in a dynamic set. Algorithm evolution uses primitive-aware operators that structurally guarantee EAP retention and cross-program transfer. Primitive selection is guided by Thompson sampling based on parent-relative performance improvements, eliminating the need for extra evaluation datasets.

Result: Experiments on four tasks show PACE discovers competitive algorithms while structurally preserving valuable algorithmic components.

Conclusion: PACE effectively addresses the coupling problem in LLM-based algorithm design by enabling persistent, transferable algorithmic primitives, leading to competitive algorithm discovery with preserved component-level contributions.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based automated algorithm design typically evolves algorithms as complete, indivisible programs. While this whole-program perspective simplifies the search space, it fundamentally couples the useful local logic to its host program. Consequently, valuable code snippets vanish when the overall program is discarded, making it highly difficult to assess the contribution of individual algorithmic components.To address this, we propose Primitive-Aware Code Evolution (PACE), which decouples local logic from complete programs by representing it as persistent units called Executable Algorithmic Primitives (EAPs). To enable code-level transfer, PACE maintains a dynamic set of EAPs. Algorithm evolution is driven by primitive-aware operators that structurally guarantee the retention and cross-program transfer of these components. To evaluate them effectively, PACE leverages Thompson sampling based on parent-relative performance improvements, guiding primitive selection from the set without requiring extra evaluation datasets. Experiments on four tasks demonstrate that PACE effectively discovers competitive algorithms while structurally preserving valuable algorithmic components.

</details>


### [182] [Circuit-Based Program Verification: Sequential Circuits as an Intermediate Representation for Verifying C Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07397)
*Po-Chun Chien,Nian-Ze Lee,Armin Biere,Dirk Beyer*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CPV translates C programs into sequential circuits, enabling hardware model checkers (BMC, k-induction, IC3/PDR) to perform software verification, achieving competitive and complementary results against traditional software verifiers on 16,000+ benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software and hardware verification communities have developed separate intermediate representations and algorithms despite sharing the common goal of reasoning about state-transition systems. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling software verification to directly leverage mature hardware model checking techniques.

Method: The CPV framework modularly compiles C programs into sequential circuits, folding control and data flows into a monolithic transition relation. It supports reachability-safety and termination analyses using off-the-shelf hardware model checkers (BMC, k-induction, IC3/PDR). Counterexamples are automatically translated back into software-verification witnesses.

Result: Evaluation on 16,000+ tasks shows CPV achieves competitive performance against five established software verifiers and demonstrates complementary strengths by uniquely solving tasks that other verifiers cannot handle.

Conclusion: Hardware model checking, accessed via a sequential-circuit intermediate representation, is a viable and complementary approach to software verification, offering distinct algorithmic strengths that can solve problems intractable for traditional path-based software verifiers.

Abstract: Formal verification of software programs and hardware designs shares the common goal of reasoning about state-transition systems, yet the two communities have largely developed separate intermediate representations and verification algorithms. This paper investigates sequential circuits as an intermediate representation for software verification, with the goal of enabling direct application of hardware-model-checking techniques. We present Circuit-Based Program Verification (CPV), a modular framework that translates C programs into sequential circuits and employs off-the-shelf hardware model checkers as backends. Unlike traditional software verifiers, which typically rely on path-based exploration, CPV reasons over sequential circuits, where a program's control and data flows are folded into a monolithic transition relation that can be analyzed as a whole. The framework supports reachability-safety and termination analyses and integrates multiple state-of-the-art hardware model checkers, which together provide access to diverse verification algorithms, including bounded model checking, $k$-induction, and IC3/PDR. Counterexamples found by hardware model checkers are automatically translated back into software-verification witnesses for users to interpret verification results. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation on a benchmark suite of more than 16000 tasks. Our results show that CPV achieved competitive performance against five well-established software verifiers and exhibited complementary strengths by uniquely solving tasks that other verifiers cannot handle.

</details>


### [183] [Taxonomy-Driven Analysis of Open-Source AI Risk Mitigation Tools](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07446)
*Afreen Alam,Evgenija Popchanovska,Ana Gjorgjevikj,Maryan Rizinski,Lubomir T. Chitkushev,Irena Vodenska,Dimitar Trajanov*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A structured protocol maps 21 open-source LLM evaluation/security tools to the MIT AI Risk Taxonomy (32 subcategories), using an LLM-assisted RAG pipeline. Results show tools cluster around technical/operational controls, while governance, legal, and financial risks remain largely unaddressed (F1=75.5%, Fleiss' Kappa=0.509). The paper proposes a layered mitigation architecture combining tool-based controls with organizational processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise adoption of LLMs introduces operational, security, and governance risks that are hard to scale with manual mitigation. Existing tooling is fragmented, designed for specific engineering tasks, and described in terms misaligned with governance frameworks and risk taxonomies, making it difficult to map tools to risks and identify coverage gaps.

Method: A taxonomy-driven analysis using the extended MIT AI Risk Mitigation and Response Taxonomy (32 subcategories). An LLM-assisted retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline analyzes source code and documentation of 21 prominent open-source tools to extract capabilities for each taxonomy category. Reliability is assessed via three independent reviewers (Fleiss' Kappa), and mapping accuracy is evaluated via F1 score after majority voting.

Result: The tooling landscape is highly skewed: tools cluster around technical and operational controls, while governance, legal/regulatory, and financial/market controls remain largely unaddressed. The mapping protocol achieved an F1 score of 75.5% after majority voting. Inter-rater reliability showed moderate agreement (Fleiss' Kappa = 0.509).

Conclusion: A layered risk-mitigation architecture is needed, combining tool-based controls with organizational and regulatory processes. The study provides a practical mapping between enterprise AI risk categories and open-source mitigation capabilities, identifies where human oversight remains necessary, and presents a taxonomy-driven framework applicable to both open-source and proprietary solutions.

Abstract: Rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in enterprise settings has introduced operational, security, and governance risks. As generative AI applications move from pilot to production, manual harm identification and mitigation are becoming difficult to scale. Although many tools support model evaluation, adversarial testing, runtime guardrails, and observability, the tooling landscape remains fragmented. Tools are typically designed for specific engineering tasks and described in technical terms that do not align with governance frameworks or risk taxonomies, making it difficult to determine which tools address which risks and where critical gaps remain. This paper proposes a structured protocol to automate AI risk mitigation through a taxonomy-driven analysis of open-source LLM evaluation and security tools. We map the capabilities of 21 prominent open-source tools to the 32 subcategories of the extended MIT AI Risk Mitigation and Response Taxonomy. An LLM-assisted retrieval-augmented generation pipeline analyzes source code and documentation to extract capabilities for each taxonomy category. Reliability assessment yielded moderate agreement (Fleiss' Kappa = 0.509) among three independent reviewers. The analysis reveals a highly skewed landscape in which tools cluster around technical and operational controls, while governance, legal and regulatory, and financial and market controls remain largely unaddressed. This motivates a layered risk-mitigation architecture combining tool-based controls with organizational and regulatory processes. The mapping protocol achieved an F1 score of 75.5% after majority voting. Overall, the study provides a practical mapping between enterprise AI risk categories and open-source mitigation capabilities, identifies where human oversight remains necessary, and presents a taxonomy-driven framework applicable to open-source and proprietary solutions.

</details>

### [184] [Towards Multi-Label Graph Foundation Models: from Single-Vector Representation Learning to Multi-Semantic Basis Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06394)
*Dongxiao He,Jiayu Zhang,Jitao Zhao,Yi Wang,Di Jin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSB-GFM addresses cross-domain multi-label node classification by representing nodes as compositions of semantic bases and employing a dual-channel architecture with domain adversarial training, overcoming the single-label limitation of existing Graph Foundation Models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) assume single-label semantics per node, which forces multi-label nodes into a single-point representation, causing semantic entanglement. Current multi-label node classification methods also lack cross-domain generalization capability, being restricted to in-domain settings.

Method: The authors propose MSB-GFM with two key components: (1) a multi-semantic basis representation learning paradigm that models each node as an adaptive composition of learnable semantic bases, enabling flexible multi-semantic modeling; (2) a semantic-structure dual-channel architecture combined with domain adversarial training to facilitate cross-domain knowledge transfer.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of MSB-GFM for cross-domain multi-label node classification, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: MSB-GFM successfully addresses the semantic entanglement problem in GFMs and enables cross-domain multi-label node classification through multi-semantic basis representations and domain adversarial training.

Abstract: Multi-label node classification is an important yet challenging task in graph learning, where nodes exhibit multiple semantics simultaneously. Existing methods for multi-label node classification can effectively model multiple labels, while only considering in-domain scenarios where the model needs to be trained and tested within the same graph domain, resulting in limited cross-domain generalization. Recently, Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for learning transferable graph representations across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks. However, existing GFMs are built upon single-label assumption, where all nodes are arbitrarily regarded as containing only one class of semantic and embedded into a single representation. For multi-label nodes, such a representation essentially approximates multiple semantics with a single point in the representation space, inevitably leading to semantic entanglement and making simultaneous discrimination of multiple labels difficult. To address these limitations, we propose a Multi-Semantic Basis Graph Foundation Model (MSB-GFM), a framework for cross-domain multi-label node classification. Specifically, we introduce a multi-semantic basis representation learning paradigm that models each multi-label node as an adaptive composition of semantic bases, thereby enabling flexible representational capacity for modeling multiple semantics. Furthermore, we develop a semantic-structure dual-channel architecture with domain adversarial training for effective cross-domain knowledge transfer. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our model.

</details>


### [185] [EntropyMoE: Entropy-Aware Sparse Expert Routing for Tokenizer-Free LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06398)
*Bo Liu,Muxuab Yu,Yu Zhang,Pengfei Gao,Yongping Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EntropyMoE introduces a Mixture-of-Experts architecture for byte-level language models that routes dynamic byte patches based on patch entropy, enabling adaptive computation that varies with patch semantics and granularity, outperforming dense baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing byte-patch architectures apply uniform dense feed-forward computation to all patches regardless of their semantic content or granularity. This is suboptimal because different patches carry varying amounts of information — some are highly predictable (low entropy) and require less computation, while others are information-dense (high entropy) and demand more model capacity. The authors aim to address this mismatch by introducing sparsity that adapts to per-patch characteristics.

Method: The authors propose EntropyMoE, which replaces dense feed-forward modules in the byte-patch Transformer with Top-K Mixture-of-Experts layers. Each dynamic byte patch serves as the atomic routing unit. Critically, routing decisions are made using the patch's entropy — the same signal that governs dynamic patch construction — creating a unified framework where patch formation and expert selection share a common granularity metric. Patch entropy and patch length jointly define the feature space that organizes expert specialization, and byte coverage determines each patch's contribution to workload accounting.

Result: EntropyMoE achieves the lowest held-out bits-per-byte among both dense and sparse baselines at matched parameter scales, while maintaining comparable downstream task accuracy.

Conclusion: Patch entropy is an effective and principled routing coordinate for sparse conditional computation in byte-level models. The work successfully extends Mixture-of-Experts modeling beyond tokenizer-based representations, establishing a new paradigm for adaptive, granularity-aware byte-patch architectures.

Abstract: Recent byte-level large language models (LLMs) have made tokenizer-free modeling increasingly competitive by grouping bytes into dynamically sized patches. However, existing byte-patch architectures still apply the same dense feed-forward computation to every patch. This uniform computation cannot adapt model capacity to variations in patch semantics and granularity. We address this limitation with EntropyMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture designed for dynamic byte patches. EntropyMoE replaces the dense feed-forward modules in the global patch Transformer with Top-K expert layers. Each dynamic patch serves as the basic unit of expert routing, and its byte coverage determines its contribution to workload accounting. The router selects experts directly from patch entropy, using the same granularity signal that underlies dynamic patch construction to organize sparse computation. Patch entropy and length jointly define the feature space for regulating expert specialization. Experiments show that EntropyMoE achieves the lowest held-out bits-per-byte among matched dense and sparse baselines while maintaining comparable downstream accuracy. These results establish patch entropy as an effective routing coordinate for sparse conditional computation and extend Mixture-of-Experts modeling beyond tokenizer-based representations.

</details>


### [186] [Beyond Routing Weights: Faithful Response-Level Interpretation of Mixture-of-Experts Reward Models via Contribution Contrast](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06400)
*Yifan Wang,Jinyi Mu,Mayank Jobanputra,Yu Wang,Soyoung Oh,Isabel Valera,Vera Demberg*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoCo introduces a response-level interpretation method for sparse MoE reward models. Unlike router-based approaches that only show which prompts an expert receives, CoCo uses chosen-rejected response pairs with the largest contribution contrasts to jointly capture both routing and preference behavior, yielding more coherent, faithful, and specialized expert characterizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sparse MoE reward model interpretations rely on routing weights, which only reveal which prompts an expert receives, not how it judges responses. This provides an incomplete picture of expert behavior, as it misses the model's preference judgments — the core function of a reward model.

Method: CoCo (Contribution-Contrast) identifies chosen-rejected response pairs that maximize the contrast in an expert's contribution. This jointly captures both routing behavior (whether the expert is activated) and preference behavior (how strongly it distinguishes chosen from rejected responses). The method is evaluated against router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based baselines via automatic metrics and human evaluation.

Result: CoCo produces interpretations that are more coherent, faithful, and specialized than all baseline methods while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy. This is the first systematic study of interpretation methods for MoE reward models.

Conclusion: CoCo provides a principled, response-level approach to interpreting sparse MoE reward models that faithfully captures both routing and preference behavior, establishing a new foundation for understanding these increasingly important architectures in RLHF pipelines.

Abstract: Reward models are central to learning from human preferences, yet identifying what drives their predictions remains challenging. Recent sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reward models seek to improve interpretability by routing prompts to specialized experts and characterizing experts through examples with high routing weights. However, routing weights only reveal which prompts an expert $\textit{receives}$, not how it $\textit{judges}$ responses, providing only a partial account of expert behavior. We therefore propose $\textbf{Co}$ntribution-$\textbf{Co}$ntrast ($\textbf{CoCo}$) response-level interpretation, which faithfully characterizes experts' roles using chosen-rejected response pairs with the largest contribution contrasts, jointly capturing routing and preference behavior. Across automatic and human evaluations, CoCo yields more coherent, faithful, and specialized interpretations than router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based alternatives while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of interpretation methods for MoE reward models.

</details>


### [187] [Interpretable Unsupervised Community Detection with LLM-Symbolized Structured Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06402)
*Aoting Zeng,Kai Wang,Jianwei Wang,Yuxiang Sun,Yizhang He,Wenjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LUCID is an LLM-guided, interpretable, training-free, and unsupervised community detection method inspired by phase-transition kinetics. It uses a four-stage pipeline where the LLM induces formal rules to translate implicit knowledge into explicit logical structures, achieving state-of-the-art performance without labeled data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classic objective-driven community detection methods struggle with complex graph structures, while deep-learning approaches sacrifice interpretability and require labeled data/training. LLMs offer strong reasoning and world knowledge, but leveraging them effectively for interpretable, label-free community detection remains an open challenge.

Method: LUCID is a four-stage pipeline inspired by phase-transition kinetics: (1) Local-View Community Initialization encodes local graph structures via k-ego contexts and unsupervised node roles; (2) Multi-factor Community Merge iteratively merges local communities using LLM-induced rules; (3) Multi-grain Community Refinement applies coarse-to-fine LLM-induced rules in parallel to reduce boundary noise; (4) Global-view Community Selection identifies high-quality communities based on topological compactness and boundary clarity. The LLM induces formal rules throughout, converting implicit knowledge into explicit, interpretable logical structures.

Result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that LUCID, as an unsupervised approach, achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently outperforms leading unsupervised and semi-supervised baselines.

Conclusion: LUCID demonstrates that LLMs can be effectively harnessed for community detection without training or labeled data, combining strong performance with interpretability through explicit, LLM-induced logical rules within a biologically-inspired phase-transition pipeline.

Abstract: Community detection is a fundamental task in graph analytics that aims to identify cohesive groups of entities with similar behaviors or interests. Classic objective-driven methods struggle with complex graph structures, while deep-learning approaches improve performance at the expense of interpretability and rely on labeled data and training. Large language models (LLMs), with strong reasoning capabilities and world knowledge, are promising for interpretable, label-free community detection. To leverage these strengths, we propose LUCID, an LLM-guided, interpretable, training-free, and unsupervised community detection method. Inspired by phase-transition kinetics in natural systems, where complex structures emerge through initialization, merging, refinement, and selection, LUCID is designed as a four-stage pipeline. Within this pipeline, the LLM induces formal rules that translate implicit knowledge into explicit and interpretable logical structures.
