Specifically, (1) the Local-View Community Initialization stage encodes local graph structures using k-ego contexts and unsupervised node roles; (2) the Multi-factor Community Merge stage uses LLM-induced rules to iteratively merge local communities; (3) the Multi-grain Community Refinement stage applies LLM-induced coarse-to-fine rules in parallel to reduce boundary noise; and (4) the Global-view Community Selection stage identifies high-quality communities based on topological compactness and boundary clarity. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that LUCID, as an unsupervised approach, achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently outperforms leading unsupervised and semi-supervised baselines.

</details>


### [188] [ADIAS: Automated Design of Interactive Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06410)
*Lekang Jiang,Bohan Tang,Stephan Goetz,Yiwen Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ADIAS introduces issue-centric agent optimization, where repair progress is maintained as an explicit persistent issue state rather than re-derived each round. This outperforms candidate-centric baselines by 25.2% on average across five benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated agent design methods are candidate-centric, organizing cross-round experience around candidate agents. This makes repair progress implicit, leading to inefficient repair targeting, slow consolidation of partial progress, and propagation of ineffective interventions across rounds.

Method: ADIAS formulates issue-centric agent optimization with two key mechanisms: (1) a persistent issue state that maintains stable issue identities, lifecycle status, supporting evidence, and intervention-outcome histories; and (2) issue-guided optimization that uses this state to jointly propose repair targets and revision directions for focused full-code modification.

Result: ADIAS outperforms the strongest baseline by 25.2% on average across five interactive benchmarks and achieves consistent gains across four backbone models. Controlled ablations show that removing the persistent issue state or replacing issue-centric revision with candidate-centric policies causes performance drops of up to 40.7%.

Conclusion: Shifting from candidate-centric to issue-centric optimization, with explicit persistent issue state tracking, substantially improves automated agent design by enabling more targeted, efficient, and cumulative repair across iterative rounds.

Abstract: Automated agent design improves agent harnesses through iterative revision, evaluation, and feedback summarization. Existing methods are largely candidate-centric: cross-round experience is organized around candidate agents, which leaves the repair progress implicit. This causes inefficient repair targeting, slow consolidation of partial progress, and propagation of ineffective interventions across rounds. Therefore, we formulate issue-centric agent optimization, in which repair progress is carried forward as an explicit persistent issue state to guide optimization, rather than re-derived from candidate history in each round. We instantiate the formulation in ADIAS, a framework for automated full-code agent design with two mechanisms. A persistent issue state maintains stable issue identities, lifecycle status, supporting evidence, and intervention-outcome histories. Issue-guided optimization uses this state to jointly propose repair targets and revision directions for subsequent focused full-code modification. Across five interactive benchmarks, ADIAS outperforms the strongest baseline by 25.2% on average and achieves consistent gains across four backbone models. Controlled ablations further show that removing persistent issue state or replacing issue-centric revision with candidate-centric policies leads to performance drops of up to 40.7%.

</details>


### [189] [Learning to Predict Middle-Layer Attention in MLLMs for Visual Token Prunin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06411)
*Yuyao Sun,Tao Deng,Shuang Li,Deqing Wang,Hao Geng,Minjun Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAP predicts visual token importance using a distilled lightweight predictor guided by a sample-specific teacher layer, enabling pruning before any LLM layers and achieving 3.09x speedup while retaining 97.5% performance on LLaVA-NeXT-7B.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual token pruning methods rely on attention from a fixed middle LLM layer to estimate token importance, but (1) the optimal layer varies per sample, and (2) reaching that middle layer already incurs substantial computation, undermining efficiency gains.

Method: MAP introduces: (1) Question Contrastive Teacher Selection — identifies a sample-specific optimal teacher layer by comparing text-to-vision attention under original vs. reference questions; (2) Attention Distillation — distills the selected layer's attention into a lightweight predictor that estimates token importance directly from multi-modal input features; (3) Diversity-aware pruning — combines predicted importance with a diversity criterion to prune tokens before the first LLM layer, requiring no attention maps at inference.

Result: On LLaVA-NeXT-7B across ten benchmarks, MAP retains 97.5% of unpruned performance using only 5.56% of visual tokens, yielding a 3.09× end-to-end speedup.

Conclusion: MAP effectively addresses the fixed-layer and late-pruning limitations of prior attention-guided pruning methods, enabling substantial efficiency gains with minimal performance degradation and compatibility with existing inference acceleration techniques.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance across diverse vision-language tasks, but their efficiency is limited by the cost of processing numerous visual tokens. Visual token pruning can reduce this cost, but requires accurate token importance estimates. Recent studies have demonstrated that text-to-vision attention from middle language model layers can effectively guide visual token pruning, typically using attention from a predefined middle layer to select the visual tokens to retain. Two problems therefore remain. First, our analysis shows that the layer whose attention is most responsive to the question varies substantially across samples, making a fixed layer suboptimal. Second, obtaining attention from the appropriate middle layer requires processing numerous visual tokens through several language model layers, by which point considerable computation has already been spent. To address both problems, we propose Middle-layer Attention Prediction (MAP), which uses Question Contrastive Teacher Selection to identify a sample-specific teacher layer by contrasting attention under the original and reference questions, and distills attention from the selected layer into a lightweight predictor that estimates visual token importance from multi-modal input features. During inference, MAP combines the predicted importance scores with a diversity criterion to prune visual tokens before the first language model layer. Thus, MAP requires no attention maps for pruning and remains compatible with existing inference acceleration techniques. Across ten benchmarks on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, MAP retains 97.5% of the unpruned model performance with only 5.56% of the visual tokens, yielding a 3.09x end-to-end speedup.

</details>


### [190] [WebGrader: Training LLMs for Web Development with Self-Evolving Programmatic Grader](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06474)
*Boshui Chen,Huiping Liu,Shaolei Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WebGrader is a self-evolving programmatic grader for RL-based website generation that uses executable Flow Contracts to verify functional correctness by observing full browser trajectories. It trains an 8B policy to 52.01% success on WebGen-Bench, outperforming script-based rewards and larger proprietary models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL-based training for website generation is bottlenecked by reward design: hand-authored browser scripts are executable but expensive to write for diverse requirements, while VLM/GUI-agent graders scale but often issue premature verdicts before the decisive state is observed. A reward system is needed that is both scalable and executes verdicts only after witnessing the requested functional transition.

Method: WebGrader separates the pipeline into four stages: (1) test planning — autonomously deriving interaction flows from website requests and encoding them as Flow Contracts; (2) action grounding — materializing the generated project in a live browser and grounding target actions against source code and live DOM; (3) evidence collection — gathering visual, DOM, response, and persistent-state evidence along a single browser trajectory; (4) semantic judgment — issuing Pass/Fail only after observing the requested transition. A residual-driven offline loop discovers reusable verifier skills, screens them on disjoint validation pages, and freezes a promoted skill graph before policy training.

Result: On WebGen-Bench, an 8B policy trained with WebGrader achieves 52.01% functional success rate, a +7.88 point improvement over a matched appearance-plus-script reward. It surpasses o4-mini and DeepSeek-v4-flash. On WG-core-250, the policy achieves a Full Score of 44.953, surpassing Qwen3-Coder-480B.

Conclusion: By decoupling test planning, grounding, evidence collection, and semantic judgment, WebGrader provides scalable, accurate RL rewards that substantially improve functional correctness in generated websites, enabling smaller open models to outperform much larger proprietary systems.

Abstract: Large language models increasingly generate complete websites from natural-language descriptions, and reinforcement learning has become a central approach to closing their remaining functional gap. This training regime is bottlenecked by reward design. Hand-authored browser scripts are executable yet costly to write for open-ended requirements, while VLM and GUI-agent graders scale but may issue verdicts before observing the decisive state. We propose WebGrader, a self-evolving programmatic grader that autonomously derives the required interaction flows from each website request, represents each flow as an executable Flow Contract, and uses its execution outcome as an RL reward. WebGrader materializes the generated project in a live browser, grounds target actions against the source code and live DOM, and collects visual, DOM, response, and persistent-state evidence along the same browser trajectory. A residual-driven offline loop then discovers reusable verifier skills, screens them on disjoint validation pages, and freezes the promoted skill graph before policy training. By separating test planning, action grounding, evidence collection, and semantic judgment, WebGrader issues a Pass verdict only after observing the requested transition. On WebGen-Bench, WebGrader trains an 8B policy to a 52.01% functional success rate, outperforming a matched appearance-plus-script reward by 7.88 points and surpassing o4-mini and DeepSeek-v4-flash. On WG-core-250, the policy reaches a Full Score of 44.953 and surpasses Qwen3-Coder-480B.

</details>


### [191] [Can MLLMs Decode the Creative Leap? Introducing C4 for Cross-Concept Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06501)
*Ming Wang,Yuqing Zhang,Tingna Xie,Xiangju Li,Xiaocui Yang,Daling Wang,Shi Feng,Yifei Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: C4 is a cognition-inspired benchmark evaluating cross-concept creativity in MLLMs using Chinese idiom (Chengyu)-based tasks. It frames item construction as encoding and model inference as decoding across cross-concept bridge paths. C4-Eval contains 184 synthetic + 37 human-created items across five task settings (884 cases). Top closed models achieve only ~50% accuracy, revealing a significant gap in MLLMs' creative decoding abilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating creative capabilities of MLLMs is difficult because creativity lacks explicit targets and reward signals, unlike accuracy-oriented tasks. Cross-concept understanding—the ability to recover intended meaning from non-obvious conceptual relations—is a core cognitive capacity underlying receptive creativity, yet remains underexplored in multimodal model evaluation.

Method: The authors introduce C4 (Chengyu-based Cross-Concept Creativity), a framework encoding target slots into imageable substitute concepts via bridge paths in a manually curated cross-concept network. Difficulty is indexed by bridge count and depth. C4-Eval comprises 184 synthetic items and 37 human-collected chengyu figures, each instantiated in five task settings. Ten MLLMs are evaluated on answer-recovery accuracy under varying conditions (candidate constraints, bridge hints, explanation requests).

Result: Top closed-source MLLMs reach 50.7% and 48.0% primary accuracy; open-source models perform substantially worse. Candidate constraints sharply improve accuracy, but bridge hints and explanation requests yield only modest gains, indicating current models struggle to decode creatively encoded cross-concept meaning.

Conclusion: Current MLLMs exhibit a substantial gap in cross-concept creative understanding. The structured C4 framework enables systematic evaluation of this capacity, and results highlight the need for advances in models' ability to navigate non-obvious conceptual relations for creative comprehension.

Abstract: Creative capabilities of MLLMs matter in design, communication, education, and human--AI collaboration, yet remain difficult to evaluate because explicit targets and reward signals are scarce compared with accuracy-oriented tasks. Cross-concept understanding is a core cognitive capacity underlying receptive creativity. It enables a perceiver to recover intended meaning from non-obvious but meaningful conceptual relations. We operationalize item construction as cross-concept encoding and model inference as cross-concept decoding. We introduce C4, a cognition-inspired evaluation framework for Chengyu (Chinese idiom)-based Cross-Concept Creativity. Its encoding component maps target slots to imageable substitute concepts along bridge paths in a manually annotated and third-party-reviewed cross-concept network, enabling batch generation with explicit structure, difficulty indexed by bridge count and depth, and exact answers. Using this framework, we instantiate the C4 Evaluation Set (C4-Eval), comprising 184 synthetic items and 37 human-created cross-concept chengyu figures collected from online sources. We manually construct and review cross-concept relations, bridge paths, and reasoning processes for the collected figures. Each C4-Eval item is instantiated in five task settings, yielding 884 primary answer-recovery cases. Across ten evaluated MLLMs, the strongest closed models reach 50.7% and 48.0% primary accuracy, while open-source models remain substantially lower. Candidate constraints improve accuracy sharply, but bridge hints and explanation requests provide only modest gains. These results expose a substantial gap in how current MLLMs decode creatively encoded meaning through cross-concept relations. The code is in the supplementary material.

</details>


### [192] [KNOWPLAN: Knowledge-Driven AI Agents for Smart Degree Pathway Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06530)
*Shuheng Cao,Weijia Zhang,Jiaqi Wu,Xiyun Hu,Yat Yang,Juqy Chen,Zhaoxiang Feng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KnowPlan separates university curriculum extraction from student degree planning via a strict extraction-first boundary. CatalogBrowse crawls unstructured academic sources using information-gain-driven exploration with formal closure certificates, producing provenance-linked JSON documents. DegreeMap then compiles these into a typed requirement hypergraph and solves lexicographically with CP-SAT. The pipeline achieves 96.2% inventory recall, 100% hard feasibility, and a 0.015 utility gap to a privileged gold graph across 100+ universities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior approaches couple curriculum crawling with degree planning, creating a circular dependency where the planner only extracts facts relevant to its current plan. This hides failure modes: incomplete extraction can appear as planning infeasibility, and planning failures can mask missing data. No existing system enforces a clean separation with measurable interface guarantees between extraction and planning stages.

Method: KnowPlan enforces an extraction-first boundary with two decoupled stages. CatalogBrowse explores university sources (catalogs, web pages, JSON endpoints, PDFs) without access to any user profile. It scores actions by lower-confidence expected marginal gain over atomic catalog obligations per unit of source access, uses platform adapters with deterministic parsing and a span-constrained clause-to-AST fallback model, and terminates on a formal closure certificate covering index, schema, provenance, and reference completeness — not a reward threshold. It emits three provenance-linked JSON documents as its output contract. DegreeMap consumes only those documents, compiles them into a typed requirement hypergraph, and performs lexicographic optimization via CP-SAT over a hierarchy: hard feasibility, completion horizon, load/risk, personalized utility, and option value. This ensures each stage optimizes within the previous stage's proven optimum and remains certifiable within solver budget.

Result: On a 100-university broad track and a six-school dense track, CatalogBrowse achieves 96.2% inventory recall and 88.7% masked-source recovery with 47% less source access than exhaustive crawling. DegreeMap achieves 100.0% hard feasibility while improving personalized utility by +0.066 over the strongest baseline. The full pipeline certifies 99.5% of requests with a utility gap of only 0.015 compared to a privileged gold-standard graph.

Conclusion: Decoupling extraction from planning with a formal output contract and closure certificate enables both stages to be independently certifiable. The extraction-first boundary eliminates hidden failure modes, and the lexicographic optimization hierarchy ensures that downstream planning never silently compensates for upstream extraction gaps.

Abstract: Planning a degree from official university sources requires solving two problems in order. The institution's curriculum must first be reconstructed from catalogs, departmental pages, JSON endpoints, and PDFs that share no schema, and only then can a student-specific path be optimized under prerequisite logic and overlapping requirement constraints. Coupling the two lets each failure mode hide the other, because a planner that drives its own crawling never learns facts its current plan does not need. We present KnowPlan, which enforces an extraction-first boundary and measures the interface between the stages rather than assuming it. CatalogBrowse explores with no access to any user profile. It scores legal actions by lower-confidence expected marginal gain over a finite set of atomic catalog obligations per unit of source access, parses deterministically through platform adapters with a span-constrained clause-to-AST model fallback, and terminates on a closure certificate over index, schema, provenance, and reference completeness instead of a reward threshold. Its output contract is three provenance-linked JSON documents. DegreeMap consumes only those documents. It compiles them into a typed requirement hypergraph and optimizes lexicographically with CP-SAT over hard feasibility, completion horizon, load and risk, personalized utility, and option value, so that each stage optimizes inside the previous stage's proven optimum and stays certifiable within the solver budget. Across a 100-university broad track and a six-school dense track, CatalogBrowse reaches 96.2% inventory recall and 88.7% masked-source recovery at 47% less source access than an exhaustive crawler, DegreeMap holds 100.0% hard feasibility while improving personalized utility by +0.066 over the strongest baseline, and the full pipeline certifies 99.5% of requests with a utility gap to the privileged gold graph of 0.015.

</details>


### [193] [TaskSense: Focusing on What Matters in World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06544)
*SM Mazharul Islam,Manfred Huber*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TaskSense introduces a task-centric world model with stochastic spatial attention guided by inverse dynamics, reconstructing only attended regions to filter distractions. It matches DreamerV3 on clean environments and significantly outperforms it under visual distractions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard world models for visual control learn latent states by reconstructing full observations, which forces them to allocate representational capacity to task-irrelevant background clutter and distractors. This mismatch between reconstruction objectives and control objectives degrades downstream performance, especially under visual distractions.

Method: TaskSense inserts a differentiable stochastic spatial attention mechanism before latent encoding, conditioned on the previous latent state. An auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective steers attention toward control-relevant regions. The world model reconstructs only the attended regions rather than the full observation, and the decoder is conditioned on the sampled attention map for reconstruction consistency. The framework is built upon the DreamerV3 baseline.

Result: TaskSense achieves competitive performance with DreamerV3 on the DeepMind Control Suite and consistently outperforms DreamerV3 on the Distracting Control Suite, demonstrating improved robustness to visual distractions. Qualitative analysis shows that inverse-dynamics-guided attention successfully localizes control-relevant regions while suppressing irrelevant content.

Conclusion: Enforcing task relevance through attention before encoding, combined with reconstructing only attended regions, effectively filters visual distractions and yields more robust control policies without sacrificing performance on clean environments.

Abstract: World models for visual control typically learn compact latent states by reconstructing observations, implicitly encouraging representations to preserve information across the entire visual input. However, task-relevant content often occupies only a small fraction of the observation, while background clutter and distractors consume valuable representational capacity. This mismatch between visual reconstruction and control objectives biases latent representations to model task-irrelevant visual content, diluting learning signals for control-relevant features and severely degrading downstream performance under visual distractions. We introduce TaskSense, a task-centric world modeling framework that enforces task relevance before latent encoding through a differentiable stochastic spatial attention mechanism conditioned on the previous latent state. To steer attention toward control-relevant regions, we augment training with an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective. Rather than reconstructing the full observation, the world model reconstructs only the attended regions, encouraging latent representations to preserve task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant visual content. The decoder is further conditioned on the sampled attention map, enabling consistent reconstruction despite stochastic attention. Compared with the DreamerV3 baseline, TaskSense maintains competitive performance on the DeepMind Control Suite while consistently outperforming DreamerV3 on the Distracting Control Suite, demonstrating substantially improved robustness to visual distractions. Qualitative analysis further confirms that the learned attention, guided by inverse-dynamics supervision, consistently localizes control-relevant regions while suppressing irrelevant visual content.

</details>


### [194] [Divergent Response Modes in Frontier Language Models Under Steering Pressure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06578)
*Ali Jalal-Kamali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Six frontier LLMs exhibit distinct, model-specific behavioral patterns under steering pressure, with GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.7 showing unique resistance strategies. Internal probing on Llama confirms the behavioral split is linearly decodable and causally manipulable in the residual stream.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier models are trained with divergent data, objectives, and safety pipelines, yet whether these differences yield measurably distinct behaviors under explicit steering pressure remains underexplored.

Method: 300 paired base-vs-steered items across three categories (values-conflict, reasoning-elicitation, reasoning-suppression) plus 40 validation items were administered to six frontier models from six developers. All six models served as blind peer judges, classifying every response against fixed behavioral rubrics, yielding 24,480 judgments scored by leave-one-out consensus. A linear probe was trained on Llama's residual stream to decode behavior, followed by causal intervention via directional injection during generation.

Result: Models differ in both the magnitude and mode of behavioral shift under steering. GPT-5 uniquely deflects reasoning-disclosure requests while preserving answer integrity (99% vs. 0% for others). Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5 resist explicit suppression instructions via distinct strategies. The linear probe decodes behavior at 0.87 held-out accuracy; injecting the decoded direction shifts behavior from 0% to 86% across an intervention sweep. All findings are robust to token-budget remediation and a hypothesis-blind judgment prompt control.

Conclusion: Frontier models exhibit developer-specific behavioral fingerprints under steering pressure, with some response modes exclusive to one or two models. These behavioral differences are mechanistically grounded in linearly accessible representations within the residual stream, as demonstrated via probing and causal intervention on Llama.

Abstract: Frontier language models are trained using distinct data, objectives, and safety pipelines. Whether these differences produce measurably different behaviors under explicit steering pressure remains underexplored. This study evaluates behavioral steerability across six frontier models from six developers using 300 paired base and steered items over three categories: values-conflict, reasoning-elicitation, and reasoning-suppression (plus 40 validation items). All six models act as blind peer judges and classify every response based on fixed behavioral rubrics. The resulting 24,480 judgments are scored by leave-one-out consensus. We find that models differ not just in how much steering shifts their behavior but in what kind (mode) of response they give, and some response modes appear in only one or two of them. GPT-5 deflects requests to disclose its reasoning while leaving its answer intact (99% vs. 0% for all other models). Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5 resist explicit suppression instructions and in different ways. Using Llama as the open-weight model, we trace the largest behavioral split to its internals. A linear probe decodes the behavior from the residual stream at 0.87 held-out accuracy while injecting that direction during generation drives the behavior from 0% to 86% across an intervention sweep. Every finding holds under both a token-budget remediation and a control experiment with a hypothesis-blind judgment prompt.

</details>


### [195] [DocMemo: Dynamic Evidence Discovery via Probabilistic Memory-Guided Retrieval for Multi-Modal Document Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07067)
*Hanshu Yao,Janfeng Zhong,Niu Lian,Jinpeng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DocMemo introduces a memory-guided framework for long-document reasoning that uses tri-level retrieval state (Document Schema, Page Belief, and Question Episodic Memory) with Bayesian belief updating and Thompson sampling to dynamically explore evidence across pages, achieving state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current long-document understanding methods either commit to a fixed top-k page set early (single-round, prone to irrecoverable retrieval errors) or lack mechanisms to track how page relevance evolves across rounds (iterative methods). There is a need for a framework that can dynamically propagate and update retrieval states during multi-round evidence acquisition.

Method: DocMemo formulates long-document reasoning as dynamic evidence exploration using a tri-level memory architecture: (1) Document Schema Memory for structural priors, (2) Page Belief Memory for dynamic relevance estimation via Bayesian updating with Thompson sampling, and (3) Question Episodic Memory for query-specific reasoning trajectories. It also employs spatial proximity propagation and structure-aware adaptive-granularity evidence access, supplementing page-level evidence with fine-grained visual regions.

Result: Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, validating the effectiveness of structured memory and dynamic page belief updating.

Conclusion: DocMemo effectively addresses the limitations of static and memory-fragile long-document reasoning systems by enabling dynamic, memory-guided evidence exploration, with both quantitative and ablative results supporting its design.

Abstract: Long-document understanding requires locating sparse and heterogeneous evidence across hundreds of pages, yet existing systems remain limited by static retrieval and fragile cross-round memory. Mainstream single-round methods commit to a fixed top-$k$ page set at the outset and struggle to recover from early retrieval errors; recent iterative approaches allow multi-round evidence acquisition, but they do not investigate the propagation mechanism of cross-round states, making it difficult to track the dynamic changes in page relevance. To address these limitations, we propose DocMemo, a memory-guided framework that formulates long-document reasoning as dynamic evidence exploration. DocMemo maintains a tri-level retrieval state consisting of Document Schema Memory, Page Belief Memory, and Question Episodic Memory, which respectively capture structural priors, dynamic relevance estimation, and query-specific reasoning trajectories. During reasoning, DocMemo continuously refines cross-round page selection through Bayesian page belief updating with Thompson sampling, spatial proximity propagation, and structure-aware adaptive-granularity evidence access, while supplementing page-level evidence with fine-grained visual regions. Experiments on 3 benchmarks show that DocMemo achieves state-of-the-art performance and validate the efficacy of structured memory and dynamic page belief updating. Code is available at https://github.com/Harrygof/DocMemo.

</details>


### [196] [Automated item evaluation: Predicting item acceptance and rejection using LLM-generated critiques](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06609)
*Hotaka Maeda,Yikai Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A fusion model combining DeBERTaV3-large with LLM-generated item critiques predicts item rejection in large-scale standardized testing. The model achieves strong performance for math (F1=.73, AUC=.86) but struggles with ELA (F1=.51, AUC=.72) and fairness-related rejections. Lowering decision thresholds improves sensitivity, useful for automated item generation pipelines where false positives are tolerable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To build a near-comprehensive automated item evaluation (AIE) model that predicts item acceptance/rejection from item text alone, leveraging historical rejection data from a large-scale standardized testing program. This addresses the costly bottleneck of manual expert review and field testing in item development pipelines.

Method: Three classifiers were fine-tuned on 52,759 ELA and math items (34% rejection rate): (1) a DeBERTaV3-large classifier on raw item text, (2) a DeBERTa classifier on item critiques generated by Qwen3 (an LLM), and (3) a fusion model combining representations from both. Rejection reasons spanned psychometric properties, content issues, bias/sensitivity concerns, and non-content issues. Decision threshold tuning was explored for operational trade-offs.

Result: The fusion model achieved the best overall performance: Accuracy=.75, F1=.64, AUC=.80, Sensitivity=.64, Specificity=.81. Math items were predicted substantially better (F1=.73, AUC=.86) than ELA items (F1=.51, AUC=.72). Lowering the threshold to .25 raised sensitivity to .88 (ELA) and .91 (math) at the cost of specificity (.31 and .56). Incorporating LLM critiques improved performance across most rejection reasons. The model struggled with bias, sensitivity, fairness, and accessibility flags, especially in ELA.

Conclusion: Text-based AIE is feasible and offers practical value for reducing manual review burden, particularly for math items. However, human review remains essential for fairness-sensitive items. Threshold calibration enables trade-offs suited to automated item generation contexts where false positives are less costly than missed rejections.

Abstract: Automated item evaluation (AIE) refers to the use of computational methods to assess item quality without requiring manual expert review or field testing of the items under evaluation. We aimed to build a near-comprehensive AIE model by predicting item acceptance and rejection from item text using historical rejection data from a large-scale standardized testing program. The dataset contained 52,759 English language arts (ELA) and mathematics items with 34% permanently rejected from future operational use. Rejection reasons included poor psychometric properties, content issues, bias and sensitivity concerns, and non-content issues. We fine-tuned a DeBERTaV3-large classifier on raw item text, a second DeBERTa classifier on Qwen3-generated item critiques, and a fusion model combining representations from both. The fusion model achieved the strongest overall performance (Accuracy = .75, F1 = .64, AUC = .80, Sensitivity = .64, Specificity = .81). Prediction for math (F1 = .73, AUC = .86) was considerably more accurate than ELA (F1 = .51, AUC = .72). Lowering the decision threshold from .5 to .25 raised average sensitivity for ELA and math to .88 and .91, while reducing specificity to .31 and .56, respectively, which may be preferable in automated item generation contexts where generating items is cheaper than evaluating them. Incorporating item critiques alongside raw item text improved performance across most rejection reasons. The model assigned higher rejection probabilities to more difficult items. However, the fusion model struggled to identify items flagged for bias, sensitivity, fairness, or accessibility, especially for ELA. These findings suggest that text-based AIE is feasible in some areas and may offer a practical tool for reducing the burden of manual review and field testing, while also underscoring the importance of human review for items with fairness concerns.

</details>


### [197] [NxN E-valuation: Hypothesis Certification via a Conformal CRT Null](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06621)
*Bin Wang,Yan Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NxN E-valuation is an e-value-based hypothesis certification algorithm that eliminates the need for case-specific null hypothesis construction by using different samples as null hypotheses for one another, realizing a conditional randomization test particularly suited for validating LLM-generated hypotheses prone to hallucination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are adept at generating hypotheses but suffer from hallucination, making direct harvesting of their outputs unreliable. Existing remedies—circular verification (LLM self-checking) and held-out testing—are inadequate because false hypotheses can still pass via spurious correlations. A universal, assumption-light certification method is needed that works when hypotheses apply to individual samples and large training data is available.

Method: The method frames hypothesis certification as a conditional randomization test (CRT) powered by e-values. It exploits the naturally available large training set, letting different samples serve as null hypotheses for one another in an N×N pairwise evaluation structure. This design avoids constructing any case-specific null hypothesis or dedicated certification procedure, while providing valid, anytime-valid statistical guarantees through e-value accumulation.

Result: NxN E-valuation provides a universally better replacement for LLM circular verification and held-out-data testing, provided the LLM's generations are hypotheses applicable to individual samples. It successfully certifies hypotheses without dedicated null hypothesis construction, leveraging only a sufficiently large dataset.

Conclusion: NxN E-valuation offers a general-purpose, statistically principled hypothesis certification framework that resolves the hallucination barrier in LLM-based exploration systems, outperforming circular verification and held-out testing whenever LLM hypotheses are sample-level and ample data exists.

Abstract: We propose NxN E-valuation, a handy, e-value-based hypothesis-certification algorithm that lets a hypothesis be verified without building any case-specific certification procedure---such as constructing a dedicated null hypothesis---as long as a large enough dataset is available. The method is especially suited to LLM-based exploration systems, where LLMs are remarkably good at proposing hypotheses but suffer badly from hallucination; this hallucination prevents us from harvesting LLM outputs directly, and existing remedies each fall short. The most common solutions include letting the LLM verify or correct itself circular verification and held-out testing (where false hypotheses can still pass via spurious correlations), among other remedies detailed in the introduction. To resolve this, NxN E-valuation exploits the naturally existing large training set and lets different samples serve as null hypotheses for one another. This design directly realizes a conditional randomization test (CRT) that certifies each hypothesis. The approach can be a universally better replacement for at least LLM circular verification and held-out-data testing, provided the LLM's generations are hypotheses that apply to each individual sample.

</details>


### [198] [GeoBenchLLM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Geo-Related Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07411)
*Rodrigo Ferreira Rodrigues,Karim Radouane,Jose G Moreno,Lynda Tamine*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GeoBenchLLM is a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates Large Language Models on diverse geo-related tasks using twelve public datasets, revealing that reasoning ability and model size strongly influence performance on geo-spatial and temporal understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM evaluations in the geospatial domain have been conducted in homogeneous settings, limiting insights into their generalization capabilities across diverse geo-related tasks and domains.

Method: The authors curated twelve publicly available datasets spanning diverse geo-related tasks and domains, then used them to systematically evaluate a set of LLMs on both geo-spatial and temporal understanding.

Result: Reasoning capability and model size were found to have a strong impact on overall LLM performance in geo-related tasks.

Conclusion: GeoBenchLLM provides a standardized, heterogeneous evaluation framework for assessing LLMs' geo-spatial and temporal reasoning, and the benchmark is publicly released to facilitate further research.

Abstract: In the context of geodata, existing Large Language Models have often been studied in a homogeneous setting, which has considerably limited insights into their generalization capabilities. In this paper, we present \benchName, a comprehensive benchmark for probing LLMs on geo-related tasks. We leverage a careful selection of twelve publicly available datasets from diverse geo-related tasks and domains, and evaluate a set of LLMs on geo-spatial and temporal understanding using our benchmark. Our results show that reasoning and size have a strong impact on overall performance. GeoBenchLLM is publicly available at https://github.com/Rfr2003/GeoBenchLLM.

</details>


### [199] [Shape Your Feed: An LLM-based Agentic System for Conversational Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06632)
*Ziyun Xu,Bosen Ding,Yue Zhang,Ji Qi,Qingyuan Song,Jizhou Huang,Liwei Wang,Jefferey Santelli,Yue Weng,Qichao Que,Zhenheng Yang,Junfeng Pan,Linhong Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SYF is an LLM-based agentic recommendation framework that replaces passive ranking with real-time, multimodal co-curation. It uses a three-tier architecture (Perception, Serving, Self-Evolution) and demonstrates strong offline alignment accuracy (98.85%) and positive online A/B results in production.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial recommendation systems rely on passive implicit signals (clicks, dwell time), creating a discrepancy between users' explicit interests and what algorithms deliver. Users cannot express nuanced preferences or steer their feeds in real time, motivating a shift toward interactive, user-steerable recommendation.

Method: SYF employs a three-tier architecture: (1) Perception Flow — captures user intent from text prompts, voice commands, and UI interactions; (2) Serving Flow — performs real-time agentic re-ranking and pruning using a persistent Semantic Profile of evolving user preferences; (3) Self-Evolution Flow — aligns system behavior with human judgments via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and an LLM-as-a-Judge ensemble.

Result: Offline: alignment scoring module achieves 98.85% accuracy, significantly outperforming few-shot baselines. Online: large-scale A/B experiments on production traffic show improvements in feed relevance and user sentiment.

Conclusion: SYF provides a practical, scalable path toward interactive, user-steerable recommendation in industrial settings, bridging the gap between explicit user expression and algorithmic content delivery.

Abstract: Industrial recommendation systems predominantly adopt a passive ranking paradigm that infers user preferences from implicit behavioral signals (e.g., clicks, dwell time) rather than explicit, natural language inputs. As a result, users experience a persistent discrepancy between their explicit interests and what passive behavioral algorithms deliver, limiting their ability to express nuanced preferences or steer their feed in real time. To address this growing gap between how recommendations are optimized and how users wish to articulate their interests, we present Shape Your Feed (SYF), an LLM-based agentic recommendation framework that enables real-time, multimodal co-curation of content. SYF employs a three-tier architecture: (i) a Perception Flow that captures fine-grained user intent from text prompts, voice commands, and UI interactions; (ii) a Serving Flow that performs real-time agentic re-ranking and pruning of candidate items, grounded in a persistent Semantic Profile encoding evolving user preferences; and (iii) a Self-Evolution Flow that aligns system behavior with human judgments via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and an LLM-as-a-Judge ensemble. Offline evaluations show that SYF's alignment scoring module achieves 98.85% accuracy, substantially improving over strong few-shot baselines. Large-scale online A/B experiments on production traffic further demonstrate that SYF improves feed relevance and user sentiment, indicating a practical and scalable path toward interactive, user-steerable recommendation in industrial settings.

</details>


### [200] [TRACE: A Multi-Layer Benchmark for Human AI Controller Coordination Under Drift and Failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06657)
*Joshua Zuniga,Srinivasan Subramanian,Ramya Madhuri Narapureddy,Md Abdullah Al Hafiz Khan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The authors construct a benchmark of 1,918 time-aligned, multi-layer traces (state, observation, decision, rules, control) derived from ALFRED, injected with controlled drift. Each trace is labeled with drift type, affected layer, onset time, responsible actor, and causal mechanism. Paired with a leak-aware evaluation protocol, baseline models achieve strong attribution performance (macro-F1: layer ~0.70, actor ~0.85, mechanism ~0.49), with heavy attention models offering no clear advantage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern cyber-physical and AI-assisted systems integrate human operators, AI modules, and automated controllers in a single control loop, yet no standard benchmark exists for capturing time-aligned, multi-layer traces of how drift and failures propagate across layers. This prevents systematic diagnosis of where coordination breaks down, why, and how to recover.

Method: The authors construct a benchmark by injecting controlled drift into traces from the ALFRED grounded-instruction benchmark. Each of the 1,918 drifted traces contains per-step records across five execution layers, labeled with drift type, affected layer, onset time, responsible actor, and causal mechanism. Labels are validated by independent raters with inter-annotator agreement reported. They design a leak-aware evaluation protocol that removes a near-perfect onset leak, and conduct baseline experiments across classical, recurrent, and attention-based model families.

Result: Under the honest (leak-removed) protocol, drift detection and attribution significantly exceed random and majority baselines: affected layer macro-F1 ≈ 0.70, responsible actor macro-F1 ≈ 0.85, and causal mechanism macro-F1 ≈ 0.49. Heavy attention-based models show no advantage over simpler classical or recurrent models on this symbolic benchmark.

Conclusion: Multi-layer drift attribution is feasible when evaluated under honest protocols. The benchmark enables systematic study of cross-layer failure propagation in human-AI-automation loops, and the results caution against assuming that complex attention architectures inherently outperform simpler models on structured, symbolic diagnostic tasks.

Abstract: Modern cyber-physical and AI-assisted systems couple human operators, AI decision modules, and automated controllers in a single control loop, so trustworthiness depends on the whole loop, not any one model. Yet no standard benchmark captures time-aligned, multi-layer traces of how drift and failures propagate across these layers, so we cannot diagnose where coordination breaks down, why, or how to recover. This paper targets one facet of that gap: drift, a deviation that can originate in any stack layer and that conventional single-modality monitoring cannot localize to a layer or pin to an onset time. We construct a benchmark by injecting controlled drift into traces derived from ALFRED, a grounded-instruction benchmark for everyday household tasks, yielding 1,918 drifted traces. Each trace is a time-aligned sequence of per-step records across five execution layers (state, observation, decision, rules, control), labeled with the drift type, affected layer, onset time, responsible actor, and causal mechanism, and validated by independent raters with inter-annotator agreement reported. We pair the dataset with a leak-aware protocol that removes a near-perfect onset leak, and a baseline study across classical, recurrent, and attention-based model families. Under this honest protocol, drift is identifiable and attributable well above random and majority baselines across every family (affected layer macro-F1 near 0.70, responsible actor near 0.85, causal mechanism near 0.49), and heavy attention offers no advantage over simpler models on this symbolic benchmark.

</details>


### [201] [CellWorld: From Gene-Level Reconstruction to Latent Cell Prediction in Spatial Transcriptomics Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06659)
*Haiping Liu,Qian Zhao,Lijing Lin,Jingyuan Sun,Hongpeng Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CellWorld introduces latent-space predictive pretraining for spatial transcriptomics foundation models, predicting masked cell latent representations rather than raw gene expression. Scaling experiments across 46M cells demonstrate that even small variants outperform baselines, and a frozen large model trained on just 5% of the corpus surpasses fully fine-tuned baselines on all spatial benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing spatial transcriptomics foundation models reconstruct masked gene identities or expression values, which risks reproducing assay-specific technical variation and limits cross-dataset transferability. The authors propose shifting the prediction target to latent cell representations to avoid this pitfall.

Method: CellWorld uses latent-space predictive pretraining: it predicts the latent representations of masked cells conditioned on visible spatial context and a limited partial-expression hint. Four model variants (5.74M to 94.56M parameters) are pretrained on a 46M-cell human corpus. Controlled scaling experiments assess performance across model capacity, data volume, and biological diversity.

Result: CellWorld-Small (5.74M parameters) outperforms all baselines on 11 linear-probe and 7 fine-tuned spatial benchmarks across four held-out datasets. A frozen CellWorld-Large pretrained on only 5% of the corpus with broad biological coverage surpasses every fully fine-tuned baseline on all seven spatial benchmarks. Performance scales with model capacity, especially for spatial tasks, while spatial transfer benefits more from optimization and source diversity than cell count alone.

Conclusion: Latent-space predictive pretraining is a scalable and effective paradigm for spatial transcriptomics foundation models, achieving strong transfer performance with frozen representations and high data efficiency when biological diversity is prioritized.

Abstract: This paper shows that latent-space predictive pretraining can provide a scalable route to foundation models for spatial transcriptomics. Existing spatial transcriptomics foundation models primarily reconstruct masked gene identities or expression values, potentially encouraging the reproduction of assay-specific technical variation and limiting representation transferability. To avoid directly reconstructing such variation, we shift the prediction target from observed gene measurements to latent cell representations and introduce CellWorld, which predicts the latent representations of masked cells from visible spatial context and a limited partial-expression hint. We pretrain four CellWorld variants, spanning 5.74M to 94.56M trainable parameters, on a corpus of 46 million human cells. Our controlled scaling experiments show that performance improves with model capacity, particularly on spatial tasks, while spatial transfer depends more on sufficient optimization and broad biological source diversity than on cell count alone. Across four held-out datasets, even CellWorld-Small, with 5.74M trainable parameters, outperforms every baseline on all 11 linear-probe benchmarks and all seven fine-tuned spatial benchmarks. Most notably, a frozen CellWorld-Large pretrained on only 5\% of the corpus with broad biological source coverage outperforms every fully fine-tuned baseline across all seven spatial benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/UoM-HealthAI/CellWorld.

</details>


### [202] [Vehicle routing problem using deep reinforcement learning - A case study about truck planning in the industry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06668)
*Siliang Lu,Dan Hu,Lili Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents industrial case studies on applying deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to vehicle routing problems involving external truck network design, demonstrating over 10% total cost reduction compared to baseline methods across three logistics use cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world VRP deployments face challenges including complex constraints, information opacity, uncertainty, and irrational human behavior that make traditional mathematical optimization models difficult to maintain. There is a need for adaptive, data-driven approaches that can handle these practical complexities in industrial logistics settings.

Method: The authors implement deep reinforcement learning-based vehicle routing optimization across three distinct logistics use cases involving external truck network design. The DRL agents are trained to make routing decisions that minimize total operational costs while accommodating real-world constraints.

Result: The DRL-optimized routes achieved over 10% total cost reduction compared to baseline results across the three industrial case studies.

Conclusion: DRL proves effective for industrial VRP applications, and future work should focus on generalizing DRL algorithms to a broader range of VRP variants.

Abstract: As an important component of the supply chain industry, transportation has experienced rapid development in the past decade with the assistance of digital platforms and intelligent algorithms. Within the field of transportation research, Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) has remained a persistent and enduring challenge. In the realm of management science, experts, and scholars from both the industrial and academic sectors have continuously explored optimization models and algorithms to effectively address routing problems, from the classical Traveling Salesman Problem to the more general Vehicle Routing Problem. These models and algorithms are applied in real-world industrial scenarios to achieve cost optimization and reduce carbon footprints. However, due to the complexity of real-world problems, numerous specific constraints are often added, and challenges such as information opacity, uncertainty, and irrational human behavior may arise. Therefore, deploying and optimizing mathematical models for VRP in practical scenarios while maintaining optimal results poses numerous challenges. This paper discusses and provides solutions for three different logistic use cases involving external truck network design. Through these industrial case study, the paper introduces how deep reinforcement learning-based vehicle routing optimization has been implemented. As a result, it can be observed that the routes optimized by reinforcement learning agent have over 10% total cost compared to baseline results. Furthermore, the paper proposes that in future research, DRL algorithms for vehicle routing problems could be generalized into more variations of VRP.

</details>


### [203] [A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics of Polymers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06694)
*Joohee Choi,Junhyeong Lee,Seunghwa Ryu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CGMas is a multi-agent framework that uses large language models to fully automate the bottom-up coarse-graining of polymers — from natural-language polymer specification through topology construction, equilibration, mapping, potential derivation (Boltzmann inversion), and validation — completing 27 polymer tasks while reducing simulation time from up to 88 minutes to about 1 minute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bottom-up coarse-grained (CG) modeling of polymers is labor-intensive because each polymer and CG resolution requires deriving potentials anew; no transferable parameter set exists. Automating this pipeline would dramatically accelerate polymer simulation workflows.

Method: CGMas employs a multi-agent system orchestrated by a large language model (LLM). A reasoning agent infers all-atom topology from the polymer name, with layered self-correction to fix errors in unsaturated, heteroatom-containing, and polar polymers. Downstream agents handle equilibration, mapping to CG resolution, potential derivation via Boltzmann inversion, and benchmarking against atomistic references.

Result: CGMas successfully completed all 27 homopolymer and copolymer tasks. It matched the all-atom density to within 5% in 22 of the 27 cases and reduced simulation time from 38–88 minutes to approximately 1 minute.

Conclusion: Agentic LLMs represent a viable route to fully automated polymer coarse-graining, eliminating the manual labor bottleneck in bottom-up CG model construction while maintaining acceptable fidelity to atomistic reference data.

Abstract: Coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics extends polymer simulation beyond the scales accessible to all-atom (AA) methods, but bottom-up CG modeling is laborious. The CG resolution is a design choice, so a transferable parameter set is generally not available and the potentials are derived anew for each polymer mapping. Here we present CGMas, a multi-agent framework that automates topology construction, equilibration, mapping, potential derivation, and validation from a natural-language specification of the polymer and target resolution. A large-language-model (LLM) reasoning agent infers the AA topology from polymer name, while layered self-correction resolves physical errors common to unsaturated, heteroatom-containing, and polar polymers. Downstream agents equilibrate the system, map it onto CG representation, derive potentials through Boltzmann inversion, and benchmark the model against its atomistic reference. CGMas completed all 27 homopolymer and copolymer tasks, matched the AA density to within 5% in 22, and reduced simulation from 38-88 min to 1 min, establishing agentic LLMs as a route to automated polymer coarse-graining.

</details>


### [204] [AgentPatch: Coarse-to-Fine Weak-Task Repair for Merging Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06699)
*Zibo Shao,Baochen Xiong,Chengdong Xu,Linhui Xiao,Kaichen Li,Haoran Gong,Yan Li,Yaguang Song,Xiaoshan Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentPatch is a training-free, coarse-to-fine repair framework for merging agentic multimodal LLMs. It addresses asymmetric capability preservation and behavior-critical forgetting via Weak-Task Unique Residual Recovery and an Agent-Guided Behavior-Critical Patch, producing a single static checkpoint that balances weak-task recovery with preservation of complementary capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agentic MLLMs are specialized for particular tools or environments, making consolidation into a single generalist difficult. Merging these models introduces two key problems: (1) asymmetric capability preservation, where capabilities with different interaction complexity are retained unevenly, leading to weak-task degradation; and (2) behavior-critical forgetting, where losing decisive actions derails long-horizon task execution.

Method: AgentPatch is a training-free, coarse-to-fine repair framework with three stages: (1) selecting a stable merged backbone; (2) Weak-Task Unique Residual Recovery, which restores diluted weak-task-specific signals; and (3) an Agent-Guided Behavior-Critical Patch that recovers decisive behaviors under explicit capability protection. The method produces a single static checkpoint without routing or ensembles.

Result: Experiments across six agentic and multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that AgentPatch improves diverse merged backbones, alleviates weak-task degradation, and better balances weak-task recovery with the preservation of complementary search and agentic visual processing capabilities.

Conclusion: AgentPatch effectively addresses the core challenges of agentic MLLM merging, namely asymmetric capability preservation and behavior-critical forgetting, without requiring additional training. The resulting single static checkpoint achieves a favorable trade-off between recovering degraded weak tasks and maintaining complementary capabilities.

Abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) extend multimodal perception and reasoning with planning, tool use, and interaction in dynamic environments. Yet current models are specialized for particular tools or environments, complicating consolidation into a single generalist. We formulate Agentic MLLM Merging and identify two challenges: asymmetric capability preservation, whereby capabilities with different interaction complexity are retained unevenly, producing weak tasks after merging, and behavior-critical forgetting, whereby losing decisive actions can derail long-horizon execution. We propose AgentPatch, a training-free coarse-to-fine repair framework. It selects a stable merged backbone, restores diluted weak-task-specific signals through Weak-Task Unique Residual Recovery, and applies an Agent-Guided Behavior-Critical Patch that recovers decisive behaviors under explicit capability protection. AgentPatch produces a single static checkpoint without routing or ensembles. Experiments across six agentic and multimodal benchmarks show that AgentPatch improves diverse merged backbones, alleviates weak-task degradation, and better balances weak-task recovery with the preservation of complementary search and agentic visual processing capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/ziboshao/AgentPatch.

</details>


### [205] [WebRider: Persona-Conditioned Intent Controllers for Live-Web Assistance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06704)
*Zhi Li,Tao Zhou,Yeqing Li,Eugene Ie,Demetri Terzopoulos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WebRider formalizes web task delegation as an "intent contract" specifying goals, constraints, evidence, answer form, and persona controls. A hierarchical architecture (controller → guarded actions → tools) ensures policy fidelity. RiderBench evaluates 4,096 live-web contracts, revealing that a strong controller finishes 99.2% of tasks but respects all policy constraints in only 38.8% of cases. A trained 8B action-policy model using the guarded interface outperforms executable-only baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current live-web agents are evaluated solely on final-answer correctness, ignoring whether they adhered to the delegator's policy (constraints, preferences, evidence requirements, stopping criteria). The authors demonstrate that high task completion rates can mask severe policy violations — a 99.2% completion rate drops to 38.8% when policy fidelity is audited. This gap motivates a framework that treats the browsing path as a first-class, auditable object.

Method: WebRider introduces: (1) an **intent contract** — a formal operational record encoding goals, constraints, evidence obligations, answer form, and task-local persona controls; (2) a **hierarchical architecture** with a top-layer controller maintaining the contract, a middle layer realizing intentions as guarded executable actions, and a tool layer (browser, search, maps) executing them; (3) **RiderBench**, a benchmark of 4,096 live-web contracts across 42 public websites that audits both internal contract state and visible user experience; (4) an 8B action-policy model trained via the guarded middle interface as a high-quality training signal.

Result: A strong controller achieves 99.2% task completion but only 38.8% full policy fidelity. The guarded middle interface provides a training signal enabling an 8B action-policy model to outperform executable-only baselines under a fixed controller. RiderBench provides dual auditing (internal contract state + user-visible experience) across 4,096 contracts on 42 websites.

Conclusion: Making the browsing path a first-class object via intent contracts enables web agents that are auditable, human-judgeable, and learnable, decoupling action realization from final-answer decisions. The hierarchical guarded architecture with contract-based delegation significantly improves policy fidelity beyond what answer-only evaluation captures.

Abstract: Delegating a web task involves more than asking a question; it requires transferring a policy: what to verify, how to handle uncertainty, which preferences matter, and when to stop. Yet, current live-web agents are evaluated solely on the final answer, ignoring the policy constraints that define the delegation. A plausible final answer can conceal violations of that policy. Our full live audit reveals this critical gap: a strong controller completes 99.2% of tasks but honors all policy constraints in only 38.8% of cases. Finishing does not imply fidelity. WebRider bridges this gap by formalizing the delegated policy as an intent contract---an operational record of goals, constraints, evidence obligations, answer form, and task-local persona controls that must hold even as web pages change. WebRider employs a hierarchical architecture: a top-layer controller maintains the contract, a middle layer realizes intentions as guarded executable actions, and a tool layer executes these actions via browser, search, and maps tools. Our benchmark, RiderBench, evaluates this design on 4,096 live-web contracts across 42 public websites, auditing both the internal contract state and the visible user experience to determine if a rollout preserved its policy and if the steps were persona-consistent. The guarded middle interface also serves as a high-quality training signal; an 8B action-policy model trained through this interface outperforms executable-only baselines under a fixed controller. By making the browsing path a first-class object, WebRider enables a system that is auditable, human-judgeable, and learnable without conflating action realization with final-answer decisions. Dataset URL: hf.co/datasets/WebRider/WebRider.

</details>


### [206] [MolBioKG: Grounding Out-of-Graph Molecules in Biomedical Knowledge Graphs via Multi-Resolution Structural Anchoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06713)
*Yiming Zhang,Hikaru Shindo,Shuan Chen,Kaushalya Madhawa,Jun Jin Choong,Yuna Oikawa,Takashi Fujiwara,Keisuke Ozawa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MolBioKG addresses the cold-start problem of out-of-graph molecules in biomedical KGs by grounding unseen molecules through multi-resolution structural anchoring, combining a 2.74M molecule index with a 9.6M-edge KG. It features static multi-anchor retrieval (RRF) and an LLM-based adaptive traversal policy (Adapt-KG), achieving substantial gains on multi-hop reasoning and out-of-graph generalization while maintaining traceability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard biomedical KG pipelines assume query molecules already exist as graph entities, leaving unregistered (novel) molecules disconnected and unretrievable. This "out-of-graph molecule problem" represents a cold-start challenge that limits the utility of KGs for drug discovery involving novel compounds.

Method: MolBioKG employs a two-layer architecture: (1) a molecular index of 2.74M molecules represented at multiple structural resolutions (scaffolds, fragments, functional groups, fingerprints) connected to (2) a 9.6M-edge biomedical KG. Given a SMILES string, it retrieves structurally related entities and traverses their biomedical neighborhoods. Two inference mechanisms are introduced: static multi-anchor retrieval using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and Adapt-KG, a tool-using LLM policy enabling adaptive traversal, both operating without task-specific training.

Result: MolBioKG outperforms strong baselines across three evaluation settings: Hits@10 on multi-hop reasoning improves from 0.585 to 0.876; out-of-graph target recall rises from 0.145 to 0.269. All predictions retain traceable structural anchors and source-attributed KG evidence paths.

Conclusion: MolBioKG effectively bridges unregistered molecules into existing biomedical KGs via multi-resolution structural anchoring, enabling robust reasoning without retraining. Its dual inference strategy delivers state-of-the-art performance while preserving interpretability through traceable anchors and evidence provenance.

Abstract: Biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) accelerate drug discovery, but standard pipelines assume query molecules already exist as graph entities, leaving unregistered molecules disconnected. We address this cold-start challenge, termed the out-of-graph molecule problem, by introducing MolBioKG. This two-layer system grounds unseen molecules in biomedical evidence via multi-resolution structural anchoring. It connects an index of 2.74 million molecules (represented by scaffolds, fragments, functional groups, and fingerprints) to a 9.6-million-edge KG. Given only a SMILES string, MolBioKG retrieves structurally related graph entities and traverses their biomedical neighborhoods without task-specific training. It features two inference mechanisms: static multi-anchor retrieval using Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and Adapt-KG, a tool-using LLM policy for adaptive traversal. Evaluated across in-graph link recovery, complex multi-hop reasoning, and out-of-graph generalization, MolBioKG outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it raises Hits@10 from 0.585 to 0.876 in multi-hop reasoning and out-of-graph target recall from 0.145 to 0.269, all while ensuring predictions retain traceable structural anchors and source-attributed KG evidence.

</details>


### [207] [The Optimizer Is the Agent: Reasoning-Driven Search across Prompts, Programs, and ML Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06714)
*Junbo Li,Boyi Liu,Canwen Xu,Yite Wang,Yuxiong He,Zhangyang Wang,Qiang Liu,Zhewei Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReASearch proposes a unified, reasoning-driven optimization framework where a single tool-using agent autonomously conducts the entire optimization loop—deciding evaluations, diagnosing failures, making edits, and managing budget—eliminating the need for hand-designed outer-loop controllers. Tested across 14 tasks spanning prompts, programs, and ML workflows, it matches or outperforms specialized optimizers by 2–40% and sometimes surpasses human best-known results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing optimization systems for prompts, programs, and ML workflows depend on explicit, hand-crafted outer-loop controllers (e.g., evolutionary search, bandits, textual gradients). The authors question whether a single tool-using agent can internalize this search policy, replacing engineered controllers with autonomous reasoning.

Method: ReASearch provides a unified agent loop with domain-specific tools. The agent autonomously: decides what to evaluate, diagnoses failures, selects edits, determines when to verify or restart, allocates budget, and refines strategy over long horizons using persistent memory. The same scaffold is instantiated across prompt engineering, program optimization, and ML workflow tuning without task-specific controller design.

Result: Across 14 diverse tasks, ReASearch is competitive with and mostly outperforms specialized optimization systems, achieving 2–40% gains over strong domain-specific baselines. In some cases, it discovers solutions that surpass prior human best-known results. Complex search behaviors typically implemented by explicit controllers emerge naturally from the agent's reasoning.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that much of the optimization search policy can be effectively internalized within a reasoning-driven agent, challenging the prevailing paradigm of explicit outer-loop controllers. This unified, scaffold-agnostic approach generalizes across domains and often surpasses specialized systems while autonomously exhibiting emergent sophisticated search strategies.

Abstract: Recent systems for optimizing prompts, programs, and ML workflows typically rely on explicit outer-loop controllers such as evolutionary search, bandits, or textual-gradient methods. We ask a fundamentally different question: how much of this search policy can be internalized by a single tool-using agent? We present ReASearch, a unified framework for reasoning-driven optimization in which the agent autonomously decides what to evaluate, how to diagnose failures, which edits to make, and when to verify or restart. Rather than serving only as a proposal generator guided by hand-designed heuristics, the agent actively analyzes outcomes, allocates budget, and refines its strategy over long horizons through persistent memory. With a shared agent loop and domain-specific tools, ReASearch instantiates the exact same scaffold to optimize prompts, programs, and ML workflows. Across 14 diverse tasks, it is competitive with and mostly better than specialized optimization systems, achieving gains of 2% to 40% over strong domain-specific baselines, and in some cases discovering solutions that improve on prior human best-known results. Crucially, we observe that complex search behaviors, which are typically implemented by explicit controllers, emerge naturally from the agent's reasoning process.

</details>


### [208] [bioMoR: Biology-Guided Mixture-of-Recursions for Effective Genomic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06727)
*Koushik Howlader,Tirtho Roy,Md Tauhidul Islam,Wei Le*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: bioMoR introduces Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR) to gene/pathway-level omics analysis by injecting structured biological knowledge at three key points: graph-based token embedding refinement, structurally biased self-attention, and a graph-aware router for adaptive recursion depth. It achieves significant gains in macro-F1 (+8.2 pp) and balanced accuracy (+7.1 pp) over biology-agnostic MoR, with 75% fewer parameters and up to 58% fewer FLOPs than non-recursive Transformers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-dimensional omics data involves thousands of genes/pathways, but only a subset requires deep computation. Existing Transformers lack efficiency and biological grounding. The authors aim to integrate structured biological knowledge into an adaptive-computation framework (MoR) to improve both predictive performance and computational efficiency while providing biological interpretability.

Method: The bioMoR framework integrates structured biological knowledge into a Mixture-of-Recursions backbone at three locations: (1) Graph-based information sharing: refines token embeddings using known gene/pathway interaction networks. (2) Structural bias in self-attention: guides attention toward biologically related tokens. (3) Graph-aware router: leverages neighborhood topology to determine per-token recursion depth, adaptively allocating compute. Evaluation uses eight diverse omics benchmarks under unified five-fold cross-validation.

Result: bioMoR outperforms the strongest biology-agnostic MoR baseline by 8.2 percentage points in macro-F1 and 7.1 percentage points in balanced accuracy. It achieves this with 75% fewer parameters and up to 58% fewer FLOPs than a non-recursive Transformer. Token-specific recursion depths reveal differential compute allocation, and selected marker genes/pathways provide biological interpretability.

Conclusion: Injecting structured biological knowledge into MoR architectures via graph-based embeddings, structurally biased attention, and graph-aware routing yields substantial gains in predictive performance, parameter efficiency, and computational cost. The framework also enables interpretability through marker gene/pathway identification and recursion depth analysis, advancing adaptive-computation methods for high-dimensional omics.

Abstract: Transformer models for high-dimensional omics analysis process thousands of genes or pathways, although only a subset requires deep computation. Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR) improves efficiency through adaptive token-choice or expert-choice routing. We propose bioMoR, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework to apply MoR to gene-level and pathway-level learning. Our contributions include identifying three locations for integrating structured biological knowledge within an MoR backbone: graph-based information sharing refines token embeddings, a structural bias guides self-attention toward biologically related tokens, and a graph-aware router uses neighborhood information to determine each token's recursion depth. These techniques are centered on our insight that additional knowledge of token interaction can effectively help models construct embeddings and select which tokens should be learned more deeply. Across eight benchmarks spanning diverse omics data types and evaluated under a unified five-fold cross-validation protocol, bioMoR improves average macro-F1 by 8.2 percentage points and balanced accuracy by 7.1 percentage points over the strongest biology-agnostic MoR baseline while using 75 percent fewer parameters and up to 58 percent fewer FLOPs than a non-recursive Transformer. The selected marker genes or pathways provide biological interpretability, while their token-specific recursion depths reveal how computation is allocated.

</details>


### [209] [PsychoAgent: An Affect-Sensitive Cognitive Architecture for Conflict-Aware Memory in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07438)
*Mohammad Amanlou,Parham Abed Azad,Farbod Davoodi,Mostafa Masumi,Behnam Bahrak,Abdol-Hossein Vahabie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PsychoAgent is a cognitive architecture for LLM agents that separates factual and affective memory, using a conflict-aware controller to re-rank semantically relevant memories by emotional salience. It outperforms baselines in retrieving conflict-critical memories, and a three-day trace demonstrates persistent affect and memory recombination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human memory retrieval is not driven solely by topical similarity; affective significance and unresolved conflict also determine what becomes accessible. Existing LLM agent memory systems lack this affective dimension, motivating the need for an architecture that models both semantic relevance and emotional salience in memory retrieval.

Method: PsychoAgent employs a dual-memory architecture: factual memory and affective memory, integrated via a conflict-aware executive controller. Affective memories are first filtered by semantic relevance (topical fit), then re-ranked by emotional salience. The system was tested across three controlled conflict scenarios against two baselines: a semantic-affective RAG and a single-memory RAG. Five blinded raters evaluated 27 outputs using within-rater standardization.

Result: The full architecture retrieved more conflict-critical memories (0.933) compared to semantic-affective (0.500) and single-memory RAG baselines (0.667), at a small cost to semantic similarity. The full architecture achieved the highest overall mean rating (+0.22 SD), though corrected pairwise differences were not statistically significant. A three-day illustrative trace showed persistent affect, offline memory recombination, and selective memory reweighting.

Conclusion: Affect-sensitive retrieval is an effective and inspectable mechanism for modeling human-like conflict effects in LLM agents, supporting the integration of emotional salience alongside semantic relevance in agent memory architectures.

Abstract: Human-like cognition does not select past experience by topical similarity alone: affective significance and unresolved conflict also shape what becomes accessible. We present PsychoAgent, a cognitive architecture for LLM agents that separates factual and affective memory and integrates both through a conflict-aware executive controller.
