Across 20,000 pairwise forced-choice comparisons per model analyzed with Bradley--Terry estimation, we observe a consistent critical acclaim orientation with all models: critically acclaimed yet commercially obscure films are selected over commercially successful yet critically unrecognized ones. This pattern grows with model scale within each family. In addition, nested OLS regression analyses show that evaluative orientation, public visibility, and popular reception distinctly help explain preferences. Adjusting for public visibility reverses the models' preference for dual-legitimacy films over critical acclaim-only films, while additionally accounting for popular reception attenuates much of the disadvantage of films with commercial success only. Finally, evaluative and recommendation-oriented prompt framings produce divergent rankings, suggesting that critical acclaim orientation may manifest indirectly in real-world LLM deployments.

</details>


### [232] [CAi Copilot: Reducing Operational Workload in Molecular Design through Intent-Driven Agentic Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06961)
*Zhu Wang,Jiangyu Chen,Yingjun Shang,Yuhui Yao,Laiao Lu,Tianfan Fu,Na Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CAi Copilot is a three-layer agent system that transforms broad molecular design intent into traceable, evidence-backed workflows, achieving an outcome score of 84.59 across 45 tasks — exceeding the next-best system by 18.07 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Early-stage molecular design is inherently iterative, requiring researchers to translate broad goals into strategies, refine candidates, evaluate multiple properties, and gather evidence — yet existing AI tools for generation, optimization, property prediction, docking, and synthesis assessment are fragmented across specialized tools. Experts must manually coordinate each step, making the process inefficient and unscalable. The core challenge is converting research intent into adaptive, traceable, scientifically grounded execution runs.

Method: The authors frame molecular design as intent-to-evidence workflow execution and introduce CAi Copilot, an expert-oriented agent with three layers: (1) a Research Interface Layer that converts user intent into executable plans, (2) an Agent Reasoning Layer that dynamically guides runs using interim results, and (3) an Execution Substrate providing molecular tools, metrics, reusable utilities, and backend services.

Result: CAi Copilot achieved an outcome score of 84.59 across 45 tasks, surpassing the next-best competitor by 18.07 points. Benchmarks also evaluate its coordination of generation, screening, and multi-criteria evaluation, while identifying limitations in long-horizon execution scenarios.

Conclusion: CAi Copilot successfully translates broad molecular-design intent into transparent, traceable workflows that link interim decisions to candidate-level evidence, demonstrating strong overall performance and exposing areas for improvement in long-horizon tasks.

Abstract: Early-stage molecular design is an iterative process, not just a task of generating molecules. Researchers turn broad goals into design strategies, refine candidates, assess many properties, and gather evidence before synthesis and tests. AI methods can generate molecules, optimize several goals, predict properties, dock compounds, and account for synthesis. Yet these functions are spread across specialized tools. Experts must still coordinate each step, judge interim results, and integrate evidence. The central challenge is thus to turn research intent into adaptive, traceable runs grounded in scientific tools. We cast this challenge as intent-to-evidence molecular design workflow execution and present CAi Copilot, an expert-oriented agent with three linked layers. The Research Interface Layer turns intent into an executable plan. The Agent Reasoning Layer uses interim results to guide each run. The Execution Substrate supplies molecular tools, metrics, reusable utilities, and backend services. Across 45 tasks, CAi achieves the strongest overall performance, with an outcome score of 84.59, exceeding the next-best result by 18.07 points. Additional benchmarks test how CAi coordinates generation, screening, and multi-criteria evaluation, while exposing limits in long-horizon execution. These results show that CAi turns broad molecular-design intent into transparent, traceable workflows that connect interim decisions to candidate-level evidence.

</details>


### [233] [Learning in Deep Networks under Dale's Constraint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06963)
*Roy Abel,Shimon Ullman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a biologically plausible neural architecture with non-negative activations and fixed-sign synapses (Dale's constraint) using dual on-off channels to represent positive/negative signals, enabling exact backpropagation-equivalent learning via local Hebbian rules, with strong empirical results on Tiny ImageNet.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing biologically plausible learning models violate Dale's constraint by allowing mixed-sign (positive/negative) neuron activations and synapses, which contradicts the biological reality that neurons are exclusively excitatory or inhibitory and synapses have fixed sign.

Method: Proposes an on-off architecture using two complementary non-negative channels (positive and negative) inspired by on-off representations in the brain. This motif is repeated in both bottom-up and top-down pathways throughout the network. Learning signals are propagated via a local Hebbian rule, using only local interactions between neurons, with theoretical proof that the scheme exactly recovers the backpropagation update despite non-negative-only error signals.

Result: The theoretically derived equivalence to backpropagation is demonstrated, and empirically the on-off architecture learns efficient representations, achieving substantial performance gains over comparable vanilla networks on the Tiny ImageNet benchmark.

Conclusion: Effective learning can emerge from biologically plausible mechanisms without mixed-sign signals. The on-off architecture provides a step toward more realistic models of neural computation by satisfying Dale's constraint while maintaining backpropagation-level learning capability.

Abstract: Biologically plausible learning models aim to explain how neural circuits can implement effective learning under the constraints of real neurons. Although significant progress has been made, a major remaining challenge is that existing models often allow neurons or synapses to represent mixed-sign values, both positive and negative, in violation of a basic aspect of cortical circuitry -- Dale's constraint: biological neurons are either excitatory or inhibitory, but not both, and synapses cannot change sign. In this work, we address this discrepancy by introducing a biologically motivated neural architecture in which both neural activations and learning signals are represented by non-negative activity, and synapses have fixed sign, while still supporting backpropagation-like learning. Our approach uses two complementary interacting non-negative channels to represent positive and negative contributions, inspired by evidence of on-off representations in the brain. These channels are implemented through a simple neural circuit motif, which is repeated throughout the network in both bottom-up and top-down pathways. Combined with a local Hebbian learning rule, the resulting model propagates learning signals and updates weights using only local interactions between neurons. We show theoretically that our learning scheme can exactly recover the backpropagation update despite relying solely on non-negative error signals. Empirically, beyond satisfying stronger biological constraints, the on-off architecture learns efficient representations, yielding substantial gains over comparable vanilla networks on the Tiny ImageNet benchmark. These results demonstrate that effective learning can emerge from biologically plausible mechanisms without requiring mixed-sign signals, providing a step toward more realistic models of neural computation.

</details>


### [234] [Finding Usable Weight Mechanisms with Tiled SVD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06969)
*Ash Manvi,Samreena Tajreen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes extracting mechanistically interpretable features directly from neural network weight matrices via column-tiled SVD, yielding "mounts" — (trigger vector, write vector, strength) triples — evaluated on Gemma-2-2B using a full-write energy lift metric, achieving 100% pass rates across all 182 site-layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability relies on proxy dictionaries (e.g., sparse autoencoders) where feature identity lives in the learned dictionary rather than in the network weights themselves. The authors aim to extract interpretable mechanism structures directly from the linear maps of the model, grounding identity in the weight rule itself.

Method: The method applies column-tiled SVD to linear sites within a transformer model. Each resulting "mount" is a triple (v, u, σ) representing a trigger vector, write vector, and strength. Evaluation uses a pre-registered suite with a "full-write energy lift" criterion (rather than tile-local lift). Experiments are run on Gemma-2-2B with a 16,384-token subsample of WikiText-2 across all seven linear maps.

Result: All seven linear maps are scored: residual writes (mlp.down, attn.o) receive full A/B/C ratings with steer after post-sublayer RMSNorm and pass 52/52 site-layers. Other maps (mlp.gate, attn.q, attn.k, effective mlp.up, attn.v) receive A/B only, passing 26/26 each. Aggregate result: 182/182 GO, indicating perfect pass across all evaluated site-layers.

Conclusion: Column-tiled SVD provides a viable method for extracting interpretable mechanism mounts directly from transformer linear weights, with identity grounded in the weight rule rather than in proxy dictionaries. The approach generalizes across all seven linear map types in Gemma-2-2B, and the authors release supporting library code, corpus builder, experiment entrypoint, and unit tests.

Abstract: The dominant approach to mechanistic interpretability trains proxy dictionaries such as sparse autoencoders and labels features from max-activating text. The best such atlases identify con- cepts, but that identity lives in the learned dictionary rather than in the network weights them- selves. We propose extracting mechanism mounts directly from linear sites by column-tiled SVD: each mount is a triple (v,u,σ) read as trigger, write, and strength. Identity is the weight rule. We evaluate mounts with a pre-registered suite judged on full-write energy lift rather than tile-local lift. On Gemma-2-2B with WikiText-2 (16,384-token subsample), all seven linear maps are scored: residual writes (mlp.down, attn.o) receive full A/B/C with steer after post-sublayer RMSNorm and pass 52/52 site-layers; other maps receive A/B only (mlp.gate/attn.q/attn.k/effective mlp.up/attn.v 26/26 each). Aggregate: 182/182 GO. We release library code, the corpus builder, the experiment entrypoint, and unit tests.

</details>


### [235] [FedLBW: A Loss-Based Weighting Strategy for Federated Learning on Non-IID Data in Wireless Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07007)
*Majid Kundroo,Tinku Singh,Taehong Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FedLBW is a federated learning aggregation method that weights client updates by inverse validation loss (computed via a server-side proxy dataset) instead of dataset size, achieving up to 7.6% higher accuracy on CIFAR-10 and superior robustness to non-IID data, outliers, and client dropouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard FL algorithms like FedAvg weight client updates solely by dataset size, introducing bias toward larger clients and making training sensitive to non-IID data distributions, outliers, and client dropouts — particularly problematic in wireless network environments where these conditions are prevalent.

Method: FedLBW introduces loss-based weighting: the server maintains a small proxy/validation dataset. Each client uploads its model update, and the server evaluates each model on the proxy dataset to compute validation loss. Aggregation weights are set proportional to the inverse of each client's validation loss, so lower-loss (more reliable) models dominate the global update.

Result: Extensive experiments on FashionMNIST (CNN), CIFAR-10 (ResNet-18), and CIFAR-100 (ResNet-34) show FedLBW outperforms FedAvg, FedAvgM, FedProx, FedNova, FedLAW, and FedDkw. Key result: up to 7.6% higher accuracy on CIFAR-10 under extreme non-IID settings, with consistently higher accuracy maintained under increasing client dropout probabilities.

Conclusion: FedLBW is an effective, resilient FL solution well-suited for wireless network environments, delivering marked improvements in model accuracy, convergence speed, and robustness to non-IID data and client dropouts.

Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative machine learning (ML) across distributed clients while preserving privacy. However, efficient model convergence in FL remains challenging, especially in wireless networks where non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data and frequent client dropouts are common. Traditional FL algorithms, such as FedAvg, rely solely on dataset size to weight client updates. This introduces biases towards clients with larger datasets and makes the process sensitive to non-IID data, outliers, and client dropouts. To address these challenges, we propose Federated Learning with Loss-Based Weighting (FedLBW), a novel aggregation method that assigns each client's update a weight proportional to the inverse of its validation loss, computed using a small proxy dataset on the server, rather than its dataset size. This ensures that lower-loss models exert greater influence during aggregation, prioritizing the most reliable updates and boosting overall performance. Through extensive experiments across multiple datasets, including FashionMNIST (CNN), CIFAR-10 (ResNet-18), and CIFAR-100 (ResNet-34), we demonstrate that FedLBW achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence compared to baseline algorithms such as FedAvg, FedAvgM, FedProx, FedNova, FedLAW and FedDkw, with notable improvements of up to 7.6 % higher accuracy on CIFAR-10 in extreme non-IID cases. Moreover, FedLBW showcases exceptional resilience to increasing dropout probabilities, consistently maintaining significantly higher accuracy even in challenging conditions. These results establish FedLBW as an effective and resilient solution for FL in wireless network environments, offering marked improvements in model accuracy, convergence speed, and robustness to non-IID data and client dropouts.

</details>


### [236] [ReQuant: Fixed-Grid Discrete Refinement for Post-Training Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07019)
*Yongge Ma,Guoan Wang,Feiyu Wang,Yaoming Li,Qian Zhang,Zihan Yan,Yinjun Han,Tong Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReQuant is a plug-and-play, backpropagation-free post-processing stage for PTQ that iteratively refines an already-quantized model's discrete weight assignments on a fixed grid, strictly reducing reconstruction error without leaving the original quantization format.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PTQ methods treat the initial quantized integer assignments as final after a one-shot heuristic or greedy optimization. The authors observe that these assignments remain improvable and propose a complementary refinement stage that can further optimize them while preserving the quantized format.

Method: ReQuant takes any existing quantized model as a feasible starting point and iteratively revisits discrete weight assignments on the fixed quantization grid. It uses a backpropagation-free, coordinate-descent-style procedure where accepted updates strictly reduce the layer-wise mean squared reconstruction error. Since only on-grid moves are permitted, the model stays within the original quantization format throughout refinement.

Result: Experiments across diverse model families, bit-widths, and downstream tasks demonstrate consistent improvement over heterogeneous PTQ initializers. Gains are especially pronounced for simple initializers (e.g., round-to-nearest) and low bit-widths. Notably, refining round-to-nearest initialization with multiple ReQuant sweeps approaches or surpasses GPTAQ performance under the same quantization format.

Conclusion: ReQuant establishes itself as a practical complementary stage that can be appended to existing PTQ pipelines, turning a one-shot quantized model into an iteratively optimizable discrete solution with consistent quality gains.

Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is widely used to reduce the memory and computational cost of large language models. Existing PTQ methods typically obtain an initial quantized model through heuristic rules or greedy optimization, and once quantization is completed the resulting integer assignments are usually treated as final. This observation motivates a complementary optimization stage within PTQ that keeps quantized weights improvable after an executable quantized model has been produced, while preserving the quantized format. We introduce ReQuant, a backpropagation-free fixed-grid refinement procedure for this stage. Agnostic to the PTQ initializer, ReQuant takes an existing quantized model as a feasible starting point and iteratively revisits its discrete weight assignments on the fixed quantization grid. Accepted updates strictly reduce the mean squared reconstruction error and remain on the original grid. In this way, ReQuant turns the initially fixed PTQ output into an iteratively optimizable discrete solution and serves as a plug-and-play post-processing stage for existing PTQ pipelines. Experiments across diverse model families, bit-widths, and downstream tasks show that ReQuant consistently improves quantized models from heterogeneous PTQ initializers, with especially large gains on simple initializers and lower bit-widths. Notably, ReQuant can refine a simple round-to-nearest initialization across multiple sweeps until it approaches or surpasses GPTAQ under the same quantization format. These results establish ReQuant as a practical complementary stage for further improving existing PTQ pipelines.

</details>


### [237] [ZIPBrain: Can EEG Foundation Models Be Faster, Locally Deployable, but Accurate?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07033)
*Lingwei Li,Yirong Kan,Peng Chen,Xu Cao,Zheng Chen,Yasuhiko Nakashima*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ZIPBrain is a training-free, plug-and-play token pooling module that exploits EEG's low SNR to merge redundant tokens, reducing Transformer inference time by up to 41.8% while improving accuracy by 1.3%–10.5% over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG foundation models suffer from quadratic computational scaling with input length, limiting deployment in resource-constrained real-time clinical settings. EEG's inherently low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) implies many tokens are redundant and compressible, motivating a redundancy-aware compression approach.

Method: ZIPBrain partitions input token sequences into redundant and unique groups, then merges each redundant token with its most similar counterpart in the unique group via similarity-based pooling. The module is training-free and plug-and-play, integrating into standard Transformer encoders with negligible overhead.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple EEG foundation models show 1.3%–10.5% average accuracy improvement over baselines, with 32.7% wall-clock inference time reduction (up to 41.8% when combined with CUDA Graph optimization).

Conclusion: ZIPBrain demonstrates that redundancy-aware token pooling can simultaneously accelerate EEG foundation models and improve their accuracy, enabling practical local deployment for real-time clinical monitoring without retraining.

Abstract: This work investigates whether Electroencephalograph (EEG) foundation models (EFMs) can be made faster and locally deployable without sacrificing accuracy. EEG foundation models are a major trend, offering strong general-purpose representations. However, their computational burden grows quadratically with input length, hindering deployment on resource-constrained scenario, particularly for real-time clinical monitoring. EEG's low SNR further suggests many of these tokens are redundant and compressible with little accuracy cost. We propose ZIPBrain, a novel redundancy-aware EEG token pooling module that leverages this low-SNR characteristic to reduce token count. Given a token sequence, ZIPBrain partitions tokens into redundant and unique groups, then merges each redundant token with its most similar counterpart in the unique group. Furthermore, ZIPBrain serves as a training-free, plug-and-play module that seamlessly integrates into standard Transformer encoders with negligible computational overhead. Extensive experiments across multiple EEG foundation models show ZIPBrain's strong versatility, achieving 1.3%-10.5% average improvement over baselines, while reducing wall-clock inference time by 32.7% (up to 41.8% with CUDA Graph) compared to the original EEG foundation models.

</details>


### [238] [Not All Problems Are Best Modeled as MILP: A DSL-Centric Framework for Flexible and Accurate Optimization Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07040)
*Shaofeng Zhang,Hongyuan Su,Qingwen Peng,Zefang Zong,Shengcai Liu,Ke Tang,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OptiDSL proposes shifting from rigid MILP-based optimization modeling to domain-specific language (DSL) representations, using LLMs to map natural language problem descriptions onto standardized DSL structures. This decoupling of formulation from execution enables seamless integration with diverse solvers, achieving 51.66% higher formulation accuracy and 91.71% faster modeling time across 44 COP types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based optimization modeling frameworks are locked into the MILP paradigm, but not all COPs are well-suited to MILP. Forcing complex domains into linear constraints leads to prohibitive modeling complexity and restricts solver flexibility, limiting both accuracy and the range of applicable solution methods.

Method: OptiDSL uses LLMs to translate natural language problem descriptions into domain-specific language (DSL) representations that follow standardized, domain-accepted structures. This decouples problem formulation from execution, allowing the framework to integrate with a diverse library of specialized solvers — including traditional heuristics and learning-based methods — rather than being restricted to MILP solvers.

Result: On a comprehensive benchmark of 44 COP types, OptiDSL achieves a 51.66% improvement in formulation accuracy and a 91.71% reduction in modeling time compared to MILP-based pipelines. On existing benchmarks, it attains 23.09% higher formulation accuracy.

Conclusion: Shifting from rigid MILP formulations to DSL-based representations significantly enhances both formulation accuracy and modeling efficiency. The decoupled architecture of OptiDSL enables flexible solver selection and better accommodates the diversity of combinatorial optimization problems.

Abstract: Solving combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) requires not only efficient algorithms but also carefully crafted formulations. While recent works have leveraged LLMs to automate optimization modeling, current frameworks predominantly rely on a rigid mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) paradigm. In this paper, we argue that not all problems are best modeled as MILP, as forcing complex domains into linear constraints can induce prohibitive modeling complexity and severely restrict solver flexibility. To address this, we propose OptiDSL, a framework that shifts the focus from rigid MILP formulations to domain-specific language (DSL) representations. By utilizing LLMs to map natural language onto standardized, domain-accepted structures, OptiDSL decouples problem formulation from execution. This paradigm enables seamless integration with a diverse library of specialized solvers, ranging from traditional heuristics to modern learning-based methods. Experimental results on the comprehensive benchmark of 44 COP types show that OptiDSL significantly surpasses MILP-based pipelines, yielding a 51.66% gain in formulation accuracy and a 91.71% decrease in modeling time. Notably, it also outperforms MILP-based pipelines on the existing benchmark, achieving a 23.09% higher formulation accuracy. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OptiDSL.

</details>


### [239] [Unsupervised Adaptation of PDE Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07053)
*Ziye Song,Zhao Wei,Xin Yu,Ivor Tsang,Yueming Lyu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An unsupervised finetuning framework for pretrained PDE foundation models that uses physics residuals and boundary conditions instead of ground-truth solution data, augmented by NSLoRA—a Newton-Schulz orthogonalized low-rank adaptation variant that rebalances learning across physical quantities—achieving performance comparable to supervised finetuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained PDE foundation models require dense solution data for adaptation to unseen PDE systems, but such data is often expensive or unavailable. The goal is to eliminate this dependency by enabling unsupervised finetuning using only governing physics.

Method: A neighborhood attention Transformer is pretrained on diverse time-dependent PDEs across varying spatial scales. For adaptation, a physics-based objective (PDE residual + boundary conditions) drives finetuning via low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The proposed NSLoRA (Newton-Schulz orthogonalized LoRA) addresses uneven learning across physical quantities by rebalancing adaptation through orthogonalization.

Result: The method achieves performance comparable to supervised LoRA finetuning without any ground-truth solutions, while consistently outperforming competitive neural operator baselines and recent PDE foundation models across heterogeneous PDE benchmarks spanning multiple spatial dimensions.

Conclusion: Unsupervised physics-based finetuning with NSLoRA is a viable and effective alternative to supervised adaptation for PDE foundation models, removing the bottleneck of requiring dense solution data while maintaining strong generalization across diverse PDE systems.

Abstract: Pretrained partial differential equation (PDE) foundation models can generalize across different equations, but adapting them to unseen PDE systems typically requires dense solution data, which is often expensive or unavailable. To address this limitation, we propose an unsupervised PDE-based finetuning framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth solutions. We first pretrain a neighborhood attention Transformer on diverse time-dependent PDEs spanning varying spatial scales, yielding transferable representations across heterogeneous equations. In the adaptation stage, we construct a physics-based objective using the PDE residual and boundary conditions, and finetune the model on unseen equations via low-rank adaptation (LoRA). To address the uneven learning across physical quantities in standard LoRA, we introduce NSLoRA, a Newton-Schulz orthogonalized variant that rebalances adaptation. Our method achieves performance comparable to supervised LoRA finetuning without requiring any ground-truth solutions, while consistently outperforming competitive neural operator baselines and recent PDE foundation models across heterogeneous PDE benchmarks spanning multiple spatial dimensions.

</details>


### [240] [BONSAI: Evolvability-Guided Tree Search over Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07056)
*Yash Priya Shastri,Anand Eswaran,Adnan Qidwai,Pankaj Thorat,Sachin Joshi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BONSAI introduces evolvability as a search criterion for optimizing textual skill prompts for frozen language agents. Using Monte Carlo tree search with a UCB variant that blends a document's own fitness with its mutational neighborhood's mean score, BONSAI outperforms budget-matched baselines by significant margins on held-out benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard skill optimization uses an "accept-if-better" loop driven by a single score, which cannot distinguish between a document on a narrow overfit spike versus one on a broad plateau — only the latter remains improvable. This blindness to evolvability (the capacity of a document region to produce viable variation under mutation) limits optimization efficiency.

Method: BONSAI grows skills via Monte Carlo tree search where each child document is a mutation of its parent. Nodes are selected using an upper-confidence-bound rule whose exploitation term blends a skill's own fitness with the mean fitness of its mutational neighborhood (estimating evolvability at no extra cost), while the exploration term keeps weak branches alive. The best-scoring document encountered is shipped at no cost beyond the accept-if-better loop it replaces.

Result: With a frozen 30B-parameter agent averaged over three benchmarks, BONSAI improves held-out accuracy over the skill-free agent by 23.13 points and outperforms two budget-matched baselines (GEPA and SkillOpt) by 3.87 and 3.97 points respectively.

Conclusion: Optimizing for evolvability rather than just present fitness yields more robust and improvable textual skills. BONSAI demonstrates that borrowing the biological distinction between fitness and evolvability can significantly improve automated prompt engineering for frozen language agents.

Abstract: A skill is a naturallanguage document that steers a frozen agent whose weights cannot be updated so any capability the agent lacks must be supplied in prose Optimising a skill is therefore optimising text against a score and the standard recipe which keeps any edit that raises a heldout score is blind in a specific way a single score cannot tell a document perched on a narrow overfit spike from one resting on a broad plateau even though only the second can still be improved We introduce BONSAI a novel skilloptimisation framework that steers instead by evolvability the capacity of a region of documentspace to keep producing viable variation under further mutation a property biology treats as separate from present fitness BONSAI grows skills as a MonteCarlo search tree in which every child document is a mutation of its parent and descends it under an upperconfidence selection rule whose exploitation term blends a skills own fitness with the fitness of its mutational neighbourhood Because every child is a mutation the mean score recorded beneath a node estimates that neighbourhoods evolvability at no extra cost so the rule concentrates budget on regions that keep improving while its exploration term keeps a currently weak branch in contention BONSAI ships the single bestscoring document it finds at no cost beyond the acceptifbetter loop it replaces With a frozen 30B agent and averaged over three benchmarks BONSAI lifts heldout accuracy over the skillfree agent by 2313 points and improves on two budgetmatched baselines GEPA and SkillOpt by 387 and 397 points respectively

</details>


### [241] [PTQ4SNN: Membrane-Aware Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07066)
*Hui Xie,Tong Shi,Haotong Qin,Aishan Liu,Xiaode Liu,Jinyang Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PTQ4SNN is a post-training quantization framework for spiking neural networks that jointly quantizes both weights and recurrent membrane states using a channel-wise unified scale bridge and mixed-precision bit allocation, achieving low-bit deployment without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SNNs enable sparse, event-driven computation, but existing low-bit quantization methods leave recurrent membrane states in floating point, even after weight quantization. Quantizing membrane states is difficult because their distributions vary across channels, differ from weight distributions, and small perturbations near the firing threshold can alter spike decisions with compounding temporal effects.

Method: PTQ4SNN introduces two key techniques: (1) a channel-wise Unified Scale Bridge that relates membrane scales to weight scales via s_mem,c = s_w,c × 2^k_c, enabling shift-compatible conversion while adapting to per-channel membrane distributions; and (2) Mixed-Precision Bit Allocation that assigns 2/4/8-bit precision per membrane channel based on firing activity and quantization sensitivity under an average-bit budget. The method operates on reusable projection-LIF pairs and supports convolutional SNNs and spike-driven Transformers without backbone retraining, requiring only a small calibration set.

Result: Experiments on static and event-based classification and semantic segmentation demonstrate that PTQ4SNN effectively preserves model accuracy under W4 quantization and approximately 4-bit membrane precision.

Conclusion: PTQ4SNN provides an effective solution for joint low-bit quantization of both weights and membrane states in SNNs, overcoming the key challenge of membrane state quantization through scale bridging and sensitivity-aware mixed-precision allocation, all without requiring retraining.

Abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) enable sparse and event-driven computation, but their low-bit deployment remains incomplete because recurrent membrane states are commonly retained in floating point even after weight quantization. Quantizing these states is challenging because their distributions differ across channels and from the preceding weights, while small perturbations near the firing threshold may alter spike decisions and accumulate over time. We propose PTQ4SNN, a membrane-aware post-training quantization framework that jointly quantizes weights and recurrent membrane states using only a small calibration set. First, a channel-wise Unified Scale Bridge constrains the membrane scale as s_mem,c = s_w,c * 2^k_c, adapting to membrane distributions while enabling shift-compatible scale conversion. Second, Mixed-Precision Bit Allocation assigns 2/4/8-bit precision to membrane channels according to firing activity and quantization sensitivity under an average-bit budget. The framework operates on reusable projection-LIF pairs and supports both convolutional SNNs and spike-driven Transformers without backbone retraining. Experiments on static and event-based classification and semantic segmentation show that PTQ4SNN effectively preserves model accuracy under W4 quantization and approximately 4-bit membrane precision.

</details>


### [242] [MemOPD: On-Policy Distillation through Memory State Alignment for Long-Horizon Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07068)
*Zhiyuan Liu,Tinghong Ye,Chenghao Liu,Yizhuo Li,Songfang Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemOPD addresses the misalignment between student and teacher states caused by memory compression in long-horizon agents by preserving per-invocation token positions and causal visibility, enabling valid on-policy distillation that significantly outperforms PPO baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In long-horizon agents, compact memory via context rewriting creates a state misalignment problem for on-policy distillation (OPD): when compressed history is re-encoded, the teacher may score a student's action under a state the student never actually visited, breaking the validity of teacher supervision. Sparse PPO rewards alone provide insufficient guidance for learning memory updates.

Method: MemOPD records the inputs and sampled outputs of each model invocation, restores original token positions and causal visibility, and packs reconstructed invocations for efficient teacher scoring. The teacher provides full-vocabulary supervision at sampled action positions, while PPO preserves the final task objective.

Result: State alignment is verified across several context updates. MemOPD improves F1 by 7.0% over persistent-history teacher scoring in a matched control. Overall, MemOPD-3B improves F1 over PPO by up to 416.2%, and packing yields up to a 1.63x speedup in actor computation during training.

Conclusion: MemOPD effectively resolves the state-alignment problem in memory-compressed long-horizon agents, enabling valid on-policy distillation that dramatically improves performance over PPO while maintaining computational efficiency through packing.

Abstract: Long-horizon agents accumulate growing contexts during interaction, impairing performance and stability. Compact memory mitigates this problem by compressing and rewriting the history retained between model invocations. Learning what to retain typically relies on proximal policy optimization (PPO) with final task rewards, but sparse rewards provide little guidance for individual memory updates. This limitation motivates on-policy distillation (OPD), which supplies dense teacher supervision on student rollouts. For such supervision to be valid, the teacher must evaluate each sampled action under the same state in which it was generated. However, the context rewriting performed during memory compression can break this alignment. When sampled responses are retained and re-encoded for later invocations, flattening the interaction into a persistent history may cause the teacher to score the action under a state that the student never visited during rollout. The action therefore remains on-policy by provenance, but not necessarily by state. We therefore propose Memory-Aligned On-Policy Distillation (MemOPD). MemOPD records the inputs and sampled outputs of each model invocation, restores its original token positions and causal visibility, and packs the reconstructed invocations for efficient teacher scoring. The teacher provides full-vocabulary supervision at the sampled action positions, while PPO preserves the final task objective. Experiments verify state alignment across several context updates and show that it improves F1 by 7.0% over persistent-history teacher scoring in a matched control. Overall, MemOPD-3B improves F1 over PPO by up to 416.2%, while packing yields up to a 1.63x speedup in actor computation during training. The code for this work is publicly available at: https://github.com/TPssp/MemOPD.

</details>


### [243] [Transformers Struggle to Use Their Emergent World Models: Revisiting the Tower of Hanoi, and the Illusion of Thinking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07077)
*Devin Pereira,Willem Zuidema*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Small Transformers and large reasoning models both develop a geometrically faithful world model of the Tower of Hanoi's state space (the Sierpiński triangle), but large LRMs fail on harder variants because they lose this representation during extended chain-of-thought planning — a failure of maintenance, not absence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed that large reasoning models struggle with the flat-to-flat variant of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle. The authors aim to mechanistically understand why these failures occur, bridging interpretability findings from small trained models to frontier LLMs.

Method: A two-stage approach: (1) Train small Transformers from scratch on precomputed solution traces and apply interpretability techniques (linear probing, causal intervention) to uncover an emergent world model. (2) Apply the same probing techniques to two frontier reasoning models (Qwen3.6-27B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B) at different stages of chain-of-thought to track world model representation fidelity over time, with causal validation via representation injection at inference.

Result: Both small Transformers and large LRMs encode a linearly decodable, geometrically faithful Sierpiński triangle representation of the puzzle's state space. However, in large LRMs solving >3-ring instances, this world model representation decays during chain-of-thought planning. Injecting the prompt-time representation at inference causally improves performance, confirming the failure is one of representation maintenance rather than absence.

Conclusion: The reported collapse in LRM performance on the Tower of Hanoi is not due to an inability to build a world model, but rather a failure to maintain it throughout extended reasoning. This reframes the problem and suggests that representation maintenance mechanisms could be a key direction for improving reasoning reliability.

Abstract: The Tower of Hanoi is a simple planning puzzle that in prior work has proven challenging for large reasoning models (LRMs). Current models solve the standard formulation of the puzzle, but still struggle with the flat-to-flat variant (where initial and goal states are not restricted to have all rings on a single peg). This paper presents an in-depth study of how both small, in-house Transformers and large, third-party LRMs solve this task. To understand the failures mechanistically, we first train small Transformers from scratch on precomputed solution traces. Using a variety of interpretability techniques, we show that these Transformers develop an emergent world model: a linearly decodable, geometrically faithful representation of the puzzle's state space (the Sierpinski triangle), that is causally involved in solving the puzzles. Second, we return to the large LLMs and apply our techniques to two frontier reasoning models, Qwen3.6-27B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, that attempt to solve the task through extended chain-of-thought. Surprisingly, we find that both models encode the Sierpinski world model near-perfectly at the end of the prompt, and yet fail at the majority of tasks when there are more than 3 rings. We locate the source of this failure in the decaying representation of the world model. We probe for the representation at different stages during planning, and establish causality by showing that performance can be improved by injecting the prompt-time representation at inference. The failure of the models is thus one of maintenance of the required representations, not their absence, and performance is at least partially recoverable. These results thus reframe the reported collapse in performance from prior work: current Large Reasoning Models build a world model, and then lose it.

</details>


### [244] [MemWM: Memory-Augmented Text-Based World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07107)
*Yujun Wang,Tao Zhang,Jinhe Bi,Aniri,Wenxuan Ye,Boliang Liu,Sikuan Yan,Shuning Wang,Xuebing Zhou,Sören Pirk,Hinrich Schütze,Yunpu Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemWM introduces a memory-augmented text-based world model that uses curated transition rules, state caches, and hard-to-predict facts to improve next-state prediction fidelity and downstream planning, achieving up to 206.3% SSF improvement and 65.4% relative task success gain across three benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard world models produce fluent but systematically incorrect next-state predictions—omitting critical facts, corrupting attributes, or applying wrong transition rules. These errors degrade planning performance. A structured memory mechanism is needed to ground predictions in reliable stored knowledge.

Method: MemWM employs a curated world memory bank containing transition rules, state caches, and hard-to-predict facts. This memory conditions next-state imagination. The policy model remains frozen; instead, retrieved task-level skills and step-wise corrective guidance are supplied to the policy side. Evaluation uses Structured State Fidelity (SSF), a metric scoring predicted states via benchmark-specific facts and fields.

Result: Memory-augmented training improves SSF by up to 206.3% over SFT. In full planning on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, memory-augmented agents achieve up to a 65.4% relative gain in downstream success over SFT-trained world-model agents. Sensitivity analyses confirm that retrieved memory consistently improves task success and efficiency across different memory and action-budget configurations.

Conclusion: Augmenting text-based world models with structured world memory substantially mitigates systematic prediction errors, yielding large gains in both state prediction fidelity and end-to-end planning success, with robustness demonstrated across diverse memory and budget settings.

Abstract: World models are increasingly used to support planning in agents by predicting how environment states evolve in response to agent actions. Yet fluent next-state predictions can still omit task-critical facts, corrupt product attributes, or apply incorrect transition rules. To address such systematic prediction errors, we introduce MemWM, a memory-augmented text-based world model. MemWM uses world memory, a curated memory bank of transition rules, state caches, and hard-to-predict facts, to condition next-state imagination. We evaluate factual state preservation with Structured State Fidelity (SSF), which scores predicted states through benchmark-specific facts and fields. Compared with SFT, memory-augmented training improves SSF by up to 206.3%. In the full planning setting, we keep the policy model frozen and provide policy-side world skill: retrieved task-level skills and step-wise corrective guidance for action selection. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, memory-augmented agents improve downstream success over an SFT-trained world-model agent, with up to a 65.4% relative gain. Sensitivity analyses further show that retrieved memory improves task success and efficiency under different memory and action-budget settings.

</details>


### [245] [How Much, Then Where: Credit-Conserving Action-to-Token Allocation for Multi-Turn Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07118)
*Lichao Ma,Yang Sun,Shuaitao Zhao,Yangyi Fang,Cong Qin,Xiaoliang Fu,Yuhang Tian,Yuchen Wei,Junbo Zhu,Yang Wei,Lu Pan,Jiaye Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FACTOR is a credit assignment method for multi-turn agent RL that decouples trajectory-level action credit (via checkpoint-calibrated TD residuals) from token-level allocation (via feedback-conditioned teacher-student likelihood gaps), with per-action normalization and action-mean reduction ensuring unbiased gradient estimates. It consistently outperforms baselines across three agent benchmarks, with gains strongest on long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-turn agent RL, credit assignment operates at two entangled levels: (1) assigning a scalar credit to each action based on its contribution to the trajectory return, and (2) distributing that action-level credit across the tokens that constitute the action. Existing methods either conflate these two decisions or use heuristics (e.g., mean pooling) that introduce biases related to token length and can cause gradient sign flips. The authors aim to cleanly separate these two credit assignment problems to improve policy gradient quality.

Method: FACTOR has two core components. First, **checkpoint-calibrated TD residuals** assign per-action credits: a telescoping decomposition ensures that the sum of per-action TD residuals equals the trajectory-level advantage, using intermediate value checkpoints to calibrate the credit of each action. Second, **feedback-conditioned teacher-student likelihood gaps** distribute each action's credit across its tokens: a frozen teacher policy (behavior policy) and student policy (current policy) produce token-level likelihood ratios, conditioned on future trajectory feedback, to allocate credit proportionally to each token's contribution to the action's outcome. **Per-action normalization** preserves the action-average coefficient and prevents token-level sign flips. **Action-mean reduction** computes the surrogate loss as the mean over actions (rather than tokens), removing dependence on action token length. Under the behavior policy and before clipping, each action's inner surrogate equals its TD credit.

Result: FACTOR consistently improves over competitive baselines (including PPO variants and other credit assignment methods) on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld. Every environment-seed comparison favors FACTOR. The largest gains appear on ScienceWorld, the longest-horizon environment. The same hyperparameters transfer without retuning to a larger backbone model and to a different model family (e.g., from one LLM architecture to another). Ablations show that TD action credit is the dominant driver of improvement, with hindsight token allocation providing complementary gains.

Conclusion: Decoupling action-level credit assignment from token-level credit allocation yields reliable and transferable improvements in agent policy optimization. The FACTOR framework provides unbiased, length-agnostic gradient estimates that scale well to long-horizon tasks and generalize across model architectures without hyperparameter retuning.

Abstract: Credit assignment in multi-turn agent reinforcement learning operates at two levels: assigning trajectory-level credit to actions and distributing each action's credit across its tokens. In this paper, we introduce FACTOR, which separates these decisions. FACTOR uses checkpoint-calibrated TD residuals to assign per-action credits that telescope to the trajectory advantage, and feedback-conditioned teacher-student likelihood gaps to allocate each credit across the realized action tokens. Per-action normalization preserves the action-average coefficient and prevents token-level sign flips. We pair this construction with an action-mean reduction, removing the implicit dependence of an action's scalar surrogate weight on its token length. At the behavior policy and before clipping, each action's inner action-mean surrogate equals its TD credit. FACTOR consistently improves over competitive baselines across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, with every environment-seed comparison favoring FACTOR and the largest gains emerging on the longest-horizon environment. The same hyperparameters transfer without retuning to a larger backbone and to a different model family. Ablations identify TD action credit as the dominant driver of the improvement, with hindsight token allocation contributing complementary gains.

</details>


### [246] [DiDPO: Diff-in-Diff Policy Optimization for Coding Agent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07147)
*Xucong Wang,Zhe Zhao,Liheng Yu,Di Wu,Xiaofeng Cao,Pengkun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DiDPO is a critic-free RL method that leverages code diff structure to perform fine-grained credit assignment for training coding agents. By splitting diffs into sub-diffs using a "groupability score" and projecting diff-level advantages back to individual tokens via anchor-based advantage groups, DiDPO significantly outperforms existing RLVR baselines, achieving over 10% improvement on Qwen2.5-7B-Coder and narrowing the gap with much larger models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RLVR methods for coding agents rely on coarse outcome-level or step-level rewards, which fail to distinguish the independent contributions of different changes packed into a single coding action. This makes the unique, finer-grained properties of code diffs invisible during training, creating a credit assignment problem specific to coding tasks.

Method: DiDPO organizes multi-turn coding interactions into thought-action steps and extracts code diffs across sampled trajectories. It introduces a "groupability score" to optimally split whole diffs into sub-diffs, selecting anchors that balance semantic scope and group mass. These anchors form advantage groups, and diff-level advantage is projected back to individual response tokens, enabling token-level credit assignment without a critic network.

Result: On long-horizon coding and reasoning benchmarks, DiDPO significantly outperforms strong agentic RL baselines. On Qwen2.5-7B-Coder, it exceeds comparable methods by over 10% and substantially narrows the performance gap with far larger models.

Conclusion: DiDPO offers a principled, critic-free framework for fine-grained credit assignment in coding agent training, directly exploiting code diff structure. The authors also open-source verl-code, an agentic RL codebase supporting various RL methods and coding benchmarks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training coding agents, where the execution feedback from compilation and tests provides objective verification. However, unlike agent tasks, coding agents face a unique and finer-grained credit assignment challenge: at each step, coding actions simultaneously pack varying changes into different regions of a code version, which makes the contribution of independent change indistinguishable. Existing RLVR methods mostly leverage the outcome reward or step-level reward, which fails to dive into a code diff and makes unique properties of coding actions invisible to training. In this paper, we propose Diff-in-Diff Policy Optimization (DiDPO), a critic-free RL method that constructs fine-grained credit units directly from the structure of code diffs. DiDPO organizes multi-turn coding interactions into multiple thought--action steps and discovers code diffs across sampled trajectories. It then selects anchors by aggregating highly similar sub-diffs split from each whole diff by our ``groupability score'', which provides the splitting schema that optimally balances the semantic scope of anchors and the group mass they may form. Finally these anchors form advantage groups and project the diff-level advantage back to individual response tokens. Experiments on long-horizon coding and reasoning benchmarks show that DiDPO significantly outperforms strong agentic RL baselines. On Qwen2.5-7B-Coder, DiDPO exceeds comparable methods by over 10\% and narrows the gap with far larger models, offering a principled framework for fine-grained credit assignment in coding agent training. We also open-source verl-code, an agentic rl codebase that supports various RL methods and coding benchmarks.

</details>


### [247] [A MARL Centered Reference Architecture for Large Language Model Augmentation in Smart Manufacturing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07148)
*Fouad Bahrpeyma,Dirk Reichelt*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a MARL-centered reference architecture for adaptive manufacturing control, analyzing where LLMs should augment (not replace) multi-agent reinforcement learning. It introduces a taxonomy of four LLM attachment points and a descriptive notation (LLM-Augmented Dec-POMDP), concluding that conventional MARL excels at fast, structured coordination while LLMs are best suited for semantic reasoning, reward design, and supervisory planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern manufacturing imposes six coupled demands (local-global decisions, partial observability, nonstationarity, reflex-speed/long-horizon effects, delayed/diffuse outcomes, and opaque dynamics) that are naturally formalized as a Dec-POMDP under CTDE. The authors seek to clarify the role of LLMs within this MARL framework—whether to augment, interface with, train, or replace the coordination core.

Method: The authors conduct a structured literature survey organized via a taxonomy of four LLM attachment points: (1) policy, (2) reward design, (3) inter-agent communication, and (4) hierarchical planning. They develop a conditional capability profile assessing each role across native mechanism, reported performance, formal guarantees, and engineering maturity. A deployment readiness analysis evaluates the evidence behind each role. The principal output is a three-layer MARL-centered reference architecture and the LLM-Augmented Dec-POMDP descriptive notation.

Result: Conventional MARL is better suited for frequent, structured, decentralized coordination after task-specific training. LLM components show promise for semantic interpretation, reward drafting, human interaction, and slower supervisory planning. Current LLM-only manufacturing controllers do not establish equivalence for strict real-time, decentralized, safety-critical control. The LLM-Augmented Dec-POMDP notation captures four attachment choices without introducing a new decision process class or algorithm.

Conclusion: A hybrid architecture is warranted: MARL should remain the coordination core for real-time decentralized control, while LLMs serve as augmentations for semantic reasoning, reward specification, and high-level planning. The conclusion that LLM-only controllers are insufficient for safety-critical manufacturing is bounded by available evidence and does not assert impossibility.

Abstract: Modern manufacturing imposes six coupled demands on adaptive control: local decisions with global consequences, partial observability, nonstationarity, reflex speed response with long horizon effects, delayed and diffuse outcomes, and dynamics that resist explicit modeling. Cooperative multiagent reinforcement learning (MARL), posed as a Dec-POMDP under centralized training with decentralized execution, is a particularly natural formalism for these demands. This paper adopts a MARL centered scope and asks where large language models (LLMs) should augment, interface with, train, or, in the strongest competitive case, replace that coordination core. A taxonomy organizes the literature through four LLM attachment points: policy, reward design, communication between agents, and hierarchical planning. A conditional capability profile separates native mechanism, reported performance, formal guarantee, and engineering maturity, and a deployment readiness analysis identifies the evidence behind each role. These stages yield the principal contribution: a three layer MARL centered reference architecture, grounded in evidence, for semantic reasoning, adaptive cooperative control, and independently assured execution. The LLM-Augmented Dec-POMDP is a descriptive comparative notation for that architecture, recording four attachment choices without introducing a new decision process class or algorithm. Under the reviewed evidence, conventional MARL is better suited to frequent, structured, decentralized coordination after task specific training, whereas LLM components are promising for semantic interpretation, reward drafting, human interaction, and slower supervisory planning. Current LLM only manufacturing controllers do not yet establish equivalence for strict real time, decentralized, safety critical control; this conclusion is bounded by the available evidence and does not assert impossibility.

</details>


### [248] [NiyamAI - An Intent-Bound AI Agent with Cryptographically Verifiable Guardrails using Zero-Knowledge Proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07167)
*Aditya Katkar,Om Karkele,Kartik Mandhane,Manisha More,Yash Kashid*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Niyam-AI introduces a provable safety framework for LLM agents using Intent Contracts and zk-SNARK proofs, achieving 88.5% F1 on Agent-SafetyBench while enabling third-party verification of tool-call enforcement without exposing model weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous LLM agents face critical security risks from prompt injection, hallucinated reasoning, and unsafe tool calls. Existing software-level defenses (system prompts, policy filters) run on the same targeted machine and offer no verifiable proof of enforcement, leaving third parties unable to confirm that safety constraints were actually applied.

Method: Niyam-AI locks permitted tools and constraints into an SHA-256-committed Intent Contract at session start. An isolated Judge model intercepts and validates every tool call; upon approval, a zk-SNARK proof is generated via EZKL. Tool execution proceeds only after proof verification, enabling third-party verification without access to Judge model weights. Evaluation uses 2,000 scenarios from Agent-SafetyBench with 5-fold stratified cross-validation, compared against NeMo Guardrails, Llama Prompt Guard 2, and GPT-OSS-Safeguard. Statistical validation employs bootstrap 95% CIs (N=1000) and McNemar's exact paired test.

Result: Niyam-AI achieves F1=88.5% with 1.1% false-positive rate (bootstrap 95% CI: [85.19%, 91.88%]). McNemar's test shows significant wins over all baselines: 390 vs 20 against NeMo, 115 vs 13 against Prompt Guard 2, and 384 vs 19 against GPT-OSS-Safeguard (p < 0.0001). Proof generation latency: 2260.6 ± 218.4 ms per approved action; verification: 53.1 ± 11.8 ms.

Conclusion: Niyam-AI provides a guardrail that is both highly accurate and mathematically verifiable, though the authors note the results reflect a classifier adapted to Agent-SafetyBench evaluated against zero-shot baselines, warranting cautious interpretation.

Abstract: Giving an AI agent the ability to send emails, query databases, or execute commands is useful--until the agent is tricked into doing something it shouldn't. Prompt injection, hallucinated reasoning, and unsafe tool calls form the primary attack surface for autonomous LLM agents. Existing defenses rely on software checks like system prompts or policy filters running on the same machine the attacker targets, offering no verifiable proof of execution. We introduce Niyam-AI, a framework that makes safety enforcement provable. At session start, permitted tools and constraints are locked into an Intent Contract committed via SHA-256. Every tool call is intercepted and validated by an isolated Judge model; upon passing, a zk-SNARK proof is generated via EZKL.
  The tool executes only after proof verification, allowing third parties to confirm enforcement without accessing Judge model weights. Evaluating Niyam-AI on 2,000 real-world scenarios from Agent-SafetyBench against NeMo Guardrails, Meta's Llama Prompt Guard 2, and OpenAI's GPT-OSS-Safeguard using 5-fold stratified cross-validation yields an F1 score of 88.5% with a 1.1% false-positive rate (bootstrap 95% CI: [85.19%, 91.88%], N=1000). McNemar's exact paired test confirms significant improvement: Niyam-AI wins 390 discordant scenarios against NeMo (vs 20 losses), 115 against Prompt Guard 2 (vs 13), and 384 against GPT-OSS-Safeguard (vs 19) with p < 0.0001 in all cases.
  Proof generation adds 2260.6 +/- 218.4 ms per approved action, while verification takes 53.1 +/- 11.8 ms. Niyam-AI provides a guardrail that is both highly accurate and mathematically verifiable--though this reflects a classifier adapted to Agent-SafetyBench evaluated against zero-shot baselines, a distinction discussed in Section IV.C.

</details>


### [249] [Agent Memory Distillation: Empowering Small LLM Agents with Hierarchical Teacher Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07169)
*Taeil Kim,Kangsan Kim,Sung Ju Hwang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AMD is a training-free memory distillation framework that transfers structured knowledge from a large teacher agent to small language model agents via three hierarchical memory types, achieving substantial accuracy improvements on tool-use benchmarks without any fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small language models (4B-8B parameters) struggle to generate sufficient successful trajectories for agent tasks, yet existing memory-based methods for improving agent performance have been underexplored for these smaller models. The authors aim to bridge this gap by leveraging knowledge from a large teacher model without requiring training.

Method: AMD constructs three complementary memory types from successful teacher trajectories: (1) Workflow memory — task-level strategic plans injected proactively at task onset; (2) Subtask memory — intermediate-granularity behavioral examples also injected proactively; (3) Function memory — per-function calling conventions and common pitfalls retrieved reactively upon tool-calling errors. The framework is training-free; student models use these memories at inference time without parameter updates.

Result: Evaluated on AppWorld, BFCL V3, and ToolSandbox using GPT-5-mini as teacher and four student models (4B-8B parameters), AMD achieves average accuracy gains of +27.2pp, +11.2pp, and +3.4pp respectively, consistently outperforming existing memory-based baselines. Subtask memory contributes the largest gains; teacher effectiveness depends on both capability and student compatibility; 4B models benefit most.

Conclusion: AMD demonstrates that structured, hierarchical memory distillation from large to small agents is an effective, training-free approach to significantly boost small LM agent performance on tool-use tasks, with subtask-level guidance being the most impactful component.

Abstract: Memory systems have shown promise for improving agent performance, but their potential remains largely unexplored for small language models, which struggle to generate sufficient successful trajectories on their own. We propose Agent Memory Distillation (AMD), a training-free framework that transfers structured knowledge from a large teacher agent to a small student agent through hierarchical memory. AMD constructs three complementary memory types from successful teacher trajectories: Workflow memory encodes task-level strategies, Subtask memory provides concrete behavioral examples at an intermediate granularity, and Function memory captures per-function calling conventions and common pitfalls. Workflow and Subtask memories are injected proactively at the start of each task, while Function memory is retrieved reactively upon tool-calling errors. We evaluate AMD on three tool-use benchmarks using four student models (4B-8B parameters) with GPT-5-mini as the teacher, achieving average accuracy gains of 27.2%p, 11.2%p, and 3.4%p on AppWorld, BFCL V3, and ToolSandbox, while consistently outperforming existing memory-based baselines. Further analysis shows that Subtask memory contributes the largest gains, teacher effectiveness depends on both teacher capability and student compatibility, and 4B-sized students benefit most from AMD.

</details>


### [250] [SetEasy: A Multi-Modal Classroom Engagement Assessment and Seating Optimization Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07188)
*Zhihao Xie,Hongye Yang,Shien Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SetEasy uses multimodal sensing and a v-Gage model to forecast student engagement, then employs CP-SAT optimization to generate seating plans that significantly improve classroom engagement in fixed-seating grids.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classroom engagement is unevenly distributed in fixed seating arrangements, with back-row students often exhibiting low activity. Existing solutions require hardware changes; a data-driven, optimization-based seating strategy could enhance engagement without infrastructural modification, offering a sustainable and transferable approach.

Method: Multimodal sensing (wristband physiology, 4K video, environmental data) feeds into v-Gage, a model grounded in a revised ISEQ (In-class Student Engagement Questionnaire). Two-week engagement forecasts are mapped to a student-seat utility matrix. CP-SAT (Constraint Programming-SAT) solver generates optimized seating plans under visual-access and social-dynamics constraints. A four-week deployment (23 students, 331 classes) validated the system.

Result: v-Gage converged across affective, behavioral, cognitive, and overall engagement dimensions, reducing RMSE from 0.75 to 0.53. Optimization raised mean engagement from 0.30 to 0.70, with over two-thirds of seats reaching high engagement. Back-row low-activity patterns were markedly reduced.

Conclusion: Interpretable, data-driven seating strategies can substantially enhance engagement without hardware changes. The multimodal "assessment + optimization" paradigm provides a transferable, sustainable path toward culturally responsive, differentiated spatial design in increasingly homogenized global educational contexts.

Abstract: SetEasy optimizes classroom engagement in fixed seating grids. It fuses multimodal sensing (wristband physiology, 4K video, environmental data) and trains a v-Gage model grounded in a revised ISEQ. Each week, two-week engagement forecasts are mapped to a student-seat utility matrix, and CP-SAT generates seating plans under visual-access and social-dynamics constraints. In a four-week deployment (23 students, 331 classes), v-Gage converged across affective, behavioral, cognitive, and overall dimensions, cutting RMSE from 0.75 to 0.53. Optimization raised mean engagement from 0.30 to 0.70, with over two-thirds of seats reaching high engagement and back-row low-activity patterns markedly reduced. These results show that, without hardware changes, interpretable, data-driven seating strategies can substantially enhance engagement. The multimodal "assessment + optimization" paradigm offers a transferable, sustainable path to culturally responsive, differentiated spatial design amid global homogenization.

</details>


### [251] [EMAS: Stabilizing Multi-Agent System Evolution through Evidence-Guided Revision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07196)
*Chao Fei,Qingyi Si,Kaihua Liang,Yanghua Xiao,Panos Kalnis,Hongcheng Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EMAS is a method that evolves multi-agent system topology and prompts based on runtime experience, improving accuracy and reducing token costs without updating LLM parameters. It uses recurring structured diagnoses from execution traces to generate and validate candidate revisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated MAS design methods perform one-shot optimization and deploy static systems, ignoring valuable runtime experience. Meanwhile, accuracy-oriented designs often incur high token costs. There is a need for a method that continuously improves MAS using sample experience, balancing accuracy and efficiency.

Method: EMAS converts execution traces into structured diagnoses specifying a revision operation and target. A candidate revision is generated only when the same diagnosis recurs across multiple samples. It is then applied only if paired validation against the current MAS meets an acceptance criterion. Revisions target topology and prompts, without LLM parameter updates.

Result: Across 4 benchmarks and 2 LLMs, EMAS achieves the highest task-weighted overall accuracy, winning or tying in 6 of 8 model-benchmark settings. Within two evolution epochs, it yields relative accuracy gains of 6.30% (Kimi-K2-6) and 20.10% (Qwen3.6-27B). On MBPP with Qwen3.6-27B, accuracy rises from 55.09% to 89.12% while token usage drops by 62.2%.

Conclusion: EMAS demonstrates that experience from new samples can be effectively consolidated into reusable MAS topology and prompt updates, achieving significant accuracy improvements and cost reductions without modifying LLM parameters.

Abstract: Many methods for automated multi-agent system design optimize prompts and topologies during an initial design stage and then deploy the resulting system unchanged on subsequent samples. Experience from these samples is rarely consolidated into reusable system updates, while accuracy-oriented designs may incur high token costs. We introduce EMAS (Evolving Multi-Agent System), which uses this experience to revise MAS topology and prompts without updating LLM parameters, either to improve accuracy or to reduce cost. EMAS converts traces into structured diagnoses that specify a revision operation and target. It generates a candidate revision only when the same diagnosis recurs across samples and applies it only if paired validation against the current MAS meets the corresponding acceptance criterion. Across four benchmarks and two LLMs, EMAS attains the highest task-weighted overall accuracy for both backbones and is best or tied in six of eight model--benchmark settings. Within two evolution epochs, EMAS achieves relative gains of 6.30% and 20.10% in task-weighted accuracy on Kimi-K2-6 and Qwen3.6-27B, respectively. On MBPP with Qwen3.6-27B, EMAS raises accuracy from 55.09% to 89.12% while reducing token use per task by 62.2%. These results show that EMAS can turn experience from new samples into reusable updates to MAS topology and prompts.

</details>


### [252] [Authoring and Management of Transparent Research Integrity Assessments of Randomised Clinical Trial Publications Using LLM-assisted Tools and Provenance Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07202)
*Milan Markovic,Goutham Indukuri,Somayajulu Sripada,Colby J. Vorland,Jack Wilkinson,Clare Robertson,Mark Bolland,Andrew Grey,Miriam Brazzelli,Alison Avenell*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: INSPECT-AI is an LLM-based interactive tool that assists human reviewers in assessing the research integrity of published RCTs, using the INSPECT-SR framework and the RIPE-O ontology, with an accompanying knowledge graph (RIPE-KG) containing 140 expert assessments of 95 RCTs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Systematic reviews of RCTs inform clinical care guidelines, requiring high integrity standards. Current manual integrity assessment is complex, labor-intensive, and subject to inconsistent human judgment. There is a need for computational support to standardize and document the assessment process.

Method: The authors developed INSPECT-AI, an interactive tool powered by large language models (LLMs) that operationalizes the community-approved INSPECT-SR framework for research integrity assessment. The tool leverages the Research Integrity Provenance and Evidence ontology (RIPE-O) to formally document the provenance of each assessment step, ensuring transparency and reproducibility.

Result: The paper presents RIPE-KG, a knowledge graph encoding 140 expert research integrity assessments across 95 RCT publications, generated using INSPECT-AI and described with RIPE-O.

Conclusion: INSPECT-AI demonstrates the feasibility of using LLMs to support and structure the research integrity assessment process for RCTs, providing both a practical tool and a formal provenance framework to enhance transparency in evidence appraisal for clinical guidelines.

Abstract: Systematic reviews of Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs) are routinely used as evidence for clinical care guidelines. Such evidence has to meet high research integrity standards to prevent low quality or false research outputs influencing the clinical care. However, assessing research integrity of published RCTs is a complex process requiring manual effort, and potentially resulting in diverse opinions of the human assessors. This paper describes INSPECT-AI, an LLM-based interactive tool that assists human reviewers with research integrity assessments of published RCTs based on the community approved INSPECT-SR framework, and the Research Integrity Provenance and Evidence ontology (RIPE-O) for documenting the provenance of the assessment process. In addition, we present the Research Integrity Provenance and Evidence knowledge graph (RIPE-KG), an initial set of 140 expert research integrity assessments of 95 RCT publications generated by INSPECT-AI and described using RIPE-O.

</details>


### [253] [Beyond the Black Box: Interpretable Models of Human Randomisation Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07220)
*Ngoc Linh Dao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Using 84,060 decisions from an O'Neill zero-sum card game, this paper finds that simple "repeat or avoid" heuristics—especially players managing their own recent action histories—account for most of the predictable deviation from mixed-strategy equilibrium, outperforming or matching complex models like LSTMs and modified EWA, while frequency tracking adds negligible out-of-sample value.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium predicts serially independent (i.i.d.) play, yet human players systematically deviate from this. Prior work showed black-box models (LSTMs) can predict these deviations, but the authors seek transparent, interpretable models that reveal the underlying behavioral structure generating the predictable patterns.

Method: The authors analyze 84,060 decisions from 2,802 pairs playing O'Neill's zero-sum card game. They benchmark naive and behavioral models against interpretable machine learning and deep learning models, evaluate modified Experience-Weighted Attraction (EWA) specifications from prior work, and apply LASSO diagnostics to motivate a nested frequency-tracking extension, comparing all models on out-of-sample predictive performance.

Result: Repeat-or-avoid behavior—specifically how players manage their own recent action histories—accounts for most of the interpretable and strategically exploitable signal in predicting deviations from equilibrium play. Frequency tracking contributes little additional predictive power out of sample. Simple behavioral models rival or surpass the predictive accuracy of black-box deep learning approaches.

Conclusion: Transparent behavioral models centered on players' management of their own action histories capture nearly all the predictable structure in strategic deviations from mixed-strategy equilibrium, rendering complex frequency-tracking or black-box models largely unnecessary for explaining and predicting human play in these settings.

Abstract: Mixed strategy equilibrium predicts i.i.d play: past actions should not help predict future decisions. Human players, however, systematically depart from this benchmark, and in O'Neill's zero sum card game, these departures can be predicted by black box sequence models such as LSTMs. This paper asks whether that predictive power can be achieved by transparent alternatives that also reveal the behavioural structure behind it. Using 84,060 decisions from 2,802 pairs, the analysis first benchmarks naive and behavioral models against interpretable machine learning and deep learning models, then evaluates the modified EWA specifications of prior work against these benchmarks and uses the LASSO diagnostics to motivate a further nested frequency tracking extension. The results show that repeat or avoid behavior, especially players' management of their own recent action histories, accounts for most of the interpretable and strategically exploitable signal, while frequency tracking adds little out of sample.

</details>


### [254] [Recipes for Creativity: Iterative Generation and Evaluation in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07243)
*Rens Anderson,Tessa Verhoef,Amirhossein Zohrehvand*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This pilot study examines whether iterative generation-selection loops improve LLM creativity in recipe generation. Using FunSearch adapted for the Pillsbury Bake-Off, results show that iterative search can match human creativity benchmarks, but more iterations alone don't help — the in-loop evaluator model size is the critical factor, with smaller scorers yielding higher creativity scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human creativity is an iterative process of generation, appraisal, and refinement, yet generative models are typically evaluated on single-shot outputs. The authors aim to investigate whether iterative search mechanisms can enhance LLM creativity, bridging this gap between human creative processes and machine evaluation paradigms.
