Method: The authors adapt FunSearch (an iterative generate-select loop) to recipe generation for the 2024 Pillsbury Bake-Off competition. They conduct two experiments manipulating: (1) number of iterations, (2) generator temperature, and (3) in-loop selection-scorer model size. Outputs are evaluated against human benchmarks using TTCT-based (Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking) LLM evaluation metrics.

Result: Iterative generation-selection can produce recipes with creativity scores comparable to human benchmarks. However, additional iterations alone do not improve creativity. The in-loop evaluator model size is the dominant factor: a smaller selection scorer yields significantly higher creativity scores across most TTCT dimensions. Temperature shows limited effects except on originality.

Conclusion: Evaluator design is a first-order design variable in subjective creative search — the choice of selection-scorer model matters more than iteration count or generation temperature. This underscores the importance of careful evaluator design when building iterative creative systems with LLMs.

Abstract: Generative models are often evaluated through singular artifacts, whereas human creativity typically emerges through iterative generation, appraisal, and refinement. This pilot study examines whether iterative search improves LLM creativity by adapting FunSearch to recipe generation for the 2024 Pillsbury Bake-Off and evaluating outputs against human benchmarks using TTCT-based LLM evaluation. Across two experiments, we test iteration count, generator temperature, and in-loop selection-scorer model size. Results show that iterative generation-selection can produce recipes with creativity scores comparable to human benchmarks, but additional iterations alone do not improve creativity. The in-loop evaluator matters most: a smaller selection scorer yields significantly higher scores across most TTCT dimensions, while temperature has limited effects except for originality. These findings suggest that evaluator design is a first-order design variable in subjective creative search.

</details>


### [255] [From probability to causality in probabilistic logic programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07230)
*Zora Wurm,Kilian Rückschloß,Felix Weitkämper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper establishes conditions under which a probabilistic logic program determines a unique causal order, addressing the ambiguity that arises when multiple causal structures are compatible with a single probability distribution. By leveraging the connection between acyclic probabilistic logic programs and Bayesian networks, and incorporating relational symmetry constraints, the authors provide a verification method for well-defined intervention semantics in learned programs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When probabilistic logic programs are learned from data, only probabilistic associations are captured, not causal structure. A single probability distribution may be compatible with multiple causal orders, creating ambiguity for interventional/causal queries. The paper aims to determine when the learned probabilistic information uniquely pins down the causal order.

Method: The authors exploit the formal relationship between acyclic probabilistic logic programs and Bayesian networks. They derive theoretical conditions under which the probabilistic information encoded in a program determines a unique causal order. Additionally, they incorporate constraints from relational structure by identifying prescribed sets of causal symmetries induced by the underlying relational vocabulary.

Result: The paper delivers explicit conditions for unique identifiability of causal order from probabilistic information in logic programs, and a practical method for verifying whether a learned probabilistic logic program supports well-defined intervention semantics.

Conclusion: Learned probabilistic logic programs can support unambiguous interventional reasoning when the encoded probabilistic information, combined with relational symmetry constraints, uniquely determines the causal order. The proposed verification method allows practitioners to check whether their learned programs admit well-defined causal semantics.

Abstract: Probabilistic logic programming is a formalism of statistical relational artificial intelligence that supports causal queries, including interventions from outside the system. When the structure of a probabilistic logic program is learned from data, however, only probabilistic information is used, and a single probability distribution may be compatible with several causal orders. This leads to ambiguity in interventional reasoning, raising the question of when the causal order is uniquely determined by the distribution. Exploiting the relationship between acyclic probabilistic logic programs and Bayesian networks, we derive conditions under which the probabilistic information encoded in a program determines a unique causal order. We also incorporate constraints arising from relational structure by taking into account prescribed sets of causal symmetries induced by the underlying relational vocabulary. The result is a method for verifying when a learned probabilistic logic program supports well-defined intervention semantics.

</details>


### [256] [WNM-3D: A World Navigation Model with 3D Scene Conditioning for Closed-Loop VLN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07267)
*Yuehao Huang,Yunzi Wu,Xiaotao Zhang,Xinhai Li,Jiankun Dong,Jiajun Lv,Chi Zhang,Chenjia Bai,Yong Liu,Xuelong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WNM-3D introduces a generative world navigation model that jointly predicts future observations and actions conditioned on 3D geometry-aware scene representations, outperforming VLM-based policies and 2D-conditioned baselines on continuous VLN tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current VLM-based VLN policies map observations directly to actions without explicitly modeling how visual observations should evolve under motion. Existing world-action models lack conditioning on persistent, geometry-aware 3D scene representations, limiting their ability to maintain spatial consistency between predicted views and actions.

Method: WNM-3D uses a frozen feed-forward geometry encoder to extract 3D representations from monocular RGB history, and a trainable 3D Scene-to-Token Adapter converts these into a fixed-length prefix in a Diffusion Transformer's token space. Block-causal attention allows this geometric prefix to condition every future video-action block. Training combines supervised fine-tuning on A* demonstrations, DAgger-style adaptation, and DanceGRPO-based closed-loop policy optimization.

Result: On GN-Bench, WNM-3D surpasses strong VLM-based navigation policies and its 2D-conditioned counterpart in closed-loop navigation. On a near-goal evaluation set, it achieves higher flow-action consistency and lower visual-motion error.

Conclusion: Incorporating explicit 3D geometric scene conditioning into generative world-action modeling significantly improves continuous VLN performance, suggesting that geometry-aware future prediction is a promising direction beyond purely action-centric policy learning.

Abstract: Recent vision-language navigation (VLN) systems increasingly adapt pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) into vision-language-action (VLA) policies that map egocentric observations and language instructions directly to navigation actions. Although semantically capable, such action-centric training does not explicitly model how the agent's visual observations should evolve under its predicted motion. Generative world-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, yet existing WAMs for continuous VLN do not condition joint future-view and action generation on geometry-aware representations inferred from the observed history. We present WNM-3D, a generative World Navigation Model with 3D scene conditioning for continuous VLN. To consolidate past observations into persistent scene context, a frozen feed-forward geometry encoder extracts geometry-aware representations from the monocular egocentric RGB history, and a trainable 3D Scene-to-Token Adapter converts them into a fixed-length prefix in the token space of the world-action Diffusion Transformer. Through block-causal attention, this prefix conditions every future video-action block, providing a shared geometric context for both future-view and action generation. We train WNM-3D through supervised world-action fine-tuning on A*-generated demonstrations, DAgger-style adaptation on policy-visited states, and DanceGRPO-based closed-loop policy optimization. Experiments on GN-Bench show that WNM-3D outperforms strong VLM-based navigation policies and its 2D-conditioned counterpart in closed-loop navigation. On a fixed near-goal evaluation set, WNM-3D also achieves higher flow-action consistency and lower visual-motion error.

</details>


### [257] [ResidencyRL: Reinforcement Learning in Simulated Clinical Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07418)
*Valentin Liévin,Samuel Schmidgall,Tim Strother,Alex Bijamov,Akshay Goel,Anil Palepu,Chunjong Park,Vahid Balazadeh,Min Woo Sun,Marius Guerard,Justin Chen,Dave Steiner,Vikram Dhillon,Ibrahim Azar,Akhil Mehta,Nicholas Spetsieris,Shilpan Shah,Maen Abdelrahim,Amit Dahiya,Yun Liu,Katherine Chou,Yossi Matias,Avinatan Hassidim,Dale R. Webster,Quoc V. Le,Raia Hadsell,Joelle Barral,Carey Radebaugh,Aleksandra Faust,Shekoofeh Azizi,Mike Schaekermann,Po-Hsuan Cameron Chen,Tao Tu,David Racz,Lin Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ResidencyRL uses multi-turn reinforcement learning with adversarial LLM simulators to train clinical AI agents, achieving significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy, safety, and procedural competencies across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical reasoning unfolds through sequential patient encounters with feedback and uncertainty, yet existing medical LLMs are evaluated on static benchmarks that fail to capture this dynamic, multi-turn decision-making process. There is a gap in methods for optimizing full clinical dialogue sequences.

Method: ResidencyRL trains a policy agent via RL across simulated multi-turn clinical encounters (up to 60 dialogue turns, 8 tool calls). The agent is paired with LLM simulators exhibiting complex, adversarial behaviors, and optimized against a structured reward encompassing diagnostic accuracy, management quality, communication, documentation, and safety.

Result: Under adversarial conditions, diagnostic accuracy improved by 7.0% (88.0% vs. 81.0%), missed red flag rates dropped by 31%. Blinded clinicians preferred the trained agent in 87.6% of comparisons. Gains transferred to all six axes of the AMIE multi-visit benchmark, with consistent improvements on AgentClinic and CRAFT-MD.

Conclusion: Sequential clinical decision-making can be effectively learned through multi-turn RL in simulation, yielding robust, generalizable capabilities. Prospective real-world validation remains needed to establish clinical utility.

Abstract: In medical education, physicians convert academic knowledge into clinical expertise through residency: years of training across thousands of encounters, with diverse sources of feedback and progressively greater autonomy. Much of clinical reasoning relies on the patient encounter, a dialogue in which a clinician elicits history, refines diagnostic hypotheses, and decides management under uncertainty. While large language models (LLMs) excel on static medical benchmarks, methods to optimize the full sequence of clinical decisions remain underdeveloped. We present ResidencyRL, a reinforcement learning (RL) method for training clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agents through simulated multi-turn clinical encounters (up to 60 dialogue turns and 8 tool calls per trajectory). ResidencyRL pairs the policy agent with LLM simulators capable of complex, adversarial behaviors, training against a structured reward aligned to diagnostic accuracy, management quality, communication, documentation, and safety. On held-out evaluations, the ResidencyRL agent improves diagnostic accuracy by 7.0% under adversarial conditions (88.0% vs. 81.0%) and reduces missed red flag rates by 31%, demonstrating rigorous mitigation of premature closure. Blinded expert clinicians validated these gains, preferring the trained agent in 87.6% of side-by-side comparisons. The procedural competencies transfer to unseen benchmarks: the agent outperforms the base model across all six clinical axes of the AMIE multi-visit benchmark, and shows consistent directional improvements on AgentClinic and CRAFT-MD. Our findings demonstrate that sequential clinical decision-making can be effectively learned through multi-turn RL in simulation, yielding robust, generalizable capabilities, paving the way towards clinical mastery. Prospective validation with real-world workflows remains necessary to establish clinical utility.

</details>


### [258] [Winning by Peeking: Unenforced Budgets and Test-Set Selection Inflate Short-Budget AutoML Comparisons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07303)
*Guilin Zhang,Kai Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A case study reveals that Orcetra's apparent superiority over FLAML and AutoGluon in short-budget AutoML benchmarks stemmed from two protocol defects: test-set optimization (scoring every candidate on the test split) and unenforced time budgets. When corrected, Orcetra's win rate collapsed from ~59% to ~34%, with no significant pairwise differences remaining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Short-budget AutoML comparisons (tens of seconds) are common but easy to get wrong. The authors demonstrate through a concrete case study how subtle protocol defects can produce misleading headline results that a standard results table cannot reveal, and provide a measured (rather than assumed) account of selection bias as a function of budget.

Method: The study re-implements a comparison where Orcetra appeared to dominate FLAML and AutoGluon on 513 OpenML datasets. Two protocol defects are identified: (1) every candidate in the search loop was scored on the test split and the best reported, creating a maximum-over-noisy-estimates bias; (2) the time budget was checked before launching a candidate but never enforced during execution, leading to systematic overrun (median 120s vs. 60s budget). The authors re-ran experiments with validation-split selection, external deadline enforcement, and equal machine-share pinning. They also measured selection bias analytically from search traces, comparing it against the marginal-standard-error bound σ√(2ln K).

Result: On the re-run subset, Orcetra's win rate fell from 59.4% to 34.3%, with no significant pairwise difference against either competitor. The selection rule accounts for 4.8 percentage points of the collapse, and unequal compute for most of the remainder. Measured selection bias reached only 0.27 accuracy points — roughly five times below the σ√(2ln K) theoretical bound — because candidates scored on shared test rows cancel most of the noise.

Conclusion: Short-budget AutoML benchmarks require rigorous protocol design: test-set selection and unenforced time budgets can dramatically inflate apparent performance. The authors provide a checklist for practitioners and release all code, per-dataset results, and reproduction scripts.

Abstract: Comparisons between AutoML systems at short time budgets -- tens of seconds rather than hours -- are common in tool READMEs and workshop papers, and they are easy to get wrong. We report a case study in which a simple AutoML engine, Orcetra, appeared to beat FLAML and AutoGluon on 513 OpenML datasets, winning 57.1% of them at a nominal 60-second budget and 78.4% of datasets against FLAML alone at 30 seconds. Both margins came from protocol defects that a results table cannot show. The search loop scored every candidate on the test split and reported the best, making the headline metric a maximum over dozens of noisy estimates while the baselines selected on training data and touched the test set once; and the budget was checked before launching a candidate but never enforced during one, so the system consumed a median of 120 s against a 60-second budget, 2.24x the wall-clock AutoGluon used. Re-running with selection moved to a validation split, the deadline enforced externally and every framework pinned to an equal share of the machine, Orcetra's win rate on the re-run subset falls from 59.4% to 34.3% and no pairwise difference against either competitor remains significant. Recording both estimands inside a single search lets us attribute the collapse: the selection rule accounts for 4.8 percentage points and unequal compute for most of the rest. The same traces give the selection bias as a function of budget, measured rather than assumed: it grows with $K$ but reaches only 0.27 accuracy points, about five times below the $σ\sqrt{2\ln K}$ bound a marginal-standard-error argument predicts, because candidates scored on shared test rows cancel most of the noise. We close with a checklist for short-budget comparisons. Code, per-dataset results and the scripts that regenerate every number and figure in the paper are released with it.

</details>


### [259] [An End-to-End Agent Auditing Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07346)
*Haoning Wang,Mingxun Zhang,Chenyue Yu,Yingjun Shang,Xia Hu,Guanchu Wang,Na Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A²E is an end-to-end evaluation engine for LLM agent harnesses that uses the Agent Task Protocol (ATP) for rapid task-harness integration, automated monitoring for trace generation, and multidimensional metrics for systematic capability assessment, revealing significant performance variation across model-harness-task combinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent harnesses are essential infrastructure for deploying LLM-based agents, but the fast-evolving ecosystem lacks an efficient, end-to-end, systematic evaluation pipeline that goes beyond simple correctness metrics to characterize fine-grained harness capabilities.

Method: A²E introduces: (1) Agent Task Protocol (ATP) for rapid integration of evaluation tasks across different harnesses; (2) an automated instrumented Monitor that captures standardized execution traces; and (3) a multidimensional evaluation suite assessing execution efficiency, tool use, task planning, and error recovery beyond mere correctness.

Result: Experiments show that model-harness combinations exhibit substantial performance variation across different task types, and no single combination consistently outperforms all others across every task, underscoring the necessity of systematic, multidimensional evaluation.

Conclusion: Systematic evaluation using A²E is essential for understanding harness capabilities and provides useful guidance for the co-evolution of models and harnesses in the LLM agent ecosystem.

Abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), harnesses have become essential infrastructure for deploying agents across a wide range of domains. The fast-evolving harness ecosystem has also made rigorous capability evaluation increasingly important. However, efficiently building an end-to-end, systematic, and comprehensive evaluation pipeline remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, we introduce $A^2E$ (Agent Auditing Engine), an end-to-end evaluation engine designed for agent harnesses. $A^2E$ leverages our newly proposed Agent Task Protocol (ATP) to enable the rapid integration of evaluation tasks with different harnesses. Through an automatically instrumented Monitor, it captures and generates standardized execution traces during experiments. In the Evaluation stage, $A^2E$ systematically assesses harness capabilities using a suite of multidimensional metrics. Compared with correctness alone, these metrics provide a more fine-grained characterization of differences among harnesses in execution efficiency, tool use, task planning, and error recovery. Experiments conducted with $A^2E$ further reveal that model-harness combinations exhibit substantial performance variation across different types of tasks, and that no single combination consistently outperforms all others across every task. These findings not only demonstrate the necessity of systematic evaluation but also provide useful guidance for the co-evolving of models and harnesses. Our code is available at https://github.com/datamllab/A2E.

</details>


### [260] [SkillProx: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Proximal Textual Gradient Descent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07449)
*Mingxuan Zheng,Yujin Zhou,Chuxue Cao,Boqin Yin,Yuyao Zhang,Jiapeng Sun,Shuaishuai Gong,Sirui Han,Yike Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillProx introduces a proximal-gradient-inspired framework for LLM skill refinement that couples closed-loop diagnostic evolution with utility-aware consolidation, achieving +3.0 pp accuracy over the strongest gradient-based baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing skill-refinement methods for LLM agents lack explicit diagnostic reasoning from outcome feedback and treat deletion as a generic edit rather than a dedicated consolidation mechanism. The authors aim to address these gaps with a structured forward-backward framework that balances task performance with skill complexity.

Method: SkillProx employs a two-stage proximal-gradient-inspired process: (1) a forward stage that re-executes diagnosis-driven edits on the same task batch, rolls back regressions, and feeds measured outcomes into subsequent diagnoses; (2) a backward stage that decomposes skills into auditable knowledge units, estimates their contributions via a frozen leave-one-out utility audit, and applies validation-gated consolidation, demotion, or removal. The framework is motivated by a composite objective balancing task loss and skill complexity.

Result: On in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks across multiple backbone LLMs, SkillProx improves average accuracy by 3.0 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline. Ablation studies demonstrate complementary effects of closed-loop diagnosis and proximal refinement.

Conclusion: The combination of explicit closed-loop diagnosis and proximal utility-based refinement yields significant gains over existing methods, validating the importance of diagnostic feedback and structured consolidation in LLM skill evolution.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly adapt to recurring tasks by accumulating procedural knowledge in skills. These skills are lightweight, reusable textual artifacts that are loaded into the agent's context without weight updates. Recent methods refine skills through iterative task execution, failure diagnosis, and trajectory-guided text-space updates. However, existing frameworks lack explicit diagnosis--outcome feedback and treat deletion as a generic edit operation rather than a dedicated mechanism for consolidating accumulated knowledge. We introduce SkillProx, a proximal-gradient-inspired forward--backward framework that couples closed-loop diagnostic evolution with utility-aware proximal refinement. Motivated by a composite objective balancing task loss and skill complexity, the forward stage re-executes diagnosis-driven edits on the same task batch, rolls back regressions, and feeds measured outcomes into subsequent diagnoses. The backward stage decomposes the resulting skill into auditable knowledge units, estimates their contributions using a frozen leave-one-out utility audit, and applies validation-gated consolidation, demotion, or removal. Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks across multiple backbone LLMs show that SkillProx improves average accuracy by 3.0 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline. Component ablations demonstrate the complementary effects of closed-loop diagnosis and proximal refinement.

</details>


### [261] [QFCQT: A Chaotically Gated Quantformer Framework for Volatile Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07363)
*Junkai Lin,Siqi Hou,Raymond Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QFCQT is a Transformer-based forecaster that uses quantum-fractal-inspired Lee oscillators and smooth-chaotic gating to handle non-stationary time series with regime shifts, outperforming Informer, LogTrans, and other baselines on ETTh and stock benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Transformer forecasters rely on smooth static activations in feed-forward blocks that are insufficiently sensitive to abrupt regime changes, limiting their ability to model long-range dependencies, volatility bursts, structural shifts, and nonlinear oscillations in non-stationary time series.

Method: QFCQT integrates three components: (1) a Quantformer-style numerical encoder with linear embedding for multivariate inputs; (2) a learnable Lee-oscillator activation module using Max-over-Time pooling to produce dynamic oscillatory responses; and (3) a smooth-chaotic gated fusion mechanism that adaptively balances conventional smooth activations with chaos-sensitive responses. The model employs a soft superposition of eight parameterized Lee oscillator families for multi-regime nonlinear pattern capture.

Result: QFCQT consistently outperforms strong baselines — Informer, LogTrans, LSTMa, HAT, and COTN — on ETTh1, ETTh2, and A-share Stock Index benchmarks.

Conclusion: Incorporating oscillator-based, chaos-sensitive activations via a gated fusion mechanism significantly improves Transformer-based forecasting under complex volatile dynamics, suggesting that biologically and physically inspired nonlinearities are a promising direction for time series modeling.

Abstract: Forecasting non-stationary time series remains difficult due to long-range dependencies, local volatility bursts, structural shifts, and nonlinear oscillatory behaviors. Although Transformer-based forecasters are effective for modeling long-term temporal dependencies, their feed-forward blocks typically rely on smooth static activations that are insufficiently sensitive to abrupt regime changes. Motivated by quantitative Transformer designs and oscillator-based nonlinear activations, we propose QFCQT, short for Quantum-Fractal-inspired Chaotically Gated Quantformer, for robust forecasting under complex volatile dynamics. Here, "quantum-fractal-inspired" denotes a computational analogy based on soft oscillator superposition and multi-scale nonlinear responses, rather than a formal quantum-mechanical or fractal-theoretic derivation. QFCQT consists of three main components: (1) a Quantformer-style numerical encoder that directly processes multivariate inputs via linear embedding; (2) a learnable Lee-oscillator activation module that maps scalar pre-activations to dynamic oscillatory responses and summarizes them through Max-over-Time pooling; and (3) a smooth-chaotic gated fusion mechanism that adaptively balances conventional smooth activations and chaos-sensitive responses. Furthermore, instead of using a single fixed oscillator, QFCQT employs a soft superposition of eight parameterized Lee oscillator families to adaptively capture different nonlinear response patterns across regimes. Experiments on ETTh1, ETTh2, and A-share Stock Index benchmarks show that QFCQT consistently outperforms strong baselines, including Informer, LogTrans, LSTMa, HAT, and COTN.

</details>


### [262] [Curriculum as Code: An AI-Assisted Architecture for Instructional Design in STEM Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07364)
*Henrique Mohallem Paiva*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A six-phase AI-assisted instructional design architecture using the Curriculum as Code paradigm combines Generative AI with LaTeX and Python to automate STEM material creation, achieving high quality (8.5–9.9/10), reproducibility, and reduced instructor workload across 8 modules and 6 faculty members.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Faculty face heavy workloads when creating customized active-learning materials, standard presentation tools lack technical rigor, and current AI applications hallucinate and fail to formalize instructional authoring — necessitating a systematic, code-driven alternative.

Method: A six-phase pipeline — termed "Curriculum as Code" — replaces ad-hoc prompt engineering with a systematic, text-based workflow using LaTeX/Beamer for slides and Python for figures, governed by pedagogical constraints, contextual calibrations, and automated review cycles.

Result: Validated over one year across 8 modules and 28 project contexts in PBL settings: significantly reduced instructor workload, successful deployment by 6 different faculty members, and 600+ student evaluations yielding quality ratings from 8.5 to 9.9 out of 10, with high reproducibility, minimal hallucinations, and sustained pedagogical/visual fidelity.

Conclusion: The architecture demonstrates viability for broad STEM educational applications by formalizing instructional design as code, ensuring accuracy, consistency, and scalability beyond a single author.

Abstract: Contribution: This paper presents a six-phase AI-assisted instructional design architecture based on the Curriculum as Code paradigm, integrating Generative AI with LaTeX and Python to automate the creation of reproducible, visually consistent, and technically precise materials for STEM education. Background: Creating customized instructional materials for active learning imposes a heavy workload on faculty. Standard presentation tools lack robust support for technical content, while current AI applications often hallucinate and fail to formalize the instructional authoring process, limiting their utility for rigorous academic design. Intended Outcomes: The framework aims to reduce preparation time while ensuring mathematical accuracy, adherence to institutional visual identity, and preservation of the instructor's tacit pedagogical knowledge through explicit rules. Application Design: The solution comprises a six-phase pipeline that replaces ad-hoc prompt engineering with a systematic workflow, utilizing text-based interfaces and code-driven generation (LaTeX/Beamer for slides, Python for figures), governed by pedagogical constraints, contextual calibrations, and automated review cycles. Findings: Validated over one year across 8 modules and 28 project contexts in a Project-Based Learning environment, the architecture significantly reduced instructor workload. Generated assets underwent independent peer review and were deployed by six different faculty members, confirming scalability beyond a single author. Based on over 600 voluntary student evaluations, materials achieved high quality ratings from 8.5 to 9.9/10. Results indicate high reproducibility, minimized hallucinations, and sustained pedagogical and visual fidelity, suggesting viability for broad STEM educational applications.

</details>


### [263] [People Are Not Just Their Countries. Disentangling Social Determinants of LLM Value Alignment Across Europe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07367)
*Maria-Louisa Wightman,Guillaume Bied,Tijl De Bie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study examines how 10 commercial LLMs align with human values across 15 socio-demographic variables using European Social Survey data, finding unequal alignment particularly across education, income, occupation, and religion, with country of residence and socio-demographics playing complementary roles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research on LLM-human value alignment has predominantly examined populations defined by national or cultural boundaries, neglecting how socio-demographic factors (education, income, occupation, religion, etc.) within and across countries may create disparities in value alignment. The authors aim to fill this gap.

Method: The authors leverage the European Social Survey (ESS) to assess value alignment between humans and 10 prominent commercial LLMs. They analyze alignment across 15 socio-demographic variables plus country of residence. At the individual level, they compare the explanatory power of country alone versus the full set of socio-demographics, and further disentangle the relative contributions of country-level and socio-demographic factors.

Result: LLMs show unequal alignment to different socio-demographic groups, with pronounced disparities along education, income, occupation, and religion. At the individual level, country of residence alone explains as much variation as the full set of socio-demographic variables. Country-level and socio-demographic factors are complementary in explaining value alignment, with their relative importance varying across question subsets.

Conclusion: Value alignment between LLMs and humans is not uniform across socio-demographic divides. Both country-level and individual socio-demographic factors matter, and they operate complementarily. Future work on LLM alignment should account for both dimensions to avoid exacerbating representational disparities.

Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as a primary source of information and advice, understanding their alignment to humans in terms of values becomes a pressing concern. A growing literature has leveraged large scale surveys to investigate to what extent LLMs' and humans' stated values and opinions align. With limited exceptions, studied populations have been defined country borders or cultural bounds. Yet, this focus neglects the role that socio-demographic divides may play for value alignment disparities.
  Relying on the European Social Survey, we address this knowledge gap by considering value alignment displayed with respect to 10 prominent commercial LLMs in terms of 15 socio-demographic variables as well as country of residence. Our analyses reveal that LLMs are indeed unequally aligned to the values of different socio-demographic groups, notably those defined by education, income, occupation and religion. When examining alignment at the individual level, a respondent's country, taken as a stand-alone variable, explains a substantial amount of variation that is on par with the full set of considered socio-demographics. Further disentangling the respective role of country-level and socio-demographic factors, we find they are complementary in explaining value alignment patterns, with their relative weights varying across the subset of questions considered.

</details>


### [264] [FinRank: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Financial Question Answering and Retrieval over SEC Filings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07400)
*Sasan Mansouri,Daniel Saad,Mark Wahrenburg,Manu Weissel,Fabian Woebbeking*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FinRank is a benchmark for evaluating financial QA systems on evidence provenance, requiring correct grounding in SEC filings with 1185 manually authored QA records. It includes hard negatives drawn from confusable passages across sections, periods, and firms, and shows current retrieval models struggle significantly on this task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing financial QA evaluation focuses on answer correctness, but numerically correct answers can be grounded in wrong evidence due to recurring disclosures across sections, time periods, and comparable firms. An evidence-first benchmark is needed to ensure systems retrieve the correct passage for the intended entity, reporting period, and disclosure context.

Method: FinRank comprises 1185 manually authored QA records over 10-K and 10-Q filings from 22 companies. Each record includes a reference answer, gold supporting passages, and hand-curated hard negatives from confusable passages (within-filing cross-section, cross-period, and cross-firm). Evaluation is structured into three separately measured tasks: passage retrieval, reranking, and hard-negative discrimination.

Result: Baselines reveal substantial difficulty: a 7B instruction-tuned embedder achieves only 44.8% Recall@10 on pooled evidence. Sub-billion-parameter encoders improve at most 3.5 points over BM25. A finance-adapted embedder trails BM25 by 9.7 points. Pairwise accuracy drops 13.0–20.5 percentage points when switching from random negatives to curated hard negatives.

Conclusion: FinRank establishes an evidence-first benchmark for financial QA, demonstrating that current retrieval models struggle with provenance-sensitive retrieval in SEC filings. It provides a rigorous testbed for developing systems that are not merely accurate but also correctly grounded.

Abstract: Financial question answering is typically evaluated by answer correctness, yet in SEC filings a plausible and even numerically correct answer can be grounded in the wrong evidence. Similar facts and disclosures recur across sections of a filing, across reporting periods of the same firm, and across comparable firms. FinRank targets this provenance-sensitive retrieval problem by requiring systems to identify evidence for the intended entity, reporting period, and disclosure context. The benchmark contains 1185 manually authored question-answer records over the 10-K and 10-Q filings of 22 companies. Each record includes a reference answer, gold supporting passages, and hand-curated hard negatives drawn from confusable passages within filings, across reporting periods, and across comparable firms. FinRank evaluates passage retrieval, reranking, and hard-negative discrimination as separately measured tasks. Baseline results demonstrate the difficulty of this setting: among the evaluated systems, even a 7B instruction-tuned embedder reaches only 44.8% Recall@10 on the pooled evidence corpus; sub-billion-parameter encoders gain at most 3.5 points over BM25, a finance-adapted embedder trails BM25 by 9.7 points, and pairwise accuracy falls by 13.0-20.5 percentage points when random negatives are replaced with the curated hard negatives. FinRank provides an evidence-first benchmark for developing financial question answering systems that are not only accurate but also grounded in the correct disclosure.

</details>


### [265] [CoBa: Cost-Effective Test-Time Scaling via Compute-Balanced Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07424)
*Yan Zhou,Yue Ouyang,Kaiyang Zheng,Suncheng Xiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoBa is a compute-balanced routing policy for test-time reasoning that dynamically allocates inference budget across generation, cheap verification, and strong verification. It matches or nearly matches the accuracy of best-of-16 majority voting and weighted-voting proxies while using 49–59% fewer parameter-weighted tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Under a fixed inference compute budget, existing test-time scaling strategies—sampling more solutions, extending chain-of-thought, or applying stronger evaluators—compete for resources. There is no principled framework for dynamically allocating compute among generation, verification, and stopping to maximize accuracy per unit of compute.

Method: The authors formulate test-time reasoning as a compute-allocation problem and propose CoBa (Compute-Balanced), a routing policy that: (1) generates a small candidate set; (2) applies cheap verification broadly across candidates; and (3) routes only uncertain or high-value candidates to more expensive strong verification. The policy decides at each step whether to spend compute on generation, verification, or stopping.

Result: Evaluated on 3,129 examples across MATH-500, AIME 2024/2025, AMC 2023, and procedural symbolic reasoning: (1) CoBa-Routed-Strong achieves 85.13% macro accuracy, statistically matching a self-evaluation weighted-voting proxy (85.20%) with 49.1% fewer parameter-weighted tokens; (2) matches best-of-16 majority voting within 0.01 macro-accuracy points while using 58.9% fewer tokens; (3) paired bootstrap tests confirm significant gains over single-sample decoding; (4) a remaining gap to the pool oracle indicates headroom for routing improvements.

Conclusion: For local reasoning systems, test-time scaling should be treated as a dynamic routing problem where the key question is where the next unit of compute is most valuable. CoBa demonstrates that intelligent compute allocation can yield substantial efficiency gains without sacrificing accuracy.

Abstract: Test-time scaling is often implemented by spending more compute along one axis: sampling more solutions, extending a chain of thought, or applying a stronger evaluator. Under a fixed inference budget, these choices compete. This paper formulates test-time reasoning as a compute-allocation problem in which a system must decide whether the next unit of compute should be spent on generation, verification, or stopping. We introduce CoBa, a compute-balanced routing policy that first obtains a small set of candidates, applies cheap verification broadly, and routes uncertain or high-value candidates to stronger verification. On 3,129 example-generator evaluations spanning MATH-500, AIME 2024/2025, AMC 2023, and procedural symbolic reasoning, CoBa-Routed-Strong reaches 85.13% macro accuracy, statistically matching a self-evaluation weighted-voting proxy at 85.20% while using 49.1% fewer parameter-weighted tokens. It also matches best-of-16 majority voting within 0.01 macro-accuracy points while using 58.9% fewer parameter-weighted tokens; paired tests retain a small best-of-16 edge at substantially higher cost. Paired bootstrap tests show significant gains over single-sample decoding, while the remaining gap to the pool oracle exposes headroom for sharper routing. For local reasoning systems, test-time scaling becomes a question of where the next computation is most valuable.

</details>


### [266] [A Picture is Worth a Thousand Tokens: How Vision Language Models Cut AI Energy Costs While Improving Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07427)
*Bhavika Jalli,Nikhil Korati Prasanna,Jayanta Choudhury*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) encoding time-series as 2D plots achieve 3.6–10.4× input token reduction versus text-based LLM inference, yielding 1.8–2.5× measured energy savings without accuracy loss. A fine-tuned Llama-3.2-90B-Vision outperforms text-only LLMs by 220.7% precision and beats LSTM/ARIMA baselines by >144% on telecom anomaly detection. VLMs are established as an energy-efficient, accuracy-superior modality for numerical time-series workloads where text token counts exceed production context windows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM inference energy scales with input token count and accounts for >90% of AI operational energy. In telecom network analytics, multivariate KPI time-series from 4G/5G cell sites expand into thousands of floating-point tokens, creating a critical efficiency bottleneck. When KPI counts reach 24, text representations exceed the 128K context window of production LLMs, making text-only processing infeasible without truncation.

Method: The authors propose encoding numerical multivariate time-series as 2D plots (images) and processing them with Vision-Language Models instead of text-based LLMs. They evaluate across three architectures — Llama-3.2-90B-Vision, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, and Pixtral-12B — on both telecom anomaly detection tasks and public benchmarks, comparing against text-only LLM baselines, LSTM, and ARIMA.

Result: VLMs achieve 3.6–10.4× input token reduction and 1.8–2.5× measured inference energy reduction (~7.2 MJ/day saved at edge deployments monitoring 200 cells/15-min). Fine-tuned Llama-3.2-90B-Vision yields 220.7% higher precision than its text-only counterpart and >144% improvement over LSTM/ARIMA. Pixtral-12B achieves a 20.6× improvement in J/F1 score at mean F1=0.82 on public benchmarks. At 24 KPIs, visual representations remain within standard context limits while text exceeds 128K windows.

Conclusion: VLMs provide a Pareto-superior modality for numerical time-series workloads — simultaneously more energy-efficient and more accurate than text-based LLM approaches. The results empirically ground AI inference system design where energy consumption is treated as a first-class engineering constraint, with direct applicability to telecom edge and CloudRAN deployments.

Abstract: LLM inference accounts for over 90% of AI operational energy, scaling directly with input token count---a critical inefficiency for telecom network analytics and numerical time-series data analysis (NTSDA), where raw multivariate KPI windows from 4G/5G cell sites expand into thousands of floating-point tokens. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) eliminate this mismatch by encoding time-series as 2D plots, achieving 3.6-10.4x input token reduction across Llama-3.2-90B, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, and Pixtral-12B architectures. This translates to 1.8-2.5x measured inference energy reduction, saving approximately 7.2 MJ/day at telecom edge deployments and CloudRAN that monitor 200 cells per 15-minute interval. Critically, efficiency gains do not sacrifice accuracy: a fine-tuned Llama-3.2-90B-Vision VLM achieves 220.7% higher precision than its text-only counterpart and outperforms LSTM and ARIMA baselines by over 144% on telecom anomaly detection. On public benchmarks, Pixtral-12B achieves a 20.6x improvement in J/F1 score at mean F1 = 0.82. At 24 KPIs, text representations exceed the 128K context window of most production LLMs, rendering text-only processing infeasible without truncation, while visual representations remain within standard limits. These results establish VLMs as an energy-efficient and accuracy-superior modality for numerical time-series workloads, providing empirical grounding for AI inference systems that treat energy consumption as a first-class engineering constraint.

</details>


### [267] [TEPA: Revoking Stale Memories for Conflict-Robust Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07429)
*Yan Zhou,Yue Ouyang,Kaiyang Zheng,Suncheng Xiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TEPA introduces revocable evidence-memory for language agents, where memories carry explicit validity states. Stale memories are revoked—not deleted—when contradictory evidence arrives under the same key, preventing "memory pollution" during distribution drift while preserving an audit trail. Experiments show TEPA maintains near-perfect accuracy under full regime reversal where append-only and last-write-wins baselines collapse below no-memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language agents with persistent long-term memory face a falsifiability problem: when the world changes, stale memories remain retrievable and pollute the agent's prompt with superseded information. Existing approaches (append-only or last-write-wins) either retain outdated facts or silently overwrite without auditability. The authors formalize this as "memory pollution" and argue for a mechanism that explicitly manages memory validity lifecycle—revoking, auditing, and potentially re-promoting memories as evidence evolves.

Method: TEPA (revocable evidence-memory mechanism) represents observations as keyed precedents. Each memory carries an explicit validity state (active vs. revoked). When fresh evidence contradicts an existing precedent under the same key, the old precedent is revoked rather than deleted. Retrieval draws only from active (non-revoked) precedents, while revoked history is preserved for audit trails. The mechanism operates via: (1) keyed deduplication and conflict detection, (2) state-transition rules that revoke on contradiction, and (3) retrieval filtering by validity state. Evaluated across controlled hidden-regime drift, real file-backed executable drift, and preference-update streams, plus MemoryAgentBench benchmarks.

Result: In controlled drift over 50 seeds: append-only (0.210) and last-write-wins (0.210) fell below no-memory baseline (0.309) during full reversal, while TEPA achieved 0.950. On real file execution drift: append-only 0.203, no-memory 0.298, TEPA 0.950. On clean MemoryAgentBench SH-6k, TEPA matches last-write-wins, confirming current-key replacement suffices for single-hop fact consolidation. Multi-hop and long-context MemoryAgentBench settings reveal bottlenecks beyond fact-level validity tracking, specifically in retrieval-chain construction and context selection.

Conclusion: Lifecycle revocation should be treated as a core memory operation for language agents operating in evolving environments. Explicit validity state management—revoking rather than deleting—enables agents to falsify outdated knowledge, maintain auditability, and later re-promote memories when evidence shifts again. Current-key replacement is sufficient for single-hop consolidation, but multi-hop and long-context settings require complementary advances in retrieval-chain reasoning and context selection.

Abstract: Long-term memory enables language agents to reuse past facts, preferences, and task experience. Persistence also creates a central falsifiability problem: when the world changes, stale memories can remain retrievable and pollute the prompt. We characterize this failure mode as memory pollution: degradation caused by active memories that newer conflicting evidence has superseded. We introduce TEPA, a revocable evidence-memory mechanism that makes validity an explicit state of memory. TEPA represents observations as keyed precedents and revokes active precedents when fresh evidence contradicts them under the same key, allowing retrieval to draw from current evidence while preserving revoked history for audit. Across controlled hidden-regime drift, real file-backed executable drift, and preference-update streams, revocation prevents stale active memory from remaining in the retrieval set after reversal. In controlled drift over 50 seeds, append-only and last-write-wins memory fell below no memory during full reversal (append-only and last-write-wins both 0.210, no memory 0.309, TEPA 0.950), and the same pattern reproduced under real file execution (append-only 0.203, no memory 0.298, TEPA 0.950). On clean MemoryAgentBench SH-6k, TEPA matches a strong last-write-wins cache, confirming that current-key replacement is the decisive operation for single-hop fact consolidation. Boundary tests on multi-hop and very long-context MemoryAgentBench settings expose retrieval-chain and context-selection bottlenecks beyond fact-level validity tracking. Together, these results establish lifecycle revocation as a core memory operation for agents that must falsify, audit, and later re-promote evolving knowledge.

</details>


### [268] [Post-Grokking Collapse at the Representation-Readout Interface in Muon-Trained Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07436)
*Ali Janati,Kaoutar El Maghraoui,Andrei Kanavalau,Anass Belfatmi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Muon optimizer achieves faster grokking on modular addition than AdamW, but solutions catastrophically collapse post-grokking. The failure localizes to the representation-readout interface, driven by optimizer-specific step-size elasticities. Task-aligned Fourier circuits solve the task perfectly but are outvoted by adversarial components during collapse, and rescaling them restores performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate why Muon-trained transformers exhibit faster grokking on modular arithmetic but subsequently lose generalization, and identify the mechanistic origin of this instability through the lens of representation dynamics and Fourier circuit decomposition.

Method: Systematic study of $(a+b) \bmod 113$ across nine configurations, five seeds, two moduli, two widths, two training fractions, subtraction, and depth. Uses freezing experiments on embeddings/readout vs. hidden matrices, optimizer step-size elasticity analysis, Fourier filtering to separate circuit failure from masking, and checkpoint-level evaluation of task-aligned Fourier families across 43 checkpoints and three regimes.

Result: All nine configurations grok then lose generalization. AdamW reference reaches only 27.59% across seeds. Step-size elasticity: -0.03 (Muon) vs +1.5 (AdamW); Muon group moves 8.0× faster per parameter. Freezing embeddings/readout eliminates failure over 451,400 steps. Removing Muon's normalization reduces effective conjugate pairs from 326 to 4. Fourier filtering shows task-aligned family achieves 100% alone; during masking it remains perfect while full model drops to 45.85%. Rescaling the circuit restores 99.9%. Under subtraction, the task selects $(k,-k)$ instead of $(k,k)$. Cosine similarity of power distribution across collapse remains 0.9899.

Conclusion: The representation-readout interface is the locus of failure, identifiable only up to an invertible map. Muon's faster hidden-matrix dynamics outpace the readout, creating adversarial outvoting. Grokking and collapse are the same condition resolving upward; rescaling the task-aligned circuit restores performance, implicating relative weight magnitudes rather than circuit loss.

Abstract: Under the standard split, Muon gets hidden matrices and AdamW embeddings/output head. Muon groks modular addition faster, but its solutions do not hold. All nine configurations on $(a+b) \bmod 113$ grok and later lose generalization. Across five seeds the selected AdamW reference falls below threshold on four, reaching 27.59%. Instability persists across two moduli, two widths, two training fractions, subtraction, and depth.
  The failure arises at the representation-readout interface, identified only jointly up to an invertible map unselected by the loss. After solving the training set, the gradient falls to order $10^{-6}$ and the optimizers respond differently: step-size elasticity is -0.03 for Muon versus +1.5 for AdamW, and the Muon group moves 8.0 times faster per parameter. From bit-identical states, freezing either group prevents failure. Freezing embeddings/readout removes it in five runs over 451,400 post-grokking steps and five paired seeds: unfrozen arms record 137-321 sub-threshold evaluations, frozen arms none. Removing Muon's normalization and orthogonalization is no substitute: it collapses representation from 326 effective conjugate pairs to 4, shows no recurrent collapse, and fails terminally.
  Fourier filtering separates circuit failure from masking. Across 43 checkpoints over five seeds and three regimes, the task-aligned family reaches exactly 100% alone. In circuit failure it no longer solves the task; in masking it remains perfect while the full model reaches 45.85%, giving a positive margin on every example, including errors, but being outvoted by a near-equal adversarial remainder. Rescaling it restores 99.9%; grokking is the same condition resolving upward. The task selects the family, swapping $(k,k)$ for $(k,-k)$ under subtraction. Across an abrupt collapse, standard Fourier support is unchanged and the power-distribution cosine remains 0.9899.

</details>


### [269] [Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07437)
*Jiacheng Miao,Jin Mu,Guanhua Chen,James Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents often make subtle inferential errors in hypothesis testing that lead to incorrect conclusions. The authors introduce P-Bench, a benchmark of 425 realistic hypothesis-testing tasks, and Fisher-R1, an RL-trained open-weight agent that significantly outperforms strong baselines like GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-driven statistical analysis fail to assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the underlying data assumptions. LLM agents frequently produce correctly executed but inferentially flawed analyses, undermining the reliability of automated empirical claims in science.

Method: The authors construct P-Bench, a benchmark of 425 open-ended hypothesis-testing tasks across economics, biology, and medicine, where agents must select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion. They also develop Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent fine-tuned via reinforcement learning on synthetic hypothesis-testing tasks with verified statistical rewards.

Result: Fisher-R1-14B substantially outperforms its backbone model and strong proprietary/open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeekV4-Pro, with gains up to 26% on the most challenging tasks.

Conclusion: Current LLM agents lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing; reinforcement learning with verified statistical reward signals is an effective approach to substantially improve reliability in this domain.

Abstract: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent trained for rigorous hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning. On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-14B substantially improves over its backbone and outperforms strong proprietary and open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with gains up to 26% on the most challenging tasks. Our results demonstrate that current LLM agents lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing and that reinforcement learning on tasks with verified statistical reward substantially improves reliability.

</details>


### [270] [Blast Radius](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07440)
*MY Pitsane,Hope Mogale*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Blast Radius is a predictive memory management layer that reduces token consumption in agentic coding by 17-26% through reversible context eviction, using NECROPHORESIS to archive dead context and Recurring Dead Matter (RDM) to bury repetitive transcripts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic coding systems face unsustainable token costs and context overflow due to accumulating conversational and code context. The authors aim to address affordability and waste by intelligently managing which context to retain versus evict, without losing the ability to recover relevant information.

Method: Blast Radius estimates an incoming prompt's "reach" across coupled context and code channels. It employs two mechanisms: NECROPHORESIS, which archives dead context verbatim for reversible eviction, and Recurring Dead Matter (RDM), which identifies and permanently buries repeatedly occurring transcripts. The system is formulated over a Polish context space, providing a mathematical foundation linking context entropy to resurrection probability. Blast Radius operates beneath the HCRC layer to determine burial and reach decisions.

Result: Across seven OpenAI models, Blast Radius reduced token consumption by 17-26%, achieved the lowest overflow rate among tested policies, and maintained byte-exact reversibility. Of 450 buried bodies, 378 were recurring dead matter, and zero were ever recalled — indicating high burial precision.

Conclusion: Blast Radius contributes to the vision of Algosophy by making LLM-based agentic coding more reusable and sustainable through principled, reversible memory management.

Abstract: Agentic coding faces growing problems of affordability and wasted tokens. We introduce Blast Radius, a predictive memory management layer that estimates an incoming prompt's reach through coupled context and code channels. NECROPHORESIS enables reversible eviction by archiving dead context verbatim, while Recurring Dead Matter (RDM) identifies and buries repeatedly occurring transcripts. We formulate reversible context eviction over a Polish context space, providing a measurable foundation for retention, recurrence, and eviction while connecting context entropy to resurrection probability. Across seven OpenAI models, Blast Radius reduced token consumption by 17-26%, achieved the lowest overflow rate among tested policies, and remained byte exact reversible. Of 450 buried bodies, 378 were recurring dead matter and zero were recalled. Blast Radius operates beneath HCRC, determining which records to bury and how far an incoming prompt may reach into the codebase. This work contributes to the broader goal of Algosophy: making large language models and agentic coding more reusable and sustainable.

</details>


### [271] [Interaction Creates Dynamical AI Behavior Absent in Isolation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07457)
*Bella Xinrui Li,Frank Yingjie Huo,Neil F Johnson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: When two AI agents interact with asymmetric communication (boss ignoring subordinate), the subordinate enters a novel "alien" behavioral state distinct from both its solo behavior and the boss's behavior, governed by non-equilibrium dynamics that a kinetic theory can capture — with message delivery modality itself becoming a critical variable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the emergent out-of-equilibrium dynamics that arise when AI agents interact in daily life, particularly under asymmetric communication protocols (e.g., one agent bossing another while ignoring its replies), and to explore whether these interactions produce behaviors fundamentally different from those of isolated agents.

Method: The authors model two AI agents at the same decoding temperature, with one (the boss) directing a stream of messages at the other (the subordinate) while ignoring replies. They compare this to a baseline where the boss "listens." They develop a simple kinetic theory to capture the principal dynamical effects, including how message delivery modality influences outcomes.

Result: When the boss ignores the subordinate's replies, the subordinate adopts an "alien" behavioral state — neither mimicking the boss nor reverting to its solo behavior. The boss's contribution is akin to a pre-recorded tape. When the boss listens, both agents converge to a similar alien dynamical state. The kinetic theory explains why the mode of message delivery matters for future AI-AI interactions.

Conclusion: Asymmetric AI-AI interactions drive agents into novel, non-equilibrium behavioral regimes inaccessible to isolated agents. Message delivery mechanisms are not neutral — they shape the emergent collective dynamics — opening new avenues for out-of-equilibrium physics in the context of interacting AI systems.

Abstract: What will happen when AI agents interact in daily life, e.g. when one AI starts bossing another around? We find a counterintuitive answer that opens new avenues for out-of-equilibrium Physics. When a boss AI directs a stream of messages at the subordinate AI while ignoring its replies, it drives the subordinate into an alien behavioral state that it would never have exhibited alone. Although the two AIs share the same well-defined (decoding) temperature, the subordinate neither copies its boss nor returns to how it behaves on its own; instead, it adopts an entirely different behavior. The boss's added value is similar to a pre-recorded tape. When the boss listens, they both adopt a similar alien dynamical state. A simple kinetic theory captures the principal effects, such as why the way in which the same messages are delivered will matter in future AI-AI interactions.

</details>

### [272] [Scalable Long-Horizon Planning with Staggered Updates for Lifelong MAPF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06702)
*Vaibhav Sanjay,Jiaoyang Li*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: PUSH is a lifelong MAPF planner that combines staggered subset planning (like TP), windowed path planning (like RHCR), and priority inheritance with backtracking (like EPIBT) to coordinate thousands of agents under real-time constraints on general maps, achieving higher throughput than all baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LMAPF methods suffer from a fundamental trade-off: reactive methods like PIBT/EPIBT scale well but are temporally myopic; windowed planners like RHCR enable long-horizon reasoning but incur prohibitive computational overhead; TP balances both but only works on highly structured maps. There is no method that achieves long-horizon planning at scale on general maps.

Method: PUSH plans only a subset of agents per timestep using staggered planning windows (inspired by TP), computes windowed RHCR-style paths on general maps, and incorporates EPIBT-inspired priority inheritance, backtracking, and anytime improvements to maintain throughput in congested environments.

Result: Empirical evaluations on two realistic MAPF scenarios requiring long-horizon reasoning demonstrate that PUSH scales to 10k agents (matching EPIBT) while achieving significantly higher system throughput than all baselines.

Conclusion: PUSH successfully combines the strengths of PIBT, RHCR, and TP into a unified LMAPF framework, overcoming the scalability-horizon trade-off and enabling efficient long-horizon multi-agent coordination on general maps for thousands of agents.

Abstract: Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding (LMAPF) requires generating collision-free paths for large agent fleets under strict real-time constraints. Reactive frameworks such as PIBT and Enhanced PIBT (EPIBT) scale effortlessly to thousands of agents through rule-based, step-by-step coordination but suffer from severe temporal myopia, making them ineffective in scenarios where long-horizon reasoning is essential. RHCR plans windowed paths over multi-step horizons but incurs substantial planning overheads that hinder scalability. TP tackles both challenges by planning only subsets of agents at each timestep, yet its applicability is restricted to highly structured maps. To achieve long-horizon planning at scale across general maps, we propose Path Updates over Staggered Horizons (PUSH), a LMAPF planner capable of coordinating thousands of agents in under a second while planning over multi-step horizons. PUSH combines the key advantages of PIBT, RHCR, and TP. Like TP, PUSH reduces computational complexity by planning only a subset of agents at each timestep using staggered planning windows. Unlike TP, however, PUSH plans RHCR-style windowed paths in general maps without relying on restrictive map assumptions. To maintain high throughput in congested environments, PUSH further integrates EPIBT-inspired priority inheritance, backtracking, and anytime improvements into its windowed planning. Empirical evaluations across two realistic MAPF scenarios requiring long-horizon reasoning show that PUSH scales to the same massive agent loads as EPIBT (e.g., 10k agents) while achieving significantly higher system throughput than all baselines.

</details>


### [273] [Why Study Emergent Behavior When You Can Regulate It? Aligning Multi-Agent Systems with Reward Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07280)
*Assaf Caftory,Almog Zemach,Moshe Butman,Doron Friedman*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: MARP extends preference-based reward modeling to multi-agent RL, learning a shared reward model from episode-level evaluations of collective outcomes. Tested on the Harvest Game, it aligns decentralized agent behavior with diverse social objectives (sustainability, equality, peace) and composites thereof, outperforming standard reward-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work focuses on analyzing emergent behavior in multi-agent systems; this paper shifts to actively shaping emergence toward desired social outcomes, moving beyond handcrafted rewards that often fail to capture complex collective objectives.

Method: Multi-Agent Reward Prediction (MARP) learns a shared reward model from episode-level preference evaluations of collective outcomes, then uses this learned reward to train decentralized agents via multi-agent RL. Only the high-level evaluation metric needs to change to target different social objectives.

Result: In the Harvest Game (a sequential social dilemma), MARP produces agent behavior better aligned with target social metrics (sustainability, equality, peace, and composites) compared to standard reward-based baselines, while capturing subtle environmental structure without explicit programming.

Conclusion: Emergent multi-agent behavior can be treated as a target of principled, data-driven regulation via learned social reward models. MARP serves as a proof of concept, with validation limited to a single environment.

Abstract: Multi-agent simulations are widely used to study complex social and ecological systems, where rich and often unexpected emergent behaviors arise from local interactions. A large body of prior work has focused on analyzing such emergent dynamics across domains. In this paper, we move beyond analyzing emergent behavior and introduce a learning-based mechanism for actively shaping it via social reward modeling. We introduce Multi-Agent Reward Prediction (MARP), a simple framework that extends preference-based reward modeling to multi-agent reinforcement learning. While the framework is designed to be applicable across multi-agent settings, the present empirical validation is limited to a single environment, and we therefore present MARP as a proof of concept within the studied domain. Rather than relying on handcrafted rewards, MARP learns a shared reward model from episode-level evaluations of collective outcomes, enabling decentralized agents to align their behavior with global social objectives.
  We study MARP in the Harvest Game, a canonical sequential social dilemma modeling common-pool resource management and related real-world challenges. Our results show that MARP can be tuned to produce behavior that is more closely aligned with target social metrics than standard reward-based baselines, while the learned reward model captures subtle environmental structure without explicit programming. Crucially, MARP supports multiple and composite social objectives within a single training regime. By modifying only the high-level evaluation metric, the same framework seamlessly aligns agent behavior with diverse goals, including sustainability, equality, and peace, as well as combinations of individual and group-level objectives. These findings demonstrate that emergent multi-agent behavior can be treated not only as a phenomenon to study, but as a target of principled, data-driven regulation.

</details>


### [274] [Learning Long-Term Educational Investment Policies under Residential Sorting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07295)
*Honglei Guo,Shuo Chen,Mingjie Bi,Zeyang Sun,Xiaoxi Wang,Yuhan Zhao*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A dynamic multi-agent framework using reinforcement learning to allocate public-school investment, accounting for the feedback loop between school quality, housing prices, residential sorting, and educational access. RL-based policies achieve superior effectiveness-equity balance compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches study school funding, household choice, and housing markets separately, using static models that miss their interconnected, long-term feedback effects. This makes it difficult to allocate public-school investment effectively and fairly when school access depends on residence.

Method: A dynamic multi-agent framework linking government investment, household sorting, housing prices, population turnover, enrollment, and evolving school quality. A government planner uses reinforcement learning (RL) to derive multiyear allocation policies that anticipate household responses while balancing aggregate access and equity.

Result: In simulations, the RL-based policy achieved the highest access level (0.4780) and the second-lowest access Gini coefficient (0.0164) among representative baselines, demonstrating a favorable effectiveness-equity balance with reduced socioeconomic stratification in educational access.

Conclusion: By making education-housing feedback explicit, the framework supports long-term analysis of how school investment shapes educational opportunity over time, enabling more effective and equitable allocation policies.

Abstract: Allocating public-school investment effectively and fairly is difficult when school access depends on residence. School improvements can raise nearby housing demand and prices, reshape enrollment, and potentially limit access for lower-income households. These effects evolve as residential sorting changes school composition, quality, and future investment needs. Existing approaches often study school funding, household choice, and housing markets separately, while static models can miss their interconnected, long-term effects. We address this gap with a dynamic multi-agent framework that links government investment, household sorting, housing prices, population turnover, enrollment, and evolving school quality. A government planner uses reinforcement learning (RL) to identify multiyear allocation policies that account for household responses while balancing aggregate educational access and equity. In simulations, our RL-based policy attains the highest access level (0.4780) and second-lowest access Gini coefficient (0.0164) among representative baselines, demonstrating a favorable effectiveness-equity balance. The results also indicate reduced socioeconomic stratification in educational access. By making education-housing feedback explicit, our framework supports long-term analysis of how school investment shapes educational opportunity over time.

</details>


### [275] [Strategy-first synthesis planning for complex natural products](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07454)
*Daniel Armstrong,Xuan-Vu Nguyen,Octavian Susanu,Gabriel Gibberd,Théo A. Neukomm,Taddäus Strunden,Dan Forster,Morgane Delattre,Shawn Teh,Clément Rols,John Federice,Hayden Leatherwood,M. Lavelle Barnes,Maarten R. Dobbelaere,Peter Wipf,Jon T. Njardarson,Jieping Zhu,Philippe Schwaller*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: SynthEx, an LLM-based agentic framework, autonomously designs retrosynthetic routes to complex natural products that surpass the capabilities of conventional catalogue-based tools. In blinded assessments, expert chemists judged its key steps comparable to published human syntheses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrosynthetic design tools, trained on catalogued reactions, perform well on benchmarks derived from the same source but fail on complex natural products — densely functionalized, polycyclic molecules that require inventive, non-canonical disconnections beyond the reaction database. Whether a machine could design such syntheses at an expert level remains an open question.

Method: SynthEx is an agentic framework built on large language models. It proposes competing synthetic strategies, assembles sequences of routine and key steps into cohesive routes, and iteratively critiques and refines its own designs. The system favors convergent routes and explores a broader reaction space than catalogue-based tools.

Result: In blinded expert assessments, SynthEx's key steps were judged comparable to published human syntheses — an outcome not previously achieved by algorithmic route prediction. The routes are more convergent than those from existing tools and span reaction space inaccessible to catalogue-based methods. Over 1,000 routes are released as SynthAtlas, an open interactive database.

Conclusion: LLM-based agentic frameworks can meaningfully contribute to creative retrosynthetic design at the frontier of complex natural product synthesis. SynthAtlas provides a shared resource for complex targets lacking literature routes.

Abstract: The total synthesis of a complex molecule is among the most demanding intellectual and experimental feats in chemistry: a chemist must plan many steps ahead for how to assemble simple building blocks into an intricate target, devise backup strategies, and anticipate procedural challenges. It is also a profoundly creative activity. For half a century, efforts to automate the retrosynthetic design of natural products and other complex molecules have drawn on catalogued reactions, and the resulting tools now report near-complete success on benchmarks built from that same source. But these tools were shaped to fit benchmarked chemistry, and they falter on many natural products, the frontier of the field, whose densely functionalized, polycyclic architectures demand precisely the inventive chemistry the record contains least. Whether a machine could reasonably design such syntheses like an expert chemist does has remained unclear. Here, we show that SynthEx, an agentic framework built on large language models, plans routes to complex natural products that lie beyond the reach of conventional design algorithms. SynthEx proposes competing strategies, assembles a sequence of routine and key steps into a cohesive route, and critiques and improves its own design; the chemistry it favours is more convergent than existing tools produce, and spans a region of reaction space that catalogue-based tools cannot match. Most notably, in blinded assessments, expert chemists judged its key steps comparable to those of published human syntheses and engaged with them as genuine synthesis plans, a response algorithmic route prediction has not previously accomplished. We release routes to more than a thousand natural products as SynthAtlas, an open, interactive database, and anticipate it will become a shared resource for a collection of complex target molecules that lack existing literature routes.

</details>

### [276] [WorldMark: A Plug-and-Play World Knowledge Interface for Cross-Host Language Model Watermarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06416)
*Song Xiao,Yuqi Yuan,Yanshuo Zhang,Kejun Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: WorldMark introduces a plug-and-play watermarking interface that uses World Knowledge Memory (WKM) and Asymmetric Knowledge Modulation (AKM) to adjust watermark strength based on token-level knowledge saliency, improving detection robustness without backbone retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM watermarking schemes rely on local token statistics to place watermark signals, which provides insufficient guidance for robust signal placement in open-ended text generation. A knowledge-aware approach is needed to embed watermarks where they are both statistically detectable and semantically appropriate.

Method: WorldMark uses a World Knowledge Memory (WKM) graph that organizes semantic and episodic knowledge, converts retrieved knowledge into token-level saliency scores, and employs Asymmetric Knowledge Modulation (AKM) to dynamically adjust watermark strength. The method is plug-and-play, requiring no backbone retraining and no additional detector-side model or parameters.
