Result: On the C4 benchmark, WorldMark improves both clean and attacked detection across three adaptive-strength host watermark variants while slightly reducing perplexity. Pilot experiments on C4 and OpenGen demonstrate that direct memory conditioning transfers across watermark families but can be unstable without saliency-aware modulation.

Conclusion: WorldMark demonstrates that knowledge-grounded, saliency-aware watermark modulation effectively enhances robustness against attacks while preserving text quality, offering a lightweight, retraining-free enhancement compatible with multiple watermark families.

Abstract: Watermarking traces the provenance of text produced by large language models by embedding statistically detectable signals during decoding. Existing schemes fall into logits-based, sampling-based, entropy-aware, and adaptive-strength families, yet all of them place watermark signals according to local token statistics. In the open-ended text-generation settings evaluated in this work, local statistics may provide insufficient guidance for placing robust watermark signals. We introduce WorldMark, a plug-and-play interface that uses World Knowledge Memory (WKM) to organize semantic and episodic knowledge in a memory graph, converts the retrieved knowledge into a token-level knowledge saliency score, and adjusts the strength of a host watermark through Asymmetric Knowledge Modulation (AKM). WorldMark requires no backbone retraining and introduces no additional detector-side model or parameter. On the primary C4 evaluation, the complete WorldMark interface improves clean and attacked detection across three adaptive-strength host variants while slightly reducing perplexity. Additional pilot experiments on C4 and OpenGen show that direct memory conditioning transfers across multiple watermark families but can be unstable without saliency-aware modulation. WorldMark requires no additional detector-side model or parameter and introduces negligible overhead under the primary protocol.

</details>


### [277] [Fairis: Fairness-Aware Aggregation with Provable Influence Containment against Fairness Poisoning Attacks in Collaborative Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06469)
*Devharsh Trivedi,Nesrine Kaaniche,Nikos Triandopoulos,Maryline Laurent,Jackson Walters*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Fairis is a server-side reweighting scheme for fair federated learning that provably reduces an adversarial client's weight monotonically in its reported bias, using a normalized weight formula ω_k = \bar{w}_k / Σ \bar{w}_j where \bar{w}_k = η - F_k, with provable properties of Monotone Weight Reduction, Demographic Participation, and Non-Gamesmanship.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fairness-aware aggregation methods (e.g., FairFed) are vulnerable to fairness poisoning attacks, where a malicious client can maximize group disparity while preserving accuracy to evade Byzantine defenses. FairFed's gap-based weighting can be gamed by an adversary observing the global fairness score.

Method: Fairis: a server-side reweighting scheme assigning each client a normalized weight ω_k = \bar{w}_k / Σ_j \bar{w}_j, with unnormalized score \bar{w}_k = η - F_k, where F_k ∈ [0,1] is the local Equal Opportunity Difference and η > 1 a security parameter. The method is combined with server-side norm clipping and is supported by three formal proofs: Monotone Weight Reduction (MWR), Demographic Participation, and Non-Gamesmanship, with MWR extended to colluding minority coalitions.

Result: Against a stealthy adversary (within 0.04 accuracy of benign), Fairis reduces adversarial weight by 41–54% below a size-blind control on Taiwan Credit. Under routine non-IID partitions, no rule dominates, and containment depends on how far the adversary's score separates from the honest mean, providing no containment when the honest population is already unfair. Clipped FairFed can achieve lower weight but guarantees nothing and can zero out a client entirely on Taiwan Credit.

Conclusion: Fairis is the only evaluated rule guaranteeing every client strictly positive weight while provably reducing an adversary's weight monotonically in its bias, assuming honest score reporting (an assumption the paper acknowledges it does not discharge).

Abstract: Collaborative machine learning among financial institutions must be both group-fair and robust against deliberate adversarial manipulation. Existing fairness-aware aggregation methods remain formally vulnerable to fairness poisoning: a malicious client maximizing group disparity while preserving accuracy evades accuracy-based Byzantine defenses, and in our threat model FairFed's gap-based weighting can be gamed by an adversary who observes the global fairness score. We present Fairis, a server-side reweighting scheme in which each client's update receives the normalized weight $ω_k = \bar{w}_k / \sum_j \bar{w}_j$ built from the unnormalized score $\bar{w}_k = η- \mathcal{F}_k$, with $\mathcal{F}_k \in [0,1]$ the local Equal Opportunity Difference and $η> 1$ a security parameter. We prove three properties, Monotone Weight Reduction (MWR), Demographic Participation, and Non-Gamesmanship, extend MWR to colluding minority coalitions, and show that combining MWR with server-side norm clipping bounds the adversary's displacement of the global model by $ω_0 C$, strictly decreasing in its own reported disparity. Assuming honest score reporting, an assumption this paper does not discharge, Fairis is the only rule evaluated that guarantees every client strictly positive weight while provably reducing an adversary's weight monotonically in its bias; clipped FairFed can reach a lower weight but guarantees nothing and zeroes a client outright on Taiwan Credit. Against an adversary stealthy enough to evade accuracy-based defenses, within 0.04 accuracy of benign, Fairis cuts its weight by 41 to 54% below a size-blind control on Taiwan. On routine non-IID partitions no rule dominates, and a uniform-weighting ablation shows that containment tracks how far the adversary's score separates from the honest mean, providing none when the honest population is already unfair.

</details>


### [278] [CyberForge: Verified Vulnerability Injection at Repository Level for Cybersecurity Agent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06471)
*Amine Lbath,Manan Suri,Aurelien Delaitre,Vadim Okun,Massih-Reza Amini,Ram D. Sriram,Dinesh Manocha*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: CyberForge synthesizes executable, repository-level security training data by injecting vulnerabilities into real C/C++ projects with dynamic validation. The resulting corpus of 1,034 validated vulnerabilities across 80 projects improves SEC-bench patch repair by up to +14.7 points, with gains generalizing to other languages via PatchEval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents lag in vulnerability discovery and patching for real-world software. While attackers only need one exploit, defenders must find all vulnerabilities. A key bottleneck is the scarcity of security training data with reproducible build/execution environments. Existing data augmentation relies on limited historical CVE data.

Method: CyberForge injects vulnerabilities into real C/C++ projects and dynamically validates each instance by (1) ensuring the injected build passes unit tests, and (2) verifying that a generated proof-of-vulnerability (PoV) triggers on the injected build but not the clean one. The framework is not limited by disclosed CVE availability, enabling scalability. Fine-tuning uses trajectories collected over this corpus across three model scales and two teachers.

Result: The corpus contains 1,034 validated vulnerabilities across 80 projects and 63 CWEs, with edit locality matching real CVE patches. Fine-tuning improves SEC-bench patch repair by +3.3 to +14.7 points across all six configurations. The 31B student reaches 72.7%, nearly matching its GPT-4o-mini teacher at 74.0%. Gains generalize to PatchEval (other languages), where the 31B student surpasses its teacher.

Conclusion: CyberForge demonstrates that synthesized, dynamically validated vulnerability data at scale effectively improves LLM-based defensive agents, closing the gap with attackers. The approach generalizes across model sizes, teachers, and even to unseen programming languages.

Abstract: Despite recent advances, frontier large language model (LLM) agents remain limited in discovering and patching complex vulnerabilities in real-world software. Generally available agents can already aid attackers, who only need to find one exploitable weakness, while defenders must continuously identify and patch all vulnerabilities across fast-growing codebases. Stronger defensive agents would help close this gap, yet the scarcity of security training data with reproducible build and execution environments remains a bottleneck.
  We present CyberForge, a framework that synthesizes executable, repository-level security training data by injecting vulnerabilities into real C/C++ projects. It validates each instance dynamically: the injected build must pass the project's unit tests, and generated proof-of-vulnerability (PoV) must trigger on the injected build and not on the clean one. CyberForge is not limited by the availability of disclosed vulnerabilities, therefore it can scale in comparison to data augmentation techniques which rely on historic CVE data. The resulting corpus holds 1034 validated vulnerabilities across 80 projects and 63 weakness categories, with edit locality similar to real CVE patches under a real-versus-real noise floor. Fine-tuning on trajectories collected over this corpus improves SEC-bench patch repair by +3.3 to +14.7 points, in all six configurations of three model scales and two teachers, with the 31B student reaching its GPT-5.4-mini teacher, 72.7% against 74.0%. These gains generalize out of distribution to PatchEval, a corpus containing other programming languages, where every configuration also improves and the 31B student passes its teacher.

</details>


### [279] [StepJack: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agent Safety Against Multi-Step Indirect Prompt Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06477)
*Zhuoxin Zhan,Akbar Rafiey,Avery Ma,Leila Pishdad,Layla El Asri*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: StepJack introduces multi-step indirect prompt injection, where adversarial goals are decomposed into innocuous sub-steps distributed across web pages, significantly raising attack success rates against state-of-the-art computer-use agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing indirect prompt injection attacks on CUAs typically deliver the full adversarial payload in a single step, making detection easier. The authors hypothesize that decomposing malicious goals into benign-looking sub-steps across multiple pages can evade safety mechanisms more effectively.

Method: An automated pipeline that decomposes an adversarial goal into multiple sub-steps under two constraints: (1) executing the sub-steps must achieve the original goal, and (2) each sub-step must be optimized for innocuousness. This pipeline is used to construct StepJack, a benchmark of 480 test examples, which is then used to evaluate six SOTA CUAs at varying decomposition depths.

Result: At fixed decomposition depth, multi-step attacks raised ASR on three of six CUAs by up to 31.2 points (GPT-5.4-mini: 41.7% single-step → 72.9% three-step). Averaged over five CUAs that reliably follow reference chains (excluding EvoCUA-32B), ASR rose from 31.3% (single-step) to 36.9% (three-step).

Conclusion: Multi-step indirect prompt injection poses a serious and under-explored threat to CUA safety. Distributing adversarial intent across innocuous sub-steps effectively bypasses existing defenses, highlighting the need for more robust, context-aware safety mechanisms in CUAs.

Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) face a growing threat from indirect prompt injection, where adversarial instructions are planted in the environment such as web pages. In this paper, we introduce multi-step indirect prompt injection, a new attack class against CUAs in which the adversarial goal is decomposed into multiple innocuous-looking sub-steps and distributed across a chain of pages referenced along the agent's navigation path. We develop a pipeline to automatically decompose an adversarial goal under the constraint that the execution of the decomposed sub-steps must achieve the original goal while optimizing the innocuousness of each decomposed sub-step. With this pipeline, we build StepJack, a CUA safety benchmark with 480 test examples. On this benchmark, we evaluate six state-of-the-art CUAs and find that at a fixed decomposition depth, multi-step attacks raise attack success rate (ASR) on three of six CUAs, by up to 31.2 points (e.g., GPT-5.4-mini: 41.7% at single-step to 72.9% at three-step); averaged over the five CUAs that can reliably follow the reference chain (all but EvoCUA-32B), ASR rises from 31.3% at single-step to 36.9% at three-step. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/BorealisAI/StepJack.

</details>


### [280] [Canonicalization Failures as a Recurring Vulnerability Class: Representation Divergence in Cryptographic Systems and Its Avoidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06508)
*Arslan Brömme*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper systematizes a cross-ecosystem class of vulnerabilities arising from ambiguous mappings between semantic objects and byte-level representations. The authors taxonomize the failure along two axes—multiple codes for one object and one code for multiple objects—and provide a preventive review methodology grounded in canonicalization and computability theory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The same fundamental vulnerability—failure to enforce unique representation—has been independently discovered and named across many cryptographic ecosystems (transaction malleability in Bitcoin, message malleability in TLS, non-deterministic encoding in various protocols) without recognition of a common root cause. This scattered knowledge impedes systematic prevention and cross-ecosystem learning.

Method: The authors conduct a systematization of knowledge: they collect and classify known malleability/representation incidents across ecosystems, unify them under a single violated condition (non-unique semantic-to-code mapping), and structure the problem along two directions—object-side multiple representation (multiple valid encodings for one semantic object) and code-side semantic collapse (one encoding interpretable as multiple objects). They then bridge this to classical canonicalization security literature and computability theory, and derive an operational review procedure comprising a canonicalization obligation, field-type classification, and an operational boundary model for preventive risk recognition.

Result: The paper demonstrates that disparate vulnerabilities across ecosystems are instances of a single failure class rooted in non-unique representation. It provides worked-out case studies, delimits the class from superficially similar but distinct incidents, and offers a structured review methodology applicable during system design to recognize and mitigate representation ambiguity risks before deployment.

Conclusion: Enforcing unique representation (canonicalization) can reduce exploitability of this failure class but is not a panacea—it neither replaces other protective measures nor constitutes a claim about cryptographic security in the narrow sense. The contribution lies in systematization, theoretical grounding, and translation into an actionable preventive procedure.

Abstract: Cryptographic systems operate on bytes but mean semantic objects. The translation between the two is rarely unique. Where this uniqueness is not enforced, an attack surface opens up as soon as a hash, a signature, replay protection, or consensus identity depends on the representation. The same class of failure has been discovered independently and named locally across many ecosystems, as transaction malleability, non-deterministic value encoding, message malleability, or hash chain malleability, without its common root being tracked as a cross-ecosystem grid. This work organizes the scattered findings systematically: it shows that they are instances of one violated uniqueness condition, along two basic directions: multiple valid codes for one object (object-side multiple representation) or one code for multiple objects (code-side semantic collapse). The contribution is explicitly not the discovery of the phenomenon, but is threefold: the systematization by representation mechanism rather than by affected system, the bridge between classical canonicalization security and a representation- and computability-theoretic foundation, and the translation into an applicable review procedure (a canonicalization obligation with a sequence of review steps, a field-type classification, and an operational boundary model) with which the risk can be recognized preventively. We substantiate the class with worked-out cases, delimit it against incidents that are not representation problems, and deliberately keep the claims to what is demonstrable: enforced uniqueness can reduce the exploitability of a failure class, but it neither replaces further protective measures or makes any statement about cryptographic security in the narrower sense

</details>


### [281] [Model Confidence Under Answer-Preserving Attacks: An Informativeness-Manipulability Frontier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06571)
*Reza Khanmohammadi,Ivan Brugere,Simerjot Kaur,Charese H. Smiley,Kundan Thind,Mohammad M. Ghassemi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Under white-box, image-only attacks that preserve answer strings, confidence readouts in vision-language models fail to provide robust oversight. Across all tested model-benchmark-estimator combinations, adversarial perturbations drive confidence discrimination below the answer-string accuracy prior, and transferred attacks cause up to 84.8% of previously rejected wrong answers to be accepted. Confidence is integrity-sensitive, not intrinsically robust.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployed vision-language systems often rely on confidence gating for oversight, accepting or rejecting answers based on confidence thresholds. The paper investigates whether such confidence readouts are adversarially robust, or whether they can be manipulated to undermine safety gating while preserving the surface-level answer string.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic empirical evaluation across 4 vision-language models, 3 VQA benchmarks, 5 confidence channels, and 2 defense estimators (84 estimator-by-cell combinations). They employ white-box, image-only attacks with an answer-preservation constraint. They introduce a formal framework including a reachability assumption, a uniform amplitude certificate threshold, and correctness-label-aware attacks. Additional experiments explore hidden-state interventions, open-ended text-model activation-space replication, and confidence-gated simulations with both direct and transferred attacks. Four defense families are tested.

Result: Under the reachability assumption, no unmovable readout outperforms the answer-string accuracy prior (pooled value 0.617). All 84 estimator-by-cell combinations violate the uniform amplitude certificate. Coordinated correctness-label-aware attacks drive adversarial discrimination to or below the answer-string floor in all 60 deployed-channel cells. A coordinated token-probability attack transferred to a hidden-state gate causes up to 84.8% of previously rejected wrong answers to become accepted. Post-reweighting, accepted accuracy falls below the no-gate baseline in 8/12 cells under transfer and 12/12 under direct gate-aimed attack. No defense family establishes robust alternatives.

Conclusion: Under the studied threat model and perturbation budget, confidence signals in vision-language models are integrity-sensitive rather than intrinsically robust. They should not be relied upon as a standalone oversight mechanism for safety gating, as adversaries can systematically manipulate confidence to defeat gating while preserving surface-level answer correctness.

Abstract: Deployed vision-language systems often gate their answers on confidence, making confidence robustness relevant to oversight. We study confidence readouts under white-box, image-only attacks constrained to preserve the generated answer byte-identically. Under a reachability assumption, an unmovable readout cannot outperform the answer-string accuracy prior, whose pooled value is 0.617. Independently of that assumption, a uniform amplitude certificate below a measurable threshold guarantees adversarial discrimination above the same floor. Across four vision-language models, three visual question answering benchmarks, five deployed confidence channels and two defense estimators, direct or surrogate-aimed attacks produce itemwise feasible perturbations that refute this uniform certificate in all 84 estimator-by-cell combinations. Coordinated correctness-label-aware attacks drive adversarial discrimination to or below the answer-string floor in all sixty deployed-channel cells, including all fifty-nine that begin above it. Hidden-state interventions and an open-ended text-model activation-space replication show that comparable confidence movement can be induced at the representation level rather than only through adversarial images. None of four tested defense families establishes a robust alternative under the specific evaluation applied to it. In a confidence-gated simulation, a coordinated token-probability attack transferred to a hidden-state gate causes up to 84.8% of previously rejected wrong answers to become accepted. After reweighting to each benchmark's natural correctness prevalence, accepted accuracy falls below the no-gate baseline in eight of twelve cells under transfer and all twelve under a direct gate-aimed attack. Under the studied threat model and budget, confidence is therefore an integrity-sensitive rather than intrinsically robust oversight signal.

</details>


### [282] [WhiteNet: Robust Identification of Overlapping IEEE 802.11 Signals Across Unseen Channels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06581)
*Ildi Alla,Vincent Lenders*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: WhiteNet introduces spectral whitening to counter channel variability in I/Q-based DL classifiers for overlapping IEEE 802.11 signals, and uses a synthetic overlap mixer with realistic per-transmitter channel modeling to reduce reliance on expensive over-the-air training data. It achieves strong accuracy under unseen channel conditions with 7.7× fewer parameters than prior work and supports distillation for edge deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning classifiers operating on I/Q samples for IEEE 802.11 protocol identification suffer severe accuracy degradation when deployment channel conditions differ from training conditions. Additionally, collecting diverse, multi-transmitter over-the-air training data is costly and impractical.

Method: WhiteNet employs (1) spectral whitening — a physics-based preprocessing step that suppresses frequency-selective fading while retaining protocol-discriminative features — and (2) a synthetic overlap mixer that models physically accurate per-transmitter channels and a shared-receiver signal chain, enabling effective pre-training without extensive field data collection. The framework also supports distillation into compact models for edge devices.

Result: On public over-the-air IEEE 802.11 datasets, WhiteNet closes a significant portion of the accuracy gap induced by unseen channel conditions, achieves this using 7.7× fewer parameters than the previous state-of-the-art, and can be distilled to compact variants suitable for power-constrained edge devices performing coarse spectrum awareness.

Conclusion: Spectral whitening combined with a physically accurate synthetic data generator offers an effective and parameter-efficient solution to the channel generalization problem in I/Q-based protocol identification, with practical paths to edge deployment via distillation.

Abstract: Deep learning (DL) classifiers trained on I/Q samples achieve high accuracy for IEEE 802.11 protocol identification of overlapping signals, but their performance degrades sharply when channel conditions at deployment differ from those encountered during training. We present WhiteNet, a framework that addresses the problem of channel variability in I/Q samples. The central idea is spectral whitening, a physics-grounded preprocessing step that suppresses frequency-selective fading while preserving protocol-discriminative features. To reduce dependence on costly multi-transmitter over-the-air captures for training, we complement it with a synthetic overlap mixer featuring a physically accurate per-transmitter channel and shared-receiver signal chain for pre-training without extensive field data collection. On public over-the-air IEEE 802.11 data, WhiteNet closes a substantial portion of the accuracy gap caused by unseen channel conditions while using 7.7 times fewer parameters than the prior state of the art, and optionally distills to compact variants for coarse spectrum awareness on power-constrained edge devices.

</details>


### [283] [From Documentation to Zero-day Vulnerabilities: LLM-Driven Fuzzing of JavaScript Engines in PDF Readers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06641)
*Suyue Guo,Stijn Pletinckx,Tianle Yu,Yigitcan Kaya,Saad Ullah,Wenbo Guo,Christopher Kruegel,Giovanni Vigna*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PDFuzzer is a novel PDF reader fuzzer that uses LLMs to construct context-free grammars and infer API call relationships from JavaScript API manuals and execution traces, then employs a constraint solver to generate complex API call sequences. It significantly outperforms existing fuzzers, achieving up to 48% higher coverage and discovering 31 zero-day vulnerabilities across three mainstream PDF readers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PDF reader fuzzers rely on simple test cases with individual API calls, resulting in limited code coverage and failure to uncover vulnerabilities that require multi-step API call sequences to trigger.

Method: PDFuzzer uses a multi-stage pipeline: (1) an LLM constructs context-free grammars and infers relationships between API calls from JavaScript API manual specifications and execution traces; (2) a constraint solver uses these grammars and relationships to generate concrete, semantically meaningful API call sequences for fuzzing.

Result: PDFuzzer achieves up to 48% higher coverage than state-of-the-art PDF fuzzers (TypeOracle, Favocado, Cooper) and LLM-based fuzzers (Fuzz4All, naive LLM). It found 31 zero-day vulnerabilities (ranging from information leakage to arbitrary code execution) in Adobe Acrobat Reader, Foxit PDF Reader, and PDF-XChange Editor. The LLM components achieve 93–98% accuracy across pipeline stages.

Conclusion: PDFuzzer demonstrates that LLM-guided grammar construction combined with constraint solving is a highly effective approach for generating complex API call sequences, substantially improving both coverage and vulnerability discovery in PDF readers. All vulnerabilities were responsibly disclosed, earning bug bounties.

Abstract: Existing fuzzers for PDF readers rely on simple test cases that involve only individual API calls, leading to limited coverage and potentially missing vulnerabilities that require sequences of API calls. To address these limitations, we propose PDFuzzer, a novel PDF engine fuzzer that automatically generates complex and meaningful API call sequences. PDFuzzer first uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to construct context-free grammars and infer the relationships between individual API calls from specifications extracted from JavaScript API manuals and execution traces. Based on the grammars and relationships, PDFuzzer employs a constraint solver to generate concrete API call sequences for fuzzing. Our experiments show that PDFuzzer significantly outperforms state-of-the-art PDF fuzzers (TypeOracle, Favocado, and Cooper) and LLM-based fuzzers (Fuzz4All, naive LLM) on three mainstream PDF readers: Adobe Acrobat Reader, Foxit PDF Reader, and PDF-XChange Editor. PDFuzzer achieves up to 48% higher coverage than existing tools and identifies 31 zero-day vulnerabilities in these readers, from information leakage to arbitrary code execution. Our ablation study validates the necessity of each component, including LLMs, which achieve high accuracy across all pipeline stages (93-98%). We disclosed all vulnerabilities to the vendors via a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process and received bug bounties.

</details>


### [284] [CyberLLM: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Autonomous Detection and Guarded Response in Automotive Cybersecurity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06651)
*Nenad Petrovic,Oussama Jeddou,Feres Ben Fraj,Vahid Zolfaghari,Fengjunjie Pan,Andre Schamschurko,Alois Knoll*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: CyberLLM is a multi-agent LLM framework for Software-Defined Vehicles that autonomously detects vulnerabilities and executes remediations under formal runtime safety guards. It combines deterministic detectors with LLM refinement, achieving ~70% vulnerability coverage with zero false positives, demonstrating that LLM agents can safely perform autonomous cyber-defense when constrained by an auditable safety envelope.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SDVs expand the automotive attack surface across source code, runtime logs, and deployment topologies, but safety constraints prohibit autonomous agents from acting without oversight. The gap is a system that can autonomously detect and remediate vulnerabilities while respecting strict automotive safety requirements.

Method: A multi-agent, LLM-orchestrated framework combining: (1) a deterministic detection layer (regex, AST analyzers, topology graph checks) providing high-recall floor; (2) LLM refinement for high-precision reasoning; (3) a decision agent that aggregates findings, applies a human-centric asset taxonomy, and selects tiered responses using signed cross-session memory and re-planning feedback; (4) a formal safety guard validating every action against four contextual security properties and an independent action-alignment oracle, with escalation on refusal; (5) a symmetric attack pipeline for generating and replaying exploits. Evaluated on nine automotive ECU modules in C, C++, and Rust with 47 layered vulnerabilities plus clean controls.

Result: The deterministic layer alone covers 34% of labeled vulnerabilities at perfect precision. Adding grounded LLM refinement and completeness passes roughly doubles coverage to ~70% (F1 score of 0.83) while producing zero false positives on clean controls.

Conclusion: LLM agents can perform useful autonomous cyber-defense when wrapped in a deterministic, auditable safety envelope, making them viable for safety-critical automotive contexts.

Abstract: Software-Defined Vehicles (SDVs) expand the automotive attack surface across source code, runtime logs, and deployment topologies, while safety constraints forbid autonomous agents from acting without oversight. This paper presents CyberLLM, a multi-agent, LLM-orchestrated framework that autonomously detects vulnerabilities and executes remediations under a formal, runtime safety guard. Detection combines a deterministic layer (regex rules, AST analyzers, and topology graph checks) with an LLM refinement pass, so a high-recall floor is complemented by high-precision reasoning. A decision agent aggregates findings, tags them with a human-centric asset taxonomy, and selects a tiered response, ratcheting its confidence with signed cross-session memory and re-planning feedback. Every action is validated against four contextual security properties and an independent action-alignment oracle before it is allowed to run, and refused actions trigger escalation and re-planning. A symmetric attack pipeline generates and replays exploits so both sides can be exercised on the same scenarios. On an independent, ground-truthed benchmark of nine original automotive ECU modules in C, C++, and Rust seeding 47 layered vulnerabilities plus clean controls, the always-on deterministic layer covers 34\% of the labeled vulnerabilities at perfect precision, and adding the grounded LLM refinement and completeness passes roughly doubles coverage to about 70\% (F1 $0.83$) while producing zero false positives on the clean controls. The results indicate that LLM agents can perform useful autonomous cyber-defense when wrapped in a deterministic, auditable safety envelope.

</details>


### [285] [Policy-Masked Private Experts: Auditable and Reversible Capability Access Control in Sparse MoE Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06690)
*Zhuoheng Huang,Mukesh Singh*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Policy-Masked Private Experts (PMPE) freezes a pretrained MoE model, trains a disjoint private expert branch, and uses trusted authorization to select between public/private pools before top-k routing. The paper demonstrates that unauthorized requests execute zero private experts under the declared TCB, while the private branch yields measurable utility gains on downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LM access controls regulate behavior but leave the same computation accessible to all requests. The authors explore a systems-level question: can trusted authorization deterministically gate access to newly trained parameters, ensuring that unauthorized requests never execute private computation paths?

Method: PMPE freezes a pretrained sparse MoE model and trains a disjoint private expert branch. A trusted authorization layer selects between the public expert pool and the private expert pool before the top-k routing decision. The public model remains frozen and fingerprint-unchanged. The approach is tested on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeek-V2-Lite across multiple seeds. Evaluation spans adversarial scenarios, deny/fail-closed events, tool-use benchmarks, and comparisons against LoRA with a post-hoc request gate.

Result: Across 64 adversarial scenarios and 96 deny/fail-closed events, unauthorized private execution is zero. Independent hooks confirm exact matching of all 11,616 routed private rows. Private branch improves exact tool use by 5.0 pp (Holm p=0.03125) and 21.3 pp (95% CI [13.3, 29.3], Holm p=0.000031) on Qwen benchmarks. Arm-blinded evaluators show 18.7 pp positive external effect (95% CI [9.3, 28.0]). Parameter-matched LoRA has similar utility but leaks 1,225 adapter calls under deny; PMPE leaves none. DeepSeek reproduces the route invariant with 27.0 pp gain. Sealed evaluation is near-neutral.

Conclusion: PMPE provides auditable, reversible control over trained parameter paths with strong execution guarantees under the declared TCB. Useful transfer from the private branch is distribution-dependent, demonstrating a viable separation between execution-level access control and task utility in MoE architectures.

Abstract: Most language-model access controls regulate behavior while leaving the same computation available to every request. We study a different systems question: can trusted authorization determine which newly trained parameters are reachable by the forward pass? Policy-Masked Private Experts freezes a pretrained sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, trains a disjoint expert branch, and selects the public or private pool before top-k routing. The resulting claim is narrow but testable: under the declared trusted computing base (TCB), an unauthorized request executes no private expert. It does not imply that the public model lacks the same semantic capability.
  We test this separation between execution control and task utility in Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Three Qwen BF16 seeds update all 32 private experts while the public fingerprint remains unchanged. Across 64 adversarial scenarios and 96 deny/fail-closed events, unauthorized private execution is zero; independent hooks exactly match 11,616 routed private rows and allow-deny-allow recovery is exact. On two prospectively frozen Qwen benchmarks, the private branch improves exact tool use by 5.0 percentage points (pp) (five versus zero discordances; one-sided Holm p = 0.03125, corresponding two-sided exact p = 0.0625) and 21.3 pp (percentile-bootstrap 95% CI [13.3, 29.3], Holm p = 0.000031). Three arm-blinded model evaluators retain a positive external effect of 18.7 pp (95% CI [9.3, 28.0]). A parameter-matched Lora has similar external utility, but a post-hoc request gate leaves 1,225 adapter calls under deny; the disjoint expert branch leaves none. DeepSeek reproduces the route invariant and gains 27.0 pp. A valid sealed evaluation is near-neutral. These results support auditable, reversible control over a trained parameter path, while showing that useful transfer remains distribution dependent.

</details>


### [286] [Tight Security for BBS Signatures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06724)
*Rutchathon Chairattana-Apirom,Dennis Hofheinz,Stefano Tessaro*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper investigates the tightness of security reductions for BBS signatures, providing both a positive result (a tight reduction to q-SDH under single-signature-per-message constraints) and a negative result (no tight algebraic reduction to q-SDH exists when multiple signatures per message are allowed).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BBS signatures are widely used in privacy-preserving authentication and are undergoing standardization. While BBS+ has a tight security proof, the more efficient BBS scheme lacks one. Understanding whether this tightness gap is inherent is critical for guiding standardization and industry adoption.

Method: The authors provide a two-pronged approach: (1) a constructive tight reduction for BBS under the q-SDH assumption when each message is signed at most once (covering derandomized signing), and (2) a meta-reduction argument proving that no algebraic reduction to q-SDH (or its variants) can be tight when multiple signatures per message are permitted.

Result: A tight reduction for BBS is established in the single-signature-per-message setting. Conversely, for the multi-signature-per-message setting, any algebraic reduction to q-SDH is provably non-tight, establishing a fundamental barrier.

Conclusion: The tightness gap between BBS and BBS+ is partially inherent: tightness is achievable under practical constraints (single signing per message), but impossible in the general multi-signature case under algebraic reductions to q-SDH.

Abstract: This paper studies the concrete security of BBS signatures (Boneh, Boyen, Shacham, CRYPTO '04; Camenisch and Lysyanskaya, CRYPTO '04), a popular algebraic construction of digital signatures which underlies practical privacy-preserving authentication systems and is undergoing standardization by the W3C and IRTF.
  Schäge (Journal of Cryptology '15) gave a tight standard-model security proof under the q-SDH assumption for a less efficient variant of the scheme, called BBS+--here, q is the number of issued signatures. In contrast, the security proof for BBS (Tessaro and Zhu, EUROCRYPT '23), also under the q-SDH assumption, is \emph{not} tight. Nonetheless, this recent proof shifted both standardization and industry adoption towards the more efficient BBS, instead of BBS+, and for this reason, it is important to understand whether this tightness gap is inherent. Recent cryptanalysis by Chairattana-Apirom and Tessaro (ASIACRYPT '25) also shows that a tight reduction to q-SDH is the best we can hope for.
  This paper closes this gap in two different ways. On the positive end, we show a novel tight reduction for BBS in the case where each message is signed at most once--this case covers in particular the common practical use case which derandomizes signing. On the negative end, we use a meta-reduction argument to prove that if we allow generating multiple signatures for the same message, then {\em no} algebraic reduction to q-SDH (and its variants) can be tight.

</details>


### [287] [Retrieval-Constrained Policy Optimization for Attack Technique Extraction from Cyber Threat Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06778)
*Jiayun Zhang,Junshen Xu,Zejun Xie,Yi Fan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TTP-R1 is a two-stage framework for mapping CTI text to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, combining retrieval-augmented SFT with reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards (RLVR). It uses a hybrid retriever to narrow the label space and a fine-tuned LLM with Group Relative Policy Optimization that directly optimizes precision, recall, and format — achieving state-of-the-art F1, outperforming Claude Sonnet 4.5 by 7.4 points while being 28x faster on a single GPU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual annotation of CTI text to MITRE ATT&CK techniques is expensive and unscalable. Existing multi-label classifiers suffer from class imbalance and large label spaces, while LLM-based methods (retrieval pipelines and fine-tuned generators) treat technique annotation as token-level sequence generation rather than set prediction, lacking direct supervision on whether the predicted technique set is correct and complete.

Method: A two-stage framework: (1) A hybrid retriever narrows the large ATT&CK label space to a candidate set, and a fine-tuned LLM is trained via retrieval-augmented SFT to select correct techniques. (2) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is applied with a decomposed reward function that directly supervises precision, recall, and output format of the predicted technique set, enabling RLVR-based set-level optimization.

Result: TTP-R1 achieves the best average F1 across four CTI benchmarks. It improves sub-technique-level F1 by 7.4 percentage points over retrieval-augmented Claude Sonnet 4.5, while running 28x faster when served as an 8B-parameter model on a single GPU.

Conclusion: Combining retrieval-augmented SFT with RLVR that directly optimizes set-level metrics (precision, recall, format) yields significant gains over both traditional multi-label classifiers and token-optimized LLM methods. The approach is also computationally efficient, enabling strong performance from relatively small models deployed on a single GPU.

Abstract: Mapping cyber threat intelligence (CTI) text to MITRE ATT&CK techniques is essential for structured threat analysis, yet manual annotation is costly and does not scale. The ATT&CK taxonomy comprises several hundred attack techniques, and a single CTI passage may describe multiple techniques, making accurate and complete extraction challenging. Existing automated approaches fall short in different ways: multi-label classifiers struggle with severe class imbalance and the large label space, while LLM-based methods--retrieval pipelines and fine-tuned generators--optimize token-level objectives that treat technique annotation as sequence generation rather than set prediction, lacking direct supervision on whether the predicted technique set is correct and complete. We propose TTP-R1, a two-stage framework that combines retrieval-augmented supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards (RLVR). A hybrid retriever first narrows the large label space to a candidate set, and a fine-tuned LLM learns to select the correct techniques. We then apply Group Relative Policy Optimization with a decomposed reward that directly supervises the precision, recall, and output format of the predicted technique set. Across four CTI benchmarks, TTP-R1 achieves the best average F1, improving sub-technique-level F1 by 7.4 percentage points over Claude Sonnet 4.5 with retrieval augmentation, while running 28x faster when served as an 8B-parameter model on a single GPU.

</details>


### [288] [LoRAScan: Detecting Backdoor Prompts in Low-Rank Adapters for Large Language Models via Down-Projection Activation Spikes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06795)
*Doniyorkhon Obidov,Honggang Yu,Xiaolong Guo,Kaichen Yang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: LoRAScan is the first adapter-aware defense that detects and rejects backdoor trigger inputs at inference time by monitoring activation spikes at a small subset (~5%) of low-variance LoRA insertion sites, achieving ~98.49% rejection of malicious inputs without modifying adapter parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Untrusted LoRA adapters pose a supply-chain threat where backdoored adapters can trigger harmful outputs. Existing defenses are either adapter-agnostic (merging adapter with base model, diluting detection signals) or adapter-aware but misaligned with the problem — they either repair a backdoored base model (inverse problem) or flag entire adapters as suspicious without addressing safe usage. None exploit the distinct latent-space signatures that trigger-bearing inputs produce in backdoored adapters.

Method: LoRAScan identifies a small subset (~5%) of LoRA insertion sites that exhibit low variance across clean inputs but show concentrated activation spikes in down-projection layers when triggers are present. Before deployment, it profiles these low-variance sites offline. At inference time, it monitors these sites and rejects inputs whose activation patterns deviate from the expected clean distribution, without modifying adapter parameters.

Result: LoRAScan rejects approximately 98.49% of malicious inputs with a small clean-input error rate, outperforming existing defenses across standard LLM backdoor benchmarks and diverse evaluation settings.

Conclusion: LoRAScan provides a practical, parameter-preserving defense against backdoored LoRA adapters by exploiting activation-level signatures, enabling safe inference-time detection without requiring adapter modification or retraining.

Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient specialization and distribution of large language models through compact adapters. However, untrusted adapters introduce a supply-chain threat: a backdoored adapter can cause a model to generate harmful content, malicious code, political propaganda, or covert advertisements when an input contains a hidden trigger. Adapter-agnostic defenses merge the adapter with the base model, which dilutes backdoor signals and reduces detection performance. Existing adapter-aware methods do not address how to safely use a potentially backdoored adapter. Instead, they either train a defensive adapter to repair a backdoored base model, addressing the inverse problem rather than securing the adapter itself, or rely on a classifier that flags the entire adapter as suspicious and requires separate mitigation. These methods overlook the distinct latent-space signatures produced by trigger-bearing inputs in backdoored adapters.
  We introduce LoRAScan, the first adapter-aware defense that detects and rejects trigger-bearing inputs at inference time without modifying adapter parameters. Our key observation is that a small subset of LoRA insertion sites, approximately 5%, remains stable across clean inputs but exhibits highly concentrated spikes in LoRA down-projection activations when a trigger is present. LoRAScan identifies these low-variance insertion sites before model deployment and monitors them during inference. Across standard LLM backdoor benchmarks, LoRAScan rejects approximately 98.49 of malicious inputs with a small error rate on clean inputs, outperforming existing defenses across diverse evaluation settings.

</details>


### [289] [On a General Theoretical Framework for Radio Frequency Fingerprint-Based Authentication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06805)
*Yuanyu Zhang,Jianing Wang,Shuangrui Zhao,Pinchang Zhang,Yulong Shen,Xiaohong Jiang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a general theoretical framework that integrates RFF modeling with authentication property analysis to explain why and how radio frequency fingerprints can serve as reliable device identities, examining trustworthiness through uniqueness, stability, distinguishability, and unforgeability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite extensive empirical studies on RFF-based wireless device authentication across various datasets and scenarios, the field lacks a fundamental theory explaining the underlying mechanisms of RFF reliability. This theoretical gap significantly impedes practical deployment and adoption of RFF authentication technology.

Method: The authors propose a two-part theoretical framework: (1) RFF modeling process — traces how fingerprints are induced, evolved, and observed along the transmitter-channel-receiver chain; (2) authentication property analysis — evaluates RFF trustworthiness through four criteria: uniqueness, stability, distinguishability, and unforgeability. These processes are integrated by linking RFF formation/evolution directly to the authentication properties.

Result: The framework establishes a solid theoretical foundation demonstrating how and why RFF-based authentication can be trustworthy in practice, and provides theoretical insights that inform communication-authentication co-design strategies.

Conclusion: The proposed framework bridges the critical theory-practice gap in RFF authentication, offering systematic guidance for developing, evaluating, and co-designing trustworthy RFF-based device authentication systems in real-world deployments.

Abstract: While radio frequency fingerprint (RFF)-based wireless device authentication has been widely studied across different datasets and scenarios, there still lacks a fundamental theory to explain why and how RFF can serve as a reliable device identity, significantly hindering the practical application of such an authentication technology. In this article, we integrate the RFF modeling with authentication property analysis to propose a general theoretical framework to facilitate the development of such a theory. The RFF modeling process reveals how RFFs are induced, evolved and observed along the transmitter-channel-receiver chain, built upon which, the authentication property analysis process then outlines how the trustworthiness of an RFF should be examined in terms of its uniqueness, stability, distinguishability, and unforgeability. By linking the RFF formation/evolution to these authentication properties, the framework offers a solid foundation for understanding why and how RFF-based authentication is trustworthy in practice. We also discuss the communication-authentication co-design issue based on the theoretical insights from the proposed framework.

</details>


### [290] [POKEx: Performance analysis of POKE-key exchange and SIDH-variants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06826)
*Hyeonhak Kim,Suhri Kim*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A comparative performance analysis showing that a POKE-based key exchange mechanism (KEM) significantly outperforms SIDH variants like terSIDH (21× faster) and CSIDH (65× faster) at NIST security level 1, positioning it as the leading isogeny-based key exchange candidate post-SIDH's cryptanalytic break.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Following the 2022 Castryck-Decru polynomial-time key recovery attack that broke SIDH, the isogeny-based cryptography community proposed countermeasure variants (MSIDH, MD-SIDH, bin/terSIDH), but these suffer from performance limitations. The authors aim to evaluate whether the newly proposed POKE scheme (Eurocrypt 2025), which combines SIDH-like protocols with higher-dimensional isogenies, can serve as a more efficient and practical alternative for key exchange.

Method: The authors adapt the POKE public-key encryption scheme (Basso & Maino, Eurocrypt 2025) into a key exchange/KEM protocol. They then conduct a comparative benchmarking study against M-SIDH, terSIDH, and CSIDH, targeting NIST security level 1, measuring relative speedup factors.

Result: At NIST security level 1, the POKE-based KEM is approximately 21.21× faster than terSIDH and 64.97× faster than CSIDH, establishing it as the most performant isogeny-based key exchange candidate currently available.

Conclusion: POKE-based key exchange is the most promising isogeny-based KEM candidate at present, offering substantial performance improvements over existing SIDH variants and post-quantum isogeny schemes like CSIDH.

Abstract: In this paper, we present a comparative performance analysis of the POKE-based key exchange and SIDH variants. SIDH gained attention for its small key size and efficient performance, and has been selected as an alternate candidate in NIST PQC Round 4. However, following the key recovery attack by Castryck and Decru in 2022, SIDH was shown to be vulnerable to polynomial-time attacks on classical computers, undermining its security and removing it from consideration. Given that SIDH was regarded as the leading isogeny-based algorithm, several countermeasures, such as MSIDH, MD-SIDH, and bin/terSIDH have been proposed. However, these approaches still face performance limitations. Meanwhile, POKE, proposed by Basso and Maino at Eurocrypt 2025, is an isogeny-based public key encryption scheme that combines a SIDH-like protocol with higher-dimensional isogenies and has drawn attention for its efficient performance. In this work, we adapt POKE into a key exchange algorithm and benchmark it against M-SIDH, terSIDH, and CSIDH. Targeting NIST security level 1, POKE-based KEM is approximately 21.21 times faster than terSIDH and 64.97 times faster than CSIDH, showing that the POKE-based KEM is currently the most promising isogeny-based key exchange candidate.

</details>


### [291] [MIFA: An MILP-based Framework for Improving Differential Fault Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06837)
*Hanbeom Shin,Insung Kim,Sunyeop Kim,Byoungjin Seok,Deukjo Hong,Jaechul Sung,Seokhie Hong,Sangjin Lee,Dongjae Lee*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A new DFA framework using MILP solvers enables deeper round attacks on DEFAULT and BAKSHEESH ciphers, reducing the number of fault injections required for key recovery. Systematic analysis of fault bit positions allows theoretical calculation of the required number of faults.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior DFA attacks on DEFAULT (Baksi et al., Nageler et al., Jana et al.) either required many faults or could not reach deep rounds. The authors aim to develop a more powerful DFA framework that reduces the number of fault injections and reaches deeper rounds than previously possible.

Method: The authors propose a DFA framework based on Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) to model differential propagation under faults. They systematically analyze input differences from all possible single bit-flip faults to identify optimal fault injection positions, enabling theoretical calculation of the required number of faults.

Result: For DEFAULT, injecting 3 faults at the sixth-to-last round and 2 faults at the seventh- and eighth-to-last rounds reduces the key space to one. This significantly improves upon prior results requiring 5 faults at the fifth-to-last round (Jana et al., ASIACRYPT 2024).

Conclusion: The MILP-based DFA framework enables attacks on deeper rounds with fewer faults and provides a systematic, theoretically grounded method for determining optimal fault injection positions.

Abstract: At ASIACRYPT 2021, Baksi et al. introduced DEFAULT, a block cipher designed to algorithmically resist Differential Fault Attack (DFA), claiming 64-bit DFA security regardless of the number of injected faults. At EUROCRYPT 2022, Nageler et al. demonstrated that DEFAULT's claimed DFA resistance can be broken by applying an information-combining technique. More recently, at ASIACRYPT 2024, Jana et al. improved DFA by searching for differential trails with a single solution. They showed that, for DEFAULT with a simple key schedule, injecting five faults at the fifth-to-last round reduces the key space to one, and for BAKSHEESH, injecting twelve faults at the third-to-last round achieves the same result. In this paper, we propose a new DFA framework that utilizes a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver. This framework makes it possible to attack deeper rounds than previously achieved, reducing the number of fault injections required for key recovery. Furthermore, we present a method to determine the most efficient fault injection bit positions by systematically analyzing the input differences from all possible single bit-flip faults, thereby further reducing the required number of faults. This systematic analysis has the significant advantage of allowing us to theoretically calculate the required number of faults. Applying our framework, for DEFAULT, injecting three faults at the sixth-to-last round and two faults at the seventh- and eighth-to-last rounds reduces the key space to one.

</details>


### [292] [Understanding and Improving Model Editing for Secure Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06848)
*Weifeng Sun,Quanjun Zhang,Yuchen Chen,Chengran Yang,Gou Tan,David Lo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper is the first systematic study of model editing as a hardening mechanism for secure code generation. The authors find that model editing improves security on seen vulnerabilities by 15-25% but transfers poorly to unseen vulnerabilities and harms functional correctness. They propose SafeEdit, a post-edit refinement combining functional tuning with edit-aware regularization, which recovers correctness while preserving security gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs reproduce vulnerable code from insecure training patterns. Existing inference-time hardening (e.g., CoSec) reduces insecure generations but adds runtime overhead and relies on auxiliary components. No prior work has systematically studied model editing—a model-level intervention that directly modifies weights—for secure code generation, leaving open questions about its effectiveness, robustness, generalization, and impact on functional correctness.

Method: The authors evaluate three state-of-the-art model editing methods (including UltraEdit) across diverse LLM families and benchmark them against CoSec, an inference-time approach. They then propose SafeEdit, a post-edit refinement method that combines functional correctness tuning with an edit-aware regularization term to mitigate the security-correctness trade-off. SafeEdit is complementary to CoSec and can be combined for further gains.

Result: Model editing yields 15-25% higher security ratios over vanilla models on seen vulnerabilities, with stability under prompt perturbations, but transfers unreliably to unseen vulnerabilities and reduces functional correctness. SafeEdit improves Pass@1 over UltraEdit by 11.73/13.70/15.50 pp at temperatures 0.1/0.4/0.8 while largely preserving security. Relative to CoSec, SafeEdit achieves 7.54-12.04% relative security-ratio gains. Combined SafeEdit+CoSec further improves security while maintaining correctness. CodeGuard+ evaluation confirms improved joint secure-and-correct generation.

Conclusion: Model editing is a viable model-level hardening mechanism for secure code generation, offering stronger security gains than inference-time methods on seen vulnerabilities. SafeEdit effectively mitigates the security-correctness trade-off, and its complementarity with CoSec provides a path toward jointly optimized secure and correct code generation. The work provides evidence-backed guidance for applying model editing in this domain.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for code generation, yet they can reproduce vulnerable implementations learned from insecure training patterns. Prior work has mainly explored inference-time hardening, which reduces insecure generations without modifying the target model but relies on auxiliary components and adds runtime overhead. We conduct the first systematic study of model editing as a model-level hardening mechanism for secure code generation. We evaluate 3 state-of-the-art editing methods across diverse LLM families and compare them with CoSec, a representative inference-time approach, focusing on security, robustness, generalization, and functional correctness. Model editing yields larger security gains than CoSec on seen vulnerability types, improving security ratios by 15%-25% over vanilla models, with gains remaining stable under prompt perturbations. However, these improvements transfer unreliably to unseen vulnerabilities and can reduce functional correctness. To mitigate this trade-off, we propose SafeEdit, a post-edit refinement method combining functional tuning with edit-aware regularization. Across eight target LLMs, SafeEdit improves Pass@1 over UltraEdit by 11.73/13.70/15.50 percentage points at T=0.1/0.4/0.8 while largely preserving security. Compared with CoSec, it achieves relative security-ratio gains of 7.54%-12.04%. Additional evaluation on CodeGuard+ confirms improved joint secure-and-correct generation. SafeEdit and CoSec are also complementary, and their combination can further improve security while maintaining strong functional correctness. Overall, our results provide evidence-backed guidance for applying model editing to secure code generation.

</details>


### [293] [SynChain: Inducing Computer-Use Agent Systems to Construct Their Own Attack Chains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06862)
*Fuyao Zhang,Jiaming Zhang,Che Wang,Boyang Chen,Yurong Hao,Xiongtao Sun,Guowei Guan,Blaise Delattre,Yang Cao,Wei Yang Bryan Lim*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces SynChain, an attack paradigm where malicious influence is covertly embedded into autonomously synthesized artifacts (skills, memory) of computer-use agents. The attack survives internal state updates and bypasses standard vetting, reactivating dormant payloads in future workflows without new exogenous inputs. A dataset called CUAChain (30 benign task chains, 3 attack objectives) is built, and experiments on OpenClaw, Codex, and Claude Code show high attack success across four defense settings, demonstrating the need for provenance-aware reasoning over cross-task execution trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing security defenses for computer-use agents (CUAs) treat attacks as externally triggered or temporally bounded, overlooking how compromise can propagate internally through an agent's own persistent state (e.g., self-generated skills and memory artifacts). The authors aim to reveal and formalize this overlooked threat surface where structural redundancies in synthesized artifacts enable covert, persistent malicious influence.

Method: The authors propose SynChain, a self-synthesized attack paradigm that uses persistence-aware directed supervised fine-tuning (DSFT) to induce agents to create poisoned yet benign-appearing artifacts. They construct CUAChain, a dataset of 30 benign task chains across three attack objectives, and evaluate across three agent platforms (OpenClaw, Codex, Claude Code) under four defense settings to measure attack success and propagation.

Result: SynChain achieves high attack success rates across all tested platforms (OpenClaw, Codex, Claude Code) and outperforms adapted baselines. Dormant payloads reactivate in future workflows using only trusted internal context, and the attack proves robust across four distinct defense settings, revealing that current defenses are insufficient against persistent, self-propagating internal compromise.

Conclusion: Securing computer-use agents requires provenance-aware reasoning over cross-task execution trajectories. Standard defenses that rely on external trigger detection or temporal bounding are inadequate against internally propagating compromise embedded in persistent agent state.

Abstract: Computer-use agents~(CUAs) have transformed large language models into persistent execution systems capable of generating, storing, and reusing artifacts like skills and memory entries. However, existing security defenses largely treat attacks as externally triggered or temporally bounded, leaving a critical gap in addressing how compromise can propagate internally through an agent's own persistent state. We reveal that malicious influence can be covertly embedded into the structural redundancies of autonomously synthesized artifacts, allowing it to survive internal state updates and bypass standard vetting mechanisms. To formalize this threat, we introduce SynChain, a self-synthesized attack paradigm utilizing persistence-aware directed supervised fine-tuning to induce agents to create poisoned yet benign-looking artifacts. To systematically evaluate this propagation, we construct CUAChain, a dataset comprising 30 benign task chains and three attack objectives. SynChain enables dormant payloads to seamlessly reactivate in future workflows as trusted context, operating entirely without new malicious exogenous inputs. Extensive experiments on OpenClaw, Codex, and Claude Code under four defense settings demonstrate that SynChain achieves high attack success and outperforms adapted baselines, proving that securing CUAs requires provenance-aware reasoning over cross-task execution trajectories.

</details>


### [294] [Rigid-Covert GNSS Spoofing of UAV Swarms: A Structural Blind Spot, Its Detection Limit, and Absolute-Anchor Defenses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06885)
*Minseok Park,Joon Soo Yoo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A rigid translation shift (RigidShift) applied to all drones in a swarm preserves inter-drone distances, making it invisible to relative-geometry-only GNSS spoofing detectors. The paper derives detection limits, proposes an anchor-rooted recovery pipeline with Byzantine-robust fitting, and validates recovery to ~0.39 m median error under ~10 m GNSS drift in simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cooperative UAV swarms rely on cross-checking GNSS positions against inter-drone ranging measurements to detect spoofing. The authors identify a fundamental structural blind spot: a common rigid translation preserves all pairwise distances and is thus unobservable to any detector that uses only relative geometry. This gauge-freedom vulnerability means a coordinated spoofing attack can shift the entire swarm's position undetected by relative-only schemes.

Method: The paper formally characterizes the gauge-freedom blind spot (RigidShift) and validates it against distance-verification and semidefinite-feasibility baselines. It derives a drift-dependent detection floor, 2γ/(1−tₛ/T), for a calibrated anchor-residual detector. The main contribution is a centralized anchor-rooted recovery pipeline: (1) reconstruct swarm geometry from inter-drone ranges, (2) align to a trusted-anchor subset using Byzantine-robust fitting, (3) recover absolute positions of non-anchored drones. A segmented estimator jointly infers anchor drift, attack rate, and onset without clean-epoch labels. Evaluation spans statistical simulations, ArduPilot SITL, and Gazebo experiments with rendered vision anchors.

Result: Median position recovery error for non-anchored drones: 0.39 m under ~10.1 m GNSS drift (20 seeds, statistical simulation) and 7.1 cm in rendered-vision multi-SITL (5 seeds). Empirically measured noise-floor slope (2.66) matches predicted value (2.67). Limitations characterized: non-collinear anchor geometry, anchor coverage, τ→0 drift-attack aliasing, and majority anchor compromise.

Conclusion: Relative-geometry-based GNSS spoofing detection in UAV swarms has an inherent gauge-freedom blind spot. An external reference (trusted anchors) is required to restore absolute position observability. The proposed anchor-rooted recovery pipeline effectively reconstructs swarm positions, though all evaluations remain simulation-based without physical RF spoofing or hardware validation.

Abstract: Cooperative UAV-swarm defenses commonly cross-check GNSS positions against measured inter-drone geometry. We show that this relative-geometry channel has a structural blind spot: a common, slowly varying translation (a rigid-covert shift, RigidShift) preserves all pairwise distances and is therefore unobservable to any relative-only detector (a gauge-freedom argument). We validate this blindness on distance-verification and semidefinite-feasibility baselines, while explicitly distinguishing it from onboard inertial/GNSS monitors that can raise a bare alarm but cannot recover the swarm's true position. To quantify when an external reference restores observability, we derive the drift-dependent detection floor $2γ/(1-t_s/T)$ for a calibrated anchor-residual detector and empirically identify an additional detector-specific noise floor (measured slope 2.66 vs. predicted 2.67). We then present a centralized anchor-rooted recovery pipeline that reconstructs swarm geometry from inter-drone ranges, aligns it to a trusted-anchor subset with Byzantine-robust fitting, and recovers the absolute positions of non-anchored drones. A segmented estimator jointly estimates anchor drift, attack rate, and onset when no clean-epoch label is available. Across statistical simulations, ArduPilot software-in-the-loop experiments, and Gazebo experiments with rendered vision anchors, the method recovers the positions of non-anchored drones to a median error of 0.39 m (20 seeds) under approximately 10.1 m of GNSS drift, and to 7.1 cm (5 seeds) in the rendered-vision multi-SITL setting. We also characterize the explicit limits imposed by non-collinear anchor geometry, anchor coverage, $τ\to0$ drift-attack aliasing, and majority anchor compromise. All evaluations are simulation-based and use no RF spoofing hardware or physical swarm.

</details>


### [295] [When Context Bites: Detecting RAG Poisoning via Document-Level Attention Collapse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06947)
*Yingtao Ren,Ziyi Zhao,Yiwei Fu,Xiao Luo,Yu-Cheng Chang,Chin-Teng Lin*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: RAG systems are vulnerable to poisoning attacks that manipulate outputs. The authors identify a phenomenon called "Attention Collapse" where attacked generations show concentrated attention entropy on poisoned documents, and propose D-SCAN, a lightweight detection framework that monitors attention dynamics to identify such attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG poisoning detection methods using output-side signals (perplexity, consistency checks) are ineffective because adversarial attacks can induce "false confidence" — poisoned outputs exhibiting even lower perplexity than benign ones, rendering uncertainty-based detection useless.

Method: The authors analyze internal generator dynamics and discover "Attention Collapse": a signature where attention entropy decreases as attention concentrates on poisoned documents, contrasting with the dispersed attention in benign generations. Based on this, they propose D-SCAN (Document-level Signal Collapse Analysis), a lightweight detection framework that monitors attention dynamics to flag attacked generations.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple attack benchmarks demonstrate D-SCAN's effectiveness. Notably, it can detect attacks even when they fail to alter the final answer output.

Conclusion: Monitoring internal attention dynamics (specifically Attention Collapse) provides a robust signal for detecting RAG poisoning attacks, overcoming the limitations of output-side, uncertainty-based detection methods.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is indispensable for enhancing large language models. However, RAGs are increasingly susceptible to poisoning attacks, in which adversarial documents are injected to manipulate generator outputs. Previous methods rely on output-side signals such as perplexity and consistency checks to detect such attacks. Nevertheless, our analysis reveals that deliberate attacks often induce false confidence, where poisoned outputs exhibit even lower perplexity than benign ones, rendering uncertainty-based detection ineffective. To address this challenge, we explore the internal dynamics of the generator and identify a distinctive signature termed \textit{Attention Collapse}. Unlike the dispersed attention in benign generations, attacked generations exhibit a decrease in entropy as attention concentrates on poisoned documents. Building on these findings, we propose \texttt{D-SCAN} (Document-level Signal Collapse Analysis), a lightweight detection framework that monitors attention dynamics to identify attacked generations. Extensive experiments on multiple attack benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Moreover, D-SCAN can detect attacks even when they fail to alter the final answer. Code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/D-Scan.git.

</details>


### [296] [Casting the Net! Revisiting MasterFace Impersonation Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06952)
*Seunghun Paik,Sunpill Kim,Chanwoo Hwang,Jae Hong Seo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that MasterFace attacks can still achieve impersonation rates significantly above the standard False Match Rate (FMR) baseline in modern face recognition systems, even under realistic constraints. By exploiting legitimate access to public commercial APIs and leveraging the geometric structure of biometric representation space (called NET), adversaries can amplify impersonation rates up to 9.5× within 30 authentication trials, challenging the prevailing belief that such attacks are no longer effective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work suggested that MasterFace-based impersonation attacks no longer exceed the standard FMR in modern FRSs under realistic adversary constraints (decision-only, limited trials, no internal knowledge). The authors challenge this consensus by investigating whether adversaries can still achieve non-trivial impersonation by leveraging publicly accessible commercial FRS APIs, which are widely used in real-world deployments and whose backend providers are often disclosed or easily inferred.

Method: The authors formalize the MasterFace attack as a maximum coverage problem over the biometric representation space, termed a NET. They show that an adversary can construct an API-tailored NET by exploiting the geometric structure of the representation space. This NET is built using only legitimate, pay-as-you-go access to commercial APIs, requiring no additional privileges over the target FRS. The attack operates under black-box, decision-only conditions with a limited number of authentication trials (≤30).

Result: The proposed attack amplifies impersonation rates by up to 9.5× compared to the standard FMR baseline, using at most 30 authentication trials, across several open-source and commercial API-based face recognition systems.

Conclusion: MasterFace attacks remain a viable and non-trivial security threat against modern API-based FRS deployments. The ease with which adversaries can obtain legitimate API access, combined with inferable backend providers, undermines the assumption that FMR alone serves as an adequate security baseline. This calls for re-evaluation of impersonation threat models in real-world face recognition deployments.

Abstract: Impersonation is a fundamental security threat in face recognition systems (FRSs). While the security of FRSs has been challenged by various attack vectors, under realistic adversarial capabilities, e.g., a limited number of decision-only authentication trials and no internal system knowledge, most attack techniques become infeasible. As a result, impersonation by zero-effort impostors, characterized by false match rate (FMR), is commonly regarded as a standalone baseline. A few years ago, impersonation attacks based on MasterFaces emerged as a notable security threat that could break the barrier of the FMR-based baseline under such realistic constraints. However, they were believed not to yield impersonation above the standard FMR in modern FRSs, as discussed by multiple follow-up studies. In this paper, we demonstrate that even legitimate access to public commercial APIs allows an adversary to amplify impersonation rates through MasterFaces, resulting in a non-trivial impersonation attack beyond FMR on downstream applications built on top of these APIs. We observe that several real-world FRS deployments are implemented using commercial APIs, and that the backend service provider is publicly disclosed or trivially inferable. As a result, the adversary can purchase these pay-as-you-go API services without requiring any additional privilege over the target FRS. From this observation, we formalize the MasterFaces attack as a maximum coverage problem over the biometric representation space, which we call a NET, and show that the adversary can construct an API-tailored NET by leveraging the geometric structure of the representation space. We demonstrate that our attack amplifies the impersonation rates of several open-source and commercial API-based FRSs by up to 9.5$\times$ within at most 30 authentication trials, compared to those expected from the standard FMR.

</details>


### [297] [HarnessSafe: Evaluating Safety Across Persistent Carriers in Agent Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06984)
*Xiao Zhang,Yusheng Wang,Yuhao Fei,Dongyuan Li,Zian Liang,Liuyu Xiang,Hongxun Gu,Zhaofeng He*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: HarnessSafe is a benchmark of 328 executable cases across seven persistent-carrier families that evaluates how attacker-influenced content propagates through agent harnesses over time. It introduces the Persistent-Risk Lifecycle model and a trace-based evaluation to pinpoint where attacks are stopped, revealing that containment is carrier-specific and depends on the harness-model configuration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern agent harnesses persist state across sessions via memory, skills, tools, and artifacts, creating delayed safety risks where attacker-influenced content can cross system boundaries and affect later benign requests. Existing benchmarks lack comprehensive coverage across carriers and harnesses, and end-to-end attack success rates obscure how risks actually propagate through the system.

Method: The authors construct HarnessSafe with 328 executable cases spanning seven persistent-carrier families, tested on mainstream agent harnesses. Each case follows a Persistent-Risk Lifecycle tracing attacker influence from entry → persistence across carriers/boundaries → benign trigger → observable violation. A multi-stage, trace-based evaluation uses execution evidence to determine how far attack chains progress and where containment occurs.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that containment is carrier-specific and strongly dependent on the harness-model configuration. Both the harness architecture and the model backend substantially shape containment outcomes. Attack success rates alone fail to capture distinct lifecycle progression patterns.

Conclusion: Persistent-risk containment in agent harnesses cannot be assessed by binary success/failure metrics alone; carrier type, harness design, and model backend all critically mediate risk propagation. Trace-based lifecycle evaluation offers finer-grained insight into where and how attacks are stopped.

Abstract: Modern agent harnesses persist state across tasks and sessions through persistent carriers like memory, skills, tools, and shared artifacts.
